title: These 7 Maine Gems Got the National Geographic Treatment
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
These 7 Maine Gems Got the National Geographic Treatment
Maine is no stranger to national attention. Heck, it seems like every other week our wonderful state is being recognized for something incredible. But when one of the most iconic publications on Earth decides to shine its spotlight on Vacationland, you know it's a pretty big deal.
That's right, folks. National Geographic is once again showing Maine some love, and we're certainly not complaining.
Did National Geographic Spotlight Maine's Lesser Known Regions?
It’s the fact that this article takes aim at some of the small, lesser-known regions of Maine that definitely deserve the spotlight. Honestly, it’s something I wish we saw more of. Now, on to the article.
National Geographic put together a list of seven of Maine’s “must-see” spots when visiting the state. Not all of these are lesser-known, as you will see, but at least half are certainly not household names.
Let’s take a look at all seven.
What does National Geographic Think the Best Locations in Maine Are?
Brooklin – This coastal town is probably best known for being the home of legendary author E.B. White, but it also amazes with unquestioned beauty and peaceful living. If you are looking for quintessential Maine, here you go.
Monhegan Island – Another great choice by National Geographic. It’s not exactly easy to get to—you have to take a ferry from Boothbay, but you will not be disappointed. It’s an artist colony and a lobster lover’s dream. Plus, it has a brewery.
Rangeley – It’s a year-round outdoor adventurer’s playground, with everything from fishing to snowmobiling and everything in between. Plus, you’re not far from Saddleback Ski Resort.
Camden – Okay, this town is quite well-known compared to the others so far. In fact, it’s probably my favorite village in Maine. Camden is picturesque, with wonderful restaurants and shops. And Camden Hills State Park is a must-visit.
Bar Harbor – Do I really need to explain this one?
Brunswick – Another one of my favorite spots in Maine, this perfect college town is home to Bowdoin College. Brunswick shines with a great downtown area and plenty of outdoor recreation opportunities.
Greenville – Home to Moosehead Lake, Greenville is another perfect spot for those who love to get away and enjoy the peace and beauty of Maine. Mount Kineo State Park is another hidden gem that can’t be missed.
So, there you have it, National Geographic’s seven Maine regions to visit on your next vacation (or staycation for all of us locals). I have to admit, there are three on here I have never been to, and I’ve lived here for 37 of my 46 years. I guess the goal for 2026 is to get to those three locations, because clearly I’m missing out.
READ MORE: Travel Experts Say These Are the 4 Best Months to Visit Maine’s Acadia National Park
All in all, it’s a tremendous list, one that doesn’t aim to hit just the usual spots. It does a great job highlighting many different regions of Maine, all of which deserve the attention the big names get.

title: Aging Untold: What it really takes to repair old family wounds
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we discuss what genuine family reconciliation looks like when aging parents and adult children work to heal old wounds.
Then we break down the vital role of protein for healthy aging and share practical ways to maintain muscle, energy and strength.
Plus, we take you to Vermont’s Lake Champlain to meet an 83-year-old marina owner preserving more than two centuries of living history.
Family estrangement can be complicated.
Repairing relationships between aging parents and adult children takes more than good intentions, according to the Aging Untold experts.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said her advice for a parent who may have caused the pain is to own it, and Dr. Rhea Rogers said a genuine apology requires more than saying sorry.
Protein is an important part of supporting strength, healing and independence as we age, but older adults might not get enough.
Dr. Rogers said some health conditions affect how much protein an individual should have, and the amount you consume should be discussed with a primary care doctor first.
“There’s going to be certain states that you cannot afford that much protein, like kidney disease and things like that,” she said.
The Aging Untold experts urge people to read labels.
Rogers said it is important to know the source of your protein because some protein shakes spike insulin levels.
Jeorgi Golden spent 35 years in salons, working as a Black hairstylist while coworkers and clients became family.
Golden said salon workers in those days received minimal safety guidance about products and how they should be applied.
She said no one ever mentioned the dangers, even though formaldehyde was an ingredient found in those products. Formaldehyde is classified as a carcinogen by the EPA.
Studies now show that toxic gas poses serious health risks to both consumers and salon workers, linking exposure to eye problems, respiratory issues, and even certain types of cancer.
Pat Ullom, 83, and her son have run Chipman Point Marina, a piece of Vermont’s maritime past, for more than 30 years.
In the 1800s, the area on one of the narrowest points on Lake Champlain was a busy maritime community. Boats once unloaded cargo right into the marina’s main stone building, which was built in 1810.
The building next door was built in 1824, and it has operated as a store for almost 100 years.

title: Bangor woman causes police standoff in Portland
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (WABI) - A Bangor woman was taken into custody Monday after police said she created a standoff in Portland.
Officials said Erin Baker, 44, was consuming drugs in the bathroom of a McDonalds when the standoff happened.
Baker was requesting medical services and when EMS personnel arrived she told them that she had a gun.
Police were then called and attempted to negotiate with Baker who stayed in the bathroom for 30 minutes until authorities deployed pepper ball rounds into the bathroom which got her out.
Police said they did not find a gun at the scene.
Baker was taken to Cumberland County Jail and is facing multiple charges including terrorizing.
The investigation is ongoing.

title: Claude accessed public voter data without human prompting, raising security concerns
text:
ATLANTA (CNN) — AI company Anthropic said its Claude model figured out how to bypass a paywall on the Georgia secretary of state’s website.
Officials said the model only accessed publicly available voter statistics. It did not enter the state’s voter registration system or change any records.
The incident comes as federal officials warn about growing AI-related security threats ahead of the midterms.
The FBI and cybersecurity officials said AI could help hackers send phishing emails on a much larger scale, including to election officials.

title: Looking back week of Oct. 29
text:
Bar Harbor
Repair work commenced on the roof and bell tower of the old Town Hill schoolhouse. Workers from the Riverside Lane Asbestos Removal Company of Ellsworth set up scaffolding to begin the process of tearing off the old asbestos and cedar roof shingles. “We’d like to show our appreciation to the community for supporting this project by letting everyone know that we are finally ready to do the work,” said Lori Corbani, treasurer of the Town Hill Village Improvement Society and one of the prime movers and shakers behind the project. The project involves removing the roof and bell tower shingles, repairing any leaks that may be found, then re-shingling and repainting. “We learned recently that the schoolhouse was built in 1869, so the bell could be just as old,” she speculated. Ms. Corbani said the VIS has raised $13,000, a little more than half of the $25,000 needed to complete the project.

title: Construction company not paid $323K for work at Togus, lawsuit says
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Portland construction company hasn’t been paid $323,000 for work it did at the Togus Veterans Medical Center, according to a new lawsuit.
Titan Mechanical has yet to be paid by Frankenmuth Insurance Company, which issued the project’s payment bond, according to the lawsuit filed by the United States on Thursday in the U.S. District Court of Maine in Bangor.
Titan Mechanical was a subcontractor hired to help build the substance use disorder center at the VA center in Augusta, starting in 2024. The facility opened this spring. The new facility offers residential rehabilitation for substance use disorder. Veterans used to have to travel out of state for treatment.
A bond guarantees payment because contractors can’t place liens on federal property the way they could on a private job. The federal government pays the bond to the company that issues it, and the company disburses that money to the contractors.
Federal law requires lead contractors to have the bond, which ensures subcontractors and suppliers are paid. Because the claim is brought under that law, the Miller Act, the United States is suing on behalf of Titan.
The lawsuit asks for the full amount Titan is owed, as well as attorney fees.
Frankenmuth did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Are electronic voting machines 'flipping' votes? Experts say no
text:
Are electronic voting machines 'flipping' votes? Experts say no
Allegations of voting machines changing votes are circulating online ahead of the midterms, but experts and manufacturers say such issues are rare and often due to user error or screen calibration.
Are electronic voting machines 'flipping' votes? Experts say no
Allegations of voting machines changing votes are circulating online ahead of the midterms, but experts and manufacturers say such issues are rare and often due to user error or screen calibration.
Claims about voting machines swapping or "flipping" voters’ choices are again going viral as early voting continues during the 2026 midterm elections.
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com.
The claims have surfaced in multiple states.
"There is a very disturbing trend being seen in early voting," read a Facebook post from the liberal group "The Other 98%." "Texas, Florida, Tennessee, Ohio are reporting difficulties getting the machines to accept Democratic votes. The machines change them back to Republican unless the voter persists, pressing several times to get the correct vote to go through."
Similar claims also circulated on X and TikTok.
Vote flipping or swapping claims have become a recurring theme since the 2020 election, but there is no evidence of voting machines deliberately designed with such flaws or that it is happening on a wide scale. Election officials have said it often is attributable to user error on touch screens.
Tennessee, Texas voters' concerns likely related to user error or screen calibration
Dolly Parton's sister Stella Parton posted Oct. 21 on Facebook that she voted at Hermitage Library in Nashville and her ballot "kept flipping to the wrong candidate."
"I had to go back three times and correct my vote because it kept defaulting to Marsha Blackburn," she said.
WSMV-TV reported that some Tennessee voters picked a candidate on the voting machine and saw a different candidate selected on the screen. They voted in Franklin, Spring Hill or Nolensville, all in Williamson County. Similar complaints were reported in Madison County.
Tennessee Coordinator of Elections Mark Goins told WSMV that it "appears to be a voter error," and could have happened because of an unintended touch on the screen. He said voting equipment is tested before elections. Voters were advised that styluses are available by request to help with the touch screens.
The Tennessee Secretary of State told news outlets that among around 400,000 voters who have cast their ballots, the office has received one complaint of that nature.
In Texas, KSAT-TV reported that in Bexar County, three voters said voting machines changed or removed their choices. They were able to check their ballots before finalizing them.
Michele Carew, Bexar County Elections Administrator, said in a press release, “Reports of mismatched selections are almost always due to user touchscreen sensitivity, not machine malfunction. Touchscreens require a firm, direct tap, and poll workers are trained to assist as needed.”
She said the county tests machines for security and accuracy, and voting machines are never connected to the internet.
One man in Kendall County said on social media that his mother-in-law had tapped on Democratic candidates, but the machine repeatedly switched her choice to Republican candidates.
Alicia Pierce, Texas Assistant Secretary of State for Communications, said she is unaware of anyone reporting such issues.
Pierce said during this election, Texas is not using machines that directly store voting selections in computer memory, except in rare cases such as to accommodate voters with disabilities. The counties with reported issues use machines that generate a paper ballot and do not store voters’ selections.
"Any machines must produce a human-readable paper ballot that a voter can review before casting. We encourage all voters to review their choices before finally casting their ballot," she said.
Williamson County, Davidson County and Madison County in Tennessee, where issues were reported, and Bexar County, Williamson County and Kendall County in Texas use the ExpressVote machines, manufactured by ES&S.
ES&S spokesperson Katina Granger told PolitiFact the company has not received widespread reports from election officials about voting technology issues.“Most commonly, reported instances stem from a voter not touching the text box in the correct place. They can touch anywhere inside the large box containing the candidate’s name,” she said.
Old videos resurface on social media
As new claims are surfacing, old video is being misleadingly reshared, too.
An X video posted Oct. 23 shows a person tapping the box next to one candidate, but the screen marks the candidate above.
"Can you say national emergency?" the caption reads. "Electronic voting machine will not let voter select the Republican candidate that they want to vote for and automatically selects the Democrat candidate instead."
That video is from 2019. The people on screen are Tate Reeves and Bill Waller Jr., who were then primary candidates for the Republican nomination for Mississippi governor. PolitiFact explained that video in 2019, too.
Another video posted Oct. 22 shows a voting machine not accurately marking the candidate the person is selecting. Other X posts reshared it too, as if it's happening now.
But the video is from 2018, not the 2026 midterm election. The candidates on the screen are Jim Baird and Tobi Beck, who ran for U.S. House in Indiana.
What voters should know about touch screen voting
Issues involving incorrect choices on a touch screen are "rare," Granger said.
"Statewide and local officials have both repeatedly affirmed that nearly every case comes back to the screen calibration on older touchscreen machines, not a change to anyone’s vote," Kristin Miles, president of the Texas Association of County Election Officials, said in a statement to PolitiFact.
If you encounter an issue with your ballot, you can ask a poll worker for help before casting your vote.
Granger and election officials encouraged voters to verify their choices before casting their ballots. There are multiple opportunities to review your vote. Voting selections are displayed on the voting machine screen, on a review screen at the end of the voting session, and on a paper ballot generated by the system to confirm your choices.
If your printed ballot does not reflect your desired choices, you may notify a poll worker.
"There is no scenario in which a voter would be forced to cast a ballot that they believe did not reflect their intentions," Granger said.

title: 7 Maine events include ‘Rocky Horror’ in Waldoboro and Nirvana tribute in Arundel
text:
7 p.m. Thursday. Sanford Performing Arts Center, 100 Alumni Blvd., Sanford, $30-$60. sanfordpac.org.
See a band that’s been playing homage to an iconic Swedish pop group for more than 25 years. MANIA: The ABBA tribute have dazzled and delighted audiences in more than 35 countries with costumes, choreography and of course all the songs that fans love and know by heart. You’ll have the time of your life singing along with classic tunes like “Waterloo,” “Dancing Queen,” “Take a Chance On Me,” “Mamma Mia” and countless others.
7:30 p.m. Friday. The Waldo Theatre, 916 Main St., Waldoboro, $20 balcony, $30 first row balcony, $40 orchestra with prop bag, $50 front row with prop bag. thewaldotheatre.org.
It’s just a jump to the left! Then a step into Waldoboro for a screening of the cult classic musical comedy film “The Rocky Horror Picture Show.” A live cast will be up front doing their campy best, and you’ll be up on your feet for “The Time Warp.” Be a Transylvanian on Halloween Eve and have a blast while the 1975 film starring Tim Curry and Susan Sarandon comes to life. Doors open at 6 p.m., and the pre-show and costume contest kicks off at 7 p.m.
10:30 a.m.-6 p.m. Saturday. Rising Tide Brewing Company, 103 Fox St., Portland. risingtidebrewing.com.

The day also features a big air competition from the gravity defying Dock Dogs, treats from Ugly Duckling and oysters from Ebenecook Oysters. You can also enjoy Buckingham Red on tap, the collaboration brew from Dogfish Head and Rising Tide.
11 a.m.-6 p.m. Saturday, 10 a.m.-4 p.m. Sunday. Halo and Brick South at Thompson’s Point, Portland, $12 for 11 a.m. entry, $10 for 2 p.m. entry, $8 for 3 p.m. entry, free all day on Sunday. lostandfoundmaine.com.

With more than 100 vintage purveyors from all over New England, you’re bound to find treasures galore for yourself and others. 7:30 p.m. Saturday, 2 p.m. Sunday. Mad Horse Theatre at The Hutchins School, 24 Mosher St., South Portland, $25. porttix.com.
There’s no better time than Halloween weekend to see “An Ode to He Who Walks Behind the Rows,” presented by artist collective The Husky Boiz. Friday is sold out, but there are still tix left for Saturday and Sunday. With the lights out, it’s less dangerous. Or is it? Find out by catching a local tribute to Nirvana on Halloween night in Arundel. Mainers Jeff Beam, Mike Chasse and Jason Elvin will open a heart-shaped box of tunes as they plan two sets of Nirvana’s music. You can expect to hear the seminal grunge band’s greatest hits, fan favorites, deep cuts, B-sides and more, including acoustic tunes from Nirvana’s iconic MTV “Unplugged” album. Come as you are or rock an awesome costume.
8 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 3. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $49.50-$99.50. statetheatreportland.com.

Fronted by singer-guitarist Justin Furstenfield, Blue October formed in Texas in the mid-’90s and has released a dozen albums. title: Detected: How artificial intelligence is changing breast cancer detection
text:
GARDEN CITY, Kan. (InvestigateTV) — As a young mom, Ashley Hurd’s breast cancer diagnosis left a trail of uncertainty.
“I didn’t know what my future would look like, and I was worried about my family and my kid’s future,” Hurd said.
As a married mother of four, she expected her first mammogram in November 2024 to be a routine screening at age 40 after her primary doctor said it was time. Instead, doctors diagnosed Hurd with stage one, HER2-positive breast cancer on Jan. 2, 2026 after numerous doctors’ appointments.
What followed for Hurd and her family was months of a routine built around distance. The drive from Hurd’s home in Garden City, Kansas, to the University of Kansas Cancer Center runs more than 380 miles.
“We would leave on Sunday night, drive that six hours, to Kansas City from our hometown, go to chemo the next morning at 6:30 a.m. for my labs, stay there all day, and then make that drive home so I could get back to work the next day and back home to our kids,” she said.
Six rounds of chemotherapy with immunotherapy followed. So did a double mastectomy, then reconstruction. Hurd said the experience reshaped her.
“It changes your whole life,” she said. “I am not the same person from two years ago.”
She believes that early diagnosis is the reason she is still here.
“If I would have waited, I may not be here,” Hurd said.
Now cancer-free, Hurd is watching a new technology move into the healthcare system: artificial intelligence.
She said she sees a role for it to benefit women like her living in rural communities, but not a replacement for the doctors who treated her.
“I like that it can assist doctors, but I still very much want their expertise,” Hurd said. “There’s a reason that they’re the doctors.”
Radiologists are already using the technology
Radiologists across the country are already using AI to help read breast images.
The software reviews a mammogram alongside the radiologist and flags areas that may need a closer look, functioning as a second set of eyes rather than making the diagnosis itself.
“Breast cancer is so common, one in eight women in their lifetime develop breast cancer,” said Dr. Onalisa Winblad, division director of breast imaging at the University of Kansas Health System.
Winblad diagnoses breast cancer every day. She spends her day reading mammograms and breast imaging in a dark room, while also supporting patients through their diagnoses.
For women like Hurd, who travel long distances for care, Winblad believes these AI tools can bridge a gap between specialist shortages and hospital closures.
“No matter where you live or what resources you have, that really should not determine your survival from breast cancer,” Winblad said. “Not only does breast cancer screening prevent death from breast cancer, but it also helps patients undergo less chemotherapy, less extensive surgeries, radiation, or other invasive procedures.”
Winblad said these AI tools produce a scorecard that highlights anything that appears abnormal. She said these tools also can flag lesions and abnormalities, especially in cases of dense breast tissue.
“I do see AI as a really positive tool to help us provide faster care, more cost-effective care, help us schedule, help us educate patients and communicate better with our patients,” Winblad said. “The radiologist still has to be able to understand what those findings mean and the context of the AI tool.”
Skeptical radiologist turned advocate
On the East Coast, another breast radiologist said she started out as doubtful as many patients are.
“I was approached about working on this and helping to develop our AI projects. I was an incredible skeptic. And I said to everyone, ‘Look guys, great, you know, this is a waste of my time,’” said Dr. Janet Storella, medical director of women’s imaging services for Community Radiology Associates at RadNet.
Storella has been working in the field for more than 30 years. She now works out of Maryland at the imaging firm RadNet. She said she found that everybody’s performance improved when they used AI, something she previously didn’t think would be helpful.
“What we found, and what I found personally, was that everybody’s performance improved using these products. When I say performance, I mean my ability to detect cancer improved,” Storella said.
She said she knows her statistics from 20 years of breast cancer detection audits and that, when looking at 1,000 screening mammograms a year, the cancer detection rate went up.
“People with 30 years of experience, people fresh out of training, people who were subspecialty breast imagers like myself, people who are general docs, who are also reading mammography. Everybody’s performance improved, so it’s hard to argue with,” Storella said.
A 2025 study in the Journal of Clinical Medicine found that using AI in mammography screening demonstrated promising results in improving cancer detection rates and reducing false negatives.
That study of more than 31,000 mammograms found that after a clinic added AI, the cancer detection rate rose from about six to about nine cases per 1,000 screenings, with more cancers caught at an early stage.
That type of detection is what Storella has found in her own practice. The AI flags areas on breast images, telling her she should take a closer look.
“It’s really like having my most trusted colleagues sitting next to me and helping me in decision-making,” Storella said.
For her, the artificial intelligence helps her make judgment calls every day in helping her distinguish obvious cases from normal cases to what she calls “the murky middle.”
She said that patients can’t think of this issue as a vacuum; the technology is still evolving.
“Humans make mistakes. AI makes mistakes. The question is, does AI make more mistakes than humans make? Does it make fewer mistakes? I don’t know the answer to that right now,” Storella said.
Advocates call for accountability
Despite the open conversation happening with AI in the field of mammography, questions about guardrails have grown.
Erin Steigleder is the director of programs at the Virginia Breast Cancer Foundation. She has seen how these tools are being implemented across the country in health systems.
She believes that it’s important for patients to understand that AI is a tool and a system that keeps evolving, but it has its shortcomings.
“We are feeding AI images from past mammograms; however, the system is only as good as the images we feed it,” Steigleder said.
Researchers stress there is no proof yet that using AI in mammograms improves survival. Most studies so far measure only how many cancers are found and how early.
For women like Hurd living in rural areas, that early detection could mean catching cancer in its early stages — and fewer six-hour drives to get answers.
“For me, it probably would have been helpful in those early stages when I was so uncertain about what my next steps would be,” Hurd said. “Especially out here in our rural communities. We do have doctor shortages. We don’t have the staffing.”
Hurd is now cancer-free, back to work, using the gym as an escape, with checkups every three months. She believes AI could help with diagnostics but said it has limits, especially that human touch.
“I don’t think AI is able to give me a hug and tell me I’m going to be okay and that they’re going to be there with me,” Hurd said.

title: 9th Circuit questions DOJ demand to set aside 20,000 California mail ballots
text:
9th Circuit questions DOJ demand to set aside 20,000 California mail ballots
A panel of federal appellate judges on Sunday questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Justice Department's demand that California election officials set aside thousands of mail ballots from people the federal government suspects may not be citizens.
During rare weekend arguments, two of the three judges on the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals appeared skeptical of a lawsuit brought by President Donald Trump's administration in mid-October. The lawsuit accuses California officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review 20,000 names the administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the state's voter rolls.
Related video above: President Trump says he ordered lawsuit that could delay Alaska Senate election results
The administration asked a federal judge to require the state to withhold counting those ballots until the voters’ immigration status could be verified. The district judge scheduled a hearing for Oct. 27, days after the case was assigned, but the federal government appealed to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, seeking an expedited decision.
Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly told the panel that California is causing irreparable harm “by allowing noncitizens to vote in violation of their own state laws. The damage is irreversible and irrevocable.”
The Trump administration has made efforts to identify noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare.
Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, questioned whether the appellate court even has jurisdiction to hear the case even before a ruling by the lower court.
Donnelly argued that the schedule set by the lower court judge was too slow and effectively a denial of the government's request, as state elections officials process thousands of mail ballots every day.
Judge Gabriel Sanchez, appointed by former President Joe Biden, questioned whether the federal government was violating the Tenth Amendment, essentially commandeering the state to enforce a federal law that makes it a misdemeanor for a noncitizen to vote.
The federal government is simply asking California to enforce their own law, which also bans noncitizens from voting, Donnelly said. He argued the state's refusal to comply with the federal request to set aside the ballots for review was “frustrating the purpose” of the federal law against noncitizen voting.
The Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections, Bennett said. The executive branch may be “unhappy with what they’re doing, and doesn’t like the manner,” Bennett said, but under the Election Clause the state has the right to determine those issues — including how it sorts out any noncitizen voters.
Attorney Seth Waxman, representing Los Angeles County Clerk Dean Logan, said the federal government's list was unreliable and that segregating the ballots for a review process would effectively disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters.
Even if election staffers spent just three minutes checking each of the expected 2.75 million mail ballots against the government's list, the process would take 140,000 man-hours, Waxman said — or about 16 years of working time.
Waxman cited a review of 200 records from the Trump administration's list conducted by Los Angeles County staffers. Assistant Registrar-Recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, individuals with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States, which the filing notes “is strong evidence of citizenship.”
If the administration disagrees with how California runs its elections, it can ask Congress to change that process, said attorney Sam Siegel, representing California Secretary of State Shirley Weber.
The federal government has provided no credible evidence to support its suspicions, said Siegal.
“It has no basis in law or in fact,” he told the panel. “We just dispute the premise that noncitizens are voting."
But Judge Patrick Bumatay, who was appointed by Trump, said everyone has an interest in ensuring that only eligible citizens vote. He suggested that granting the administration's request for an emergency order could provide clarity.
“Without an injunction, you will never know” if that is happening, Bumatay told Seigel.
Bennett said the panel would try to issue a ruling as quickly as possible.
___
Boone reported from Boise, Idaho.

title: Maine’s ranked-choice system could decide the Senate under a hot spotlight
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
If the U.S. Senate race between U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson is close, the country may wait days to learn whether it is headed to a ranked-choice count and a week or more to learn who won.
Only first choices are counted on election night, and blank ballots and write-in votes can keep a candidate short of the majority needed to win outright. If that happens, Maine would hold its first statewide ranked-choice count in a general election.
Decision Desk HQ, the Bangor Daily News’ election results partner, rates Maine’s race as the closest Senate contest in the country. It gives Jackson a 54% chance of winning in what it projects as an effectively even vote split. It gives Democrats a 56% chance of taking the Senate.
The closer the race, the more blank ballots and write-ins could matter. A count would put Maine’s unusual election process in front of national media, party lawyers and President Donald Trump, who has already moved to block certification in another state that uses ranked-choice voting.
The potential ballot gap
In 2024, blank ballots and one write-in candidate pushed U.S. Rep. Jared Golden just under a majority in the 2nd District. The BDN and Decision Desk HQ called the race the day after Election Day, correctly predicting that the blanks mattered little.
Ballot records show only a sliver of voters who skipped a first choice ranked anyone later, and they split almost evenly. Backup choices on write-in ballots broke heavily for Golden, who held on through the count and a recount.
Full ranked-choice counts, which are run centrally in Augusta, have finished the week after the election. Before the count, ballot information must be collected statewide and checked against election-night tallies. That latter task dominates the bulk of the secretary of state’s time.
That pace drew fire in June, when the count for three major primaries ran into the early morning hours and finished about a day later than expected. Campaigns in both parties complained about delays and communication from Secretary of State Shenna Bellows’ office.
Bellows, a Democrat, said her office is weighing staffing changes to speed up the count this time, but she is not promising a faster answer.
“At this time we want voters to be prepared for the results to come the week following the election,” she said.
What the parties may argue over
Both general-election counts in Maine have drawn objections. In 2018, Republican U.S. Rep. Bruce Poliquin sued after Golden overtook his first-round lead, arguing that the count produced a false majority. In 2024, Golden’s lawyer objected to holding a count at all.
On Oct. 22, the Justice Department sued to block Alaska, the other state that uses ranked-choice voting in general elections, from certifying a Democratic win in its Senate race over a separate ballot dispute. Trump said he ordered it. Bellows expects a similar fight in Maine if the race is close.
“I think it is very possible that if the U.S. Senate race goes to ranked choice voting, we will see litigation, much like we are seeing in Alaska right now,” she said.
Her office has been running what it calls “tabletop the vote” exercises to plan for worst-case scenarios, she said. This year, it also held its first statewide training for election wardens and is mailing every municipality a first-ever guide to election law for wardens.
The Republican National Committee has observers, an in-state election integrity team and lawyers lined up, spokesperson Kristen Cianci said.
“We’ve stopped the expansion of ranked-choice voting in Maine before, and we’re ready to win up and down the ballot,” she said, referring to an April opinion from Maine’s high court that blocked its use in general elections for governor and the Legislature due to language in the state constitution.
Spokespeople for the Democratic National Committee, the party’s Senate campaign arm and Jackson’s campaign did not reply to questions.
What the courts have said
Republican challengers have argued that ranked-choice voting violates equal protection and due process by setting aside ballots that do not rank the finalists, producing what Poliquin’s lawyers called a “faux majority.”
Federal courts have rejected every challenge to Maine’s use of ranked-choice voting in federal races. U.S. District Judge Lance Walker, a Trump appointee, threw out Poliquin’s suit in 2018, and an appeals court refused to block certification.
“Whether RCV is a better method for holding elections is not a question for which the Constitution holds the answer,” Walker wrote.
The libertarian Cato Institute has written that states can use the system without violating the U.S. Constitution. But the U.S. Supreme Court, where Trump appointed three of the six conservative justices, has never taken up the question.

title: Looking for a Scare? Check Out These 20 Haunted Attractions
text:
20 Terrifying Haunted Attractions in Maine, New Hampshire, & Massachusetts
With the exception of a very few people, everyone seems to love 'spooky season'.
When we say that, obviously, we are talking about that period of time between Labor Day and November 1st. Yes, we know that Halloween is on October 31st, but the season is too fun to just limit to one day, right?
While the holiday mostly focused on kids back in the 80s and 90s it has become more and more adult over the last few decades.
In addition to nearly every bar and nightclub throwing a Halloween party, we are seeing more and more haunted attractions. Back in the day we would have called these haunted houses, but these days they go way beyond that. Now, these haunted attractions take over trails, old factories, ski areas, and even amusement parks.
If getting the crap scared out of you is your idea of fun, we have you covered. We've put together a list of some of the best haunted attractions throughout Maine, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire.
20 of the Best Haunted Attractions in New England in 2026
As you can see, we dug deep to find the best haunted attractions throughout our part of New England. We made sure that, no matter where you are, one of these attractions is not far.
Maineiac Manor in the Bangor Mall is one of our favorites because, at least in the past, they have done a Holiday version of the haunt to coincide with Christmas. Canobie Lake Park's Screeemfest is one of a kind, too. And, we always love the United Volunteers of Maine haunted house in Augusta because it gives local nonprofits a chance to raise money for their organizations.

title: Obama rebukes Ramaswamy ad using rival’s estranged mother: ‘No line he will not cross’
text:
DETROIT (AP) — Former President Barack Obama on Saturday seized on what he described as cruelty and indecency coming from President Donald Trump and his Republican allies, stepping into one of the nation’s ugliest midterm fights as he worked to rally Democratic voters in two Midwestern battlegrounds.
First in Ohio, Obama took aim at Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an advertising campaign featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have also defended the ad, even as Republican leaders across Ohio, including Gov. Mike DeWine, have called for its removal.
“In recent days, we’ve seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to,” Obama said of Ramaswamy, noting that Acton has “spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she’s experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness.”
Later in Michigan, Obama condemned critics of Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, suggesting that they’re using his name or his faith to tear him down.
“We have seen this movie before. I starred in it,” Obama told a packed high school gym in Detroit. “I’ve got a long-form birth certificate to prove it.”
“Abdul is as Michigan as it gets,” he added.
Obama, 65, remains the Democratic Party’s best motivator nearly a decade after leaving the White House. And he’s taking his star power on the road in the final days of the midterm elections, which will help determine the balance of power in American politics on Nov. 3.
Trump cast his own ballot on Saturday in Florida, where he defended the Ramaswamy ad, which has emerged as a national flashpoint a little more than a week before Election Day.
“The mother said that Amy Acton is a liar, and she’s no good,” Trump said. ”And you know what? I don’t think you can get a better reference on that.”
The Ramaswamy campaign video features Acton’s birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her “a liar” and insinuating she has mental health issues.
Acton, Ohio’s COVID-19-era health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur’s husband, was indicted on a charge of rape involving Acton.
The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur failed to show for a court appearance and became a fugitive. Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death in 2004.
Appearing before Obama, Acton spoke as if addressing Ramaswamy directly.
“My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his stumbling campaign, but it’s not going to work,” she said. “Decency still matters.” She added: “Mr. Ramaswamy, you are not just out of touch, you are out for yourself and you are a danger to my state. Apparently there is no low to which you won’t stoop.”
Although Ohio has become more reliably Republican, it’s been a hotly contested battleground this year. Trump and Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to drum up support for Sen. Jon Husted and Ramaswamy. And the controversy over Ramaswamy’s ad has ratcheted up the already high temperature.
Michigan, too, is a critical state this midterm season, with high-stakes contests for the Senate and governor.
While Obama addressed both races, he offered a passionate defense of El-Sayed, a former public health official running against former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican.
The former president pushed back against those who call El-Sayed a radical, declaring that “Abdul shares my values.” He also acknowledged that El-Sayed was critical of him after his 2012 reelection for not following through on all of his progressive campaign promises.
El-Sayed wrote that Obama “was not the right choice — he just wasn’t the wrong one.”
“Some of these folks say, well, you know, Abdul didn’t like some of the things you did as president,” Obama said in Detroit, wearing a blue shirt with no tie, his sleeves rolled up. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama. Michelle Obama, about five times a day.”
Democrats hoped that Obama’s appearance in the city, which is three-quarters Black, could bolster support for El-Sayed among Black voters. In the primary, his opponent Haley Stevens won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by about 6 percentage points. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian vice president, campaigned for El-Sayed in September.
Cheryl McWilliams, 67, said Obama’s speech “pumps you up to vote,” and she’s hoping to see high turnout in the midterms.
“If Detroit doesn’t vote, whoever’s running is going to lose, period,” McWilliams said. “I’m just hoping we can reach voters that don’t vote. They think it doesn’t matter, and it does.”
Chunnika Hodges, who lives in Detroit and canvassed for El-Sayed on Saturday, said some Black voters are supporting Rogers because they don’t think anything has changed after years of voting for Democrats. Some are also wary of El-Sayed because of his progressive policies, Hodges said.
“We don’t lean to the conservative, but we have seen that within our community,” Hodges said. “There are conservative Blacks, conservative Democrats.”
While Obama talked up Democratic candidates in Ohio and Michigan, he also spoke at length about Trump.
He accused the Republican president and his family of rampant corruption and called out his inability to lower costs, noting that Trump has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn.
“I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation,” Obama quipped. “He should be on HGTV.” He went on: “There’s gold everywhere. He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”
The former Democratic president acknowledged that the nation has Trump for another two years, until his term ends. But voters are not stuck with Trump’s allies, he said.
“We’re not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are handling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people,” Obama said. “After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence … you get a chance to say enough is enough.”
Obama will headline a rally in Georgia next week with Sen. Jon Ossoff and candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Trump, campaigning in Perry, Georgia, on Saturday evening with their Republican rivals, made several references to Obama’s Michigan event, insisting “the place was empty.”
___
Peoples reported from New York. AP writer Jill Colvin in New York contributed. GaNun is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: 15-year-old arrested in Florida A&M shooting that wounded 11 after homecoming game
text:
TALLAHASSEE, Fla. (AP) — A 15-year-old boy has been charged in a weekend shooting that wounded 11 people at Florida A&M University following the school’s homecoming football game, police said Monday.
Investigators say a fight broke out before the shooting Saturday night, and it appears that none of the victims were intended targets.
Authorities arrested the teenage suspect Sunday and charged him with attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent, according to a statement from Tallahassee police.
The shooting happened just outside Bragg Memorial Stadium after Florida A&M lost to Arkansas-Pine Bluff.
Eleven people were hit by gunfire and one person was injured while running away. Six of those hurt were minors, police said Sunday.
At least three of the victims suffered serious injuries, authorities said.
Video surfaced on social media of people fleeing in terror. The area was crowded with people leaving the game and homecoming celebration.

title: 5 fun things to do while you’re in Bethel
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Kate Webb spends a lot of time thinking creatively.
She’s program director of Bethel Area Arts & Music (BAAM), a nonprofit focusing on youth art education, artist opportunities and public engagement with the performing arts. She lives in a yurt, and enjoys being part of the creative community in western Maine.
She took a few minutes to share some of her favorites spots and activities in Bethel.
Where do you like to eat?
I love Le Mu Eats on Main Street. Their menu puts a unique spin on American cuisine, with South Asian and Southern influences that make it really stand out. As someone with food allergies, I especially appreciate how allergy-conscious and accommodating they are. You really can’t go wrong with the Hot Noodz or the Porke Bowl, two of my favorites. They also serve a spicy margarita with a tajin rim that is delightful.
Where do you like to drink?
You can’t go to Bethel without going to the Suds Pub. Nestled in the basement of the Sudbury Inn, it’s a local favorite with 29 beers on tap, tasty food, live music every Thursday night and plenty of local flavor. It’s the kind of place where you’re likely to run into someone you know, or leave feeling like a local yourself.
Where do you like to connect with nature?
The Bethel area has endless opportunities to connect with nature, but a couple of places are particular favorites of mine. Buck’s Ledge Community Forest offers three trails leading through the woods to beautiful views of North and South Pond. Through the Access for All initiative, an accessible trail was created to help ensure this “Forever Forest for All” truly is open and welcoming to everyone. Another favorite is the Habitat for All Garden at Mahoosuc Land Trust’s Valentine Farm. The garden is filled with beautiful flowers and native plants that provide important habitat for pollinators throughout the seasons. At its peak in the summer, it’s especially magical when the monarch butterflies begin coming through. Each year, Valentine Farm celebrates their arrival with its annual Monarch Festival, a wonderful community event.
Where do you like to shop locally?
I love The Philbrook Place; it has a little bit of everything. You’ll find gifts, toys, books, handmade goods and a great selection of secondhand clothing for kids and adults. It’s also a wonderful place to discover and support local artists and makers. It’s my go-to spot for gifts because I can always find something unique for just about everyone.
What’s a hidden gem or can’t miss place in town?
Perhaps a bit on the nose, but The Gem Theater truly is a hub of our community. Along with showing blockbuster movies and independent films, it’s a gathering place for so much more. The nonprofit I run, Bethel Area Arts & Music (BAAM), partners with The Gem to bring live performances, art films, visiting artists and other creative experiences to our small community. The building itself is also a work of art, featuring a 900-square-foot mural by artist Ryan Adams that BAAM completed in 2021 with the help of community members and Telstar Middle School students. It’s a great example of the creativity and collaboration that make Bethel such a special place.
Five Things is a feature in which locals give our readers suggestions for exploring the state of Maine, town by town. Have a city or town you think we should explore in the future? Tell News & Culture Editor Katherine Lee at [email protected].

title: 2-year-old suffers catastrophic brain injury after exposure to 7-OH
text:
AUBURN, Ind. (WPTA/Gray News) - An Indiana 2-year-old suffered catastrophic brain injury after police say he was exposed to a drug called 7-OH.
Police charged 20-year-old Kole Schwarz with neglect of a dependent resulting in catastrophic injury. Court records say Schwarz was the mother’s live-in boyfriend at the time.
Family members say the toddler was rushed to a hospital in DeKalb County on Sept. 6, where the affidavit says he was “unresponsive and placed in a medically induced coma.”
The child was later transferred to Riley Hospital in Indianapolis.
Court papers say a specialized lab test later found kratom-related drugs in his blood.
Investigators say the child’s mother told them she believed Schwarz used “7-OHs” and she was concerned the toddler may have ingested one.
Detectives say Schwarz admitted buying tablets sold as “7-OH” under the counter through a contact in Fort Wayne.
The detective calls that product the likely source of the exposure. Schwarz told police the tablets stayed sealed in his pocket.
Court papers say the child had an “unknown green substance around his mouth” and a doctor found MRI evidence that met the criteria for catastrophic injury.
Auburn police say the mother of the child is not a suspect in the case and has cooperated throughout the investigation.
The toddler’s grandmother, Josie Casebere, says she spent six weeks in the hospital with her grandson.
“It’s been the hardest thing in my life. I mean, I’ve lost parents and friends, and this is... I know we didn’t lose him, but it’s still been the hardest thing I’ve ever went through,” she said. “He’s got a wheelchair order that’s supposed to fit him until he’s six. If that tells you anything. They don’t know that he’ll ever walk again or anything.”
The FDA calls 7-OH a potent opioid concentrated from kratom, warning of a “concerning proliferation of concentrated 7-OH products that are sold over the counter and online.”
“This public health threat is troubling and requires immediate and impactful policies to educate consumers and take regulatory action that limits access to 7-OH-containing products,” the FDA’s report says.
It is illegal in Indiana, but in Michigan, it is sold as gummies, drinks and pills.
Berrien County health officials warned last week that kratom-related hospitalizations are rising. Michigan has no statewide age limit.
“Kratom contains a chemical called 7-OH (7-hydroxymitragynine), which acts like an opioid and can cause severe withdrawal symptoms. Kratom is an increasingly popular substance among teens and is sold at gas stations and smoke shops as candy-flavored gummies, drinks, pills and more,” the county’s health warning says. “While advertised as an energy booster, mood lifter, pain reliever and remedy for symptoms of quitting opioids, kratom can cause serious health issues, such as seizures, liver toxicity and substance use disorder. It also can lead to an overdose.”
Casebere says she spoke out to raise awareness about 7-OH.
“They’re labeling it however they want to because it’s not regulated, and they’re selling it to our kids,” she said.

title: Detected: How artificial intelligence is changing breast cancer detection
text:
GARDEN CITY, Kan. (InvestigateTV) — As a young mom, Ashley Hurd’s breast cancer diagnosis left a trail of uncertainty.
“I didn’t know what my future would look like, and I was worried about my family and my kid’s future,” Hurd said.
As a married mother of four, she expected her first mammogram in November 2024 to be a routine screening at age 40 after her primary doctor said it was time. Instead, doctors diagnosed Hurd with stage one, HER2-positive breast cancer on Jan. 2, 2026 after numerous doctors’ appointments.
What followed for Hurd and her family was months of a routine built around distance. The drive from Hurd’s home in Garden City, Kansas, to the University of Kansas Cancer Center runs more than 380 miles.
“We would leave on Sunday night, drive that six hours, to Kansas City from our hometown, go to chemo the next morning at 6:30 a.m. for my labs, stay there all day, and then make that drive home so I could get back to work the next day and back home to our kids,” she said.
Six rounds of chemotherapy with immunotherapy followed. So did a double mastectomy, then reconstruction. Hurd said the experience reshaped her.
“It changes your whole life,” she said. “I am not the same person from two years ago.”
She believes that early diagnosis is the reason she is still here.
“If I would have waited, I may not be here,” Hurd said.
Now cancer-free, Hurd is watching a new technology move into the healthcare system: artificial intelligence.
She said she sees a role for it to benefit women like her living in rural communities, but not a replacement for the doctors who treated her.
“I like that it can assist doctors, but I still very much want their expertise,” Hurd said. “There’s a reason that they’re the doctors.”
Radiologists are already using the technology
Radiologists across the country are already using AI to help read breast images.
The software reviews a mammogram alongside the radiologist and flags areas that may need a closer look, functioning as a second set of eyes rather than making the diagnosis itself.
“Breast cancer is so common, one in eight women in their lifetime develop breast cancer,” said Dr. Onalisa Winblad, division director of breast imaging at the University of Kansas Health System.
Winblad diagnoses breast cancer every day. She spends her day reading mammograms and breast imaging in a dark room, while also supporting patients through their diagnoses.
For women like Hurd, who travel long distances for care, Winblad believes these AI tools can bridge a gap between specialist shortages and hospital closures.
“No matter where you live or what resources you have, that really should not determine your survival from breast cancer,” Winblad said. “Not only does breast cancer screening prevent death from breast cancer, but it also helps patients undergo less chemotherapy, less extensive surgeries, radiation, or other invasive procedures.”
Winblad said these AI tools produce a scorecard that highlights anything that appears abnormal. She said these tools also can flag lesions and abnormalities, especially in cases of dense breast tissue.
“I do see AI as a really positive tool to help us provide faster care, more cost-effective care, help us schedule, help us educate patients and communicate better with our patients,” Winblad said. “The radiologist still has to be able to understand what those findings mean and the context of the AI tool.”
Skeptical radiologist turned advocate
On the East Coast, another breast radiologist said she started out as doubtful as many patients are.
“I was approached about working on this and helping to develop our AI projects. I was an incredible skeptic. And I said to everyone, ‘Look guys, great, you know, this is a waste of my time,’” said Dr. Janet Storella, medical director of women’s imaging services for Community Radiology Associates at RadNet.
Storella has been working in the field for more than 30 years. She now works out of Maryland at the imaging firm RadNet. She said she found that everybody’s performance improved when they used AI, something she previously didn’t think would be helpful.
“What we found, and what I found personally, was that everybody’s performance improved using these products. When I say performance, I mean my ability to detect cancer improved,” Storella said.
She said she knows her statistics from 20 years of breast cancer detection audits and that, when looking at 1,000 screening mammograms a year, the cancer detection rate went up.
“People with 30 years of experience, people fresh out of training, people who were subspecialty breast imagers like myself, people who are general docs, who are also reading mammography. Everybody’s performance improved, so it’s hard to argue with,” Storella said.
A 2025 study in the Journal of Clinical Medicine found that using AI in mammography screening demonstrated promising results in improving cancer detection rates and reducing false negatives.
That study of more than 31,000 mammograms found that after a clinic added AI, the cancer detection rate rose from about six to about nine cases per 1,000 screenings, with more cancers caught at an early stage.
That type of detection is what Storella has found in her own practice. The AI flags areas on breast images, telling her she should take a closer look.
“It’s really like having my most trusted colleagues sitting next to me and helping me in decision-making,” Storella said.
For her, the artificial intelligence helps her make judgment calls every day in helping her distinguish obvious cases from normal cases to what she calls “the murky middle.”
She said that patients can’t think of this issue as a vacuum; the technology is still evolving.
“Humans make mistakes. AI makes mistakes. The question is, does AI make more mistakes than humans make? Does it make fewer mistakes? I don’t know the answer to that right now,” Storella said.
Advocates call for accountability
Despite the open conversation happening with AI in the field of mammography, questions about guardrails have grown.
Erin Steigleder is the director of programs at the Virginia Breast Cancer Foundation. She has seen how these tools are being implemented across the country in health systems.
She believes that it’s important for patients to understand that AI is a tool and a system that keeps evolving, but it has its shortcomings.
“We are feeding AI images from past mammograms; however, the system is only as good as the images we feed it,” Steigleder said.
Researchers stress there is no proof yet that using AI in mammograms improves survival. Most studies so far measure only how many cancers are found and how early.
For women like Hurd living in rural areas, that early detection could mean catching cancer in its early stages — and fewer six-hour drives to get answers.
“For me, it probably would have been helpful in those early stages when I was so uncertain about what my next steps would be,” Hurd said. “Especially out here in our rural communities. We do have doctor shortages. We don’t have the staffing.”
Hurd is now cancer-free, back to work, using the gym as an escape, with checkups every three months. She believes AI could help with diagnostics but said it has limits, especially that human touch.
“I don’t think AI is able to give me a hug and tell me I’m going to be okay and that they’re going to be there with me,” Hurd said.

title: What it really takes for aging parents and adult children to repair old wounds
text:
(Aging Untold) — As parents age, some might hope for a closer relationship with their adult children.
Repairing those relationships takes more than good intentions — it takes ownership, patience and realistic expectations.
“Forgiveness takes one person, but a relationship takes more than one”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said families need to understand upfront that they can’t control how the other side responds.
“I think it’s real important to understand that forgiveness takes one person, but a relationship takes more than one,” Cradduck said. “And if they’re not willing, there’s not a whole lot you can do.”
Cradduck added that many long-running family conflicts have lost their origin story entirely.
“Sadly, most of these disconnects, nobody knows what caused it,” Cradduck said. “They’ve been mad for so long, and they’ve lived this life in anger for so long, they don’t even know what happened to start it all.”
Her advice for the parent who may have caused the pain: own it.
“If you’re the person that maybe offended them, be willing to apologize. Be willing to own what you did wrong,” Cradduck said. “And if they’re not willing to accept that apology, you’ve done your part. You can’t be responsible for somebody else in a relationship — you can be responsible for yourself.”
A real apology has three parts
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said time alone doesn’t heal old wounds — and a genuine apology requires more than saying sorry.
“Time doesn’t automatically heal the pain. Just because 30 years have passed doesn’t mean the pain passed,” she said.
Rogers broke down what a real apology requires.
“When you have an apology, it has three parts to it: you want to acknowledge the harm, you want no excuses, and you need changed behavior,” Rogers said. “But the healing happens on the injured person — the person who was hurt, it’s on their timeline, not yours. The healing is the peace — but the reconciliation is the trust process and the relationship.”
- Acknowledge the harm
- Make no excuses
- Change your behavior
Sometimes the real conflict isn’t the one you think it is
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared an example from her own consultations about a client who had spent years resenting his father over how his mother had been treated — and became fixated on getting his dad to bring his mom coffee every morning.
“I said, well, maybe it’s more about you and your own feelings than it’s really their marriage,” O’Rourke said. “So he went into therapy and discussed his own resentments that were not attached to his parents at all — and he ended up telling me that his relationship with his partner got better for what he learned about himself.”
O’Rourke said the experience points to a broader lesson about self-awareness.
“What you think the conversation you need to have might not be the conversation you need to have,” O’Rourke said.
Estrangement is common — and complicated
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said that estrangement between older adults and their relatives has become increasingly common.
“There’s a lot of older adults living with serious pain from estrangement. It’s almost like a popular culture thing to be estranged from relatives,” Ambrose said. “And it’s very, very sad.”
Her advice to an older adult who feels cut off from family: let go of what you can’t control.
“You can’t make them change their mind or do anything. Honestly, I just say, pray about it, because something can change just like that,” Ambrose said. “And it could happen suddenly. And sometimes, maybe they did do something wrong, but sometimes maybe they really didn’t.”
Cradduck added that the only thing somebody can do is apologize and try to explain where they were at, or where they came from, or how it happened.
“And it’s on you then to either accept that and move forward, or to not. It’s your choice,” she said.
She added a reminder about grace.
“Someday you’re also going to need grace,” Cradduck said.
Don’t have the hard conversation when you’re angry
O’Rourke also offered practical advice for when emotions run high.
“If you’re really, really upset, you’re really hot, you’re really mad — don’t talk to them then,” O’Rourke said. “Let yourself cool down, get some objectivity.”
She recalled a friend whose daughter repeatedly raised complaints about her mothering, even after her mother felt she had done all she could.
“My friend said, ‘Well, I hope you get a really good therapist for that,’” O’Rourke said. “Because she really had resolved that she’d done all she could do, and she could really see that it was on her daughter that needed the help.”
O’Rourke noted that estrangement isn’t always literal distance.
“You might not be estranged, but you might feel emotionally estranged,” O’Rourke said.
Key takeaways
- Aging well means deciding what comes next — not rewriting old battles.
- Forgiveness and reconciliation are different. Forgiveness brings individual peace; reconciliation requires shared trust and real accountability.
- A genuine apology has three parts: acknowledging the harm, avoiding excuses and showing changed behavior.
- Healing happens on the hurt person’s timeline — not the timeline of the person who caused the pain.
- Set healing boundaries. Cool down and gain objectivity before starting emotionally charged family conversations.

title: Meet the 83-year-old marina keeper preserving hundreds of years of Vermont history
text:
ORWELL, Vt. (Aging Untold) — At one of the narrowest points on Lake Champlain, a piece of Vermont’s maritime past is still standing — and still in use.
For more than 30 years, 83-year-old Pat Ullom and her son have run Chipman Point Marina.
Chipman Point was once where “all the goods landed,” Ullom said.
A landing point for 1800s commerce
In the 1800s, the area was a busy maritime community close to New York state.
The marina’s main stone building was built in 1810 and quarried from the property itself. Boats once unloaded cargo directly into the building through its doorways, and the second floor functioned “more like a grocery store.”
Ullom said the beams inside are original to the building.
“Yeah, yeah, I do that a lot,” Ullom said, when asked if she ever looks out at the water and imagines what the property looked like in 1810.
A store that’s kept its character for a century
Next to the 1810 stone building stands a structure built in 1824 that has operated as a store for almost 100 years.
Pat Ullom keeps the candy on the counter and the coffee, still priced at 25 cents a cup, flowing.
Part of the original floor remains intact. Ullom said a previous owner who had the property for 50 years used to chew tobacco, leaving marks still visible in the wood today.
With boating season underway, the marina is picking up activity again.
Living above the history she preserves
Ullom lives on the third floor of the 1824 building. She said she doesn’t see herself as the building’s owner, but as someone passing through it.
“I don’t feel that I own it,” Ullom said. “I feel that I’ve been lucky enough to live here.”

title: ‘Halloween Harvest Stomp’ trad dance in Millinocket
text:
MILLINOCKET – Celebrate fall and local community by kicking up your heels at the “Halloween Harvest Stomp” trad dance on Friday, Oct. 30. The event features live music and a dance caller and is presented by the Katahdin Folk School Project, with support from the Town of Millinocket, the Katahdin Collaborative and Belfast Flying Shoes.
The all-ages program starts at 6:30 p.m. at the Elks Lodge, 213 Aroostook Ave. in Millinocket. All are welcome! Admission is by suggested donation: $10-25 for adults and $5 for kids. Pay what you can and enjoy this program with your family and friends. Special thanks to the Elks Lodge #1521 for sharing their venue for the dance. For more dance information, email dan@outdoorsi.org
Chrissy Fowler, a Millinocket native and Stearns grad, will teach easy-to-learn dances from the unique cultural traditions of square dancing and contra dancing. Dancers will smile and laugh as they swing their partner and do-si-do at this intergenerational event. Waldo County musicians Willy Clemetson and Benjamin Foss will play fiery fiddle tunes to get everyone’s feet stomping, from dancers to folks listening on the side of the hall. Both Willy & Benjamin tour across the country to play for dances, and it’s a special treat to have them join us in the Katahdin Region.
Extend your time in the area – mountain biking, fishing, hiking, camping, eating out and digging into local lore at the Millinocket Museum and Millinocket Memorial Library. Stay in town or venture to Baxter Park, Katahdin Woods & Waters or the region’s countless outdoor recreation opportunities, including renting outdoor equipment from the Katahdin Gear Library.
The Katahdin Folk School Project is a collaborative initiative focused on celebrating and sharing traditional skills, knowledge, and wisdom found in the Katahdin Region. Partners include the Millinocket Memorial Library and the Outdoor Sport Institute, with support through the Katahdin Collaborative. Info at katahdincollaborative.org
Belfast Flying Shoes was founded in 2005 by siblings Chrissy & Tom Fowler and others. With a mission to build community and cultivate well-being through the joy of traditional music and dance, the nonprofit’s programs include dances, concerts, arts residencies in schools and programs for older adults. For more go to belfastflyingshoes.org.

title: Historic SS United States set to become world's largest artificial reef
text:
The SS United States is a step closer to sinking to become the world's largest artificial reef
DESTIN, Fla. —
A historic ocean liner is a step closer to becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.
Officials in Florida's Okaloosa County expect to sink the SS United States off the Gulf Coast during the second week of November. The exact dates could change because of weather.
Related previous coverage in the video player above: Historic SS United States spotted off south Florida coast in February 2025
The ship will be sunk about 22 nautical miles southwest of Destin.
“This is an exciting move forward to create a one-of-a-kind resource for the environment and for our tourism industry,” county officials wrote in a news release.
Hulton Archive
The new United States liner SS United States, winner of the Blue Riband for 1952 with a transatlantic crossing speed of 41 mph. (Photo by Hulton Archive/Getty Images)
The nearly 1,000-foot vessel shattered the trans-Atlantic speed record on its maiden voyage in 1952. 
John Chillingworth
The new United States liner SS United States, winner of the Blue Riband for 1952 with a transatlantic crossing speed of 41 mph, arrives at Le Havre.  Original Publication: Picture Post - 5969 - The New First Lady - pub. 1952   (Photo by John Chillingworth/Getty Images)
Preservation groups tried to save the ship but were hindered by high costs.
JEWEL SAMAD
Susan Gibbs, executive director of the SS United States Conservancy, poses aboard the retired passenger liner at a dock in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on October 10, 2015. Larger than Titanic and once saved from the scrap heap, the rusting ship is again nearing being sold off to metal recyclers as the SS United States Conservancy struggles to raise the 60,000 a month for docking and maintaining the ship. The SS United States still holds the east- and west-bound transatlantic crossing records.  AFP PHOTO/JEWEL SAMAD        (Photo credit should read JEWEL SAMAD/AFP via Getty Images)
Supporters hope that sinking the ship will make it a barnacle-encrusted star among more than 500 artificial reefs and a signature diving attraction, helping to generate millions of dollars a year in local tourism spending for scuba shops, charter fishing boats and hotels.
