title: Bangor will fund an as-needed overnight warming center this winter
text:
The Bangor City Council unanimously approved funding Monday night for an as-needed overnight warming center at the Together Place recovery center that will open on the coldest nights this winter.
The added capacity will provide needed beds after two of the city’s warming centers were denied state funding this year. Warming center leaders and volunteers who spoke at Monday’s council meeting emphasized that those extra beds will save lives as the city continues to struggle with a homelessness crisis.
The as-needed warming center, which was proposed by the city’s public health department, will open on nights when the temperature drops below 15 degrees.
The city is directing up to $5,000 of the city’s heating assistance funds, about $11,000 in general assistance funds and $90,000 in Community Development Block Grant funds to support 40 beds at the Together Place for the warming center.
Beds at the nonprofit will supplement those at the Brick Church and the Bangor Area Homeless Shelter, both funded by MaineHousing, and at the Mansion Church, which plans to open using volunteers despite being denied state funding. Those three shelters can support about 95 beds combined — about 30 fewer than the maximum number of people who visited a warming center in a single night last year.
The council also awarded $10,000 in Community Development Block Grant funds to The Well, a daytime warming center.
Speakers during the meeting’s public comment period were overwhelmingly supportive of the measure, with 12 people speaking in favor, and the council chamber filled with applause when it passed.
“You are saving people’s lives with this simple act,” resident Katie Coe said.
Pastor Leon Licata of the Brick Church told councilors he worried that people would be left out on the street this winter if the Together Place didn’t get funding for its shelter, and noted that all the warming centers work together to get people to the shelter that’s the best fit for them. For example, Licata noted that his warming center is more accessible for wheelchair users, while he often calls Joe Hartel, the director of the Together Place, when he has a visitor who needs psychiatric or substance use-related services.
Shea Mullaney, the board president for the Together Place, noted that “this proposal will allow unhoused individuals access to a bed, food, one-on-one and group recovery support, monitored bathrooms and resource navigation on the coldest nights.”
Some residents also urged the council to consider more sustainable, long-term solutions for future years.
Former City Councilor Charlie Longo said that while the warming center funding was necessary, he didn’t believe community development block grants were the best funding source, and that the council should think about how to prevent this situation next year
“This is more like treading water or putting a Band-Aid on a wound,” he said.
Correction: A previous version of this story misspelled Katie Coe’s name. It has been updated.

title: Susan Collins will regret this descent into sleaze
text:
One of the saddest developments of this year’s U.S. Senate campaign in Maine has been watching Susan Collins, a senator once renowned for civility and decency, damage her own legacy in an attempt to win a sixth term in office.
It has been obvious for months that Collins is pinning her reelection hopes on juicing turnout among voters who support President Donald Trump — something highlighted by her casual embrace of the Maine Wire’s sickening racism and vulgar politics.
Perhaps the clearest preview of this turn came during the late summer interview Collins gave to Politico, during which she pretended she wouldn’t sink to slamming her challenger, Democrat Troy Jackson, for his decades-long relationship with his partner.
“I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin,” Sen. Collins said. “I don’t know whether people know that or not.”
Gosh, senator. Thanks for not bringing that up.
The Senate Leadership Fund’s radio ad last week called Jackson a creep, adding, in a jingle, “If he’ll screw his own family, he’ll screw yours too.”
Sen. Collins called for the super PAC that paid for the ad to take it down. But let’s be clear: This PAC wasn’t some obscure, disconnected outfit. It was an arm of Senate Republican leadership with ties to Majority Leader John Thune.
Two other events last week showed voters how rapidly Sen. Collins is losing her way.
After the Maine Wire posted clips of Somali citizens voting at Lewiston’s city hall, Sen. Collins weighed in on one of the right-wing website’s manufactured controversies by declaring that “only Americans should be voting in American elections.” Instead of defending the right of Somali-Americans to cast ballots, Sen. Collins chose to cater to the MAGA lie that foreigners are swarming the polls.
When Collins brought former Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia to Maine to laud her record, she had him stand beside her as she posed for a photo with the Maine Wire’s awful “sword of truth,” a prop that was previously waved around in front of mosque-goers in Lewiston. Collins is no stranger to the sword.
Asked what Sen. Collins thinks it stands for, a Collins spokesperson said Monday in a memorable bit of PR: “The sword of truth symbolizes a willingness to take steps toward fiscal responsibility.”
(This spokesperson didn’t waste an opportunity to take a shot at me: “But we also believe that truth itself is very important — we know that when you were a reporter you used to put a premium on that; it seems that it has been less of a priority for you as a columnist.”)
Make no mistake: Sen. Collins is trying to rouse Trump loyalists to vote for her in big numbers. As long as Trump is telling penny-pinching Americans they shouldn’t worry about rising costs, it probably won’t work.
Democratic candidates in Maine, as around the country, are soaring in the polls and feeling confident.
“We’re all peaking at the right time,” congressional candidate Matt Dunlap told a small crowd Sunday at the Auburn home of Jordan Wood, an unsuccessful primary challenger.
Dunlap, who is angling to defeat Republican Paul LePage in the 2nd Congressional District, said the president is at the heart of the campaign. Voters have a stark choice, he said: “We can either stop Trump or succumb to him.”
Sen. Collins had that choice, too. She’s opted to succumb. Her willingness to engage in slimy campaigning is going to tarnish her legacy.

title: Maine’s wild blueberry rake maker dies at 84 but business may live on
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Ike Hubbard, a longtime designer and maker of harvesting rakes for Maine wild blueberries and many other crops, died this month. He was 84.
An industrial engineer, he returned from southern Maine to a family homestead Down East in 1990, where he created a durable new rake for harvesting Washington County’s iconic crop and expanded into designs for other small farmers across the country.
“I’m the rake manufacturer of the United States, to be honest with you,” Hubbard said in July, shortly after his Jonesport shop burned to the ground. “Everything that’s got a berry on it, I build a rake for.”
His was the last business in Maine, and possibly the country, to make such rakes by hand. Efforts to rebuild and reopen the shop will continue, his employee Debbie Salisbury wrote on a GoFundMe page that has raised $26,000 toward recovery efforts.
Salisbury and her husband, Ken, had been training to take over the company and Hubbard wanted them to continue it, she said Monday, but she’s not sure yet what will happen as the business goes through probate.
Hubbard died in his sleep on Oct. 3 after his health declined following several falls, according to Salisbury.
During Hubbard’s lifetime, advances in technology and field management nearly quadrupled Washington County’s wild blueberry yields, and mechanical harvesters that came on the scene in the 1980s changed the harvest from an event that drew many migrant rakers into a more mechanized affair with fewer workers.
But hand rakes still have a place in smaller fields, areas with difficult terrain and operations selling berries for the fresh market instead of frozen. Hubbard still built and repaired them, and kept inventing. He was most recently working on designs for a walk-behind flame weeder and a rake on wheels that could be used from a standing position; one of his latest creations was a specialty rake researchers used to scoop up lizards.
Hubbard spent his early childhood in Jonesport, when blueberries were still raked entirely by hand into wooden containers. His family moved to southern Maine when he was a teenager.
He served in the Army and worked as a manufacturing engineer, returning to Jonesport in 1990 and opening a rake shop next to the old family home.
The lighter, wider-panned, two-handled design he came up with was like the “Cadillac of rakes,” early users told the Bangor Daily News at the time.
He continued inventing with input from rakers, eventually offering rakes from 12-tooth miniatures to 35-foot spans.
Skilled workers using his rakes can harvest berries as intact as those picked by hand so they stay covered in whitish “bloom,” a natural coating believed to preserve the fruit’s quality.
“When you get these berries with the bloom on them … it’s like they glow,” Hubbard previously told the BDN.
The company also branched out into rakes for harvesting herbs, highbush blueberries, huckleberries and elderberries, along with tooth-based garden tools like broadforks and weeding claws for Maine-based Johnny’s Selected Seeds.
That seed company calls the tools that Hubbard helped develop part of a “small scale farming revolution.”
He chose not to work on mechanical harvesters, because he promised himself when he started not to build anything that would put a person out of work, Hubbard said last summer.
His uninsured shop burned from an unknown cause in late June, taking tens of thousands of dollars in tools, supplies and finished orders with it. A phased fundraiser to clear the site, pay employees, rebuild and replace equipment has so far raised about $26,000.
Rebuilding is still underway, with a foundation poured and a local builder taking the lead on constructing a shop, according to the fundraiser. But how the building would be used and by whom is also up in the air, Salisbury said Monday.
After the fire, Hubbard only became more determined to keep working, according to the page.
“He was an original: a veteran, a brilliant craftsman, an inventor, and a welder, with a true Maine work ethic and a wicked sharp sense of humor,” the fundraiser update announcing his death reads. “For 40 years, the rakes and farm tools he created have served Maine farmers. We hope that tradition continues.”
His funeral will be held at the Bayview Cemetery on Mason Bay Road at 9 a.m. on Saturday, Nov. 7, followed by a celebration of life at the American Legion’s Machias post.

title: Letter: Democrats favor prosperity, equality
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
As we approach this year’s crucial election, we face an important choice about our nation’s future. I believe voting for Democratic candidates is the most effective way to ensure a future built on shared prosperity, equality, and progress for all Americans.
Democrats consistently advocate for policies that invest in everyday citizens rather than concentrating benefits for corporations and the ultra-rich as Republican policies often do.
From lowering prescription drug and health care costs to supporting infrastructure improvements and clean energy, Democratic leadership has focused on building a stronger, more equitable future.
Conversely, the current Republican platform has shifted away from consensus-building. It favors an agenda that threatens civil liberties and economic fairness, placing an unfair burden on the working class. Their national economic proposals consistently favor large corporations and the wealthy who spend billions of dollars per year lobbying Republican elected leaders.
No political party is perfect, and healthy debate is essential to a healthy democracy. However, at this pivotal moment, I believe Democratic candidates offer the clearest commitment to protecting democratic institutions, personal freedoms, and economic opportunity for everyone.
Democracy works best when every voice is heard. I urge every eligible citizen to register, research the issues, and vote for Democratic leaders. The fate of our country is in our hands.
Ron Sadler
Bangor

title: 6 citizens sue Trump, saying media ban deprives them of news as audience stakeholders
text:
(AP) - In the increasingly bitter legal standoff between President Donald Trump and media outlets whose reporting he dislikes, a new and crucial third party has emerged: citizens who watch and read the news and need it to do their jobs.
A lawsuit filed Monday on behalf of six such citizens — essentially representing the wider public audience — argues that it’s not only the rights of news organizations that are violated when Trump bans them from White House premises. Even more fundamentally, the lawsuit argues, such bans violate the public’s right to independent reporting about its president and government.
“The ultimate injury here … is to the democratic public,” says the suit, filed in federal district court in New York against Trump and three key aides, including the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles.
“The First Amendment protects the public’s right to know what its government is doing,” said Katie Fallow, deputy litigation director at the Knight First Amendment Institute, which filed the lawsuit on behalf of the plaintiffs, along with the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic at Yale Law School.
“The White House cannot decide what information Americans receive by punishing critical reporting,” Fallow said in a statement. ”When the White House expels reporters because of their coverage and threatens others with expulsion, it isn’t just the press that suffers — the public loses access to independent reporting and gets something closer to government propaganda.”
The Trump administration, asked for comment on the lawsuit, responded in a statement that it attributed to an unidentified White House official: “No person may demand access to the Oval Office.” It said media that peddle “misinformation and defamation are completely capable of reporting their manufactured stories from directly outside.”
The plaintiffs all rely on White House news for their work
The six plaintiffs are all people who say they rely on independent and diverse White House reporting for their teaching, journalism or advocacy. They include a noted human rights advocate, a political journalist, a Yale history professor, a high school civics teacher, a legal journalist, and a student journalist at the University of Pennsylvania.
The complaint filed Monday recounts how various news organizations that have been targeted by Trump are already battling the administration in the courts. These cases include the current lawsuit by CNN, MS NOW and Politico, whose journalists were banished from the White House in September.
A federal judge recently extended an order preventing the White House from enforcing the ban while the case makes its way through the legal system. Still affected, though, is CNN’s pool coverage of Trump. The White House has been denying the network its usual slots in the video pool covering the president’s activities and travel, and CNN has threatened further action.
Also continuing is the legal case involving The Associated Press, whose reporters were barred last year from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some events in retaliation for the outlet’s decision not to follow Trump’s lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters, to the Gulf of America.
The New York Times is also involved in litigation, over a Pentagon policy requiring escorts for journalists on its grounds. And ABC is fighting back against the Trump administration in a dispute over renewal of its broadcast licenses.
This lawsuit seeks more wide-ranging relief
The new lawsuit filed Monday, though, is different from previous legal action against the president — first, in that the plaintiffs are ordinary citizens, shifting the focus from news gatherers to news consumers, and thus implying a much larger pool of stakeholders.
The lawsuit reframes the current debate over White House access in at least one key way. The public right to receive information is part of established law, said Jameel Jaffer, executive director of the Knight Institute. However, nobody has yet asserted this right in relation to the White House press corps and the issues currently at stake.
“We wanted to put the injury to the public at the center of the conversation,” Jaffer said.
“It’s one thing for CNN to say, ‘We are here because the public needs us,’” he said. “It’s another for a member of the public to say that interference with the White House press corps undermines our right to information about the government.”
In addition, the litigation seeks more wide-ranging relief.
The suit, which names Trump as defendant along with Wiles, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung and Secret Service Director Sean M. Curran, calls not merely for reinstatement of access that has already been impacted, but for a broad injunction that would protect from retaliation every news outlet that covers the White House —- now, and in the future.
“Defendants’ policy of restricting the access of disfavored news organizations deprives the public of the reporting of those organizations,” the complaint says. It also “inevitably deprives them of the independent reporting of other news organizations as well, since every journalist who reports from the White House must now account for the possibility that a critical or ill-advised word about the president may result in their access being summarily restricted or revoked.”
“Plaintiffs ... seek a declaration that the policy is unconstitutional because it imposes restrictions on a limited public forum that are viewpoint-based and unreasonable,” the complaint adds. ”They also seek an injunction barring defendants from enforcing the policy.”
Plaintiffs include a human rights advocate, a high school teacher and a student journalist
Plaintiff Ethan Young, a student at the University of Pennsylvania and editor-in-chief of The Daily Pennsylvanian, said in an interview that White House reporting has become increasingly important at his college newspaper during Trump’s second term.
“Over the last two years we’ve seen college campuses be a key avenue where President Trump’s policies have really affected people across the country, and Penn’s campus is no stranger to that,” he said.
“So I use White House reporting almost daily to look at what’s happening in both national higher education trends, but also just general federal policy changes, to see what might impact Penn,” Young said. “You never know what policy could have an impact on the Penn student body.”
Especially important to Young and his colleagues at the paper is a diversity of news outlets to choose from.
“We are not in the room. We are not in Washington,” Young said. “The benefit of having access to a variety of publications ... means I am constantly seeing different questions being asked of White House officials.”
And more often than not, he said, that means he’ll get the answer to a question he has, too.
The other plaintiffs are:
— Kenneth Roth, former longtime executive director of Human Rights Watch and a lecturer at Yale’s law school and school of global affairs.
— Daniel Froomkin, media and political journalist and editor of Press Watch, a nonprofit that encourages political journalists to “fulfill their essential mission of creating an informed electorate and holding the powerful accountable.”
— Beverly Gage, Pulitzer Prize-winning historian and professor at Yale University.
— Peter Schmidt-Nowara, a social studies and civics teacher at Brooklyn Technical High School in New York.
— Benjamin Wittes, editor-in-chief of Lawfare and a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

title: Cause of death revealed for Eric Bauza, the modern voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and more
text:
(Gray News) — Eric Bauza, the Emmy Award-winning voice actor who was the modern voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and many more Looney Tunes characters, died suddenly at the age of 46, his family said.
Bauza’s family announced the voice actor’s sudden death in a statement on Instagram.
The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner said Bauza died from hypertensive cardiovascular disease. Other contributing factors included sleep apnea and type 2 obesity, according to the medical examiner.
His manner of death was ruled natural.
Bauza lent his voice to such iconic Looney Tunes characters as Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, as well as Tweety, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Porky Pig and more in “Coyote vs. Acme.” He also voiced characters in “Space Jam: A New Legacy” and “Looney Tunes Cartoons.”
He also voiced characters in DreamWorks Animation’s “Forgotten Island.”
“Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world,” said Channing Dungey, chairman of Warner Bros. Television Group and U.S. Networks, in a statement. “He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc. Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life.”
Bauza won three Children’s & Family Emmy Awards for “Teen Titans Go!,” “Bugs Bunny Builders” and “Looney Tunes Cartoons,” according to Variety.
He was born on Dec. 7, 1979, in Toronto.

title: School reorganization: Not a radical change, but a step in the right direction
text:
As a Bar Harbor parent and school board member, I’ve heard many thoughtful questions about the reorganization plan on the Nov. 3 ballot. The biggest are simple: Why do this, and why now?
For me, the answer starts with our students.
Every fall, many children from across MDI, Trenton, and the outer islands walk into MDI High School together. We are proud of that school and the opportunities it provides. But before they get there, they attend separate elementary schools with different resources, staffing levels and programming. Dedicated educators work hard in every school, yet students do not always arrive with the same foundation. A stronger regional system would give us the opportunity to better align curriculum, services and support so that every child enters high school with the same opportunities to succeed.
Our elementary schools are small, and that is one of their greatest strengths. Small schools create close-knit communities where students are known and valued. But their size also creates challenges. District figures show Conners Emerson with 335 students and the other elementary schools with 554 students combined, and Conners Emerson does not have pre-K. In our four largest schools after Conners Emerson, the average grade has about 13 students.
Each school does wonderful work, but alone, providing specialized services becomes more difficult and expensive. Two schools that each need a part-time special education teacher must recruit and support two separate part-time positions. In a regional system, those resources can be shared, making it easier to attract and retain highly qualified professionals while giving students better access to the services they need. The same principle applies to counseling, intervention programs, enrichment opportunities, and other specialized support.
Just as important is the question of timing. Why now? Because big decisions are coming, whether we act or not.
We are going to continue facing major decisions about facilities, staffing and long-term financial sustainability. I would rather we make those choices together, with a plan, than one town at a time. I believe our communities are stronger when we solve problems collectively rather than waiting until circumstances force our hand.
Many residents are understandably concerned about taxes and local control. The facts matter. Bar Harbor taxpayers are already committed to paying for the Conners Emerson building, a necessary and long-overdue need. That cost exists regardless of this vote. Under an RSU, every member town would share responsibility for the building and its long-term upkeep. The same for all other schools.
Bar Harbor would also keep a strong voice. Seats on the 15-member RSU board are assigned by the same split as high school voting today. Teachers keep their contracts, no town can be forced to consolidate schools, and no school can be closed unless it is replaced by a new building and approved by that town’s voters.
This plan is not a radical change. It does not try to do everything at once, as many residents asked. It is a step in the right direction, and whatever comes next — like a shared middle school — starts here. It will remain the board’s job to protect what we have built and keep pushing it forward. Future decisions are up to future voters.
More than 50 years ago, our towns came together to build MDI High School because they recognized that some opportunities are greater when we work together than when we work apart. That same principle is before us today.
This reorganization is a practical, measured step toward giving every child access to the strongest education we can provide while preserving local voices and local schools. I hope you’ll join me in voting yes on Nov. 3.
Tyson Starling is a Bar Harbor resident, parent and school board member.

title: 'Picasso of Pumpkin Carvers' brings artistry to a Halloween tradition
text:
HALF MOON BAY, Calif. (AP) — When fall arrives and leaves start changing color, Mike Valladao, a systems engineer at a cybersecurity company, slips into his alter ego, “Farmer Mike,” also known as the “Picasso of Pumpkin Carvers.”
Farmer Mike has been chiseling whimsical faces and comical creatures into big pumpkins for more than four decades. Wearing his trademark orange overalls and farmer hat, he’s sculpted hundreds of gourds into ghoulish faces, seaside landscapes, witches, dragons and pop culture figures such as Yoda and Charlie Brown.
Valladao doesn’t have any formal artistic training, but he’s always looking for inspiration. He gets ideas from looking at art in a museum or just walking down the street.
“Sometimes I’ll look at somebody and I’ll think, oh, I like the teeth or I like ears or the way the nostrils flare,” Valladao said.
This year, “Farmer Mike” celebrated 40 years of Halloween artistry at the Half Moon Bay Art & Pumpkin Festival, which is held in mid-October and is best known for its giant pumpkin weigh-off. At the two-day festival on the coast south of San Francisco, Valladao works on stage so people can watch.
His pumpkin carvings have drawn requests from across the US
Valladao stumbled into his artistic hobby after he began growing big pumpkins at his San Jose home in the mid-1980s. He didn’t know what to do with the massive gourds, so he pulled out a knife and started slicing faces into them.
“I’m an engineer by trade and I tend to look at it as building something the same way I would build a piece of hardware, one layer at a time,” he said.
In 1986, festival organizers saw a picture of Valladao’s pumpkins and invited him to showcase his carving skills in Half Moon Bay, where his family opened the town’s first feed and seed store in the 19th century. He grew an 800-pound (363-kilogram) pumpkin once, but it was a lot of work, so he doesn’t participate in the giant pumpkin contest.
His art has since taken him to different parts of the country, including an appearance on “The Tonight Show.” He has gotten requests to carve pumpkins at venues such as the San Diego Zoo, the California Academy of Sciences and the State Fair of Texas.
‘It’s about the illusion of depth’
He uses Atlantic pumpkins that weigh from 100 to 1,000 pounds (45 to 454 kilograms). They have thick skins that allow him to cut protruding facial features shallow or deep.
“It’s really about the illusion of depth,” Valladao said. “I can make it so that it’s three-dimensional, such that the eyes are inset and the nose sticks out. So it’s a little bit of carving, but it’s just adding a little more magic to it.”
Valladao said he doesn’t name his creations because he recognizes the ephemeral nature of his art, which only lasts a few days.
“It never really bothers me when a pumpkin starts to age because in some cases they’ll build character,” Valladao said.
And there are always more pumpkins to be carved.
After 40 years at Half Moon Bay, Valladao doesn’t have any plans to hang up his carving knives.
“It’s fun, it’s enjoyable and, quite frankly, it’s a piece of me,” he said.

title: Is It Really Illegal To Drive in the Left Lane On I-95?
text:
Is It Really Illegal To Drive in the Left Lane On the I-95 in Maine?
If you spend a lot of time driving the I-95 through Maine there is a good chance that you have broken the law without even realizing it.
Is It Illegal To Drive In The Left Lane On The I-95?
Without hashing out the specifics of how fast you drive, I think we can all agree that many of us frequently drive faster than the posted speed limit. A lot of times this happens when we're on the highway. This often causes us to drive faster than the flow of traffic. When that happens we tend to camp in the left lane of the highway.
Is it legal to do this? Technically, no.
According to the Maine Legislature website:
An operator driving on a limited-access way with a speed limit of 65 or more miles per hour is restricted in ordinary operation to the right-hand lane and may use adjacent lanes for overtaking and passing another vehicle, but must return to the right-hand lane at the earliest opportunity. This requirement does not apply to an authorized emergency vehicle, or to a vehicle otherwise directed by posted signs, a law enforcement officer or a highway maintenance crew.
So, will you get pulled over for riding in the left lane? As long as you are actively passing a line of cars, probably not. But, you're going to want to slip back into that right lane as soon as you can.
If you do get pulled over for camping in the left lane you could be facing a $152 ticket!
You can read more about the laws HERE.
It is just another reminder to always be aware of the rules of the road in the states where you travel.

title: Charles campaign fined more than $22K by Maine Ethics Commission
text:
Campaign for Bobby Charles fined more than $22K by Maine Ethics Commission
Penalty stemmed from the Charles campaign accepting over-the-limit campaign contributions totaling $45,315
Campaign for Bobby Charles fined more than $22K by Maine Ethics Commission
Penalty stemmed from the Charles campaign accepting over-the-limit campaign contributions totaling $45,315
The Maine Commission on Governmental Ethics and Election Practices voted to fine the campaign for Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles more than $22,600 for violating election laws by means of accepting over-the-limit contributions.
Jonathan Wayne, executive director of the Ethics Commission, said during Monday's meeting that the commission received a complaint from the Maine Democratic Party claiming that the Charles campaign accepted a number of over-the-limit campaign contributions.
Wayne said apparent over-the-limit contributions totaling $45,315.98 were found, and that commission staff recommended to the Ethics Commission a penalty between $11,329 and the total amount by which the contributions went over the limit.
The recommendation from commission staff was conveyed in writing to the Charles campaign Thursday evening. Wayne said that the following day, the Charles campaign asked for the Ethics Commission to delay a decision until its Nov. 18 hearing because the campaign wanted more time to respond.
Brittany Hausle, a lawyer representing the Charles campaign, spoke during Monday's meeting and did not dispute the over-the-limit contributions, but she did note that the campaign has been working diligently to correct the overages and wanted more time to gather information.
Hausle also said that although the campaign does understand Maine election laws, discussion of a penalty never came up during informal meetings with commission staff.
“This came as a surprise, frankly, to the campaign, regarding the penalty," Hausle said.
The Charles campaign's treasurer, Bill Riley, also spoke during the meeting and claimed a national consultant ignored his warnings about there being over-the-limit contributions and filed the paperwork anyway.
“There was nothing malicious here. It was an outside consultant who didn’t follow our protocol, and that’s what has put us in a mess," Riley said.
A lawyer for the Maine Democratic Party said during the meeting that the Charles campaign's request for the Ethics Commission to delay until after the Nov. 3 election "feels like a dodge."
The bipartisan Ethics Commission ultimately voted 4-1 to levy a fine against the Charles campaign that equaled 50% of the total overages, which was $22,657.99.
"We would have preferred a different outcome, but we respect the Commission's process," the Charles campaign said in a statement. "Our focus remains on the issues Maine families are facing right now, especially record heating costs heading into winter. With one week until Election Day, that is the conversation Maine voters deserve."
The Maine Democratic Party said it will continue to monitor the situation, but said that as long as the Charles campaign pays the fine, then the filing regarding the violations will be complete.
A group held a gathering Monday afternoon following the commission's decision.
One of the speakers was Rep. Marc Malon, D-Biddeford, who called the overpayments unethical, extreme, reckless and sloppy. Malon added it's a testament on how Charles would govern if elected.
"This is a desperate man folks, willing to say or do anything to win," added Malon. "But he won't win. And I'm glad the Ethics Commission is holding him accountable. Maine voters will, too."

title: Trump failed to stop inflation. Now Republicans may pay the price in the midterm elections
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump would prefer that voters not worry about inflation. But it’s hard for them to ignore.
Filling up a basic Ford F-150 truck now costs about $100, up $30 from a year ago. Mortgage rates have jumped to levels that have depressed home sales. And for the past 12 months, consumer prices have risen faster than paychecks, making the average family poorer.
One week before midterm elections that will serve as a referendum on his second term, Trump is struggling to deliver on his campaign promise to bring down costs, even as he insists the country has entered an economic “golden age.” The same frustration that powered his comeback two years ago could now cost Republicans control of Congress.
“Our nation is doing better now than ever before,” Trump insists while campaigning, vowing that interest rates and oil prices will plunge once the war with Iran — which he started — comes to an end.
The word “affordability,” he says, is nothing but “a con job by the Democrats,” adding that “it doesn’t mean anything to anybody.”
Trump’s rosy rhetoric meets voters’ reality
That rhetoric comes as voters say they’re struggling to afford basics like fuel and groceries and as they blame Trump for higher costs, pointing to the Republican president’s aggressive tariff policies and the ongoing, unpopular war with Iran.
Record-high diesel prices, in particular, have driven up shipping and farming costs, creating trouble for Republicans in typically conservative states such as Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas, where Democrats appear uniquely competitive in races that will shape Trump’s final two years in office.
“The costs of things are absolutely the first thing people talk about, but also it’s their pay not keeping up with the cost,” said AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler. “It’s a double whammy.”
Prices at the pump have become a preeminent issue for voters.
“People hate paying more money for gas, and the prices have gone up a lot,” said Stephen Moore, who has previously advised the president on the economy. “It’s frustrating because Trump’s done so many good things for the economy. But with the Iran situation, that’s really had a big effect on the economy, and Republicans may pay a high price for that.”
Misty Reeder, 48, said she considers herself “in the middle” politically but picked all Democrats on her ballot in Easley, South Carolina.
“I’ve noticed that things have been getting a lot harder,” said Reeder, who receives disability payments. “You hear about it everywhere you go.”
In the six years that she and her husband have been renting their home, Reeder said their rent had increased by hundreds of dollars.
“Something’s gotta give,” she said. “It’s like a dam — the pressure’s too much, and it’s going to break.”
Sandra Capell, 69, said she wants “to see some change” when it comes to the economy even though she voted Republican in Easley, which is part of South Carolina’s conservative Upstate region.
“I think everybody is kind of suffering when it comes to groceries, gas, everything really,” she said. “I’m looking at the Republican Party to jump on the wagon, get in the saddle and let’s bring it back.”
Beti Rosales, 47, said higher prices have taken a toll on her family’s Mexican restaurant in Allentown, Pennsylvania, part of the Lehigh Valley that has seesawed between the parties in recent years. Limes and avocados cost more than before. So does the plumber who’s occasionally needed.
Two years ago, Rosales decided to give Trump and Republicans a chance, hoping for relief from inflation.
“The reality now is that it actually didn’t get better,” she said. “It actually got worse. The prices of everything have increased.”
Rosales is now considering voting Democratic in the midterms.
“Maybe fresh new faces might make a difference?” she said.
Trump promised he’d bring prices down
While running in 2024, Trump hammered President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris, his Democratic opponent in the election, for high inflation, which climbed as high as 9.1% in June 2022. He promised voters he would lower gasoline prices and unlock roaring growth.
“With your vote in this election, I will end inflation,” he vowed.
In less than two years, Trump has aggressively remodeled the U.S. economy. He’s slapped double-digit tariffs on many trading partners — including the European Union, India, Japan, Canada and Mexico — and sparked trade wars with allies. The U.S. government now holds stakes in several dozen private companies. He’s signed broad income tax cuts into law.
But the persistent challenge of inflation has continued, overshadowing the positives of continued economic growth and a low unemployment rate. Inflation was 3% when Trump took office and reached 3.7% last month.
The president has played down the intensity of inflation, claiming that it is under 2% and “under control.”
Democrats have seized on the discontent, using the same high cost of living that sank them before to pressure vulnerable Republicans and put congressional districts Trump won by even double digits in play.
“Now remember, they promised to lower prices on Day One. Instead, under the failed President Donald J. Trump, it costs more than ever in American history to fill up your truck, stock your fridge, visit the doctor or power your home,” said Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, a Democrat running for reelection, at a recent rally in Atlanta.
“You work harder and harder, but the treadmill gets faster and steeper and the bills get higher and higher,” he told the crowd.
Cait Conley, a Democrat running in New York against Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, one of his party’s most vulnerable incumbents, harkened back to his tweet from the last midterm elections, when Biden was president. Lawler had advised voters to “fill up your tank and go grocery shopping — it will inform your decision.”
In a new ad, Conley said voters should follow that advice this year “and then tell me if the system’s working for you.”
“You deserve better. It shouldn’t be this hard,” she says.
Democrats turn Trump’s attacks back on him
Conley and other candidates have pounded on a theme that Democrats believe will be especially effective this cycle: accusing Trump and other Republicans of compounding voters’ economic pain by corruptly pursuing policies that help their billionaire donors at the expense of everyday Americans.
“I know you’re frustrated. Washington politicians get rich while you get hurt. Corporations make huge profits while your costs go up,” North Carolina Senate candidate Roy Cooper says in an ad airing in the competitive state.
That has included a particular focus on the war with Iran.
“Trump’s war abroad costs taxpayers a billion dollars a day on a war we have no business fighting. Our schools crumble, our factories shutter, our gas prices skyrocket. But when they want war, billion-dollar blank checks,” says Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in another spot.
The president “thinks that the economy is doing well because he and his family have enriched themselves to the tune of several billion dollars,” said Amy Richards, 56, a onetime Republican who has voted Democratic since Trump became his party’s 2016 nominee.
“He has zero idea what it is like to receive a paycheck and have to feed yourself and your family,” said Richards, standing outside a polling place in her town of Round Rock, Texas, on Friday, “and he doesn’t care.”
Republicans, meanwhile, have tried to cast Democrats as extreme, pointing to an ascendant populist wing that includes a number of Democratic socialists.
Moore, who advised Trump’s campaigns, said he wished Republicans would spend more time talking about the economy’s strengths, including rising median incomes and a record-setting stock market, even as he acknowledged those numbers might not resonate with voters.
“What matters is how people feel, and clearly people are feeling stressed out financially,” he said.
Some Trump supporters remain satisfied. Renee Blood, 57, an executive assistant in Round Rock, feels the economy has “improved quite well.”
“Of course we see gas prices up and down, but things are much more affordable,” she said.
She plans to vote Republican because she worries things will get worse if Democrats return to power.
Trump’s golden age might not have arrived, she said, but “we are still working on it.”
___
Colvin reported from New York. Associated Press writer Meg Kinnard in Easley, S.C.; Mike Catalini in Allentown, Pa.; and Jesse Bedayn in Round Rock, Texas, contributed to this report.

title: Eric Bauza, known as the iconic voice behind Looney Tunes' Bugs Bunny, dies at 46
text:
Eric Bauza, known as the iconic voice behind Looney Tunes' Bugs Bunny, dies at 46
Eric Bauza, the modern voice behind iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, among several others, has died.
Bauza's family took to his Instagram page on Sunday, saying the Emmy Award-winning voice actor "passed away suddenly."
“Eric Bauza, Emmy Award-winning voice actor and the modern voice of iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, along with dozens of other beloved cartoon characters, has passed away suddenly,” they wrote. “More details to come.”
According to Variety, the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner said he died at his home as a result of hypertensive cardiovascular disease.
He was 46 years old.
Throughout his career, Bauza was one of the industry’s most in-demand voiceover actors, Variety said, lending his voice to characters like Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck. He also was the voice of Tweety, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Porky Pig, Road Runner, Charlie the Dog and others in this year’s Looney Tunes film “Coyote vs. Acme.”
Alongside Looney Tunes, the Emmy winner voiced characters in “Avatar: The Last Airbender,” “Chowder,” “Alvin and the Chipmunks: The Squeakquel,” “Scooby-Doo! Mystery Incorporated,” “Fanboy & Chum Chum,” “Ben 10: Omniverse” and many more.
Bauza has more than 400 acting credits to his name.
This year, Variety said the actor was a part of the productions “Chibiverse,” “Minions & Monsters,” “Forgotten Island,” “Rick and Morty,” “SuperKitties” and “Avatar: Seven Havens."
According to Newsweek, the voice actor won three Children's & Family Emmy Awards for his work on "Teen Titans Go!," "Bugs Bunny Builders" and "Looney Tunes Cartoons."  
According to his SBV talent bio, he began his animation career as a character designer at a production studio in Hollywood.

title: New report calls for changes, transparency when it comes to AI impact on Maine workforce
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
New report calls for changes, transparency when it comes to AI impact on Maine workforce
A new report from the Maine Center for Economic Policy points to several recommendations for how the state can address the impacts of artificial intelligence on the local workforce and workplace.
The report is called State of Working Maine 2026: Protecting Workers from Artificial Intelligence and looks at how AI can benefit Maine and Maine workers while also providing safeguards.
The report finds AI’s future effects are uncertain, but the risks, which are familiar, include: job displacement, weakened worker power, intrusive surveillance, discrimination, and widening inequality.
The report does include personal stories from people affected by and connected to AI, including one person who lost their job within the last year as a result of AI.
The report finds that AI is affecting jobs in office support, production, transportation, retail, and customer service the most, mirroring similar trends to the rest of the country. Data within the report shows that workers in Cumberland, Androscoggin and Kennebec Counties have the highest exposure to AI in the state.
"These areas of the state have higher costs of living, which higher average earnings currently balance. But if AI adoption causes a depression in wages, Mainers in these areas could be burdened with higher costs without the wages to pay for them," the report says. "Despite its rural nature, Somerset County also scores highly on the geographic measure of AI because of a relatively large proportion of workers employed in health care, education, and retail."
Workers in Piscataquis County have the lowest exposure, according to the report.
Workers in York, Oxford, Franklin, Sagadahoc, Lincoln, Knox, Hancock and Washington Counties have below-average exposure while those in Aroostook, Penobscot, Somerset and Waldo Counties have above average exposure.
The report finds that, in mid-2026, one in four employed Mainers used AI at work multiple times a week, and only 55% of users reported increased productivity as a result of AI use.
The report says that a May 2026 survey found 70% of Mainers predicted the growth of AI would result in fewer jobs over the next decade, making it the most common concern about the technology among those surveyed. However, most Mainers who used AI at work did not think their own job was at risk from the technology. Still, one-quarter of AI users in Maine thought they were likely to lose their job to AI in the next decade.
Researchers say the report suggests that Maine does not need to predict AI’s exact trajectory to act and they urge Maine lawmakers to pair innovation with accountability.
The report says that growth and use of AI does not necessarily mean there will be a loss of jobs. The report says AI may complement workers, more efficiently do certain tasks or jobs, or raise profits without increasing pay.
The report also says there is no evidence at this time of broad AI-driven unemployment in Maine, but there are some warning signs among technology firms, call centers, early-career workers, and within certain communities.
If left unchecked, the report says AI could deepen the financial divide between owners/investors and employees.
Possible policy solutions
The report also highlights several possible policy solutions to help manage the growth of AI in Maine.
Researchers suggest that employers be required to disclose any layoffs related to AI. They also say that all safety-critical and public-interest jobs be legally protected from full automation.
The report recommends expanding unemployment insurance eligibility, duration, and wage replacement benefits and recognizing education and retraining as qualifying activity.
Researchers say there should be enforceable AI rules in the workplace, including limiting surveillance, banning algorithmic wage-setting, requiring impact assessments and human review of employment decisions, protection of employee data, and requiring consent before using a worker’s voice, likeness, or work to create a digital replacement.
The report also calls for making sure that large corporations, technology companies, and wealthy investors pay fair taxes on AI-driven profits and digital services; removing tax incentives that reward replacing workers with machines; and implementing policies to prevent corporations from accumulating too much economic and political power.

title: Understanding the importance of pelvic floor therapy for women
text:
LAKE OSWEGO, Ore. (InvestigateTV) - It’s a condition that can affect women at any age whether they’ve had children or not.
Doctors say one in three women experience a pelvic floor disorder in their lifetime, but getting treatment can drastically improve their quality of life.
With every throw, jump and stretch, Mackenzie Devine is strengthening muscles, including important ones that aren’t visible.
It’s exercise, physical therapy and personal time all rolled into one. For her, it’s a top priority.
“For me pelvic floor therapy is non-negotiable for my time and schedule,” Mackenzie Devine said.
Devine has quite the schedule. She’s a mother of five, including two sets of twins.
“I’ve got two sets of twins. One set is 10 months old, the other set just turned four. And then a 5-and-a-half-year-old,” Devine said.
She said pelvic floor therapy has been a helpful tool throughout all of her postpartum journeys. Pelvic floor therapy is a treatment for the group of muscles in the pelvic girdle.
“I think it’s huge with regard to your overall confidence in motherhood. For example, if you don’t know how to engage your pelvic floor, just putting your baby into the crib can be painful,” Devine said.
Dr. Jessica Hund, founder of The Floor PDX in Lake Oswego, works with women of all ages and stages who come to her seeking relief from common ailments that are not commonly spoken of, even among close friends.
“It’s not normal to be like hey, let’s go grab lattes and tell you about how sex has been killing me for 10 years,” Hund said. “Or I don’t feel confident in anything down below my waistband since having a kiddo, or perimenopause is wrecking me and this part of me is not what I knew it to be before.”
Hund said many people have the wrong idea about pelvic floor therapy.
“I think there has been a long-held misconception that if something is leaking or broken that you need to do Kegels or pelvic floor contractions and that’s all you need to do. The problem with that is your pelvic floor is a dynamic system that’s supposed to involuntarily react to the tasks you’re doing,” Hund said.
When patients come in for the first time, Hund said it usually starts with a quick internal assessment.
“We can feel all these muscles and see how are they resting, are they acting really guarded, are they able to move, are we touching pain points you’ve never experienced before,” Hund said.
But patients actually spend most of their time strength training.
“That’s why we’re in the gym because that’s how life is being lived, with the load that’s being passed to you when you’re jumping and landing and going back to the things you’re doing in real life, which is our greatest goal,” Hund said.
Whether someone is five months postpartum or five years, Hund said it’s never too late.
Hund said there’s a close connection between pelvic floor health and mental health.
“This area of your body also matters, and it’s so closely tied to mental health presentation of I don’t feel worthy, I’m not meeting exercise goals I want, my relationship is struggle because I can’t connect on an intimate level I want to,” Hund said.
Rachael Adair also reached out for help after giving birth to her baby boy, Finnegan.
“He entered the world in a bit of a dramatic fashion, and I found myself needing pelvic floor therapy,” Adair said.
Adair said a weakened pelvic floor played into a weakened sense of self-esteem. For a new mother already facing changes, she knew she didn’t want to face it alone.
“I left the hospital in shambles and tears — and the shift to motherhood has been a big one for me, but having the support from this team and being able to understand my body better and who I am has built a lot of confidence and love for myself which has changed a lot for me,” Adair said.
Pelvic floor therapy is often covered by insurance.

title: Route 94 reopens after crash that seriously injured a man in Dexter
text:
DEXTER, Maine (WABI) - A man was seriously injured in a major traffic incident that shut down State Route 94 between Garland and Dexter on Monday afternoon.
The crash happened just before 1 pm when a car went off the road and rolled over according to Dexter Police Chief Kevin Wintle.
The only person in the vehicle, a 48-year-old man, was flown via LifeFlight to the hospital.
The road was reopened as of 5:30 PM.
Route 94 was closed between Haskell Lane in Garland and Carr Road in Dexter for much of the afternoon as crash reconstruction took place with the assistance of the Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office.
Wintle said that authorities do believe that speed was a factor in the crash.

title: What it really takes for aging parents and adult children to repair old wounds
text:
(Aging Untold) — As parents age, some might hope for a closer relationship with their adult children.
Repairing those relationships takes more than good intentions — it takes ownership, patience and realistic expectations.
“Forgiveness takes one person, but a relationship takes more than one”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said families need to understand upfront that they can’t control how the other side responds.
“I think it’s real important to understand that forgiveness takes one person, but a relationship takes more than one,” Cradduck said. “And if they’re not willing, there’s not a whole lot you can do.”
Cradduck added that many long-running family conflicts have lost their origin story entirely.
“Sadly, most of these disconnects, nobody knows what caused it,” Cradduck said. “They’ve been mad for so long, and they’ve lived this life in anger for so long, they don’t even know what happened to start it all.”
Her advice for the parent who may have caused the pain: own it.
“If you’re the person that maybe offended them, be willing to apologize. Be willing to own what you did wrong,” Cradduck said. “And if they’re not willing to accept that apology, you’ve done your part. You can’t be responsible for somebody else in a relationship — you can be responsible for yourself.”
A real apology has three parts
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said time alone doesn’t heal old wounds — and a genuine apology requires more than saying sorry.
“Time doesn’t automatically heal the pain. Just because 30 years have passed doesn’t mean the pain passed,” she said.
Rogers broke down what a real apology requires.
“When you have an apology, it has three parts to it: you want to acknowledge the harm, you want no excuses, and you need changed behavior,” Rogers said. “But the healing happens on the injured person — the person who was hurt, it’s on their timeline, not yours. The healing is the peace — but the reconciliation is the trust process and the relationship.”
- Acknowledge the harm
- Make no excuses
- Change your behavior
Sometimes the real conflict isn’t the one you think it is
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared an example from her own consultations about a client who had spent years resenting his father over how his mother had been treated — and became fixated on getting his dad to bring his mom coffee every morning.
“I said, well, maybe it’s more about you and your own feelings than it’s really their marriage,” O’Rourke said. “So he went into therapy and discussed his own resentments that were not attached to his parents at all — and he ended up telling me that his relationship with his partner got better for what he learned about himself.”
O’Rourke said the experience points to a broader lesson about self-awareness.
“What you think the conversation you need to have might not be the conversation you need to have,” O’Rourke said.
Estrangement is common — and complicated
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said that estrangement between older adults and their relatives has become increasingly common.
“There’s a lot of older adults living with serious pain from estrangement. It’s almost like a popular culture thing to be estranged from relatives,” Ambrose said. “And it’s very, very sad.”
Her advice to an older adult who feels cut off from family: let go of what you can’t control.
“You can’t make them change their mind or do anything. Honestly, I just say, pray about it, because something can change just like that,” Ambrose said. “And it could happen suddenly. And sometimes, maybe they did do something wrong, but sometimes maybe they really didn’t.”
Cradduck added that the only thing somebody can do is apologize and try to explain where they were at, or where they came from, or how it happened.
“And it’s on you then to either accept that and move forward, or to not. It’s your choice,” she said.
She added a reminder about grace.
“Someday you’re also going to need grace,” Cradduck said.
Don’t have the hard conversation when you’re angry
O’Rourke also offered practical advice for when emotions run high.
“If you’re really, really upset, you’re really hot, you’re really mad — don’t talk to them then,” O’Rourke said. “Let yourself cool down, get some objectivity.”
She recalled a friend whose daughter repeatedly raised complaints about her mothering, even after her mother felt she had done all she could.
“My friend said, ‘Well, I hope you get a really good therapist for that,’” O’Rourke said. “Because she really had resolved that she’d done all she could do, and she could really see that it was on her daughter that needed the help.”
O’Rourke noted that estrangement isn’t always literal distance.
“You might not be estranged, but you might feel emotionally estranged,” O’Rourke said.
Key takeaways
- Aging well means deciding what comes next — not rewriting old battles.
- Forgiveness and reconciliation are different. Forgiveness brings individual peace; reconciliation requires shared trust and real accountability.
- A genuine apology has three parts: acknowledging the harm, avoiding excuses and showing changed behavior.
- Healing happens on the hurt person’s timeline — not the timeline of the person who caused the pain.
- Set healing boundaries. Cool down and gain objectivity before starting emotionally charged family conversations.

title: 15-year-old arrested in connection with mass shooting after Florida homecoming, police say
text:
TALLAHASSEE, Fla. (WCTV/Gray News) – A 15-year-old was arrested in connection with a mass shooting that took place near Florida A&M University’s Bragg Memorial Stadium Saturday night.
Police Chief Lawrence Revell announced Monday morning during a press conference that Anthony Rivers III was charged with 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent.
At least 11 people were shot and injured, including six minors who, the chief said, did not appear to be the intended targets. The youngest victim was 11 years old. Revell said he believes one of the victims is a FAMU student.
“It is incredibly troubling when violence of this magnitude occurs in the very community I grew up in,” Revell said.
The shooting happened just hours after a homecoming football game at Bragg Memorial Stadium, where the visiting Arkansas-Pine Bluff Golden Lions beat the Rattlers, but it is unclear whether the shooting was related to the game.
Police believe the shooting likely stemmed from a fight between two or three people.

title: Drone Technology Helps Maine Emergency Crews Find Missing Bangor Woman

First Responders, at both the state and federal level across Maine, have started to make add drones into their toolkits.

title: Bodycam video shows moments after parents say cops were called on 3-year-old for being ‘too good’ at soccer
text:
WINTER PARK, Fla. (Gray News) — Parents in Florida claim their 3-year-old son had the police called on him because he was too good at soccer.
A viral Instagram video posted by the parents shows 3-year-old Nevada playing in a soccer game. Nevada can be seen dribbling the ball and scoring goals.
Then, the video shows police officers on the field as Nevada’s father says, “They called police on a 3-year-old ‘cause he’s too good.”
The parents later claimed that Nevada was kicked out of the i9 Sports league for the same reason.
The video gathered thousands of comments.
“Why would police waste their time responding to this?” one user wondered.
“This level of ridiculousness shouldn’t have happened to him, however his future looks very bright since he’s obviously a born champion,” another wrote.
Gray News obtained body camera video from Winter Park police that shows more of the story. Responding officers are shown speaking with a coach who said the boy’s parents were causing a disturbance.
“So, the kid is good, right? He’s great. Real good. So, what happened is, he’s very advanced compared to the other ones. So, he scores a lot of goals, but he’s pushing the other kids … so I try to tell him, play without pushing, right?” the coach said.
He continues, “There was like six kids on the team. I swap the kids out, because he’s so good I take him out, everyone deserves their time … They [the parents] don’t like that. They tell me I’m ignorant, I’m this, I’m that, blah blah blah … I just want them out. Immediately.”
The video then shows the two officers speaking with the boy’s parents, who dispute the coach’s account.
“I guess he was calling because I guess he believes that you guys were causing a disturbance that was interfering with the gameplay,” one officer told the parents.
“They’re mad at my son because he actually plays soccer. So I’m a little confused and I’m a little baffled because I signed my kid up for soccer. So they’re literally kicking him out of this place because he’s good at soccer,” the boy’s mother said.
“He specifically mentioned that your son is very good, but he doesn’t like how the parents become aggressive,” the officer said.
After speaking with officers, the parents agreed to leave the park with their son.
A police event report obtained by Gray News said, “Parents left field without issue and were cooperative with request of league personnel.”
The event report goes on to say, “Parents were upset that their child was being scorned for playing too well and was being taken out of game.”
One officer can be heard laughing at the end of the video and saying, “I kinda want to see him play. I bet he’s good.”
A news release from Winter Park police said:
“The Winter Park Police Department was contacted by a soccer league official who requested response to a disturbance between league officials and the parents of a player. The league requested the family leave and offered to refund the league cost to family. Shortly after arrival, the officers were requested by the league official to communicate with the family as he did not want to further a disturbance. The family stated the game was over and they were leaving. The family was cooperative with the officers and were provided with an event number for the incident at their request. The incident was a civil matter between those parties and not criminal. No one was arrested, trespassed, or forced to leave the park. The Officers body worn cameras confirm the above information.”

title: Your Choice, Your Voice: Election security in Maine
text:
Your Choice, Your Voice: Election security in Maine
One of the issues our viewers said is important to them to learn more about heading into the midterms is election security.
Your Choice, Your Voice: Election security in Maine
One of the issues our viewers said is important to them to learn more about heading into the midterms is election security.
We asked you, our viewers, what issues matter most to you and what you want to know the most about heading into the midterm election. One of the top issues, election security.
Maine is seeing record-high voter turnout. This, for a state that normally sees high turnout anyway.
The state's highest-ranking election official, Secretary of State Shenna Bellows says often that elections in Maine are safe and secure.
"We are going to run yet another free, safe and secure election," she said in an interview last month.
But some people, like Patrick Davis, from the nonprofit Maine Election Integrity Network, said there are some red flags.
"We look and look at all things election related. [The] main job is to protect the vote," he said.
Davis said he is mostly concerned about the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act (UOCAVA) voters. A law that Davis said is not necessarily being used as intended in Maine.
"There are more citizens voting today than there are military," he said about UOCAVA voters in Maine.
Davis is an election observer and takes photos of things he sees as worrisome, as well as election workers, because he said Mainers should know who is handling their ballots.
"These are our ballots. You know, it's important to know who's handling it," he said. "We have no idea what goes on when they're transcribing a ballot."
Another Maine nonprofit, the League of Women Voters, said the way Maine handles elections is completely safe.
"There's a reason we have nation leading voter participation in Maine," Chrissy Hart from the League said.
She added that issues surrounding elections are few, and far between and anyone who commits a crime related to elections is prosecuted.
She also said the League does election audits.
"Looking at how our elections are run, ensuring that everything we see adheres to election law and the way a polling place should be set up, how things should be run, how our elections should be conducted," she said.
Election security has been top of mind for many people in recent years. Last year, Maine voters failed to approve a measure that was aimed at voter ID and at the federal level, Congress could still take up the SAVE Act, which would require voter ID to cast your ballot nationwide.

title: Appeals court declines to rule on federal bid to set aside California ballots of alleged noncitizens
text:
Appeals court declines to rule on federal bid to set aside California ballots of alleged noncitizens
An appeals court on Monday declined to rule on whether California elections officials can count roughly 20,000 ballots that the Justice Department alleges belongs to noncitizens voters.
The decision sets the federal government and state officials up for another legal showdown on the matter on Tuesday in front of a federal district judge, giving the federal government a very short window to compel California to sequester votes before the Nov. 3 elections.
The Republican administration sued election officials in the heavily Democratic state in mid-October, accusing them of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a list of 20,000 people it alleged were likely noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls. The administration asked the judge to stop the state from counting those ballots until immigration status checks could be completed.
After a district judge had scheduled an Oct. 27 hearing on the issue, the federal government appealed to the 9th Circuit Court, arguing that a faster decision was needed to prevent the further counting of votes.
But two of the three 9th Circuit Court judges rejected that argument on Monday, writing that the federal government “failed to allow the district court adequate opportunity to consider” their initial request to sequester the ballots in question.
The Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to an emailed inquiry.

title: Mother dies trying to save her 2 sons after they were swept away while snorkeling
text:
(Gray News) - A British woman visiting the Bahamas with her family died attempting to rescue her two sons after they were swept out to sea.
According to the Royal Bahamas Police Force, the 36-year-old was snorkeling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island. Police reported a strong current swept the children away and the woman, in an effort to rescue them, “also was swept away.”
She was later rescued and taken to a ferry dock where CPR was administered before she was transported to a local medical clinic. Police reported a local doctor pronounced her dead “despite efforts to save her life.”
The BBC identified the woman as Leanne Gregory from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire. According to People, her husband, Nathan Gregory, set up a GoFundMe to raise funds for their two sons.
“This loss is unimaginable for our family, she was our foundation, our support, she made us who we are,” Nathan Gregory said, adding that the couple were childhood sweethearts and had been together for 22 years.
In the GoFundMe, Nathan Gregory described the moments after their sons were swept away.
He said that Leanne Gregory held their son until he was rescued but “didn’t have the energy to save herself.” He recounted that a “freak wave” swept her away from the boat that was helping them.
“I just have to be thankful for the hero she was in life and in death, and totally grateful for the fact my boys got out safely,” Nathan Gregory said. “Mainly thankful to my brave, amazing wife for keeping my boy above the water even as you were sinking ... you will be forever loved by everyone you knew, and I know you will continue to watch over us.”
The Royal Bahamas Police Force said an autopsy will be conducted.

title: Wearing the “college of our hearts” on your sleeve: The purpose of the homecoming court
text:
Homecoming is a time each fall when alumni, friends and current students come together to celebrate the college that unites them all. Homecoming is framed by sporting events and tailgating, but perhaps the most iconic part is the homecoming court. At the University of Maine, applications come out at the beginning of the year, with eight members selected for the court in the weeks leading up to homecoming weekend.
The court this year is made up of five fourth-year students, two third-year students and one second-year student, representing four different colleges. But what is the point of having a court? Is it just something to do during halftime at the football game, or is there a deeper meaning?
The members of this year’s court all had a variety of reasons for applying, ranging from community involvement and club representation to encouragement from friends. One member of the court, Malachi Lowery, a fourth-year student studying electrical engineering, cited his friend and UMaine alum Keegan Tripp as his inspiration for applying. Lowery said that Tripp is someone he “looks up to as a role model” and that he is an “example of a great leader.”
Friendships like these seem to be what ties students to UMaine. You can find hockey rinks, libraries and student unions on a host of college campuses, but it seems to be the relationships made here that keep people coming back.
Lowery is not alone in his inspiration. Helena Kay, a fourth-year student studying ecology and environmental science, said that many of her friends asked if she had applied, and she felt that “it would be a good opportunity to put a spotlight on the student organizations” she is a part of. Though the court may seem trivial to some, most are not attempting to get onto the court for the purpose of it being a popularity contest.
What does the court represent? For some, like Kaylie Strong, a third-year mechanical engineering student, the court represents the “spirit, pride and community that makes UMaine special.” While the court and the subsequent royalty are symbolic, Kasper Birgfeld, a fourth-year student studying mechanical engineering, said that the symbolism “serves as a vehicle to help engage the greater UMaine community in our collective traditions and festivities.” The people who are selected for the court come from many different majors and a plethora of clubs.
Lydia Rabideau, a third-year student studying art education, sees homecoming as an amazing way to spotlight all of the campus organizations. They said, “They are so beautiful and unique in their own ways and each and every one deserves to be shown to the world.”
Some members of the court will be on display for more than just the presentation of the court. Helena Kay is a member of the dance team, and Alexis Williams serves as a drum major for the Pride of Maine Black Bear Marching Band. Williams, along with the other two drum majors, is responsible for conducting the peppy tunes that are a quintessential aspect of the football games, and if you’ve attended a pregame, you have seen her pride on display as she leads the song “Let Me Clear My Throat.”
The students on this court are clearly full of pride for UMaine, and though symbolic, they are still important to campus culture. These students are involved, and as it feels like a long time coming to actually get to the game, the members of the court have a mix of emotions. Cami Juskiewicz, a fourth-year nursing student, said that she’s “very excited to be on the homecoming court” because being from Arizona, UMaine has “felt like her home away from home.”
Meanwhile, Rigel DeLisle, a second-year student studying business administration, said that while he is excited, he’s “nervous being the only sophomore on the court.” These emotions show that this matters enough to the court members to think about it longer than the moments it took to submit the application.
So although symbolic, the court matters because it shows off the students who are not only involved in a multitude of clubs but also love this school and truly think of UMaine as the “college of our hearts,” always.

title: Eric Bauza, the modern voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and more, dies at 46
text:
(Gray News) - Eric Bauza, the Emmy Award-winning voice actor who was the modern voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and many more Looney Tunes characters, has died at the age of 46, his family says.
Bauza’s family announced the voice actor’s sudden death in a statement on Instagram. Citing Los Angeles County Medical Examiner records, Variety reports he died Sunday as a result of hypertensive cardiovascular disease.
Bauza lent his voice to such iconic Looney Tunes characters as Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck as well as Tweety, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Porky Pig and more in “Coyote vs. Acme.” He also voiced characters in “Space Jam: A New Legacy” and “Looney Tunes Cartoons.”
He also voiced characters in DreamWorks Animation’s “Forgotten Island.”
“Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world,” said Channing Dungey, chairman of Warner Bros. Television Group and U.S. Networks, in a statement. “He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc. Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life.”
Bauza won three Children’s & Family Emmy Awards for “Teen Titans Go!,” “Bugs Bunny Builders” and “Looney Tunes Cartoons,” according to Variety.
He was born on Dec. 7, 1979, in Toronto.
