title: ‘I get very angry’: Mother speaks out after 10-year-old shot by another child
text:
VALDOSTA, Ga. (WALB/Gray News) — The mother of a 10-year-old boy shot in the face by a 9-year-old in September says she has not been told of a court date in the case, and that the mother of the boy involved still lives a few houses down from her.
Marshania English’s son, Javion, was shot at Brittany Woods Apartments on Monday, Sept. 7, according to the Valdosta Police Department. Police said the boy and a 9-year-old were playing with a gun when it went off.
Javion has since returned home and is not back in school full time with his usual activities, according to English.
“For the first few days, you know, it was very emotional. It was a lot going on,” English said. “And now that we’re home and he’s just not going back to school, he had his days with his ups and downs.”
English said she now watches her son more closely.
“And now, like, I have to pay a lot more attention to him,” English said.
Mother, 9-year-old facing charges
Police said detectives obtained arrest warrants on Sept. 9 for 46-year-old Andrea McClendon, the mother of the 9-year-old and the owner of the firearm. McClendon is charged with second-degree cruelty to children and reckless conduct. Police said she turned herself in at the Lowndes County Jail on Sept. 14.
Through the Department of Juvenile Justice, detectives also charged the 9-year-old with reckless conduct and possession of a firearm by a minor.
Mother describes neighbor living nearby
English said McClendon still lives a few houses down from her.
“I think that’s my biggest thing, because she still lives down from me, a couple houses down from me,” English said. “You know, I see them every day, which I don’t allow J.B. on to come outside, only when I’m outside. But when I’m out the door, I see them, and it’s just, I get angry.”
English said she feels no justice has been served.
“I feel like my son has been shot, and no justice has been served,” English said. “Like, they’re still able to go out, grocery shop, and still live their life. But my son is here, having to tell people, oh, what happened to his teeth, or the mark on his neck. And I don’t think it’s right, to be honest. I really don’t.”
Javion back in school
English said Javion is back in school. He is not currently participating in PE activities.
Asked how he is adjusting, Javion said, “Good.”
Javion described sitting outside as peaceful.
“It’s really peaceful, because I really just sit down,” Javion said.
PREVIOUS COVERAGE: 10-year-old shot in the face by 9-year-old while playing with a gun in Valdosta, police say
Recounting the shooting
Javion said the other boy asked whether Javion wanted to see his mother’s gun.
“Then, when I came inside, he asked me did I want to see his mama gun,” Javion said. “Then I said, ‘Yeah, just don’t point it at me. Turn that gun. I don’t want no bullets at me.’ He did the opposite. Then pointed at me and put bullets in it. Then he cocked it back. Then he locked the door.”
Javion said he tried to get the gun away before the shooting.
“Then I ran. Then I pushed the gun down to try to take it. He pointed it at me, and I really didn’t know. I locked the door. And then I stayed in there for some minutes,” Javion said. “Then it got quiet. So I went to the door... And then I got shot.”
Mother describes being overwhelmed
When asked how important his mother is to him, Javion said, “A hundred percent. Important to me.”
English said she is overwhelmed by what her son now has to go through.
“I’m overwhelmed. I really am. I’m overwhelmed,” English said. “You know, because now he has to start therapy. And it’s just something that he has to deal with for the rest of his life.”
Mother wants distance from suspect’s family
English said she would feel more at peace with distance between the two families.
“I probably would feel more at peace is either I moved or they moved,” English said.
English said she believes the legal system failed her after McClendon was released from custody quickly.
She said she has not been told of any court date in the case.
“To be honest, I haven’t heard anything about a court date or anything like that,” English said.
GoFundMe set up for dental work
English said a GoFundMe has been set up to help pay for Javion’s dental costs.
“People can support our GoFundMe so that Javion can get his teeth fixed,” English said. “It would go towards his teeth cosmetics, which we would try to get him some veneers.”

title: Election Day in Maine may come with tensions over poll watching
text:
Maine elections officials are warning of potential friction at the polls ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3.
Last week, the U.S. Department of Justice announced plans to send election monitors to Portland and Lewiston — cities with large immigrant communities.
Meanwhile, recent reports of possible voter intimidation in Lewiston have prompted a nonprofit coalition of military veterans to launch its own poll-watching program. Their intention is to stake out the polls to make sure federal agents or other groups aren’t intimidating voters.
But their efforts have prompted a word of warning from Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, the state’s top elections official.
“While well-meaning, the presence of large groups at polling locations may actually have the opposite effect (and discourage) some voters from voting,” Bellows said in a written statement.
“We’ve instructed wardens to ensure that no voters are intimidated on Election Day, and we will be working closely with local clerks and the Office of the Attorney General to safeguard the right to vote for every Maine citizen.”
The expected surge in poll watching comes amid concerns that President Donald Trump will somehow try to influence the midterm elections using the power of the federal government. Trump has repeatedly made unproven claims of widespread voter fraud and has been trying to exert more control over state-run elections. His Department of Justice has already sued Alaska over its ballot, claiming that if the Republican candidate there loses, the result should not be certified.
Maine’s Senate race is one of a handful nationally that could determine control of the upper chamber and set the course for Trump’s final two years in office. It’s one of the Democrats’ top pickup opportunities, since incumbent Sen. Susan Collins is the only Senate Republican running in a state won by Democrats in the 2024 presidential election. Polls show Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson in a tight race.
Mainers will also choose a new governor and a new 2nd District congressman, since Democratic Rep. Jared Golden, of Lewiston, is not running for reelection.
Last week, the DOJ announced that it plans to send about 1,000 staffers to monitor elections across the country — the most ever.
The DOJ has been increasing voting monitoring efforts in recent years. CBS News reported that the agency had 289 watchers in 2022 and 714 people across 26 states in 2024.
At least two municipalities in Maine have been put on notice by the DOJ ahead of the midterms. Portland and Lewiston received letters on Wednesday about the federal government’s plans to send election monitors from its Civil Rights Division on Nov. 3.
The letter says staff will be onsite to make sure federal voting laws are being followed, including the Voting Rights Act; National Voter Registration Act; Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act; Voting Accessibility for the Elderly and Handicapped Act; Civil Rights Act; and Help America Vote Act.
“If any issues arise on election day, the Team Lead or I will call you or your designee,” DOJ regional coordinator and senior trial attorney James Tucker wrote to the city clerks. “We will also provide you with our contact information if you have any concerns.”
Bellows said in a written statement that the state will ensure that the federal monitors comply with state laws. She said DOJ staffers cannot interact with voters, handle ballots or equipment, or disrupt voting in anyway.
“It’s important to note that DOJ has sent monitors to observe elections for decades,” Bellows said. “We will monitor their activities to ensure that they follow state and federal law, and that every voter is able to cast their ballot free from interference or intimidation.”
The effort comes as the Trump administration has been seeking more control over elections. Several states, including Maine, have resisted attempts by the White House to require that they provide sensitive voter information to the federal government, saying the U.S. Constitution delegates control of elections to the states.
Outside groups, such as the League of Women Voters of Maine and the ACLU of Maine, routinely monitor elections as well. But even more groups are expected to have a presence at the polls this cycle.
A spokesperson for the Maine People’s Alliance said the group plans to have faith leaders and military veterans watching the polls.
Over the weekend, the MPA-affiliated Maine Veterans Alliance issued a call to action for service members to observe polling locations on Election Day. The group said it’s worried that the Trump administration will deploy “federal forces in ways that intimidate voters.”
“Our goal is to stand in solidarity with voters who may feel intimidated, offer reassurance and support to those who are concerned, and remain vigilant while maintaining a peaceful presence,” wrote organizer Tristin Friend.
The 29-year-old Herman resident said in an interview Monday that about 30 veterans have already signed up. He said poll watchers will likely be wearing matching blue T-shirts to they can be identified. He stressed that the group will follow all local, state and federal election laws.
“We very much care about being there peacefully,” said Friend, who said he served in the Army National Guard from 2015-21.
Friend said he and other veterans were alarmed about reports last week of immigrants being targeted in Lewiston by staff of the Maine Wire, a conservative website affiliated with the Maine Policy Institute.
Several voters have claimed that the outlet’s reporters have been staking out the polls and harassing voters as they try to cast their ballots with the help of interpreters.
Videos that have circulated on social media showed a confrontation at the polls between a Maine Wire reporter and Safiya Khalid, a local advocate and former city councilor.
Lewiston City Hall now has posted notices advising visitors that since City Hall is a voting place, video recording and photography is prohibited within 15 feet of voters, per state statute.
On Monday, Lewiston City Clerk Kathleen Montejo said early voting was brisk and problem-free.
“I don’t believe we are having any more issues with voter intimidation; I have not received any additional complaints beyond the one from last week,” Montejo said. “We have posted signs regarding the limits under the law about photos and video and everyone seems to be abiding by that.”
This story contains reporting from The Associated Press.

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Barbara Sundberg, of Damariscotta, passed away on Oct. 14, 2026 at the age of 88.
She was born Barbara May Chrystie on Oct. 23, 1937. She and her brother, Richard, grew up in East Providence, R.I., spending summers in Oak Bluffs on Martha’s Vineyard, where her father was a minister.
Barbara attended MacMurray College in Jacksonville, Ill., and later received a master’s degree in education. She worked as an elementary school teacher in Warwick, R.I. until her retirement. Barbara was an accomplished pianist (with a repertoire including “The Star-Spangled Banner,” “The Entertainer,” and “Bad, Bad Leroy Brown”), loved experimenting with new recipes, and never passed up the chance to make a corny joke.
Barbara met her future husband, Richard (“Dick,” who predeceased her in 2024), when they were 16. They and their children, Karen and David, spent as much time as possible exploring Narragansett Bay on the various sail- and motorboats they owned over the years (Sunburst, Tijuana Taxi, Dodo, Alewife, Maker’s Mark, and Sedna, among others). They also took family cruises to Block Island, Cape Cod, Martha’s Vineyard, and Maine.
Barbara fell in love with the Maine coast on those summer cruises. She and Dick retired to Newcastle and later moved across the river to Damariscotta. They quickly embraced, and were embraced by, their new community, getting involved with local fundraisers and the Damariscotta River Association (now the Coastal Rivers Conservation Trust).
They spent their retirement sailing and motoring Maine’s coast and taking road trips to Quebec and Canada’s Maritime Provinces. Barbara cherished winter weather and found every single snowflake magical. She also loved planning family summer vacations when David, his wife Laura, Karen, and her husband Erik would gather for coastal hikes, lunches at lobster pounds, and happy hours with live music amongst their Damariscotta family.
Barbara, her quick wit, and her impeccable sense of fashion will be missed by all who knew her. A celebration of life for Barbara and Dick is being planned for spring 2027. To honor their passion for the natural wonders of Midcoast Maine, please consider a donation in their memory to the Coastal Rivers Conservation Trust at P.O. Box 333, Damariscotta ME 04543 or coastalrivers.org.

title: Study looks at changes to Mt. Katahdin’s tree line
text:
BAXTER STATE PARK, Maine (WABI) - According to a new study, the landscape atop Maine’s highest peak is changing through a process known as alpine greening.
“This study uses satellite imagery from the past 40-plus years to look at long-term changes in kind of the environment of the alpine zone on the summit of mountains across New England and eastern Canada, above tree line, where the climate is too harsh for trees to grow,” said Jonathan Chipman, the researcher at Dartmouth College who commissioned the study.
“What we found is that over the past four decades, there’s been a gradual greening process above tree line on these mountains,” said Chipman, notably, “Mount Katahdin, other mountains in Maine, in New Hampshire, and in eastern Quebec.”
“In some cases, trees are starting to spread up into areas that were formerly above tree line. Climate warming is contributing to this.”
Chipman went on to say that alpine zones, meaning zones above the tree line where larger vegetation cannot grow, are likely to keep shrinking.
“What we will probably see is the alpine zones, especially the smaller ones, disappearing on these mountains,” and “many of the smaller alpine summits will basically be turning over into forest,” said Chipman.
Nava Tabak, Natural Resource Director at Baxter State Park, said long-term data is key.
“It’s very hard to detect these changes year to year. And that’s why these studies like the ones that you’re asking about are so important because they allow us to look over longer periods of time to see that, to actually be able to detect those changes,” said Tabak.
Tabak also said alpine sedge communities appear to be bearing the brunt of these long term changes.
“Rare plants are, by their definition, somewhat more sensitive to these changes in population, sensitive to becoming extinct,” said Tabak.
Operating as a public trust, Baxter State Park takes a hands-off wilderness approach, focusing on managing people, not plants, to let systems adapt naturally.
On stewardship, Tabak stressed staying on the trails.
“One of the most impactful thing, things people can do when they come to visit an alpine area is to stay on the marked trails.”

title: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson fight over this torn group of Maine women
text:
The increasingly heated toss-up race between Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson could hinge on a crucial bloc of voters both campaigns have appealed to in the final push before Election Day: women 50 and older.
In a late September AARP poll that Jackson led 50%-47%, Collins held a 4-point edge among women 50 and older, who make up about a third of Maine’s likely voters. Jackson’s lead among women overall came from younger women. AARP Maine gave more data on this group exclusively to the Bangor Daily News. Other polls also show older voters closely divided.
These women favored Democrats for Congress and governor but still leaned toward Collins, while men their age backed her by a wide margin. They are also among the most motivated to vote in a race with almost no undecided voters that could decide control of the U.S. Senate.
Several women interviewed by the BDN described the race as more nerve-wracking than any they had experienced. They were starkly divided over the candidates’ abilities and character and whether President Donald Trump’s low approval and relationship with Collins loomed over the race.
“The reason I voted for [Collins] is I think she’s a capable, honest person, smart as a whip,” Clara Payne, a retired lawyer from Brooksville, said in an interview. “Unfortunately, she’s running against Trump, not Troy Jackson. I think it’s a tougher year for her.”
Trump’s approval rating in Maine was 37% in a Fox News poll released Thursday, and only about a third of women and voters 65 and older approved. Collins still drew support from 1 in 5 voters who disapprove of the president, and the race was tied.
Susan Kolm, a 79-year-old Jackson supporter from Waterford, said she believed the former logger from Allagash is a good and genuine person whose competence was evident from his time as Maine Senate president, even if he’s an unpolished speaker.
But she worried about Jackson’s name recognition compared to that of Collins, combined with an onslaught of negative ads from Republican groups. More attack ads have dominated the airwaves on both sides of the race in recent days. Last week, Collins called on an allied group to pull a radio ad referencing Jackson’s family.
Collins also recently touted efforts to advocate for healthcare in Maine, one of the top issues for older voters in AARP’s poll. She campaigned alongside former independent U.S. Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia, appealing to moderates and undecided voters by highlighting bipartisan work.
Her campaign has pointed to Jackson losing his temper in Augusta, where he once threw a plastic water bottle during an argument over prescription drug prices and later apologized. An ad that began running Friday highlighted Jackson telling the senator to “shut up” during their final debate, arguing that’s his message to Maine women.
“Troy’s pattern of angry outbursts toward women who disagree with him — which was on full display at all four debates — clearly isn’t helping him win over independent voters,” Blake Kernen, a Collins spokesperson, said.
Jackson received a boost from U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who in a Portland town hall made a direct push to Maine women frustrated by Trump administration cuts to healthcare and Collins’ vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh.
Jackson in a Portland event Friday shrugged off the ad on the “shut up” moment, noting the progressive Maine Women’s Lobby endorsed him last week. He said he wished “more people would get animated about these things.”
“People know that women’s rights are being taken away,” he told reporters. “I’ve fought for them. I’ve believed in them. I’ve worked with so many great women leaders that I’m so inspired by.”
Collins voted against the final version of Trump’s signature tax and spending law, which cut Medicaid, but Jackson and Democrats have focused on a procedural vote to bring it to the Senate floor. She says she did that to write a rural health fund into the bill, while Jackson has billed it as a deciding vote for the cuts.
“[Jackson] seems like a decent person and seems uncomplicated, and that’s what I want,” Anita Haviland, a retiree from Deer Isle backing the Democrat, said.
Roberta Bowden, a 67-year-old Collins supporter from Etna, described the healthcare system as “crashing around us right now.” Despite Medicaid cuts under Trump, she credited the senator for previous work on health care and veterans issues, and said her bipartisan wins were a sign she could be more productive than Jackson.
Healthcare is among the top reasons that Vickie Wallace, a retired medical technician from Holden, is backing the Democrat. After throat cancer and four heart attacks, cuts to healthcare over the last two years have threatened her life and family, she said.
“[Jackson] thinks all people should have healthcare, and he is not going to be a rubber stamp for what Donald Trump wants,” she said.
Social Security is a major issue in Maine, the nation’s oldest state, with the trust fund projected to run short in 2032. Collins said in their second debate that high earners should pay more into the program, while Jackson joins many other Democrats in wanting to scrap the program’s cap on taxable income and expand benefits.
Chris Partridge, 76, a former Democrat turned independent from Bangor, said she was a “nervous wreck” about the midterms. She defended Trump and Collins from Jackson’s critiques, and credited the senator for the 2025 law she championed to secure Social Security and retirement benefits for more Mainers.
“She’s one of the few honest politicians we have,” she said.

title: 'All My Children' star Alan Dysert dead at 75
text:
'All My Children' star Alan Dysert dead at 75
'All My Children' star Alan Dysert dead at 75
Alan Dysert, an acclaimed actor best known for his role on "All My Children," has died. He was 75.
Dysert, who played Sean Cudahy on the ABC soap opera from 1980 to 1990, died Friday, his wife, Michele Dysert, announced in a social media post.
"While I am struggling to imagine life without him, I am forever grateful to have experienced what so many people spend their lives searching for — the love of a lifetime," she wrote.
A cause of death has not been revealed, but Michele Dysert said he "faced more than his share of health challenges over the years."
Dysert made an early television appearance on the sitcom “Soap” before joining “All My Children.”
He played Cudahy between 1980 and 1990, appearing in 79 episodes.
After his daytime television run, Dysert continued acting and worked as a producer and director. He also taught acting and coached performers in Nashville.
In his 2023 book, “Lights, Camera, Cancer!,” he wrote about living with a rare, aggressive cancer and undergoing multiple surgeries and chemotherapy.
Dysert is survived by his wife and two sons, Cody and Cooper.

title: Peculiar paranormal phenomena have a history in Presque Isle
text:
An early 19th-century hospital. A ghostly fire station protector. Vestiges of a 1990s murder.
You might think you know Presque Isle, but you may not know some of the unexplained phenomena in Aroostook County’s largest city.
When the Presque Isle Historical Society, which maintains two museums and offers tours of local landmarks, invited paranormal investigators north a few years ago, no one knew what they’d find. The results spawned surprises the society revisits every year, especially as Halloween rolls around. Come on, jump into a haunted hearse and follow along.
Wait. Haunted hearse?
For many years, the society has held haunted lantern tours, both by car and on foot, where they visit a few places around the city and share “slightly scary, kind of creepy” tales, secretary-treasurer Kim Smith said.
But they wanted to do more. They found inspiration in such places as Bangor, which offers tours of the Mount Hope Cemetery, and Salem, Massachusetts, which has built a tourism industry around centuries of stories of witches, pirates and more. They invited the South Paris-based Maine Paranormal Investigation Team to visit 20 sites around the city in 2018.
“Presque Isle dates from 1828, and we have a lot of Victorian-era homes,” Smith said. “They’d never been this far north, and they came up two weekends in a row. They had so much fun they came back.”
Their stipulation was that they didn’t want to know anything about the places they were to visit. They wanted to make their own conclusions, which they shared with the society that fall. The results sparked the city’s first Haunted Hearse Tour in 2019, a tradition that’s grown in popularity each year, especially at Halloween.
Yes, it does include an old hearse. The historical society’s president, Craig Green, acquired the 1996 Cadillac from the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home in Damariscotta, which was going to discard it.
The tours stop at 13 sites and allow people to follow along in their cars, with their radios tuned so they can hear Smith narrate.
“In my research, I had found no ghost stories from our past,” Smith said.
But the investigators posited there were, indeed, eerie echoes in the city. Here are just a few.
An actual home
The team came equipped with dowsing rods and a pendulum, which are supposed to react to questions or spirit energy with movement, and high-tech gear such as infrared cameras and a 360-degree motion sensor, Smith said.
They also used a spirit box, which scans radio frequencies and creates white noise, according to Amazon.com. Spirits can supposedly communicate audible messages through the noise.
The first place Smith took investigators to was her own home. They described two spirits, whom Smith recognized as her mother and great-grandmother, she said.
A team member told Smith she had an impression of an object with scalloped gold edges and a red stone, which was in an upstairs bedroom. Smith said the description matched a bracelet that had belonged to an ancestor, but told them it was downstairs.
But when she went to her jewelry box, it wasn’t there, she said.
She found it in that upstairs bedroom, hanging behind a closet door.
Historic fire station
The team went next to Presque Isle’s former fire station on Church Street, which the society now owns and uses for tours and storage.
“We had a volunteer for the society who, every time he would walk into the building and use the staircase, would talk to a ghost. He’d say, ‘Hi, Mr. Ghost,’” Smith said.
As they explored inside, the investigators stopped at the same spot on the staircase. Using the spirit box, they suggested the entity’s name was Xavier. He had been in the Army and was there protecting firemen.
Upstairs, Smith watched as an investigator used an infrared camera. An image of a tall, big man moved quickly across the viewer. She speculated it may have been “Big Jim” Cullen, whose handcuffs hang in the old fire station.
Cullen, famously the only person ever lynched in Aroostook County, was accused of stealing a pair of size 14 boots in Mapleton and murdering two lawmen before being killed by a lynch mob on April 30, 1873.
No one was ever found responsible for the lynching. Cullen’s head was severed and used in phrenology demonstrations. The mystery gave rise to two books by historian and author Dena Winslow, who determined the head had been buried illegally somewhere in the Lewiston-Auburn area.
The old hospital
Before A.R. Gould Hospital, now part of Northern Light Health, opened on Academy Street, Presque Isle started a hospital in a Second Street house and built a new facility next to it in 1920, which is now City Hall.
The adjacent house was converted into a dormitory for nurses, and an underground tunnel connected to the hospital, Smith said.
While touring the building, one investigator received an impression of a young woman being assaulted in a tunnel. Another reported hearing a voice screaming, “My baby, don’t take my baby” when they visited the City Council chambers on the third floor — which was where the maternity ward used to be.
“The assumption they made was that, perhaps, the woman who had been assaulted had a baby and they took it away from her,” Smith said. “That’s an assumption, of course. We have no proof.”
A murder and a mystery
One of the more famous tales involves the A.M. Smith building on the corner of Main and State streets and a mysterious murder.
Smith led the paranormal team around the building’s perimeter. The sunny day should have revealed their reflections in a window, she said.
“But that’s not what came out in the photos. In the photos, you see what appears to be a woman wearing a shroud or hoodie,” Smith said. “At that point, they asked me to tell them what was going on.”
George Jaime of Presque Isle owned a pawn shop in that building. His girlfriend, Starlette Vining, disappeared in 1998. More than a decade later, a firefighter inspecting the building noted a brand-new furnace and an old one discarded in a corner. He opened the old furnace door and saw what he thought were bones, Smith said. That kickstarted the investigation into Vining’s disappearance and suspected death.
The case riveted Presque Isle. Jaime was arrested in 2012. At his 2013 trial, he was accused of murdering Vining, 38, in 1998, then dismembering and burning her body, the Bangor Daily News reported. His son and another man testified Jaime told them he stabbed and dismembered Vining, and they helped Jaime burn the body.
A jury found Jaime guilty in November 2013, and in December he was sentenced to 40 years in prison. Jaime appealed the following year, but Maine’s high court upheld the conviction, the BDN reported.
Jaime died last year at the Maine State Prison.
If you’re in for more eerie stories of Presque Isle’s past, you’ll have a chance on Halloween night, when the historical society will host three haunted hearse tours.
Tours will take place at 6 p.m., 7:30 p.m. and 9 p.m. and cost $10 per person. Reservations are required by emailing pihistoricalsociety@hotmail.com.
People are flocking to events where they can have adventures or encounters, Smith said.
“Experiential events are the museum and history trend today,” she said. “To be able to offer that is really nice for us.”

title: Local elections deserve students’ attention too
text:
EDITORIAL: When people think about voting, they think about the big races: President, senator, congressman. However, they often fail to think about “smaller” races and the impact they have on their communities.
Don’t get it twisted — elections that decide our president, senators and congressmen are very important. They affect laws and regulations that impact our everyday lives, the economy, how we interact with other countries abroad and so much more. However, they are not the only government officials that matter. Smaller, local elections for state government positions matter a tremendous amount. These are the types of positions that can make our lives better or worse no matter what the federal government is doing in Washington.
We know this can sound daunting. On top of all the homework you have to do, the extra shift you pick up, societal anxiety and all the other time constraints a college student might have, we are asking you to become more educated on local races. We can hear it now, “Local election? I barely have time to look into the presidential election!” and “It doesn’t affect my life in any way who the sheriff or state senator is.” We know the burden a full time college schedule can put on someone, but it’s really important that you are educated and vote for people representing you in local office.
For example, this year in District 8, our district, there is a very important state legislature race between incumbent Democratic State Sen. Mike Tipping and Republican challenger Leo Kenny. The outcome of this race could have significant implications for UMaine students.
The University of Maine is going through some hard times. Earlier this year, administrators projected a $19 million budget shortfall for fiscal year 2028, raising concerns about faculty layoffs and potential program cuts. State elections, including the District 8 Senate race between Tipping and Kenney, can influence how these challenges will be addressed. While the University of Maine System Board of Trustees oversees the system’s budget, state legislators play a role in determining how much funding our public universities receive through state appropriations.
When Roe v. Wade was overturned, it put abortion rights back in the hands of the states. Luckily, the Maine State Legislature upheld the rights of women and Maine is one of the lead states when it comes to protecting a woman’s right to an abortion. That’s the kind of impact results of local elections can have on your life.
Beyond issues of rights, state legislators have an impact on the economy, cost of living and many other things. Earlier this week, Maine Campus published a Q&A with both candidates to see where they stand on certain issues concerning UMaine students. That could be a great resource for students starting to research which candidate they would like to see influence the future of Maine’s laws. Many local news outlets also offer plenty of information for you to make an educated vote.
The outcomes of these November elections are going to decide a lot of things, but it’s important to remember it’s not only senators and congressmen who make a difference. Change starts down the street before it makes it to Washington.

title: Man dying of cancer renews his vows with his wife of 22 years as his last wish
text:
BENTONVILLE, Ark. (KFSM) - An Arkansas man with terminal cancer renewed his vows with his wife of 22 years the same week he was admitted to hospice.
Bryan Rose has Stage 4 colon cancer and was admitted to hospice last week. Even through his terminal illness, he wanted to make sure his promises to Terri Rose, his wife of 22 years, were restated.
The Roses renewed their wedding vows Wednesday at Circle of Life hospice care in Bentonville. After the ceremony, there was a reception attended by family and friends. With vendors, entertainment and – of course – cake, it was meant to highlight Bryan and who the Roses are as a couple.
Event planner Kristin Hoops with Blushing Gypsy Events says she realizes the Roses are a special couple.
“Bryan and Terri, what I’ve learned about them is before his illness, they were full of life. Just a very fun couple, they enjoyed all the things and were very outgoing,” Hoops said.
She says she had been figuring out details for the vow renewal for several weeks.
Wish Upon a Wedding is part of the team that made it all possible. The program, which is similar to Make-a-Wish, grants weddings and vow renewals to couples facing terminal illness.
Circle of Life also helps to find a way to have their patients’ last wishes granted.
“We’ve done airplane rides, but we also get requests for milkshakes and apple pie and a favorite meal or just to be able to pet a horse again,” said Nancy Desler, marketing manager for Circle of Life.
After 22 years together, the Roses chose each other again – and one of Bryan’s last wishes was granted: renewing his promise to the woman he loves most.

title: 3 moments from Troy Jackson and Elizabeth Warren’s latest appeal to progressives
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson joined Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts in a Waterville town hall Monday evening, marking the latest visit from a handful of leading national progressives in his bid to oust Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
Coming after recent visits by U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and independent U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Warren’s visit came a day before Jackson was poised to welcome the more moderate Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona in Freeport.
Collins and her allies have invested heavily in ads targeting Jackson over his temper and tone during a contentious battle over the airwaves and media that has ramped up as Election Day approaches. Jackson has sought to hammer home the message that Collins is too strongly aligned with President Donald Trump, whose approval rating has sunk to 37% in Maine according to the latest Fox News poll.
Here are a few key takeaways from the event, which featured several students from Bates College and Colby College.
Warren pins higher prices on Trump and GOP
Warren said the midterm election would determine who controls our government: billionaires or Americans “slammed harder than ever and working harder than ever.” She reminded guests that two years ago on the campaign trail, Trump pledged to lower prices if sent back to the White House.
The senator then joked that it was now “day 668,000” of Trump’s second administration, and the cost of gasoline, heating oil, groceries, health care, housing and utilities are “up, up, up, up, up.”
Warren and Jackson called on Congress to blunt Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran. Warren didn’t name Collins directly in her opening, but said, “Every Republican in the Senate has had their spine surgically removed.”
Collins’ team recently accused Jackson of campaigning “with far-left progressive office holders who either don’t know or don’t care about the difficulties that he has had working with women.”
Jackson says Trump, Collins can’t be trusted on tariffs
Collins is against Trump’s tariffs, particularly against Canada, and successfully pushed for exemptions on a handful of goods, including a round from the president last week that The Wall Street Journal reported was aimed at helping her win. She has also voted in favor of war powers resolutions after previously siding with Republicans on the war, citing its impact on prices.
But Jackson told the Waterville crowd that even if Trump is trying to expand exemptions on tariffs to give Collins a last-minute boost in the race, there’s no guarantee those exemptions will hold after the election.
“What do you think is gonna happen on Nov. 4, after there’s no reason to help her out anymore?” he said. “He’s shown us time and time again, he doesn’t care about us.”
Who decides on AI?
Warren and Jackson emphasized that young people have become increasingly concerned about the impacts of AI on the workforce, safety and privacy. Warren said AI firms have incentivized a lack of safeguards and oversight from Congress.
“If that is the path of decision-making, then we are just at the mercy of … Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk,” she said.
Warren added that many across the country from all stripes are pushing back against advances of AI due to environmental, cost, privacy and safety implications. If Democrats become the majority, a potential major tech bill will focus on jobs, safety, profits, and international relationships including China and Europe, she said.
Collins has taken a cautious approach to AI and data centers, expressing support for projects at former mill sites with an energy source built in. Jackson, who cited Musk’s boost to Collins’ reelection bid, pledged to fight for stronger regulations.
“We’re not that far from ‘Terminator,’” Jackson said. “And I don’t want to be, ‘hasta la vista, baby.’”

Mother dies trying to save her 2 sons after they were swept away while snorkeling
text:
(Gray News) - A British woman visiting the Bahamas with her family died attempting to rescue her two sons after they were swept out to sea.
According to the Royal Bahamas Police Force, the 36-year-old was snorkeling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island. Police reported a strong current swept the children away and the woman, in an effort to rescue them, “also was swept away.”
She was later rescued and taken to a ferry dock where CPR was administered before she was transported to a local medical clinic. Police reported a local doctor pronounced her dead “despite efforts to save her life.”
The BBC identified the woman as Leanne Gregory from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire. According to People, her husband, Nathan Gregory, set up a GoFundMe to raise funds for their two sons.
“This loss is unimaginable for our family, she was our foundation, our support, she made us who we are,” Nathan Gregory said, adding that the couple were childhood sweethearts and had been together for 22 years.
In the GoFundMe, Nathan Gregory described the moments after their sons were swept away.
He said that Leanne Gregory held their son until he was rescued but “didn’t have the energy to save herself.” He recounted that a “freak wave” swept her away from the boat that was helping them.
“I just have to be thankful for the hero she was in life and in death, and totally grateful for the fact my boys got out safely,” Nathan Gregory said. “Mainly thankful to my brave, amazing wife for keeping my boy above the water even as you were sinking ... you will be forever loved by everyone you knew, and I know you will continue to watch over us.”
The Royal Bahamas Police Force said an autopsy will be conducted.

title: Windham church hosts Palestinian ‘peacebuilder’
text:
The Chaplaincy Institute of Maine hosted Mohamad Jamous, a Palestinian public speaker and self-described “peacebuilder,” for an “Evening of Conversation and Hope” at Windham’s Unity Center for Spiritual Growth on Oct. 23.
Jamous, a resident of Ramallah in the West Bank, serves as director of the Children of Abraham Project, a nonprofit organization that promotes interfaith dialogue and humanitarian work in Israel and Palestine. Jamous said the goal of the organization is to stop the circle of hatred between Israelis and Palestinians.
Jamous grew up in Jericho as one of eight siblings. He recalled how, as a young man, he wanted to resist the occupation of his homeland, and would frequently throw rocks at Israeli soldiers. One day, Jamous was shot by an Israeli soldier and hospitalized. Although doctors did not expect him to make it, Jamous survived, and began asking questions about what the cycle of violence was meant to achieve for the Palestinian people.
Jamous began engaging with peace organizations in Palestine, and recalled going on an interfaith trip with 150 Jews, Christians and Muslims. Watching people of three religions praying in the same space, Jamous realized there was another way for people to follow.
Jamous’ organization has held similar gatherings. In 2025, the group organized an interfaith iftar, the breaking of the fast during Ramadan, which drew more than 1,000 attendees in spite of the ongoing war. Last December, they held an event called 100 Stories, One Voice for Peace, in which 100 people, including an Israeli man who lost his parents on Oct. 7, 2023, and a man from the West Bank who lost his brother to settler violence, gathered to commit to stopping the cycle of violence.
The Children of Abraham Project plans to hold another iftar in 2027 and hopes to attract 2,000 attendees.
Last week’s event in Windham was part of Jamous’ larger tour of the United States. Jamous said he plans to speak at college campuses, churches, synagogues, and other organizations, and said the mission of the tour is to spread awareness of his organization’s work in the Middle East.
In addition to the Levant, the Children of Abraham Project, which was established in 2019, also runs programs in conflict zones such as Uganda, Ethiopia, and Myanmar.
Jamous spoke at length on the humanitarian situation in the West Bank, noting how military checkpoints mean that what should be a 30-minute drive to visit his family in another city can stretch to up to six hours. He also spoke about the epidemic of violence committed by Israeli settlers against Palestinians, saying that, when settlers surround someone, they are left with no choice but to either let themselves be attacked or try to escape and be branded a “terrorist.”
“We just want to live like any other people, and other nations in the world,” said Jamous of the Palestinian people.
At the same time, Jamous also emphasized that the settlers are not representative of all Jews or Israelis, and that the actions of extremist groups like Hamas are not representative of all Palestinians. He said that everyone was traumatized by the violence that has engulfed the region since Oct. 7, 2023, and that he does not expect change to come through government action, but from peace-minded people.
Jamous also spoke about the importance of the Oct. 27 election in Israel, widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s leadership. He said the security situation in the West Bank is entirely dependent on the Israeli government, and expressed hope that, should Netanyahu’s government lose power, people in the West Bank would receive some respite from settler violence.
Toward the end of the event, as Jamous was taking questions from the audience, Pat Bessie, minister at the Unity Center, asked if it was possible for her congregation to build a “pen pal” relationship with people in the region. Jamous said that, while humanitarian organizations in Palestine unfortunately could not reach all families, he would try to connect the congregation to families and people in the region.

title: Maine Colleges Shine in New Ranking of America's 500 Best Schools
text:
Maine Colleges Shine in New Ranking of America’s 500 Best Schools
Whether it’s on the field, on the court, or in the classroom, college is all about competition. And nothing beats having bragging rights over a rival school.
That’s what makes this time of year so much fun. It’s college ranking season, when publications release their annual lists, giving schools plenty of reasons to celebrate...or complain.
The latest list to drop comes from the financial experts over at WalletHub. The popular publication releases an annual ranking of colleges and universities across the country, featuring the top 500 schools.
WalletHub evaluates numerous metrics, including cost, student selectivity, campus experience and safety, education and career outcomes, and faculty resources. Believe me when I say this is a very detailed ranking.
What Maine Colleges Have the Best National Rankings
Maine performed relatively well in this year’s rankings, with three schools earning top spots, particularly in the liberal arts college category. Here’s a closer look:
28. Colby College – Waterville
This Central Maine “Little Ivy” earned the highest ranking among Maine schools. It received high marks for its academic opportunities, campus facilities, and strong post-graduation salary outcomes. Its best ranking was 11th in campus experience.
29. Bowdoin College – Brunswick
The Brunswick college finished right behind its rival in the standings. Bowdoin is recognized for its high graduation rate, strong job placement, and outstanding faculty recommendations. Its highest ranking was 12th in education outcomes.
89. Bates College – Lewiston
Bates rounds out Maine’s trio of elite liberal arts colleges. It's particularly noted for student development, innovative learning environments, and its unique “Short Term” spring semester, which focuses on immersive, experiential learning. Its top ranking came in campus experience, finishing 39th.

title: Cat safe after being tied in plastic bag and thrown in Maine dumpster
text:
'Absolutely no excuse': Kitten safe after being tied in plastic bag and thrown in Bingham dumpster
A cat is safe after town officials say it was tied inside a plastic bag and thrown into a dumpster at the Bingham Transfer Station.
Town officials shared information about the incident on Sunday morning.
The town says staff at the transfer station heard something and were able to rescue the cat before it was physically injured. As of Sunday morning, the cat was being cared for by the town Animal Control Officer and officials said the animal seemed to be doing well.
"There is absolutely no excuse for animal cruelty. We understand that sometimes people have hard choices and may be struggling financially. If you find yourself unable or unwilling to care for an animal, there are safe, legal, and humane resources available right here in our community," the town wrote. "To the individual or individuals who thought it was acceptable to tie a cat inside a plastic bag and throw it into a dumpster at the Bingham Transfer Station: Human decency and basic compassion should have guided you to a completely different choice."
The town said people who need help with a pet can reach out to a local animal shelter, the Animal Control Officer, local town office or police.
"Please do the right thing next time. Our community is better than this, and we will continue to look out for those who cannot speak for themselves," Bingham town officials wrote.

title: UMSG calls for improved lighting at Lengyel Field, approves $14,600 in funding
text:
The University of Maine General Student Senate (UMSG) approved more than $14,600 in funding for three student organizations during its Oct. 6 meeting, including money for a hair care event, a Model United Nations conference and a national engineering conference.
The Senate also granted preliminary recognition to the Arctic Protection Club, elected two senators to committee positions and approved resolutions concerning Senate procedures and additional lighting at Lengyel Field.
The 1,621st meeting began at 6 p.m. in the Bangor Room of the Memorial Union, with 20 senators in attendance.
Club business
The Black Student Union received $3,393.80 to expand its Hair Care Fair into a semesterly event. President Adora Olise and Vice President Emilia Faustino said the organization provides a supportive space for Black students and has between 38 and 55 members. The event brings in professional braiders to provide hair care services to students. Organizers said they plan to hire two braiders and have already raised approximately $500 through a bake sale.
According to the club representatives, freelance braiders in the Orono area typically charge between $250 and $300 per head, but the organization has negotiated contracts that reduce the cost to $115 per head. During the previous semester’s event, organizers provided services to 40 people in one day and also hired two barbers who served 20 people.
The International Affairs Association received $6,333 to send 11 or 12 students to a fall Model United Nations conference. The organization gives students opportunities to develop debate and communication skills through simulations of international diplomacy.
The American Institute of Chemical Engineers Student Chapter also received $4,912 to attend its fall national student conference. Club President Logan Beaupre and Treasurer Zachary Arnold said the conference offers networking, career development and competitions. The organization has 30 members and plans to bring 11 students, three or four of whom have not attended the conference previously.
The Senate approved all three funding requests following committee recommendations.
The Senate also approved three smaller allocations through its consent agenda: $400 for the Ballet Club, $537.41 for Sophomore Owls and $400 for the UMSG Services Committee.
Club maintenance
During club maintenance, senators granted preliminary recognition to the Arctic Protection Club. Vice President Samuel Landry said the organization advocates for Arctic protection and environmental awareness. He said the club’s work last year contributed to a vote for an Arctic referendum.
The organization currently has eight members but expects to grow to between 16 and 20 members based on a recent interest poll. Club representatives said they may request funding for an event featuring a guest speaker and artist, similar to one held the previous year.
The Senate also welcomed Hanniel Nyanutse, the new assistant vice president of student entertainment, who briefly introduced himself and discussed his background and enthusiasm for working with student government.
New business
During new business, senators approved a resolution moving guest speakers to a position on the meeting agenda immediately after new senators, officer appointments and resignations. The change is intended to establish a consistent order for Senate meetings.
Another resolution designated the Machias Student Representative position as an ex-officio position. During discussion, senators clarified that the role is not an executive position but counts as one point toward a senator’s requirements.
The Senate also approved a resolution requesting additional high-rise stadium lighting at Lengyel Field. Senators Juliannah Soper and St. Lawrence presented the resolution, explaining that the Services Committee can submit funding requests directly to the university.
Committee updates
In committee updates, Vice President of Student Entertainment Elle Granat announced plans for a Halloween carnival in collaboration with the Center for Student Involvement. Student government allocated $5,000 toward the event, with the center providing tables and 15 volunteers.
Granat also announced that the Collins Center for the Arts will screen “The Rocky Horror Picture Show” on Oct. 24 at 8 p.m. Student government plans to purchase 200 tickets for students, with tickets and prop bags costing $5 each through the arrangement.
The Senate’s Voter Involvement and Education Committee reported that its first voter registration drive resulted in five registrations in Orono and one in Bangor. The committee planned another registration event for Oct. 7 in the Memorial Union.
The Services Committee also continued preparations for its campus Night Walk, scheduled for Oct. 15 at 5:30 p.m. The walk allows students to identify general campus concerns, including potholes and other infrastructure issues.
The meeting adjourned at 7:10 p.m.

title: Trump administration asks Washington to set aside ballots from 400 voters it says may be noncitizens
text:
SEATTLE (AP) — The Trump administration on Monday asked Washington state to set aside any ballots received from more than 400 people it suspects registered to vote without U.S. citizenship.
In a letter to the Washington Secretary of State’s Office, the Justice Department said it had identified 1,500 votes cast by the over 400 people in prior elections. It asked the state to set aside any ballots the people might cast in next month’s midterm until state officials can confirm they are legally eligible to vote. The state has more than 5 million registered voters.
“We are asking the state to set aside those ballots until we can confirm they are legal voters,” Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd said in a news conference.
Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs was reviewing the administration’s demand. His office noted that it had received about 60 subpoenas from the Justice Department since last month seeking information about voters.
“We take our responsibility to protect voter information seriously and will only respond to requests that follow due process,” Hobbs said in an emailed statement. “We see what’s happening in California and don’t want Washingtonians to be harassed.”
The effort is the latest by the administration to identify noncitizen voters, even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. President Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine public confidence in elections. The request in Washington is similar to Justice Department attempt to require California to sequester mail ballots from up to 20,000 people the federal government suspects may not be citizens.
California has challenged that, and during rare Sunday arguments a panel of federal appellate judges questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Justice Department’s demand. The Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections.
Los Angeles County Assistant Registrar-Recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that her staff went through a sample of 200 records from the Trump administration’s list. They found the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, people with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States.
The Justice Department told Washington it anticipates sending the state an additional list of people it suspects are not citizens prior to Election Day. It also noted that some of the people it suspects registered without citizenship may have since become naturalized.
Investigations into prior allegations of noncitizen voters have revealed far fewer instances than the Trump administration has claimed. In Nevada, Trump’s administration alleged there were 1,500 potential noncitizen voters on the rolls but subsequent investigation found zero.
In Maricopa County, which includes Phoenix, the county Recorder, who is a Trump supporter, announced that there were 207 possible noncitizens on the county’s rolls. The Republican County Attorney determined there were actually eight.

title: Trump administration attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey again
text:
Trump administration attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey again
The Trump administration is attempting to prosecute James Comey for what it calls a decade-old leak of classified information, an effort the former FBI director's lawyers immediately dismissed as invalid and outside the legal time limit for when the Justice Department can file a criminal indictment.
The allegations from the Justice Department were revealed Monday in newly unsealed court documents that shed light on a closed-door fight that represents a clear escalation in the administration's targeting of Comey, a longtime critic and foe of President Donald Trump who has faced two other criminal cases since the Republican returned to the White House last year. The effort to prosecute Comey is also part of a series of politically charged investigative actions the department has undertaken in the run-up to next week's midterm elections.
"Well, they're back — again," Comey said in a video statement released after the documents dropped. "It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice – one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing's changed with me; I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in an independent federal judiciary."
The Justice Department, for its part, said it had filed what's known as a "criminal information" to extend the 10-year statute of limitations for bringing a case.
"Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further," a department spokesperson said.
A criminal information is typically filed with a defendant's consent accompanying a plea deal, but Comey's lawyers made clear that they intend to fight the charges as invalid and barred by the statute of limitations.
"For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence," his attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement.
The allegation was previously investigated
The latest allegation concerns an October 2016 New York Times story related to a secret court order that required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. The story cited two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity about the order from a judge on the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court that Yahoo was barred from publicly disclosing.
Federal authorities, including then-Special Counsel John Durham, began investigating the FBI's Oct. 5, 2016, disclosure to The New York Times in early 2017. Durham wrote a classified memo in December 2018 recommending no criminal charges against anyone in connection with the disclosure, Comey's attorneys said in a recent court filing.
In January 2019, the U.S. Attorney's office for the District of Columbia opened a second investigation of the same matter under the code name "Tropical Vortex." But that investigation was closed without any charges filed in February 2020.
"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone. Now, ten years after the article was published, the Government filed an "Information" against Mr. Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit," Fitzgerald said.
Trump and Comey have a long and uneasy history
The first case against Comey was dismissed after the judge found that the prosecutor who brought the indictment was illegally appointed. Comey was charged in a separate case in April over a social media post depicting seashells on the beach that officials said constituted a threat against the president.
Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush's Republican administration.
But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president -- an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum.
Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump's campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, found that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration.

title: RSU reorg question hits the ballot Nov. 3: What voters need to know
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MOUNT DESERT ISLAND — It’s been a long and winding road for the proposed school reorganization plan on MDI, but the question of whether to reorganize the Mount Desert Island Regional School System into an RSU will ultimately be in voters’ hands on Nov. 3.
Island towns, including Trenton, will have a referendum on the ballot this year about whether the school system should be reorganized into a Regional School Unit or RSU.
The question will read, “Do you favor approving the school administrative reorganization plan prepared by the MDIRSS-AOS #91 Reorganization Planning Committee to reorganize Trenton, Bar Harbor, Southwest Harbor, Tremont, Mount Desert, Swans Island, Cranberry Isles, and Frenchboro into a Regional School Unit with an effective date of 7/1/2028?”
For the plan to pass, Trenton, Bar Harbor, Mount Desert, Southwest Harbor and Tremont must all vote in favor of the reorganization. If any of the mainland towns reject the plan, it does not move forward. If all mainland towns vote to approve it and any of the outer islands vote to reject it, the plan still moves forward.
Some towns have started to weigh in on the issue. Both the Bar Harbor Warrant Committee and Town Council voted to recommend the town reject the plan. However, the Bar Harbor school committee voted 3-2 to recommend the adoption of the RSU reorganization plan. The Mount Desert Warrant Committee and Tremont Select Board each voted unanimously to recommend rejection for their respective towns as well.
The Reorganization Planning Committee has hosted numerous forums around the island for community members to learn about the plan and share their thoughts.
What would change under an RSU reorganization?
The proposed reorganization includes a restructuring of the school boards. Currently, each elementary school has its own school board and a separate, overarching AOS board. In the proposed RSU, there would be one 15-person board of directors that would govern the entire RSU. Towns would have a predetermined number of elected seats on the board based on population.
To help maintain local control, each town would also have a local school advisory council that would include the principal and a local RSU board member.
In the reorganized structure, the RSU would become the single employer for the entire district, meaning all staff across schools would be employed by one entity, the RSU.
The hope is that by restructuring so the RSU is the single employer for the district, staff will be able to move between schools to fill gaps that might be missing elsewhere, according to the RPC.
In the proposed plan, the RSU would assume ownership of all school buildings within the district. Part of that means that the RSU would also absorb capital debt from construction and renovations and operational debt such as equipment leases.
Cost sharing under the RSU proposal would follow MDI High School’s current structure, which takes 67% of a town’s valuation and 33% of its enrollment to determine how much taxpayers in each town will contribute.
In terms of tax increases, according to data on the reorganization website, taxpayers in Bar Harbor, Mount Desert, and Cranberry Isles would see an increase in taxes. In Southwest Harbor, Tremont, Trenton, Frenchboro and Swan's Island, taxpayers would pay less under the reorganized RSU.
Originally, the reorganization plan included a proposal to create one island-wide middle school, however, that is not a part of the plan that will be on the ballot on Nov. 3. The reorganization plan was revised after a series of community forums in which residents raised concerns over creating one island-wide middle school.
In community discussions about the reorganization, Superintendent Mike Zboray has underscored that one of the goals of the proposed plan is to spread district resources more evenly across the island.
“Instead of asking ‘what can my town provide with the students and resources inside its boundaries?’ we can ask, ‘what can we provide when we put our resources together,” said Zboray at a panel discussion of the reorganization plan in Bar Harbor in September. “Because eventually, regardless of which community they grew up in, our kids are going to put on the same jersey.”
He also emphasized that students would not experience much change, if any, if the reorganization plan were to pass. Other long-term goals identified by the RPC are to provide equitable educational access, deliver financial fairness, empower educators and develop a sustainable system.
If the referendum passes, the current AOS board will appoint a temporary RSU board to manage the transition for the RSU to be organized by July 1, 2028.

title: Several trailers at Brunswick mobile home park condemned
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Several trailers at Brunswick mobile home park condemned; residents place blame on landlord
Some residents of a mobile home park in Brunswick have been displaced after several trailers were condemned, and the residents are blaming it all on the landlord.
Eric Harris and Kristie Miquelon call their mobile home at Zoe Court a danger zone. Code enforcement officials deemed that four trailers at the park are not safe to live in, saying the homes are considered electrical and structural hazards.
Harris said he fell through rotted floorboards in his living room.
"When I stepped here, my foot went through," he said. "My ankle rolled towards the vent and I fell."
The couple moved into the rental trailer in May 2025 and pay $1,500 a month in rent; utilities are not included.
Miquelon said she suffers from asthma and that mold test results were off the charts. She also said an electrical outlet caught fire and burned the cord to her asthma nebulizer.
The couple pointed to sagging ceilings and leaky windows to a Maine's Total Coverage crew on Monday.
Harris and Miquelon said they got fed up when the property management company said they were coming to fix things and never showed up, so they went to town officials. Code enforcement officials condemned the couple's trailer and three others in the mobile home park at the end of September.
The town has been paying for the families to live in a hotel, while the deputy fire chief said the company that owns the park and the trailers has been responsive and submitted a corrective action plan on Friday, Oct. 23. Harris and Miquelon said they will believe it when they see it.
"Even the things that they're fixing, they are not actually like fixing them. It's all just band-aid work," Miquelon said.
The couple has a 6-year-old daughter who loves her school. Harris is an assistant football coach for Brunswick High School. The couple wants to stay in Brunswick, but they do not want to give another dime to the trailer park owners, so they are looking for another place to live.
"You can't treat people this way. This is where we make our home," Harris said. "This is home base and our sanctuary, and to lose that because somebody didn't do their job ... it's very stressful. It's a lot on us."
The Town of Brunswick continues to help the displaced Zoe Court residents. Maine's Total Coverage has contacted Hekla Ventures, the Massachusetts company that owns the trailers, with a request for comment, but the company had not responded as of Monday evening.

title: Man completes 12,000-mile walk across America’s four corners in Lubec for mental health awareness
text:
LUBEC, Maine (WABI) — A Florida man who traveled across the United States to raise money and awareness for mental health completed his historic journey in Washington County over the weekend.
Kyndal Ray Edwards, a mental health coach from Jacksonville, Florida, crossed the finish line at West Quoddy Head Lighthouse in Lubec on Sunday afternoon after visiting all four corners of the contiguous United States.
For Edwards, walking across America was a dream years in the making following his own battles with depression and addiction.
“I got arrested August 9, 2017, and then April 12, 2019, while I was in prison, I made a conscious decision that I didn’t want to be the person that I was anymore,” Edwards said.
Inspired by a story of a local who traveled coast to coast, Edwards began his walk across America on Jan. 1, 2022. Along the way, he raised funds for the nonprofit Never Alone Recovery while carrying “A Walking Testimony”—a dedication honoring 180 people who lost their lives to drug overdose or suicide.
Edwards documented every step of his trek on social media, building a following of hundreds of thousands of followers. On Sunday, supporters, friends, and family traveled from across the country to greet him at the easternmost point of the Lower 48.
“I found Kyndal’s story on Facebook through my algorithm. Ever since discovering him, he’s been a huge inspiration to me. I’m somebody who’s colossally passionate about mental health and advocacy, and I just incredibly appreciate the work that he’s doing,” said Heather Rotman of Massachusetts.
“I think his whole premise is very admirable. We’ve been following him and we wanted to be here to congratulate him,” said Laurie Schoen of Connecticut.
“I get people reaching out to me all the time who have either lost children or have adult children who are struggling with addiction themselves. And so just the fact that he’s made an impact in people’s lives—for us as parents, that’s incredible,” said Kyndal’s mom.
In total, Edwards spent nearly five years on the road, walking for 1,022 of those days and logging 12,144 miles.
“Words could never express just how grateful and thankful I am for the support,” Edwards said. “For people to come out here and make human connection, it’s important because there’s not enough unity in community. There are not enough people in their communities actually getting together... We need more hugs, handshakes, and high-fives in the world.”
Looking back on more than 12,000 miles on foot, Edwards said one memory stands out above all the rest.
“Any time that somebody has pulled over on the side of the road saying that they were on their way home to take their life, and the ‘You Matter’ sign was the sign that they needed to still be here,” Edwards said. “That’s definitely going to be the number one.”
To learn more about Edwards’ mission, visit kyndalray.com or follow the Kyndal Ray Edwards Facebook page.

title: Man dying of cancer renews his vows with his wife of 22 years as his last wish
text:
BENTONVILLE, Ark. (KFSM) - An Arkansas man with terminal cancer renewed his vows with his wife of 22 years the same week he was admitted to hospice.
Bryan Rose has Stage 4 colon cancer and was admitted to hospice last week. Even through his terminal illness, he wanted to make sure his promises to Terri Rose, his wife of 22 years, were restated.
The Roses renewed their wedding vows Wednesday at Circle of Life hospice care in Bentonville. After the ceremony, there was a reception attended by family and friends. With vendors, entertainment and – of course – cake, it was meant to highlight Bryan and who the Roses are as a couple.
Event planner Kristin Hoops with Blushing Gypsy Events says she realizes the Roses are a special couple.
“Bryan and Terri, what I’ve learned about them is before his illness, they were full of life. Just a very fun couple, they enjoyed all the things and were very outgoing,” Hoops said.
She says she had been figuring out details for the vow renewal for several weeks.
Wish Upon a Wedding is part of the team that made it all possible. The program, which is similar to Make-a-Wish, grants weddings and vow renewals to couples facing terminal illness.
Circle of Life also helps to find a way to have their patients’ last wishes granted.
“We’ve done airplane rides, but we also get requests for milkshakes and apple pie and a favorite meal or just to be able to pet a horse again,” said Nancy Desler, marketing manager for Circle of Life.
After 22 years together, the Roses chose each other again – and one of Bryan’s last wishes was granted: renewing his promise to the woman he loves most.

title: Ike Hubbard, owner of Hubbard Rake Company, dies at 84
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Ike Hubbard, the owner of Hubbard Rake Company has died.
WABI met Ike back in July just after his workshop in Jonesport, where he had been making aluminum blueberry rakes for nearly 40 years, burned down.
He was known as someone who could make anything from virtually nothing and in the early 90s was asked by local growers in his hometown of Jonesport to design a a blueberry rake that wouldn’t break.
In Hubbard’s words, he didn’t say no.
In the decades to follow, Hubbard Rake Company became the choice supplier to berry harvesters.
Born in 1942, Hubbard never gave up on his hopes of revamping Hubbard Rake Company.
His funeral is scheduled for November 7th at Bayview Cemetery in Jonesport.

title: Cause of death revealed for Eric Bauza, the modern voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and more
text:
(Gray News) — Eric Bauza, the Emmy Award-winning voice actor who was the modern voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and many more Looney Tunes characters, died suddenly at the age of 46, his family said.
Bauza’s family announced the voice actor’s sudden death in a statement on Instagram.
The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner said Bauza died from hypertensive cardiovascular disease. Other contributing factors included sleep apnea and type 2 obesity, according to the medical examiner.
His manner of death was ruled natural.
Bauza lent his voice to such iconic Looney Tunes characters as Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, as well as Tweety, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Porky Pig and more in “Coyote vs. Acme.” He also voiced characters in “Space Jam: A New Legacy” and “Looney Tunes Cartoons.”
He also voiced characters in DreamWorks Animation’s “Forgotten Island.”
“Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world,” said Channing Dungey, chairman of Warner Bros. Television Group and U.S. Networks, in a statement. “He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc. Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life.”
Bauza won three Children’s & Family Emmy Awards for “Teen Titans Go!,” “Bugs Bunny Builders” and “Looney Tunes Cartoons,” according to Variety.
He was born on Dec. 7, 1979, in Toronto.
