title: 6 citizens sue Trump, saying media ban deprives them of news as audience stakeholders
text:
(AP) - In the increasingly bitter legal standoff between President Donald Trump and media outlets whose reporting he dislikes, a new and crucial third party has emerged: citizens who watch and read the news and need it to do their jobs.
A lawsuit filed Monday on behalf of six such citizens — essentially representing the wider public audience — argues that it’s not only the rights of news organizations that are violated when Trump bans them from White House premises. Even more fundamentally, the lawsuit argues, such bans violate the public’s right to independent reporting about its president and government.
“The ultimate injury here … is to the democratic public,” says the suit, filed in federal district court in New York against Trump and three key aides, including the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles.
“The First Amendment protects the public’s right to know what its government is doing,” said Katie Fallow, deputy litigation director at the Knight First Amendment Institute, which filed the lawsuit on behalf of the plaintiffs, along with the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic at Yale Law School.
“The White House cannot decide what information Americans receive by punishing critical reporting,” Fallow said in a statement. ”When the White House expels reporters because of their coverage and threatens others with expulsion, it isn’t just the press that suffers — the public loses access to independent reporting and gets something closer to government propaganda.”
The Trump administration, asked for comment on the lawsuit, responded in a statement that it attributed to an unidentified White House official: “No person may demand access to the Oval Office.” It said media that peddle “misinformation and defamation are completely capable of reporting their manufactured stories from directly outside.”
The plaintiffs all rely on White House news for their work
The six plaintiffs are all people who say they rely on independent and diverse White House reporting for their teaching, journalism or advocacy. They include a noted human rights advocate, a political journalist, a Yale history professor, a high school civics teacher, a legal journalist, and a student journalist at the University of Pennsylvania.
The complaint filed Monday recounts how various news organizations that have been targeted by Trump are already battling the administration in the courts. These cases include the current lawsuit by CNN, MS NOW and Politico, whose journalists were banished from the White House in September.
A federal judge recently extended an order preventing the White House from enforcing the ban while the case makes its way through the legal system. Still affected, though, is CNN’s pool coverage of Trump. The White House has been denying the network its usual slots in the video pool covering the president’s activities and travel, and CNN has threatened further action.
Also continuing is the legal case involving The Associated Press, whose reporters were barred last year from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some events in retaliation for the outlet’s decision not to follow Trump’s lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters, to the Gulf of America.
The New York Times is also involved in litigation, over a Pentagon policy requiring escorts for journalists on its grounds. And ABC is fighting back against the Trump administration in a dispute over renewal of its broadcast licenses.
This lawsuit seeks more wide-ranging relief
The new lawsuit filed Monday, though, is different from previous legal action against the president — first, in that the plaintiffs are ordinary citizens, shifting the focus from news gatherers to news consumers, and thus implying a much larger pool of stakeholders.
The lawsuit reframes the current debate over White House access in at least one key way. The public right to receive information is part of established law, said Jameel Jaffer, executive director of the Knight Institute. However, nobody has yet asserted this right in relation to the White House press corps and the issues currently at stake.
“We wanted to put the injury to the public at the center of the conversation,” Jaffer said.
“It’s one thing for CNN to say, ‘We are here because the public needs us,’” he said. “It’s another for a member of the public to say that interference with the White House press corps undermines our right to information about the government.”
In addition, the litigation seeks more wide-ranging relief.
The suit, which names Trump as defendant along with Wiles, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung and Secret Service Director Sean M. Curran, calls not merely for reinstatement of access that has already been impacted, but for a broad injunction that would protect from retaliation every news outlet that covers the White House —- now, and in the future.
“Defendants’ policy of restricting the access of disfavored news organizations deprives the public of the reporting of those organizations,” the complaint says. It also “inevitably deprives them of the independent reporting of other news organizations as well, since every journalist who reports from the White House must now account for the possibility that a critical or ill-advised word about the president may result in their access being summarily restricted or revoked.”
“Plaintiffs ... seek a declaration that the policy is unconstitutional because it imposes restrictions on a limited public forum that are viewpoint-based and unreasonable,” the complaint adds. ”They also seek an injunction barring defendants from enforcing the policy.”
Plaintiffs include a human rights advocate, a high school teacher and a student journalist
Plaintiff Ethan Young, a student at the University of Pennsylvania and editor-in-chief of The Daily Pennsylvanian, said in an interview that White House reporting has become increasingly important at his college newspaper during Trump’s second term.
“Over the last two years we’ve seen college campuses be a key avenue where President Trump’s policies have really affected people across the country, and Penn’s campus is no stranger to that,” he said.
“So I use White House reporting almost daily to look at what’s happening in both national higher education trends, but also just general federal policy changes, to see what might impact Penn,” Young said. “You never know what policy could have an impact on the Penn student body.”
Especially important to Young and his colleagues at the paper is a diversity of news outlets to choose from.
“We are not in the room. We are not in Washington,” Young said. “The benefit of having access to a variety of publications ... means I am constantly seeing different questions being asked of White House officials.”
And more often than not, he said, that means he’ll get the answer to a question he has, too.
The other plaintiffs are:
— Kenneth Roth, former longtime executive director of Human Rights Watch and a lecturer at Yale’s law school and school of global affairs.
— Daniel Froomkin, media and political journalist and editor of Press Watch, a nonprofit that encourages political journalists to “fulfill their essential mission of creating an informed electorate and holding the powerful accountable.”
— Beverly Gage, Pulitzer Prize-winning historian and professor at Yale University.
— Peter Schmidt-Nowara, a social studies and civics teacher at Brooklyn Technical High School in New York.
— Benjamin Wittes, editor-in-chief of Lawfare and a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

title: Judge rules Maurene Comey, daughter of ex-FBI director, was unlawfully fired by Trump administration
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The Trump administration illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of ex-FBI Director and Trump critic James Comey, as a Justice Department prosecutor, a judge ruled Monday in a sharp rebuke of the administration’s authority to terminate career federal employees it dislikes.
The ruling is tailored to Maurene Comey but its import stretches beyond her case, repudiating the claim of President Donald Trump’s administration that the Constitution permits such firings for any reason. Administration officials have cited that belief repeatedly in a sweeping purge of the federal workforce.
Comey, an assistant U.S. attorney for a decade, was fired in July 2025 despite consistently receiving “the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike,” Judge Jesse M. Furman found.
The judge said her firing violated laws passed by Congress that were intended to abolish the spoils system, under which newly elected presidents regularly purged government workers and replaced them with loyalists.
Furman’s decision didn’t address the validity of Comey’s claim that she was fired because she is the daughter of James Comey, whom Trump has long viewed as an enemy.
Trump fired James Comey as FBI director in May 2017 as the bureau was investigating ties between Russia and the Republican’s successful 2016 campaign for the White House. Trump in the years since has repeatedly called for Comey to be jailed, and his Justice Department has worked with mixed success to make that happen.
Hours after Furman’s ruling Monday, unsealed court filings showed that the Justice Department had quietly brought another criminal case against James Comey, accusing him of leaking classified information.
Furman, who was nominated to the bench in 2011 by then-Democratic President Barack Obama, granted Maurene Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay from the date of her firing through Dec. 20, 2025, when she began a new, private-sector job.
In a statement, the Justice Department said it disagreed with this decision and would appeal.
Comey’s lawyers, Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan, lauded the ruling.
“This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law,” they said in a statement. “This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law.”
Comey was fired two weeks after leading the prosecution of music mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs, which ended in a conviction on prostitution-related charges but an acquittal on others. She also worked on the sex trafficking prosecutions of Jeffrey Epstein, the financier who killed himself in jail a month after his arrest in 2019, and Epstein’s former girlfriend and longtime confidant Ghislaine Maxwell, who was convicted in 2021 and is serving a 20-year prison sentence.
The Justice Department during the Trump administration has fired scores of career employees, including prosecutors and FBI agents, who participated in investigations of Trump or who were perceived as opposed to the administration’s agenda. Some of those firings have also resulted in federal lawsuits.
The firing of Maurene Comey was seen as particularly personal, given her father’s longtime adversarial relationship with Trump.
An earlier criminal case accusing James Comey of having lied to Congress in 2020 was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who filed the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47,” a case he has sought to dismiss that some legal experts have greeted with skepticism.
In his ruling on Maurene Comey’s termination, Furman said the Justice Department’s claim that Congress is barred from regulating the removal of federal prosecutors “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent.”
He didn’t rule on Comey’s claim that her firing violated her free speech rights, though he said he was inclined to dismiss it because she is now in private practice and no longer seeks reinstatement to her old job.
___
Tucker and Durkin reported from Washington.

title: ‘All My Children’ actor Alan Dysert dead at 75 following incurable cancer diagnosis
text:
(Gray News) - Actor Alan Dysert, known for his role in “All My Children,” died at age 75.
In a social media post, his wife, Michele Dysert, announced his death on Oct. 26.
“Alan lived an extraordinary life. From his humble beginnings as a farm boy in Illinois, he went on to become an actor, musician, writer, filmmaker, producer, and beloved acting teacher,” she wrote.
His cause of death was not immediately confirmed, but Dysert was diagnosed with cancer. In his autobiography, “Lights, Camera, Cancer!,” published in 2023, he wrote about his struggles with a “rare, aggressive and incurable cancer.”
“Alan faced more than his share of health challenges over the years, yet he continued to approach life with determination, humor, and gratitude,” Michele wrote about her husband. “He fought hard for the life he loved, and I was honored to stand beside him through it all.”
In addition to his wife, Dysert is survived by his sons, Cody and Cooper.

title: Voter intimidation reported in Lewiston
text:
Voter intimidation reported in Lewiston
The Secretary of State's Office says it has received a complaint of a "political operative" intimidating voters at Lewiston City Hall.
Voter intimidation reported in Lewiston
The Secretary of State's Office says it has received a complaint of a "political operative" intimidating voters at Lewiston City Hall.
The Maine Secretary of State's Office and the Lewiston City Clerk's Office said they have received complaints of voter intimidation in Lewiston.
"She felt that, someone who was here observing, approached them and was having a dialog with them. And then another observer and this particular observer and the voter and the family member who complained about it, all three of them were videoing, the discussion of the transaction," Lewiston City Clerk Kathy Montejo said detailing the complaint.
"We have all seen that the immigrant community in general has been experiencing increased levels of harassment and intimidation," Jodi Hayashida, who works with Maine People's Alliance, said of the interaction with the political operative who allegedly intimidated voters. "[It's] really intimidating and violating some, very significant cultural norms for some immigrant communities where being photographed is not okay. And he persisted in filming, persisted in photographing."
"One of the most serious complaints included documentary evidence that a political operative was harassing voters by asking them unwanted questions," Secretary of State Shenna Bellows added, referencing the complaint her office received.
The complaint has led to additional signage and instructions about where election observers and media outlets can be at polling locations.
A candidate for the legislature said she had an interpreter ask her questions she could not answer within the polling location and say other things that concerned her.
"It certainly is alarming to hear an interpreter say that he was going to tell somebody how to vote if I was [from] a certain party," Janet Beaudoin, Republican candidate for House District 94, said.
She alleged an interpreter was breaking election laws and telling a voter who to vote for. She said she told Montejo and received a "thoughtful response" and again, more signage and instructions are now up at city hall. She said she did not report it to the Secretary of State's Office.

title: Helen Catherine Hoch Martin
text:
Helen Catherine Hoch Martin, 99, passed on July 12, 2026 in West Palm Beach, Fla. She was born on March 16, 1927, the daughter of Elmer and Thelma (Cuthberson) Hoch, in Waldoboro.
Helen and her husband, Howard, built their home and family in Tolland, Conn. They raised three sons, Tyrone Hoch Martin, Philip Lawrence Martin, and Larry Howard Martin, as well as two daughters, Sharon Ann Martin DallaCorte and Barbara (Lynn) Martin Howlett.
Helen was educated in Waldoboro schools. Later in life, she earned an associate degree in business administration (1977) from Manchester Community College.
Helen has been an active member of every community she lived in well into her 90s – always becoming a member of the local church. She held offices of president, treasurer, chaplin, and hospital chairlady in the Women’s Auxiliary of the VFW Post 241. She was instrumental in starting a ladies drill team, which won recognition for the Post. She also worked with children in 4-H while raising her family.
After raising their children, Helen and Howard moved back to Maine and their home in Waldoboro, where they enjoyed a farming life. Helen rekindled many old friendships from her childhood, and continued to build friendships until she passed.
Every summer, she hosted a lobster feed during the weekend of the Lobster Festival. It was a huge gathering during which her children brought family and friends from their hometown in Connecticut to the Wagner Bridge residence.
An artist at heart, she opened a studio and business — Misty Pine Creations in Waldoboro. There, she created her blueberry kitchenware that became popular, selling throughout New England. In addition, she was active in many hobbies, entering her artwork in the local fair exhibit halls. She loved gardening, creating oil paintings, square dancing, sewing costumes for many organizations, and making ceramic Santas.
Helen was predeceased by her loving husband, Howard, of 50-plus years. She was also predeceased by daughter, Sharon; daughters-in-law, Mary and Claudette; and siblings, Pat and Sara.
She leaves behind her beloved brother, Elmer R. Hoch Jr. – her “Buddy”; and his four girls. Helen is sadly missed by her large extended family with many grandchildren, great-grandchildren, great-great-grandchildren, and nieces and nephews, as well as lifelong friends.
A graveside service will be held Friday, Oct. 30 at 1 p.m., followed by the interment of Helen and Howard at the Old German Church Cemetery in Waldoboro.

Judge rules Maurene Comey, daughter of ex-FBI director, was unlawfully fired by Trump administration
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, was unlawfully fired from her job as a federal prosecutor in New York last year, a federal judge ruled Monday.
Judge Jesse M. Furman said that Comey, who was an assistant U.S. attorney for a decade, was illegally fired in July 2025 despite her work on some of the nation’s highest-profile cases and consistently receiving “the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike.”
After her firing, Comey sued the Justice Department and others, saying her termination violated the constitutional separation of powers, the First Amendment and the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment.
She asserted that she was fired because she was the daughter of James Comey, a longtime foe of President Donald Trump, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, the judge noted.
Furman rejected the government’s claim that Comey could be fired because federal prosecutors exercise the president’s “conclusive and preclusive” powers.
“The Court concludes the Defendants are wrong,” the judge wrote.
He said the government’s claim that Congress is barred from regulating the removal of federal prosecutors “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent.”
Furman added: “Indeed, to accept Defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.”
The Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment.

title: These 7 Maine Gems Got the National Geographic Treatment
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
These 7 Maine Gems Got the National Geographic Treatment
Maine is no stranger to national attention. Heck, it seems like every other week our wonderful state is being recognized for something incredible. But when one of the most iconic publications on Earth decides to shine its spotlight on Vacationland, you know it's a pretty big deal.
That's right, folks. National Geographic is once again showing Maine some love, and we're certainly not complaining.
Did National Geographic Spotlight Maine's Lesser Known Regions?
It’s the fact that this article takes aim at some of the small, lesser-known regions of Maine that definitely deserve the spotlight. Honestly, it’s something I wish we saw more of. Now, on to the article.
National Geographic put together a list of seven of Maine’s “must-see” spots when visiting the state. Not all of these are lesser-known, as you will see, but at least half are certainly not household names.
Let’s take a look at all seven.
What does National Geographic Think the Best Locations in Maine Are?
Brooklin – This coastal town is probably best known for being the home of legendary author E.B. White, but it also amazes with unquestioned beauty and peaceful living. If you are looking for quintessential Maine, here you go.
Monhegan Island – Another great choice by National Geographic. It’s not exactly easy to get to—you have to take a ferry from Boothbay, but you will not be disappointed. It’s an artist colony and a lobster lover’s dream. Plus, it has a brewery.
Rangeley – It’s a year-round outdoor adventurer’s playground, with everything from fishing to snowmobiling and everything in between. Plus, you’re not far from Saddleback Ski Resort.
Camden – Okay, this town is quite well-known compared to the others so far. In fact, it’s probably my favorite village in Maine. Camden is picturesque, with wonderful restaurants and shops. And Camden Hills State Park is a must-visit.
Bar Harbor – Do I really need to explain this one?
Brunswick – Another one of my favorite spots in Maine, this perfect college town is home to Bowdoin College. Brunswick shines with a great downtown area and plenty of outdoor recreation opportunities.
Greenville – Home to Moosehead Lake, Greenville is another perfect spot for those who love to get away and enjoy the peace and beauty of Maine. Mount Kineo State Park is another hidden gem that can’t be missed.
So, there you have it, National Geographic’s seven Maine regions to visit on your next vacation (or staycation for all of us locals). I have to admit, there are three on here I have never been to, and I’ve lived here for 37 of my 46 years. I guess the goal for 2026 is to get to those three locations, because clearly I’m missing out.
READ MORE: Travel Experts Say These Are the 4 Best Months to Visit Maine’s Acadia National Park
All in all, it’s a tremendous list, one that doesn’t aim to hit just the usual spots. It does a great job highlighting many different regions of Maine, all of which deserve the attention the big names get.

title: Campaign for Bobby Charles fined more than $22K by Maine Ethics Commission
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - The Maine Commission on Governmental Ethics and Election Practices voted to fine the campaign for Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles more than $22,600 for violating election laws by means of accepting over-the-limit contributions.
Jonathan Wayne, executive director of the Ethics Commission, said during Monday’s meeting that the commission received a complaint from the Maine Democratic Party claiming that the Charles campaign accepted a number of over-the-limit campaign contributions.
Wayne said apparent over-the-limit contributions totaling $45,315.98 were found, and that commission staff recommended to the Ethics Commission a penalty between $11,329 and the total amount by which the contributions went over the limit.
The recommendation from commission staff was conveyed in writing to the Charles campaign Thursday evening. Wayne said that the following day, the Charles campaign asked for the Ethics Commission to delay a decision until its Nov. 18 hearing because the campaign wanted more time to respond.
Brittany Hausle, a lawyer representing the Charles campaign, spoke during Monday’s meeting and did not dispute the over-the-limit contributions, but she did note that the campaign has been working diligently to correct the overages and wanted more time to gather information.
Hausle also said that although the campaign does understand Maine election laws, discussion of a penalty never came up during informal meetings with commission staff.
“This came as a surprise, frankly, to the campaign, regarding the penalty,” Hausle said.
The Charles campaign’s treasurer, Bill Riley, also spoke during the meeting and claimed a national consultant ignored his warnings about there being over-the-limit contributions and filed the paperwork anyway.
“There was nothing malicious here. It was an outside consultant who didn’t follow our protocol, and that’s what has put us in a mess,” Riley said.
A lawyer for the Maine Democratic Party said during the meeting that the Charles campaign’s request for the Ethics Commission to delay until after the Nov. 3 election “feels like a dodge.”
The bipartisan Ethics Commission ultimately voted 4-1 to levy a fine against the Charles campaign that equaled 50% of the total overages, which was $22,657.99.

title: The SS United States is scheduled for sinking to become the world’s largest artificial reef
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
DESTIN, Fla. (AP) — A historic ocean liner is a step closer to becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.
Officials in Florida’s Okaloosa County expect to sink the SS United States off the Gulf Coast during the second week of November. The exact dates could change because of weather.
The ship will be sunk about 22 nautical miles (41 kilometers) southwest of Destin.
“This is an exciting move forward to create a one-of-a-kind resource for the environment and for our tourism industry,” county officials wrote in a news release.
The nearly 1,000-foot (305-meter) vessel shattered the trans-Atlantic speed record on its maiden voyage in 1952. Preservation groups tried to save the ship but were hindered by high costs.
Supporters hope that sinking the ship will make it a barnacle-encrusted star among more than 500 artificial reefs and a signature diving attraction, helping to generate millions of dollars a year in local tourism spending for scuba shops, charter fishing boats and hotels.

title: Chris Brown avoids prison time for brawling at a London nightclub
text:
LONDON (AP) — Grammy-winning singer Chris Brown avoided prison time Monday for beating a music producer with a tequila bottle at a London nightclub three years ago.
The 37-year-old was given an eight-month sentence, suspended for a year.
He had faced up to three years in prison after pleading guilty to a count of affray in July for the attack on the dance floor of Tape, a private club in the swanky Mayfair neighborhood in February 2023.
Video footage played in court showed Brown having to be pulled away from the victim, his former friend Abraham Diaw, after striking him twice in the head with a bottle.
“The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous. It carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained,” Judge Tony Baumgartner said in Southwark Crown Court.
Despite the seriousness of the attack, Baumgartner said Brown did not qualify for a custodial sentence because he pleaded guilty and there were several mitigating circumstances, including stable employment and charity work. The judge acknowledged Brown’s previous convictions but said he had maintained a clean record in recent years.
Previous brushes with the law
Brown has faced repeated legal trouble since his felony conviction in the 2009 assault of his then-girlfriend, Rihanna, hours before the pair were due to perform at the Grammys.
He has been arrested in several U.S. states over altercations but was either not charged or prosecutors later dropped the charges. In 2019 he was arrested in Paris and questioned on suspicion of rape, but was released without charge.
In return for his guilty plea, prosecutors dropped charges of assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm and having an offensive weapon, a bottle.
Brown’s friend and vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu also pleaded guilty to affray and was given a four-month suspended sentence.
Affray is the use or threat of unlawful violence that leads someone to fear for their safety.
Brown has apologized for the attack
Prosecutor Heidi Stonecliffe said Brown played a leading role in the attack.
“By any circumstances, when one watches that footage, it is Mr. Brown that moves first,” Stonecliffe said.
Defense lawyer Sallie Bennett-Jenkins said Brown apologized to all those at the club that night, though she emphasized the attack lasted no more than 20 seconds.
“This is an ugly and unattractive incident,” Bennett-Jenkins said. “It is something which undoubtedly would have caused distress to those who are present and for which Mr. Brown … offers a profound apology to all those present.”
Diaw was discharged from the hospital with head and knee injuries, Stonecliffe said.
Crowds greet Brown outside court
Brown was cheered outside the courthouse by fans who came from as far as Italy and the Netherlands.
His face was covered by a black mask and dark glasses and his bleached hair was mostly hidden from view under a black ball cap. He wore a black leather jacket and light-colored turtleneck.
He blew a kiss to one fan and appeared to sign an autograph for another as he moved through a pack of photographers and onlookers.
Not everyone was cheering for him. When he arrived at court in the morning, a lone voice could be heard shouting at him to ask when he was going to learn that violence is not OK.
Brown left the United Kingdom after the brawl but was arrested in May 2025 at a Manchester hotel after flying to the city for a concert. He had been free on bail of 5 million pounds ($6.7 million), which allowed him to tour Europe and North America the past two summers.
Brown rose to stardom as a teen in 2005 and won his first Grammy for best R&B album in 2011 for “F.A.M.E.” He earned his second in the same category for “11:11 (Deluxe)” in 2025.

title: Peace Ridge Sanctuary marks 25 years caring for farm animals
text:
BROOKS, Maine (WABI) - Peace Ridge Sanctuary is the largest animal shelter and sanctuary system on the eastern seaboard. The organization recently celebrated its 25th anniversary.
Growing up, Peace Ridge Sanctuary founder and director Daniella Tessier spent a lot of time on her grandparent’s large farm.
“so I grew up with cows, particularly, they’re one of my favorites,” she says smiling.
Tessier began volunteering for the Humane Society at age 12. She said that experience shaped her future work.
“There was no help for farmed animals because the shelters don’t have the facilities that you need,” Tessier said.
From seven acres to five facilities
Tessier started Peace Ridge Sanctuary in 2001, on about seven acres in the town of Penobscot.
“Once we opened our doors, it didn’t take very long until we realized that we were going to have to do some development,” Tessier said.
In 2015, the nonprofit purchased property in Brooks. The sanctuary now spans more than 1,000 acres.
“We have goats, sheep, alpaca, we have over 50 pigs, over 50 cows, donkeys, horses, birds as well. And then we have a really, really large dog program,” Tessier said.
Staff, volunteers and daily care
The sanctuary cares for more than 650 animals across its five facilities. It employs 24 staff members and has about 20 volunteers.
“We start at 6 o’clock in the morning and sometimes it goes until 11 o’clock at night,” Tessier said.
Tessier said most animals arrive needing medical care.
“Most of them are arriving really underweight, heavy parasite burdens, untreated medical conditions,” Tessier said.
Peace Ridge Sanctuary goes through 224,000 pounds of grain, 32,000 bales of hay and about $84,000 in wholesale medications every year.
Special privileges and recovery
Some animals are allowed to roam free, in part because of a mile-long driveway on the property.
“The reason they have special privileges is because maybe they’re older animals and they get injections every day. So instead of having to pull them out of their flock or herd every day, we let them walk around and enjoy themselves,” Tessier said.
Tessier said some animals arrive in poor condition.
“Sometimes we get animals in and you can’t even touch them,” Tessier said.
She said animals already living at the sanctuary help new arrivals adjust.
“The animals that have lived here for a long time, they sort of them them into the folds. And very quickly they realize, because the other animals aren’t scared, that they don’t have to be scared anymore. And I feel like that’s where the real healing begins,” Tessier said.
Long-term commitment
Tessier and her staff have taken in well over 2,000 animals since the sanctuary started. While some animals are adopted out, most remain at the sanctuary for the rest of their lives.
“When we take an animal in, we’re making the promise to them that they have a place to be forever. I made a long-term commitment to this. And we will create it for more animals as long as we have community support,” Tessier said.
Ways to help
People can donate through the sanctuary’s home page, you can click here for that link. And right now, all donations will be matched up to $15,000 thanks to an offer by a current Peace Ridge Sanctuary donor.
Monthly donors can receive special access to the facility.
Peace Ridge Sanctuary is also seeking volunteers. Companies can host a Sanctuary Work Day. All of that information is also on the Ways to Give page.
The sanctuary holds Open House Days starting in the spring, summer and fall. And they also host fundraisers periodically.
You can follow their Facebook page for the latest updates on all that is going on at their five facilities throughout the year.

title: FBI arrests man accused of orchestrating 14-year-old girl’s suicide over Discord
text:
INDIANAPOLIS (WPTA/Gray News) - The FBI says a German man has been arrested on a count of murder in relation to an Indiana teenager’s suicide.
Warning: This article contains disturbing details that may be upsetting to readers.
The Fort Wayne Police Department says officers responded to a death investigation involving a 14-year-old girl earlier in October. The department’s Homicide Unit identified a suspect who allegedly contributed to her death, working with the FBI and authorities in Germany.
The FBI Indianapolis Field Office says German authorities recently arrested an 18-year-old man on suspicion of murder in the teen’s death. The Hamburg Public Prosecutor’s Office said he was 17 at the time of the alleged crime, according to a translated article by NDR, a German television broadcaster.
___
This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org
Suspect allegedly manipulated teen into taking her own life
German prosecutors say the suspect communicated with the 14-year-old victim over Discord, manipulating her into hurting herself and ultimately taking her own life, according to NDR.
NDR reports that the suspect allegedly demanded that the victim record her self-harm. After the 14-year-old died, prosecutors allege he tried to obtain recordings of her suicide.
Investigators say the suspect is believed to have orchestrated her suicide, threatening that he would release compromising video of her, according to NDR. The article says police also found that the girl made references to the group “NMK,” which stands for ”Nefarious Maniac Cult,” in her recordings.
The Fort Wayne Police Department recently warned the community about similar dark web groups.
Police warn parents about dangerous dark web groups
Fort Wayne Police held a press conference Oct. 14 to warn parents, guardians, educators and young people about such online networks that they say are leading to deaths across the United States.
They say the perpetrators reportedly use Discord, Roblox, Telegram and other online platforms to build relationships with children and other vulnerable individuals.
They say messages and friend requests from such predators can escalate to grooming, sextortion, threats and psychological manipulation. Information and photos victims send can then be used by the groups to manipulate, threaten, blackmail or extort children.
“Anyone who targets or exploits a child should understand this: There is no safe haven from justice. It doesn’t matter where you live or where you try to hide. The FBI will work with our partners around the world to find you and hold you accountable,” said FBI Indianapolis Special Agent in Charge Timothy J. O’Malley. “When children are victimized, we will pursue every lead and use every available resource. Wherever you go, justice will find you.”

title: What is ‘moneymaxxing’ and how can it help your budget?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — “Moneymaxxing” is a viral social media trend focused on making the most out of every dollar already being earned.
Clay Cooper, a wealth management advisor with Northwestern Mutual, said the concept covers things like moving money to a higher-yield savings account, maximizing credit card rewards or cutting unused recurring subscriptions.
Cooper said the trend is essentially a positive spin on traditional financial planning, and it starts with a thorough budget review. He recommends pulling bank and credit card statements from the past year and closely examining spending patterns.
Cooper said one of the most valuable steps is identifying unused subscriptions.
“The other thing I think is great to do while you’re looking at your bank statements is go through it with a fine-tooth comb and go, ‘What subscriptions am I paying for that I don’t even know, or I’m not using?’” Cooper said. “I am embarrassed to say my wife and I just did this at the beginning of the year — we cut out 12 subscriptions.”
Cooper said credit card rewards should only be viewed as a bonus on planned spending, not a motivation to spend more.
“Normal expense — automate the cash back and pay the full balance every single month,” Cooper said. “If you’re buying something just to earn credit card points, you’re no longer moneymaxxing, in my opinion.”
Cooper said the goal of moneymaxxing should not come at the cost of overall well-being. When optimizing credit cards or squeezing extra interest out of savings, the effort needs to be worth it and sustainable over time. He said the goal is progress, not perfection.

title: When is it too late to get a flu shot?
text:
As the colder seasons approach, many people start preparing for fall and winter routines. For most people, this should include getting a yearly flu shot. The flu vaccine is effective and safe and provides protection against flu illness — both for you and for those around you.
Getting a flu vaccine can keep you from missing work or school due to illness. The flu vaccine also protects you against severe symptoms, which could require hospitalization. And the flu vaccine can be lifesaving for people at greater risk. This includes pregnant women, older adults, and children, as well as people with chronic medical conditions.
But what if it’s already flu season, or you’ve already had the flu? Is it ever too late to get the flu shot? Below, GoodRx, a platform for medication savings, has the answers.
Key takeaways:
- The best time to get a flu shot is right before flu season starts. Flu season usually starts by the end of October.
- The flu shot is safe, effective, and recommended for most people.
- The flu shot protects you even if you’ve already had the flu. So it’s almost never too late to get a flu shot.
Is it too late to get a flu shot?
It’s almost never too late to get a flu shot. A flu shot will provide protection as long as the flu is circulating in the community. Since the flu circulates until late May in most parts of the U.S., even getting your shot in late winter or early spring will help keep you healthy.
When is the best time to get a flu shot?
The best time to get a flu shot is right before flu season begins, which usually means in September or October. In most areas of the U.S., flu season is from October through May. Peak activity is usually from December through February.
It’s best to get your flu shot by the end of October. It takes two weeks for your immune system to fully respond to a vaccine. So, it’s important to plan accordingly and get the vaccine before flu activity increases in your community.
Early vaccination — that is, getting a flu shot in July or August — is sometimes an option. This can make sense for young children who need two doses of the flu vaccine in the same year. You may also benefit from early vaccination if you’re pregnant or close to delivery.
But, in general, most people shouldn’t get vaccinated early. The flu shot gets less effective over time, so it works best if you wait until closer to flu season.
How long does the flu shot last?
It’s not clear exactly how long a flu shot lasts. Studies show that vaccine protection likely lasts at least six months for most people — but fades over time. That’s why it’s important to get a yearly flu shot for the best protection against the flu virus during flu season.
Should you get a flu shot if you’ve already had the flu?
Yes, you should get a flu shot if you’ve already had the flu. Every year, several strains of flu spread through communities. Immunity to one strain of flu doesn’t protect you against other strains.
That means you can get the flu more than once in a single year. The flu shot is designed to protect you against several of the most troublesome strains each season. So it makes sense to get vaccinated even if you’ve already recovered from the flu.
Where to get a flu shot
Flu vaccines are widely available during the flu season. There are many places you can go to get a flu shot, including:
- Your doctor’s office
- Most large chain retail pharmacies
- Drive-thru flu-shot clinics
- Pop-up flu-shot clinics at community centers and hospitals
- Your local health department
There’s no “right” place to get the flu shot. You can go to any licensed healthcare professional offering a licensed flu vaccine.
When not to get a flu shot
Just about everyone should get a flu shot. However, the flu shot isn’t recommended for:
- Anyone with a severe allergy or anaphylaxis to the flu vaccine or its ingredients
- Infants younger than 6 months old
Anyone with a history of Guillain-Barré syndrome should talk with their healthcare team before getting a flu shot.
In rare situations, the risks of the flu shot can outweigh the benefits. In these cases, people need to talk with their healthcare team before getting a flu shot.
The flu shot is safe for people with egg allergies. Before 2023, people with egg allergies needed to take special precautions when getting a flu shot, but according to the CDC, that’s no longer the case.
If you or your child is sick on the day of your flu shot appointment, make sure you let the healthcare professional know. Some people can still get vaccinated if they only have a minor illness. In some cases, rescheduling the flu shot may be recommended.
Frequently asked questions
Is it too late to get a flu shot in January?
No, it’s not too late to get a flu shot in January. In the U.S., the flu tends to stick around through May. You can even get the flu in the summer. Getting a flu shot in January still provides important protection.
Can you get a flu shot anytime during the year?
Yes, you can get the flu shot pretty much any time of the year. But keep in mind that you’re more likely to have better protection if you get a flu vaccine right before the start of flu season, around September or October. Protection goes down over time, so the idea is to make sure you’re protected during the peak of flu season.
How effective is the flu shot this year?
The flu shot’s effectiveness varies from season to season, depending on how well the vaccine matches the strains actually circulating. In seasons with a good match, flu vaccination cuts the risk of a flu-related healthcare visit by 40% to 60%. But one thing holds up every year: Even when the match is imperfect, the vaccine still lowers your odds of severe illness and hospitalization.
Does the flu shot make you sick?
No, the flu shot doesn’t make you sick with the flu. Flu shots contain inactivated (killed) virus or single viral proteins. Neither of these can cause a flu infection. Some people can feel ill after a flu shot with:
- Low-grade fever
- Headache
- Muscle aches
- Fatigue
But that’s your immune system responding to the shot, not the flu.
What to avoid after a flu shot?
There’s not much you need to avoid after a flu shot. That being said, you may want to skip heavy arm workouts if your arm is sore and avoid alcohol for a day or so. Alcohol can cause dehydration, which could make any side effects feel worse.
The bottom line
The best time to get a flu shot is two weeks before the flu season begins — usually by the end of October. But it’s really never too late to get a flu shot, as the virus is normally circulating in communities through May of each year. The flu vaccine can keep people safe from flu illness, and it’s lifesaving for people at risk for severe flu disease. The flu shot is recommended for nearly everyone older than 6 months.

title: Eric Bauza, Voice of Bugs Bunny, Dies at 46
text:
Eric Bauza, Voice of Bugs Bunny and Many More Cartoon Characters, Dies at 46
Since the death of original Looney Tunes voice talent Mel Blanc, several other actors have voiced Bugs Bunny and his other cartoon characters. But in recent years Eric Bauza has been Bugs in most of his onscreen appearances — including HBO Max’s Looney Tunes Cartoons, Bugs Bunny Builders, and 2026’s Coyote vs. Acme.
Bauza also voices many other Looney Tunes favorites. In 2024’s hilarious The Day the Earth Blew Up, Bauza played both lead characters — Daffy Duck and Porky Pig — and at different times and on different projects he’s also voiced Marvin the Martian, Pepe Le Pew, Sylvester, Tweety Bird, Yosemite Sam, Foghorn Leghorn, Elmer Fudd, and more.
Which makes this news all the more shocking: Bauza has passed away at the age of 46. His family announced his death on his official Instagram account earlier tonight, writing...
“Eric Bauza, Emmy Award-winning voice actor and the modern voice of the iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, along with dozens of other beloved cartoon characters, has passed away suddenly.”
READ MORE: The 20 Best Animated Superhero Shows
Bauza was born in Canada and grew up loving Looney Tunes and animation in general. His first voice credit was as Stimpy on 2003’s Ren & Stimpy: Adult Cartoon Party. His first work with the Looney Tunes came in 2011’s The Looney Tunes Show, where he voiced Marvin the Martian, but over time he gradually added more of the franchise’s characters to his repertoire.
Here’s a video where you can see Bauza in action, showing off his remarkable vocal dexterity:
Outside of Looney Tunes, Bauza’s notable credits include portraying Puss in Boots in The Adventures of Puss in Boots animated TV series spun off from the DreamWorks movies, voicing Splinter on Rise of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, and playing Fozzie on the recent Muppet Babies revival.
But that’s only a couple of shows he worked on; Bauza’s voice could be heard in everything from Big Hero 6: The Series to Star Trek: Lower Decks, to Gremlins: Secrets of the Mogwai to Star Wars: Young Jedi Adventures to X-Men ’97. (He voiced the Sentinels.) He can currently be heard on the latest Avatar sequel series, Seven Havens. And only a few months ago he was heard doing a slew of Looney Tunes characters (including the Road Runner) in the wonderful Coyote vs. Acme.
It’s just a sudden, terrible loss.

title: Family steps in, detains man who tried to kidnap girl at gunpoint outside her home, sheriff says
text:
SALEM, Ind. (WDRB+WAVE/Gray News) — A family in Indiana is being credited with saving a girl from being kidnapped at gunpoint.
According to the Washington County Sheriff’s Department, deputies responded at 4:30 p.m. to a home after receiving a report of a man attempting to abduct a girl at gunpoint.
Police said Jeffrey Mauck, 53, approached the girl outside her home and attempted to force her into his vehicle.
The girl told police that Mauck grabbed her and threatened her with a gun.
Police said she screamed for help and struggled to break free. The struggle caught the attention of her family members, who came outside and detained Mauck until police arrived.
Mauck had a revolver, ammunition, handcuffs and two folding knives, according to police.
“This is an extremely disturbing incident, and we are thankful this young girl was able to get away and that her family acted quickly,” Washington County Sheriff Brent Miller said in a news release. “Anyone who attempts to harm or abduct a child in Washington County will be met with the full force of law enforcement. Protecting our children and keeping our families safe will always be among our highest priorities.”
Mauck was arrested and charged with attempted kidnapping, criminal confinement, aggravated battery, pointing a firearm and operating a vehicle while intoxicated.

title: Does the moon determine when Maine’s deer rut peaks?
text:
Many sportsmen count the November deer hunt as the highlight of all their outdoor pursuits. It is a special time. Frosty mornings and quiet moments in a tree stand, with hand warmers, a thermos of hot coffee and the anticipation of a big buck in the crosshairs, are part of a deer hunter’s daydream. For the hardiest and most driven hunters, the dream is to follow a big, dew-clawed track in fresh snow.
And, of course, the Maine deer camp is also a centerpiece of the hunt, part of its heritage and history. These camps come in all sizes and are scattered across the state. Many have been passed down from generation to generation, along with their unique histories and hunting yarns that get retold year after year.
A mouse in the corner — a graying one that has been hiding in the food bin for more than a year or two — knows that many of the same topics get debated around the card tables year after year. Among them are the best deer gun, the time of day bucks move, tracking methods and the granddaddy of them all: when is the peak period of the all-important rut?
In general, knowing when the rut peaks gives you the best chance of catching a buck distracted by breeding activity, with his guard down and less focused on danger. But predicting the peak involves educated guesswork and anecdotal evidence, making the timing of the deer rut a subject of spirited debate at deer camp.
There are two schools of thought on the subject. The conventional wisdom of respected wildlife biologists such as Gerry Lavigne is straightforward and has nothing to do with moon phases. Lavigne maintains that the rut peaks around Nov. 15 every year. This theory holds that the breeding season is driven by day length.
The more romantic theory, if you will, is that although the rut occurs over a period of several weeks, there is a “sweet spot” lasting about 10 days. This is the lunar theory advanced by well-known deer researcher Charles Alsheimer of Bath, New York. In a chapter of his book, “Anatomy of the Rut,” Alsheimer proposed that the whitetail rut is regulated by the lunar cycle.
According to Alsheimer’s theory, the Rutting Moon, also known as the Beaver Moon, is the second full moon after the autumnal equinox. He proposed that the 10-day rutting “sweet spot” begins three days after the full moon.
In 2026, the full moon falls on Nov. 24, meaning the predicted window would begin around Nov. 27, much later than last year. Unlike the theory that the rut peaks around Nov. 15 each year, the lunar theory predicts a different peak period from year to year.
However, Maine’s firearms season ends Nov. 28, followed by the muzzleloader season, which begins Nov. 30. So smokepolers, take note.
So what does this mean for hunters? It depends on which theory you believe: the lunar cycle or day length. If you favor the lunar theory and want to maximize your chances of encountering a buck distracted by breeding activity, you might want to reconsider when you schedule your hunting vacation. If Alsheimer’s theory is right, a buck may be more likely to make a mistake in your favor late in November.
One other thing: If you really want to cover your bases and account for both the lunar and day-length theories, spend as much time as possible in a tree stand in good deer country during the dates mentioned above.
Good luck and hunt safely.

title: Judge rules Maurene Comey, daughter of ex-FBI director, was unlawfully fired by Trump administration
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The Trump administration illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of ex-FBI Director and Trump critic James Comey, as a Justice Department prosecutor, a judge ruled Monday in a sharp rebuke of the administration’s authority to terminate career federal employees it dislikes.
The ruling is tailored to Maurene Comey but its import stretches beyond her case, repudiating the claim of President Donald Trump’s administration that the Constitution permits such firings for any reason. Administration officials have cited that belief repeatedly in a sweeping purge of the federal workforce.
Comey, an assistant U.S. attorney for a decade, was fired in July 2025 despite consistently receiving “the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike,” Judge Jesse M. Furman found.
The judge said her firing violated laws passed by Congress that were intended to abolish the spoils system, under which newly elected presidents regularly purged government workers and replaced them with loyalists.
Furman’s decision didn’t address the validity of Comey’s claim that she was fired because she is the daughter of James Comey, whom Trump has long viewed as an enemy.
Trump fired James Comey as FBI director in May 2017 as the bureau was investigating ties between Russia and the Republican’s successful 2016 campaign for the White House. Trump in the years since has repeatedly called for Comey to be jailed, and his Justice Department has worked with mixed success to make that happen.
Hours after Furman’s ruling Monday, unsealed court filings showed that the Justice Department had quietly brought another criminal case against James Comey, accusing him of leaking classified information.
Furman, who was nominated to the bench in 2011 by then-Democratic President Barack Obama, granted Maurene Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay from the date of her firing through Dec. 20, 2025, when she began a new, private-sector job.
In a statement, the Justice Department said it disagreed with this decision and would appeal.
Comey’s lawyers, Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan, lauded the ruling.
“This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law,” they said in a statement. “This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law.”
Comey was fired two weeks after leading the prosecution of music mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs, which ended in a conviction on prostitution-related charges but an acquittal on others. She also worked on the sex trafficking prosecutions of Jeffrey Epstein, the financier who killed himself in jail a month after his arrest in 2019, and Epstein’s former girlfriend and longtime confidant Ghislaine Maxwell, who was convicted in 2021 and is serving a 20-year prison sentence.
The Justice Department during the Trump administration has fired scores of career employees, including prosecutors and FBI agents, who participated in investigations of Trump or who were perceived as opposed to the administration’s agenda. Some of those firings have also resulted in federal lawsuits.
The firing of Maurene Comey was seen as particularly personal, given her father’s longtime adversarial relationship with Trump.
An earlier criminal case accusing James Comey of having lied to Congress in 2020 was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who filed the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47,” a case he has sought to dismiss that some legal experts have greeted with skepticism.
In his ruling on Maurene Comey’s termination, Furman said the Justice Department’s claim that Congress is barred from regulating the removal of federal prosecutors “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent.”
Furman added: “Indeed, to accept Defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.”
He didn’t rule on Comey’s claim that her firing violated her free speech rights, though he said he was inclined to dismiss it because she is now in private practice and no longer seeks reinstatement to her old job.
___
Tucker and Durkin reported from Washington.

title: Earthquake shook Piscataquis County town
text:
An early Friday morning earthquake rattled Guilford.
The magnitude 1.8 temblor shook the ground at a depth of more than 6 miles northwest of the Piscataquis County town about 12:13 a.m., according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
Since 1997, there have been more than 170 recorded earthquakes in the state, according to the Maine Geological Survey.
The strongest quake in recent memory occurred on Oct. 16, 2012, when a 4.5 magnitude earthquake shook the ground in East Waterboro, according to the Maine Geological Survey. But Maine has felt the impact of much larger earthquakes that hit as far away as Plattsburgh, New York, and Quebec City.
Recorded quakes tend to be clustered near Passamaquoddy Bay, the Dover-Foxcroft-Milo area and southwestern Maine. Of course, earthquakes have been felt across Maine, even as far north as the St. John Valley, according to a Maine Geological Survey report.
Every so often quakes happen in clusters. That happened off York Harbor between Jan. 27 and Feb. 2, 2024, when three quakes ranging from magnitude 2 to 3.8. It happened again near Jonesboro between Aug. 11 and Sept. 1, 2022, when about nine earthquakes ranging from magnitude 1.7 to 3 shook the ground. Before that there was the cluster of six quakes east of Cadillac Mountain on Mount Desert Island from Sept. 22 to Dec. 29, 2006, the strongest of which measured a magnitude 4.2.

title: York County emergency management director to retire
text:
York County Emergency Management Agency Director Arthur “Art” Cleaves announced he will retire from the position on Jan. 1. Cleaves, who took the helm of the agency in January 2015, will be much missed in the role, York County commissioners said when they accepted the decision at the Oct. 21 meeting.
“I think everybody should retire at some point — but not you,” Commissioner Richard Clark said with a smile. He thanked Cleaves for his work over the past 11 years: “I appreciate what you’ve done; thank you for what you have done for the county.”
Cleaves has led the agency through multiple milestones in York County: The emergency management team mobilized in 2021 to open a COVID-19 vaccination site that dispensed more than 100,000 vaccines; the agency under Cleaves’ leadership in early 2024 coped with punishing coastal storms that ripped away dunes and caused massive erosion — and found ways to mitigate the damage.
Cleaves and the team worked hard to get York County’s dredge program up and running to aid in the coastal recovery, among many other initiatives. Early in his tenure at the agency, in 2015, the agency instituted its first drone acquisition that is vital to first responders in search-and-rescue operations and with hazardous materials incidents when it isn’t safe to place people in the area.
His name is synonymous with emergency management. Cleaves became administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s New England region in 2005, and oversaw 34 major disaster declarations, including the Patriots’ Day Storm in 2007 and the 2008 ice storm.
Earlier, he spent 30 years with the Maine Army National Guard, retiring as a colonel, and directed the Maine Emergency Management Agency and the state’s Homeland Security office. He worked in Haiti after an earthquake and served as liaison for FEMA and coordinated recovery operations for the New York Office of Emergency Management following Hurricane Sandy.
“I want to thank you all for all … that you’ve done for York County,” said Commissioner Donna Ring. “I’ve been here a long time, and I know what you’ve done for EMA and for the county, and it’s second to none. I appreciate everything that you’ve done.”
“You’ve been a really steady hand in lifting up … so many vulnerable communities that have really needed help in some dark moments,” said Commissioner Justin Chenette, particularly noting work carried out in coastal regions. “York County EMA is there, always.”
“You’re the heart and soul … and I just thank you for everything you’ve done for this county,” said Commission Vice Chair Robert Andrews. “People often joke about ‘Who do we call?’ and it’s always ‘1-800-CALL-ART,’” said York County Manager Greg Zinser.
Zinser said he has learned a lot from Cleaves, like the value and power of building relationships. “It’s those relationships that you rely (on) when you are trying to get something done,” said Zinser.
Deputy Director Megan Arsenault will serve as interim director following Cleaves’ retirement until next steps are determined.
“With all of my work in life I have been driven by tasks and missions at hand to make people more prepared for emergencies, and help after a disaster,” said Cleaves, reflecting on his
career over the years. “This is bittersweet. I am engaged every day … the goals here are compelling, and I want always to contribute.”
Tammy Wells is a media specialist for York County Government.

title: Trump says US is 'making a fortune' from higher oil prices. Who benefits?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Trump says US is 'making a fortune' from higher oil prices. Who benefits?
President Donald Trump says higher oil prices are making America wealthier. But economists say the gains are concentrated among producers and investors, while consumers face rising costs.
Trump says US is 'making a fortune' from higher oil prices. Who benefits?
President Donald Trump says higher oil prices are making America wealthier. But economists say the gains are concentrated among producers and investors, while consumers face rising costs.
President Donald Trump says the United States is "making a fortune" from higher oil prices, even as American consumers are paying significantly more for gasoline and diesel.
Speaking at a campaign rally in Perry, Georgia, on Saturday, Trump anticipated criticism of his remarks.
"I could just see the fake headlines. 'President Trump is talking about all the money they're making while people are suffering at the pump.' That'll be the headline," Trump said.
"But I said, 'I don't give a damn. I'm gonna say it.' We're making a freaking fortune."
A White House official said in a statement provided to Hearst Television that America's oil production and exports are making the country wealthier and strengthening national security.
The official pointed to oil tankers now coming to Texas and Louisiana, bringing business to American producers rather than Iran.
Where is the money going?
An Oil & Gas Journal analysis found that 38 U.S. oil producers and refiners reported a combined $62.2 billion in profits during the second quarter of 2026, nearly triple the $22.3 billion they earned during the same period last year.
Their combined revenue also climbed from $299.3 billion to $439.1 billion. But oil companies aren't the only ones benefiting.
In a statement to Hearst Television, the Interior Department said energy production on federal lands and waters generated $7.53 billion for the U.S. Treasury, more than $6.6 billion for states and over $1 billion for conservation efforts in fiscal year 2026.
For context, Interior reported distributing $5.01 billion to the Treasury and $4.07 billion to states in fiscal year 2025.
"These aren't just numbers on a ledger; these are billions of dollars flowing into American communities, schools, infrastructure and more," the Interior Department said.
The department's figures cover revenue from federal energy production throughout the fiscal year, not just oil revenue generated since the war began. The two years' figures also have not been confirmed as directly comparable.
Energy economist Ed Hirs, of the University of Houston, said governments are among the beneficiaries of higher energy prices.
"The federal government is gaining, as are some of the state governments with higher tax collections," Hirs said.
He explained that higher prices can also support jobs and local businesses in oil-producing communities. Americans who own energy stocks, including through retirement accounts, may benefit as well.
But those financial gains aren't shared equally.
"It's a redistribution of wealth from the consumer to the producers right now," Hirs said.
The cost to consumers
Hearst Television's Get the Facts Data Team found gasoline prices have risen more than 50% in 20 states since the war began on Feb. 28.
Brown University estimates Americans have spent nearly $143 billion more on gasoline and diesel than they would have without the war with Iran.
Higher diesel prices can also increase transportation and delivery expenses, potentially pushing up prices for groceries and other everyday goods.
Abhi Rajendran, an energy expert at Rice University's Baker Institute for Public Policy, said the financial benefits to American oil producers do not necessarily outweigh the broader costs to consumers.
"I would say a net-net, it is a drag on the economy because, you know, it's more of a consumption tax, the higher price environment, than it is a, you know, production benefit," Rajendran said.
The White House maintains that stronger American energy production benefits the country. However, its statements did not quantify how much of the additional wealth generated by higher oil prices ultimately reaches ordinary American households.
Trump predicts gas prices will fall sharply when the war ends. But Hirs cautioned that disruptions to global oil markets could keep prices elevated for months, even if the fighting stopped immediately.

title: How going outside in nature could ease stress
text:
(Aging Untold) — There is something about nature that makes us feel instantly connected.
For the Tomlinson family, spending time outdoors is a daily routine.
“Nature makes me feel happy and excited when I always get around it because it makes me feel like I’m at home,” said Gibbs Tomlinson, who enjoys spending time in nature.
“See the sun come through the trees and being able to put a shadow on a leaf, the fish glistening in the creek, and it just makes you feel wholesome,” Brent Tomlinson, Gibbs’ father, said.
Reconnecting with the outdoors
Research shows nature could ease symptoms of depression, stress and ADHD.
Aging Untold expert and gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said human history was not built around pavement or concrete.
“Human history wasn’t built in a concrete jungle. It wasn’t built around pavement. It was built around nature. And we are natural beings that need to connect back to fresh air, to the earth, to having nature around us,” Cradduck said.
Cradduck said being outside is one of the most powerful treatments for what she described as the “mental exhaustion” of the digital age.
“We’re living in a world that’s constantly throwing information our way - we’re in information overload, and we’re not getting back to just the basics and the roots of society, you know, grounding getting in there and just being part of the community that you live in, not having everything thrown at you all the time,” Cradduck said.
Benefits without a hike
Cradduck said people do not need extensive access to wilderness to benefit from nature.
“Not everybody has the opportunity to walk over to Central Park in the middle of their city. Not everybody has the opportunity to go for a walk in nature and go for a hike in the mountains, but everybody has an opportunity to go outside, get that sunlight, let your rhythms reset, let your body understand that there is a great outdoors. We know how valuable it is for our own health,” Cradduck said.

Justice Department to send federal observers to Portland, Lewiston on Election Day
Maine's Secretary of State says she is prepared to welcome federal observers from the DOJ at polling locations in Lewiston and Portland to "put more eyes on the process."
The U.S. Department of Justice plans to send election observers to Portland and Lewiston for the Nov. 3 election, according to Maine's Secretary of State.
In an interview with C-SPAN, Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said DOJ observers are "not new" and she welcomes their presence because they build public confidence in elections.
Bellows said her office will ensure that the monitors follow the law and she is confident that they will do so across the country.
"We will ensure that they follow the same protocols as anyone observing the election," said Bellows on Friday on C-SPAN's "Ceasefire." "They cannot interact or intimidate voters in any way. We safeguard the voting booths and the tabulators themselves."
Bellows also emphasized that federal law prohibits armed federal agents, such as ICE personnel, from being at polling locations. She said Maine is prepared to "fight back" and stop that immediately if it were to happen.
It's unclear how many federal observers are coming to Maine, but their deployment is part of a larger effort that the Justice Department has called the "biggest DOJ election observer effort in history."
President Donald Trump plans to dispatch more than 1,000 monitors on Election Day, which is hundreds more than the Biden administration deployed in 2024.
Speaking to CNN in Georgia on Saturday, Trump downplayed concerns that the monitoring efforts would disrupt polling places or prevent anyone from voting.
"They're not going to do anything other than watch," Trump said. "If they see something wrong, we want to all have honest elections. And the one thing we have to have is honest elections."
Bellows says that recent federal attempts to obtain voter information and impose limits on voting have raised concerns among voters. She said her office has trained election workers and law enforcement on how to respond to potential disruptions, including questions about federal agents at polling places.
One vocal critic of the plan has been Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson, who says federal observers could scare people away from voting.
"If there's anyone that was doing anything wrong in Lewiston, I'm sure those poll workers are going to catch it and make it stop," said Jackson to reporters after a campaign rally in Westbrook on Saturday. "We don't need people coming from Washington to make it harder or scare people from voting."

title: NASCAR race at Talladega stopped after Joey Logano’s car goes airborne in scary 15-car wreck
text:
TALLADEGA, Ala. (AP) — The NASCAR Chase race at Talladega Superspeedway was stopped under the red flag with five laps remaining after a scary wreck involving three-time Cup Series champion Joey Logano, whose car went airborne and landed on its roof.
Safety crews needed several minutes to turn Logano’s No. 22 Ford back over on its wheels, and Logano was able to climb from the car to cheers from the crowd.
Logano was running in fourth when he lost control off a push by Carson Hocevar and started a 15-car pileup on the frontstretch that also included Chase Briscoe, Brad Keselowski, Austin Cindric, Josh Berry and Riley Herbst, who appeared to lose the brakes in his No. 35 Toyota before hitting the inside wall at virtually full speed.
“I just got a push in the wrong spot there,” Logano said. “It was very much a ‘Talladega Nights,’ Oh no, I’m upside down, this is not good’ moment. I can’t thank the safety crew enough. They did an amazing job flipping that thing over.”
Herbst, who missed the Daytona race in August with a concussion from a crash at New Hampshire Motor Speedway, was able to exit his car with help from safety workers. He took a moment to lean against his car before removing his helmet.
In a postrace interview with USA Sports, Herbst had a soft cast on his left hand and a wrap around his wrist and forearm.
“I’m OK; it was a big one,” Herbst said. “But just thank you to 2311 Racing and Toyota for the support. It’s been an up-and-down year, to say the least. I thought we had a shot at it there at the end. We got shuffled out a little bit, but came back and ultimately just got caught up in that wreck at Talladega.
“My dad always said, ‘If you’re going to be dumb, you better be tough.’ So, cheers.”
Logano is a three-time winner at Talladega. He has been involved in airborne crashes before at the 2.66-mile oval that is infamous for its big crashes.
After a similar incident in the April 2021 race at Talladega, Logano expressed frustration that his car had gotten up in the air and had its roof crushed. “I got a roll bar in my head,” Logano said. “That is not OK. I am one hit away from the same situation Ryan Newman just went through (in the 2020 Daytona 500). I just don’t feel like that is acceptable.”
NASCAR made safety enhancements to address airborne wrecks in recent years, and the Team Penske driver praised his car’s integrity after the wreck Sunday at Talladega.
“The car did a great job,” Logano said. ”The last time I flipped it was crushed on my head. This time, I don’t think any of the roll cage crushed at all, so I appreciate what NASCAR’s done. Thank you and the safety team for getting me out of there. There was some vicious hits in this one. Just happy to be alive.”
___

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Margaret Louise Simmons died peacefully at the Sussman House in Rockport on Oct. 22, 2026. She was the youngest daughter of John Edward Fortman and Sophia (Dreyer) Fortman. Margaret lived and worked in Baltimore until 1966 when she moved to Maine, where she remained the rest of her life.
She loved the northern Maine woods and the oceanfront of Midcoast Maine. She lived for many years raising her two youngest daughters in New Harbor, where she developed many friendships over the years. She later moved to Waldoboro and eventually married Carleton Simmons Jr. and began their life together with their blended families. They filled their days full of love, fun, and adventures with their dog Molly and a few cockatiels over time.
Margaret loved to go fishing, hunting, camping, and boating whenever she could with her late husband, Junior. Together they made lifelong friends in their travels in Maine. They also loved to go to lawn sales where they found their treasures of “eclectic” taste.
Margaret loved her family and friends fiercely and once you were in her fold, she held you there forever. She was famous for her Maryland crabcakes, none better in Maine have been found. She was a lover of ketchup, which became family hilarity when she’d slather it on most everything, even prime rib! She even woke from a morphine state to tell the nurse “I’m OK, I just need ketchup.”
Always, spiritual … Margaret devoted her faith in Jesus and church after Junior died. Her friends of West Waldoboro Church sustained her through their fellowship and love until her passing. She loved to cook and share her foodies with her church friends who in turn enjoyed every morsel.
Margaret was predeceased by her beloved husband, Carleton Simmons Jr.; her sisters, Anna Mae Kreutzer and Ida Kreutzer; a brother and oldest sibling, John Edward Fortman, who died a toddler; granddaughter, Crystalle Rose Johnson; and her very best friend, Ellen Farrin Rice.
Margaret is survived by her daughters, Deborah (Weinhold) Furlong, of Parsons, Tenn., Rose (Poland) Prior and husband, Robert, of Damariscotta, Margaret (Poland) Eustis and husband, Mark, of Auburn; her loving stepson, Johnny Simmons and wife, Stephanie, of Greenville, and their children, all of which Margaret considered her grandchildren; special grandson, Larry Reed and wife Amanda, their daughter Cheyanne, another loved as her grandchild; adored granddaughter, Miranda Prior; granddaughter, Michelle Muhl and spouse, Mike, of Maryland; granddaughter, Lisa Martin and spouse, J.T., of Tennessee; and several great- and great-great-grandchildren of Maryland and Tennessee that she was thankful to see by way of social media.
Per Margaret’s wishes, there will be no formal services or celebration of life. A private gathering will be held by boat off Pemaquid Point to commit her ashes to the ocean with the love of her life, Junior Simmons.
In Margaret’s memory, donations may be made to the Midcoast Humane animal shelter in Edgecomb or to the National Kidney Foundation at 30 East 33rd St., New York, NY 10016.
Arrangements are under the care of Hall Funeral Home and Cremation Services of Waldoboro. To share a condolence or memory with Margaret’s family, visit hallfuneralhomes.com.
