title: FBI arrests man accused of orchestrating 14-year-old girl’s suicide over Discord
text:
INDIANAPOLIS (WPTA/Gray News) - The FBI says a German man has been arrested on a count of murder in relation to an Indiana teenager’s suicide.
Warning: This article contains disturbing details that may be upsetting to readers.
The Fort Wayne Police Department says officers responded to a death investigation involving a 14-year-old girl earlier in October. The department’s Homicide Unit identified a suspect who allegedly contributed to her death, working with the FBI and authorities in Germany.
The FBI Indianapolis Field Office says German authorities recently arrested an 18-year-old man on suspicion of murder in the teen’s death. The Hamburg Public Prosecutor’s Office said he was 17 at the time of the alleged crime, according to a translated article by NDR, a German television broadcaster.
___
This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org
Suspect allegedly manipulated teen into taking her own life
German prosecutors say the suspect communicated with the 14-year-old victim over Discord, manipulating her into hurting herself and ultimately taking her own life, according to NDR.
NDR reports that the suspect allegedly demanded that the victim record her self-harm. After the 14-year-old died, prosecutors allege he tried to obtain recordings of her suicide.
Investigators say the suspect is believed to have orchestrated her suicide, threatening that he would release compromising video of her, according to NDR. The article says police also found that the girl made references to the group “NMK,” which stands for ”Nefarious Maniac Cult,” in her recordings.
The Fort Wayne Police Department recently warned the community about similar dark web groups.
Police warn parents about dangerous dark web groups
Fort Wayne Police held a press conference Oct. 14 to warn parents, guardians, educators and young people about such online networks that they say are leading to deaths across the United States.
They say the perpetrators reportedly use Discord, Roblox, Telegram and other online platforms to build relationships with children and other vulnerable individuals.
They say messages and friend requests from such predators can escalate to grooming, sextortion, threats and psychological manipulation. Information and photos victims send can then be used by the groups to manipulate, threaten, blackmail or extort children.
“Anyone who targets or exploits a child should understand this: There is no safe haven from justice. It doesn’t matter where you live or where you try to hide. The FBI will work with our partners around the world to find you and hold you accountable,” said FBI Indianapolis Special Agent in Charge Timothy J. O’Malley. “When children are victimized, we will pursue every lead and use every available resource. Wherever you go, justice will find you.”
The FBI says information about potential federal crimes can be reported here.

title: Don’t rake those leaves
text:
New England is known for its fall foliage, and this year did not disappoint. After each rainstorm or gust of wind, I’m convinced the leaves will drop, but so far, they’re clinging on, delighting leaf peepers and locals with the canopy of reds, oranges, yellows, browns and purples. As a landscaper, I’m often asked what to do with leaves. The answer is simple: leave them be.
Colder temperatures and shorter days prompt leaves to change color and eventually fall. These leaves, as well as small twigs, seeds, and other woody debris, are considered “leaf litter.” Many people treat this “litter” as literal trash — raking, bagging it up, and taking it to the local transfer station. However, leaf litter is a natural part of the woodland cycle, and throwing the leaves away is not only wasteful, but also detrimental to the entire ecosystem.

title: Cooper Flagg has double-double in return from injury to lift Mavs
text:
MIAMI — Cooper Flagg had 29 points and 11 assists, plus blocked a shot that would have given Miami the lead in the final moments, and the Dallas Mavericks sent the reeling Heat to 0-4 with a 113-109 win on Monday night.
PJ Washington added 20 points, Kyrie Irving scored 18 and Walter Clayton Jr. had 15 for Dallas. Flagg had 12 of his points in the fourth, and his block of a 3-point try by Andrew Wiggins with 31 seconds left preserved a two-point Mavs lead.
Giannis Antetokounmpo had his first triple-double since joining the Heat, finishing with 29 points, 15 rebounds and 11 assists. Davion Mitchell scored 21 for Miami.
The Heat are 0-4 for the fifth time in team history, the first since 2008-09.
Miami started slowly, getting down 19-11 midway through the opening quarter — then outscoring Dallas 37-17 over the next 12 minutes to take a 12-point lead, its biggest so far this season.
It didn’t last.
Dallas was up 53-52 at the half. The back-and-forth continued in the third, with Miami going up 10 not long after halftime but settling for an 84-83 lead going into the final 12 minutes.
Dallas took the lead back midway through the fourth and kept it the rest of the way, on a night where Miami missed 11 of 25 free throws.
It was the first meeting between first-year Dallas coach Dusty May and Miami coach Erik Spoelstra. May coached nearby Florida Atlantic to the 2023 Final Four and his son, Jack, worked in Miami’s video room before joining his father’s Dallas staff.
“He’s a heck of a coach,” Spoelstra said of May, who led Michigan to the 2026 NCAA title. “There’s no doubt about it.”
Up next
Mavericks: Host Oklahoma City on Wednesday night.
Heat: Visit Atlanta on Wednesday night.

title: Where the candidates in Maine stand on election security
text:
Your Choice, Your Voice: Where the candidates for office in Maine stand on election security
Maine's Total Coverage asked viewers what issues they are most interested in learning more about heading into the midterm election.
After hundreds of submissions, one of the top issues on voters' minds is election security. Maine's Total Coverage asked all the candidates for governor and congressional offices about their stance on the issue.
Gubernatorial candidates
The race for the Blaine House began with two crowded primaries. Republican Bobby Charles was the winner of a seven-way ranked-choice voting primary and Democrat Hannah Pingree won in a five-way race. Independent Rick Bennett, who left the Republican Party last year, was the only independent who got the required number of signatures to get on the November ballot.
Last year, Maine voters failed to approve a measure that was aimed at election security, but at the federal level, Congress could still take up the SAVE Act, which would require voter ID to cast your ballot.
Bennett said people need to look at the facts on this matter.
"Every time that there is actual voter fraud, people have been prosecuted and they've been arrested and convicted," he said. "So every time, people look at this, they can't find much of it. And when they do find it, it is pursued through law enforcement."
Charles said he understands why there is distrust in elections.
"The first thing you've got is a state that's encouraging the influx of a lot of illegal aliens who do not have the right to vote," he said. "The second thing people see is that there was Democrat opposition to voter ID, which is it gives people confidence and other states have used it. In fact, there's a federal bill up right now, but they try to give people confidence that only citizens will be voting."
Pingree said Mainers should be proud of the elections here.
"I think the good thing about our elections is they really are run at the local level. You know, your town clerk, you know your city clerk who's running the election," she said. "They do it safely and securely. We have absentee voting. So I think people should feel good about elections in Maine. We have huge voter turnout."
Senate candidates
The midterms are high stakes for both parties. Democrats are hoping to take the majority in Congress, heading into President Trump's final two years in office. Republicans, who hold the majority in both chambers, want to keep it.
The highly anticipated Senate race has been closely watched for months. Senator Susan Collins is seeking a historic sixth term in Washington. Democrat Troy Jackson replaced Graham Platner as the party's nominee in late July after Platner dropped out following a sexual assault allegation he denies. Jackson, seeking to help Democrats flip the U.S. Senate.
Jackson says elections are very safe and secure in Maine. However, he raises concerns for other states, saying it's harder to vote for some people.
He also says Republican candidate for governor Bobby Charles' pitch for immigration enforcement to be at the polls is just a way to ensure low voter turnout.
"I didn't see any election wrongdoing happening when I was a Republican, I didn't see any wrongdoing when I was independent and I don't see any as a Democrat," Jackson said. "I mean, it's a very small amount of people that try and vote. And, you know, typically they get caught doing it when they do. So I feel very good about our system here in Maine."
Collins said she is troubled by the Newburgh ballot situation, where roughly 250 ballots were incorrectly delivered, ending up at a Mainer's house in 2025.
The senator says she does not want to put additional restrictions on absentee ballot voting, saying it's really important for voters to have that option.
"I do believe, however, that when someone goes to register to vote for the first time, they should show proof of citizenship because only Americans should be voting in American elections," Collins said.
Candidates for Congress in Maine's 1st District
The race for Maine's 1st Congressional District is a rematch. Army veteran Ron Russell is challenging Congresswoman Chellie Pingree for her seat in Washington.
Pingree has held the CD1 seat for nearly two decades. Russell ran against her back in 2024, but lost.
Russell secured the Republican nomination back in June, defeating newcomer Joshua James Pietrowicz.
Congresswoman Pingree, who is fighting to keep her seat, says Maine does a good job conducting its elections. However, she also says she doesn't trust President Trump since she says he has fought back in the past based on election results.
Pingree says she's been telling voters to cast their ballot early at their local town office.
"I know we will do everything we can to keep them safe, but we are not taking it for granted and that's a bizarre thing to say as an American citizen," Pingree said. "But we are worried about the president interfering with elections, and we're going to do everything we can to protect them."
Russell says Maine elections are generally secure, but he wants voters to show proof of citizenship and photo ID when voting. He says if he's elected, he'll do what he can to get that change passed, saying non-citizens should not be voting in American elections.
"Whoever controls the majority in the legislature in Maine controls the secretary of state, the auditor and the attorney general, those positions," Russell said. "So those are pretty important positions in Maine government. So there could have been a significant impact there as a result of fraud in our last elections."
Candidates for Congress in Maine's 2nd District
The race for Maine's 2nd Congressional District began when Congressman Jared Golden still planned to run for his seat.
Former two-time Republican Governor Paul LePage got in the race to take on Golden. LePage was uncontested in the primary. Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap filed paperwork to primary Golden.
Golden eventually left the race, and three other candidates got in to primary Dunlap.
Dunlap won in a four-way ranked-choice voting primary in June to take on LePage.
Dunlap used to be the Secretary of State and oversaw elections in Maine for years. He credited the Maine Legislature with making sure elections are free, fair and secure.
"I had a great working relationship with all of our town clerks, who actually are the election administrators. The warden and the individual polling station hold all the power in our elections and our job was to support them," he said. "I think that Maine voters could feel very good about this upcoming election, the way it's going to be conducted, because of their local election officials."
LePage overlapped with Dunlap when he was governor and Dunlap was secretary of state. LePage agreed with Dunlap in that the clerks and local election officials do a great job, but said he does not trust Secretary of State Shenna Bellows and his opponent did not enforce election laws when he was in that position.
"He refused to enforce election laws on campuses. I mean, we sent him ballots and he refused to enforce them," LePage said, recalling when Dunlap was secretary of state while he was governor. "Now, in Maine, if you go to college from out of state and you want to register to vote, you have to have your license, your registration, your hunting and fishing license, like, everything's going to be changed to Maine if you're calling it your residence while you're in college. He refused to enforce that."

title: Bangor will offer free bus rides on Election Day
text:

title: Republican ads call Troy Jackson's family corrupt. Are they?
text:
Mainers have almost certainly seen the ads accusing Troy Jackson of corruption. There are nearly $14 million worth of them blanketing state’s airwaves.
Republicans nationwide have used personal attacks prominently in their campaign messaging. Last week, Ohio Republicans aired an ad featuring a Democratic candidate’s estranged parent calling her a liar. In Texas, Republicans used AI-generated ads to take aim at a Democratic candidate’s Christian faith.
Now, as Maine’s U.S. Senate race heats up, Sen. Susan Collins and allied super PACs have looked to label her Democratic challenger as “a creep” and his family as “corrupt.”
“Special interests paid Jackson’s son. And Jackson pushed their agenda,” one ad states.
“Troy Jackson’s family got paid. We got played,” says a female voiceover in another.
But many of the ads calling Jackson corrupt lean into innuendo rather than verifiable facts.
Most of the ads point to Jackson’s son Chace, who worked for years as a lobbyist in Augusta while his father was Senate president.
But while Chace Jackson’s line of work and his father’s position may give the impression of a conflict of interest, there have been no complaints lodged with the state ethics commission regarding the Jackson family, according to its assistant director, Martha Currier.
“As far as we’ve seen, there’s been nothing — no red flags or anything like that,” Currier said.
Still, ethics experts say politicians generally should avoid behavior that even raises the appearance of a conflict of interest — regardless of whether they actually violated ethics rules or norms.
“The concern we have is not even necessarily that there’s this improper behavior,” said Delaney Marsco, director of ethics at Campaign Legal Center, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit that offers guidance to candidates and advocates for stricter ethics laws locally and nationally.
“It’s more the question of access and influence, and who gets that?” she said. “And in this case, it could raise the appearance that because he’s the son of a powerful legislator, (Chace) gets better access, more influence than other people do.”
Chace Jackson did not respond to requests for comment. Troy Jackson’s campaign called the ads misleading and claimed Republicans are attacking Jackson’s family because they are “unable to defend (Collins’) voting record.”
“Susan Collins and her allies are dragging Troy’s son through the mud with ads that fall apart as soon as anyone checks the facts,” campaign spokesperson Maggie Amjad said in a statement. “Mainers deserve an honest debate about the candidates’ records.”
The Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican super PAC that has spent millions of dollars producing and airing ads accusing Troy Jackson of corruption, did not respond to requests for comment.
SOUTH PORTLAND POLLUTION
The Senate Leadership Fund has spent nearly $3 million on one ad claiming a company hired Chace Jackson to lobby against a bill that would have cracked down on emissions during his father’s tenure as Senate president.
“With Jackson in charge, the bill went up in smoke,” the voiceover says. “Coincidence or corruption?”
The ad’s claims omit important context about the legislation and Troy Jackson’s role in its defeat — or lack thereof.
It cites a 2019 Portland Press Herald article about legislation drafted in response to a South Portland petroleum tank farm violating emissions standards. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency knew the tanks had been exceeding emissions limits for years, but the extent of the pollution only became public after the owners settled with the federal government in 2019.
A pair of bills meant to address the problem were introduced into the Maine Legislature shortly after. The company that owned the tank farm, Global Partners LP, retained the Maine law firm Preti Flaherty to lobby in the State House that year.
Chace Jackson and the firm lobbied on both bills. The first, which required state regulators to notify municipalities when the EPA issued a notice locally, was signed into law. The second, which would have strengthened emissions testing, was killed in committee — but there is no evidence that was because of work done by either Jackson.
Troy Jackson was not on the Environment and Natural Resources Committee that considered and ultimately killed the proposal, which was also opposed by a number of other groups, including the Maine Department of Environmental Protection. Global Partners LP did not submit testimony for or against either bill.
SLF ads also claim Chace Jackson “raked in almost $200,000 from special interests.” But that total was paid to the firm he worked for over the course of the entire session: Not to Chace specifically.
State law doesn’t require lobbying firms to break down their associates’ pay, noted Currier, with the state ethics commission. As a result, she said there’s “no way for us to know” how much Chace Jackson was paid. Still, it’s unlikely it was anywhere near the total cited on the contract and in the ads.
MAINE MARITIME ACADEMY
One of SLF’s largest ad buys lays out a bombastic, and false, claim: Troy Jackson steered $13.4 million in taxpayer funding toward one of his son’s clients.
The Maine Maritime Academy, a public college in the coastal town of Castine, had retained Chace Jackson as a legislative liaison before a bill was introduced to bolster the school’s funding in 2024.
The bill would have given the academy some $13 million to offset rising inflation. It was a bipartisan effort. Troy Jackson was one of 10 legislators from both parties who co-sponsored it.
While the bill passed the Senate, it ultimately died in the House. The Maine Maritime Academy received no additional funding from the legislation — a far cry from the $13.4 million SLF PAC’s ad claims.
Still, Marsco with the Campaign Legal Center said Troy Jackson co-sponsoring a bill that his son lobbied for leaves the impression of unethical behavior.
“Here, again, there’s no evidence of illegality,” Marsco said. “But if somebody is getting special access or special influence by virtue of their family ties, that raises concerns in the minds of the public.”
The TV spot also distorts unrelated news reports to further its claims. In the first, a WGME anchor describes “allegations of fraud and wrongdoing.” The second clips a News Center Maine reporter saying “rot and corruption in Augusta.” But neither clip has anything to do with the Jacksons or the bill.
AROOSTOOK CELL TOWER
The SLF PAC started airing an ad last weekend that calls Jackson a “crook and a creep” and references a claim that he made a deal with communications company to get a cellphone tower put on his in-laws’ land.
“The taxpayer dough secured by Jackson is now exposed as a sleazy deal with Jackson’s cousins, who are also his in-laws,” the ad’s voiceover says. Troy Jackson and his partner are reportedly second cousins, which means they share a great-grandparent. Their relationship is legal across the country.
The ad’s portrayal of how the cell tower deal came about and where the money came from is disputed by those involved in it.
The company behind the tower, Wireless Partners LLC, used a $180,000 grant from the Maine Connectivity Authority to build it in December 2022.
But the Maine Connectivity Authority’s president, Andrew Butcher, said that the $180,000 didn’t come from Maine — it was federal funding secured through the American Rescue Plan Act, and it didn’t go toward a tower in Allagash.
“That funding was awarded by the MCA after board evaluation and recommendation — not due to any recommendation or involvement from Troy Jackson,” Butcher said in a statement.
Jackson did applaud the tower’s construction; he had been advocating for years to improve cell service in northern Maine, his campaign noted, which has historically been sporadic and routed through Canada.
GUN CONTROL
For much of his career, Troy Jackson was one of Maine’s most staunchly pro-gun Democrats. He had previously received support and high marks from the National Rifle Association.
That changed abruptly in 2023.
That October, a gunman killed 18 people at a bowling alley and a bar in Lewiston. It remains the deadliest mass killing in state history.
Soon after, Maine legislators began drafting bills to strengthen gun laws that could have helped prevent the killings. Jackson, then the Maine Senate President, began publicly rethinking his positions.
Shortly after, the Maine Gun Safety Alliance retained a Portland lobbying firm to garner support for a suite of gun control bills. Chace Jackson was one of the firm’s employees.
There’s no evidence that he directly influenced his father’s position. But the appearance of a conflict of interest has given Collins and PACs supporting her a line of attack.
“If you look at the number of times that Troy has flip-flopped his position on issues, it usually has to do with the issues that his son has been hired to lobby him on,” Collins said during an Oct. 8 debate.
Troy Jackson has maintained since the shootings’ immediate aftermath that the carnage in Lewiston prompted his policy reversal. He reiterated that at a campaign event this month.
“Eighteen funerals changed me,” he said. “Sometimes leadership means having the guts to admit that what you believed before isn’t good enough anymore. I couldn’t look at those families and tell them nothing had to change. So I changed.”
Staff Writer Billy Kobin contributed to this story.

title: 15-year-old arrested in connection with mass shooting after Florida homecoming, police say
text:
TALLAHASSEE, Fla. (WCTV/Gray News) – A 15-year-old was arrested in connection with a mass shooting that took place near Florida A&M University’s Bragg Memorial Stadium Saturday night.
Police Chief Lawrence Revell announced Monday morning during a press conference that Anthony Rivers III was charged with 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent.
At least 11 people were shot and injured, including six minors who, the chief said, did not appear to be the intended targets. The youngest victim was 11 years old. Revell said he believes one of the victims is a FAMU student.
“It is incredibly troubling when violence of this magnitude occurs in the very community I grew up in,” Revell said.
The shooting happened just hours after a homecoming football game at Bragg Memorial Stadium, where the visiting Arkansas-Pine Bluff Golden Lions beat the Rattlers, but it is unclear whether the shooting was related to the game.
Police believe the shooting likely stemmed from a fight between two or three people.

title: Judge rules Maurene Comey, daughter of ex-FBI director, was unlawfully fired by Trump administration
text:
Judge rules Maurene Comey, daughter of ex-FBI director, was unlawfully fired by Trump administration
The Trump administration last year illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, from her job as a federal prosecutor in New York, a federal judge ruled Monday.
Maurene Comey, who was an assistant U.S. attorney for a decade, was illegally fired in July 2025 despite her work on some of the nation's highest-profile cases and consistently receiving “the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike," Judge Jesse M. Furman found.
After her firing, Comey sued the Justice Department and others, saying her termination violated the constitutional separation of powers, the First Amendment and the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment.
She asserted that she was fired because she was the daughter of James Comey, whom President Donald Trump has long viewed as an enemy, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, the judge noted.
Furman rejected the government's claim that Comey could be fired because federal prosecutors exercise the president's “conclusive and preclusive” powers.
He said the government's claim that Congress is barred from regulating the removal of federal prosecutors “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent."
Furman added: “Indeed, to accept Defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.”
The firing violated the separation of powers, the Administrative Procedure Act and her Fifth Amendment due process and statutory rights, the judge ruled.
Furman reserved judgment on Comey's First Amendment claim pending further arguments to be submitted by each side, though he said he was inclined to dismiss the claim because it was largely moot since she is now in private practice and no longer seeks actual reinstatement.
The judge granted Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay from the date of her firing through Dec. 20 to “make her whole” and ensure that she doesn't suffer adverse employment consequences for the “unlawful termination.”
Comey’s lawyers, Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan, lauded the ruling.
“This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law,” they said in a statement. “As the Court correctly held, to accept the government’s argument about unlimited executive power ‘would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.’ This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law.”
The Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment.
The Justice Department during the Trump administration has fired scores of career employees, including prosecutors and FBI agents, who participated in investigations of President Donald Trump or who were perceived as opposed to the administration’s agenda. Some of those firings have also resulted in federal lawsuits.
The firing of Maurene Comey was seen as particularly personal, given her father’s longtime adversarial relationship with Trump.
The president fired James Comey as FBI director in May 2017 as the bureau was investigating ties between Russia and the Republican’s successful 2016 campaign for the White House. Trump in the years since has repeatedly called for Comey to be jailed, and his Justice Department has worked with mixed success to make that happen.
An earlier criminal case accusing James Comey of having lied to Congress in 2020 was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who filed the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47,” a case he has sought to dismiss that some legal experts have greeted with skepticism.

title: 6 citizens sue Trump, saying media ban deprives them of news as audience stakeholders
text:
In the increasingly bitter legal standoff between President Donald Trump and media outlets whose reporting he dislikes, a new and crucial third party has emerged: citizens who watch and read the news and need it to do their jobs.
A lawsuit filed Monday on behalf of six such citizens — effectively representing the audiences for the news media — argues that it’s not only the rights of news organizations that are violated when Trump bans them from White House premises. Even more fundamentally, the lawsuit argues, such bans violate the public’s right to independent reporting about its president and government.
“The ultimate injury here … is to the democratic public,” says the suit, filed in federal district court in New York against Trump and three key aides, including the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles.
“The First Amendment protects the public’s right to know what its government is doing,” said Katie Fallow, deputy litigation director at the Knight First Amendment Institute, which filed the lawsuit on behalf of the six plaintiffs, along with the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic at Yale Law School.
“The White House cannot decide what information Americans receive by punishing critical reporting,” Fallow said in a statement. “When the White House expels reporters because of their coverage and threatens others with expulsion, it isn’t just the press that suffers — the public loses access to independent reporting and gets something closer to government propaganda.”
The plaintiffs all rely on White House news for their work
The six plaintiffs are all people who say they rely on independent and diverse White House reporting for their teaching, journalism or advocacy. They include a noted human rights advocate, a political journalist, a Yale history professor, a high school civics teacher, a legal journalist, and a student journalist at the University of Pennsylvania.
The complaint filed Monday recounts how various news organizations that have been targeted by Trump are already battling the administration in the courts. These cases include the current lawsuit by CNN, MS NOW and Politico, whose journalists were banished from the White House in September.
A ederal judge recently extended an order preventing the White House from enforcing the ban while the case makes its way through the legal system. Still affected, though, is CNN’s pool coverage of Trump. The White House has been denying the network its usual slots in the video pool covering the president’s activities and travel, and CNN has threatened further action.
Also continuing is the legal case involving The Associated Press, whose reporters were barred last year from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some events in retaliation for the outlet’s decision not to follow Trump’s lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters, to the Gulf of America.
The New York Times is also involved in litigation, over a Pentagon policy requiring escorts for journalists on its grounds. And ABC is fighting back against the Trump administration in a dispute over renewal of its broadcast licenses.
This lawsuit seeks more wide-ranging relief
The new lawsuit filed Monday, though, is different from previous legal action against the president — first, in that the plaintiffs are ordinary citizens. And it seeks more wide-ranging relief.
The suit, which names Trump as defendant along with Wiles, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, and Secret Service Director Sean M. Curran, calls not only for reinstatement of access that has already been impacted, but for a broad injunction that would protect from retaliation every news outlet that covers the White House.
The complaint says: “Defendants’ policy of restricting the access of disfavored news organizations deprives the public of the reporting of those organizations, and it inevitably deprives them of the independent reporting of other news organizations as well, since every journalist who reports from the White House must now account for the possibility that a critical or ill-advised word about the president may result in their access being summarily restricted or revoked.”
“Plaintiffs … seek a declaration that the policy is unconstitutional because it imposes restrictions on a limited public forum that are viewpoint-based and unreasonable. They also seek an injunction barring defendants from enforcing the policy.”
Plaintiffs include a human rights advocate, a teacher and a student journalist
The plaintiffs are:
—Kenneth Roth, former longtime executive director of Human Rights Watch and a lecturer at Yale’s law school and school of global affairs. Roth “relies on newsgathering and reporting from members of the White House press corps to inform his public writing and commentary,” the suit says.
—Daniel Froomkin, media and political journalist and editor of Press Watch, a nonprofit that encourages political journalists to “fulfill their essential mission of creating an informed electorate and holding the powerful accountable.”
—Beverly Gage, Pulitzer Prize-winning historian and professor at Yale University who “relies on newsgathering and reporting from the White House press corps to inform her scholarship, public writing and commentary.”
—Peter Schmidt-Nowara, a social studies teacher at a New York City high school, who teaches civics courses and considers White House reporting “essential to his work as an educator.”
—Benjamin Wittes, editor-in-chief of Lawfare and a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, whose publication is “especially reliant on the White House press corps to provide accurate and timely coverage of the president.”
—Ethan Young, a student at the University of Pennsylvania and editor-in-chief of The Daily Pennsylvanian, who, as a student journalist, “relies on a diverse, independent and trustworthy cohort of White House reporters to serve as his proxy.”
Schmidt-Nowara, who teaches at Brooklyn Technical High School, is quoted in the lawsuit as saying: “As a social studies teacher, I want my students to have access to accurate, independent reporting about their government.” He adds he is “gravely concerned that the Trump administration’s restrictions on White House reporters are cutting off access to crucial information.
“I joined this lawsuit because my students deserve to know what’s happening in their government and to hear from a free and independent press,” he says.
Young, the student journalist, contends that since he can’t personally access White House press spaces, he relies on “a diverse, independent and trustworthy cohort” of White House reporters to serve as his proxy.
The effect of federal policy changes has been “acutely felt on college campuses, Penn’s included,” Young is quoted as saying. “As a student journalist, I rely on reporting from the White House press corps to understand the decisions made in Washington, their consequences, and how they impact my college community. A vibrant free press allows me to do just that.”

title: Co-founder of Firehouse Subs, Chris Sorensen, dies at 65
text:
Co-founder of Firehouse Subs, Chris Sorensen, dies at 65
A former firefighter and co-founder of an American restaurant chain has died at the age of 65.
The Jacksonville Fire and Rescue Department said in a post on Facebook that Chris Sorensen followed in his father's footsteps and became a firefighter, later opening Firehouse Subs with his brother.
"Before his business accomplishments, Chris was first and foremost a firefighter. Following in the footsteps of his father, Rob 'Captain Video' Sorensen, Chris began his JFRD career on March 14, 1988, before launching Firehouse Subs in 1994. He retired at the rank of Engineer four years later," the department said. "In 2005, he volunteered alongside his father and brother in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina, and that experience led to the creation of the Firehouse Subs Public Safety Foundation, turning a commitment to disaster relief into a lasting mission to support first responders."
The Firehouse Subs Public Safety Foundation, the department said, has helped equip fire departments and public safety agencies across the country with lifesaving equipment and critical resources.
According to Sorensen's obituary, the foundation has awarded more than $118 million in grants to 7,700 departments in the United States and Canada.
In 1994, Chris co-founded Firehouse Subs with his brother, Robin. The first location opened in their hometown of Jacksonville, Florida.
After being sold in 2021 for $1 billion to Restaurant Brands International, which also owns Burger King, the Firehouse Subs fleet grew to more than 1,200 locations.

title: Aging Untold: What it really takes to repair old family wounds
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we discuss what genuine family reconciliation looks like when aging parents and adult children work to heal old wounds.
Then we break down the vital role of protein for healthy aging and share practical ways to maintain muscle, energy and strength.
Plus, we take you to Vermont’s Lake Champlain to meet an 83-year-old marina owner preserving more than two centuries of living history.
Family estrangement can be complicated.
Repairing relationships between aging parents and adult children takes more than good intentions, according to the Aging Untold experts.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said her advice for a parent who may have caused the pain is to own it, and Dr. Rhea Rogers said a genuine apology requires more than saying sorry.
Protein is an important part of supporting strength, healing and independence as we age, but older adults might not get enough.
Dr. Rogers said some health conditions affect how much protein an individual should have, and the amount you consume should be discussed with a primary care doctor first.
“There’s going to be certain states that you cannot afford that much protein, like kidney disease and things like that,” she said.
The Aging Untold experts urge people to read labels.
Rogers said it is important to know the source of your protein because some protein shakes spike insulin levels.
Jeorgi Golden spent 35 years in salons, working as a Black hairstylist while coworkers and clients became family.
Golden said salon workers in those days received minimal safety guidance about products and how they should be applied.
She said no one ever mentioned the dangers, even though formaldehyde was an ingredient found in those products. Formaldehyde is classified as a carcinogen by the EPA.
Studies now show that toxic gas poses serious health risks to both consumers and salon workers, linking exposure to eye problems, respiratory issues, and even certain types of cancer.
Pat Ullom, 83, and her son have run Chipman Point Marina, a piece of Vermont’s maritime past, for more than 30 years.
In the 1800s, the area on one of the narrowest points on Lake Champlain was a busy maritime community. Boats once unloaded cargo right into the marina’s main stone building, which was built in 1810.
The building next door was built in 1824, and it has operated as a store for almost 100 years.

title: The Dos and Don’ts of Howl-o-ween
text:
Halloween may be the spookiest night of the year, and keeping our kids safe is a given. We check costumes, remind them to say thank you and inspect the candy haul. But what about the other members of the family? The ones with four legs, curious noses and absolutely no idea why a skeleton is ringing the doorbell?
In Maine, where late October can bring anything from a crisp, clear evening to cold rain, wind or even an early taste of winter, keeping pets safe deserves a little planning, too.
The ASPCA Poison Control Center (aspca.org) recommends some simple precautions to keep four-legged family members safe and out of trouble.
No tricks, no treats
Kids may think they’ve found the perfect hiding place for their Halloween stash, but a dog’s nose is hard to fool. Chocolate, particularly dark and baking chocolate, can be dangerous for dogs and cats. Sugar-free candy containing xylitol can also cause serious problems.
Keep candy, trick-or-treat bags and wrappers out of reach, and remind kids that sharing their loot with the family pet is never a good idea, no matter how convincing those puppy-dog eyes may be.
When the doorbell gets scary
Doorbells, excited children and strangers dressed as ghosts, witches and who-knows-what-else can be stressful for pets. Consider setting up a quiet, comfortable room away from the front door during peak trick-or-treating hours.
Add a favorite bed, toys or treats to keep them occupied and away from the activity.
Decorations deserve attention, too. A glowing jack-o’-lantern looks great on a Maine porch, but candles and curious paws aren’t a good combination. Consider battery-operated candles, and keep cords, wires and small decorations out of reach.
Getting into costume
Not every pet dreams of becoming a moose, Lady Gaga or Buzz Lightyear for Halloween. If your dog or cat doesn’t enjoy dressing up, skip the costume. A festive bandanna or collar may be all the Halloween spirit they need.
If your pet does tolerate a costume, make sure it doesn’t restrict movement, vision or breathing. Check for dangling pieces that could be chewed off or swallowed, and give the costume a trial run before the big night.
Human costume accessories can be tempting, too. Small plastic pieces, fake jewelry and other props can become choking hazards for curious pets.
No disappearing acts
Halloween means more people on the streets, open doors and unfamiliar sights and sounds. Even a pet that normally sticks close to home can become frightened and bolt. Make sure your pet has current identification, and keep dogs securely leashed outside. Reflective collars, harnesses or other visibility gear are particularly helpful after dark.
If you suspect your pet has eaten something toxic, contact your veterinarian or the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center at 888-426-4435 immediately.
Did your pet dress up for Halloween? If so, send a picture to [email protected] with their name and your contact information to be entered to win a family four-pack of movie tickets to Nordica Theatre in Freeport.

title: Bodycam video shows moments after parents say cops were called on 3-year-old for being ‘too good’ at soccer
text:
WINTER PARK, Fla. (Gray News) — Parents in Florida claim their 3-year-old son had the police called on him because he was too good at soccer.
A viral Instagram video posted by the parents shows 3-year-old Nevada playing in a soccer game. Nevada can be seen dribbling the ball and scoring goals.
Then, the video shows police officers on the field as Nevada’s father says, “They called police on a 3-year-old ‘cause he’s too good.”
The parents later claimed that Nevada was kicked out of the i9 Sports league for the same reason.
The video gathered thousands of comments.
“Why would police waste their time responding to this?” one user wondered.
“This level of ridiculousness shouldn’t have happened to him, however his future looks very bright since he’s obviously a born champion,” another wrote.
Gray News obtained body camera video from Winter Park police that shows more of the story. Responding officers are shown speaking with a coach who said the boy’s parents were causing a disturbance.
“So, the kid is good, right? He’s great. Real good. So, what happened is, he’s very advanced compared to the other ones. So, he scores a lot of goals, but he’s pushing the other kids … so I try to tell him, play without pushing, right?” the coach said.
He continues, “There was like six kids on the team. I swap the kids out, because he’s so good I take him out, everyone deserves their time … They [the parents] don’t like that. They tell me I’m ignorant, I’m this, I’m that, blah blah blah … I just want them out. Immediately.”
The video then shows the two officers speaking with the boy’s parents, who dispute the coach’s account.
“I guess he was calling because I guess he believes that you guys were causing a disturbance that was interfering with the gameplay,” one officer told the parents.
“They’re mad at my son because he actually plays soccer. So I’m a little confused and I’m a little baffled because I signed my kid up for soccer. So they’re literally kicking him out of this place because he’s good at soccer,” the boy’s mother said.
“He specifically mentioned that your son is very good, but he doesn’t like how the parents become aggressive,” the officer said.
After speaking with officers, the parents agreed to leave the park with their son.
A police event report obtained by Gray News said, “Parents left field without issue and were cooperative with request of league personnel.”
The event report goes on to say, “Parents were upset that their child was being scorned for playing too well and was being taken out of game.”
One officer can be heard laughing at the end of the video and saying, “I kinda want to see him play. I bet he’s good.”
A news release from Winter Park police said:
“The Winter Park Police Department was contacted by a soccer league official who requested response to a disturbance between league officials and the parents of a player. The league requested the family leave and offered to refund the league cost to family. Shortly after arrival, the officers were requested by the league official to communicate with the family as he did not want to further a disturbance. The family stated the game was over and they were leaving. The family was cooperative with the officers and were provided with an event number for the incident at their request. The incident was a civil matter between those parties and not criminal. No one was arrested, trespassed, or forced to leave the park. The Officers body worn cameras confirm the above information.”

title: I regret voting for Susan Collins
text:
Despite years of Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s anti-vaccine rhetoric, Sen. Susan Collins voted to confirm him for secretary of health and human services — based on personal assurances that he would “trust the science.” Since then, he mass-fired the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention vaccine advisory panel. Collins, meanwhile, tells us she does not regret her vote.
Despite years of Brett Kavanaugh’s demonstrating he might have the capacity to overturn Roe v. Wade, Collins voted to confirm him based on private, personal assurances to her that he considered Roe v. Wade “established law.” He later voted to overturn it. Collins does not regret that vote, either.
Despite years of voting in sync with President Trump and her recent knee-jerk endorsement of ultra-conservative candidates Paul LePage for U.S. Congress and Bobby Charles for governor, Collins has given assurances to Mainers that she will conduct herself in a bipartisan manner and will be independent of Trump.
I voted for Susan Collins once. I regret that vote.
Fred Wolff
Cumberland

title: Expect Hearts of Pine to make sweeping roster changes for 2027
text:
PORTLAND — The Portland Hearts of Pine season finale Saturday showed what Fitzpatrick Stadium can be like with a winning team.
It was a wonderous night of fun and exciting soccer by the home team. A 4-1 victory against Charlotte Independence, the top team in USL League One. A storybook finish for retiring captain Mikey Lopez. Exciting goals. Gritty defense. A fervent packed house.
It was also the exception during the third-tier soccer franchise’s second season. Only the fans showed up every game. The team was 6-7-3 at home and finished 8-14-10 overall, finishing a disappointing 14th in the 17-team league, 12 points out of the playoffs.
Now it’s time to start building for 2027 and figuring out how to make sure the Hearts of Pine won’t field a team that concedes tying or winning goals in 12 matches as in 2026, when they coughed up 26 potential points.
The roster will “see a decent amount of turnover,” in 2027, sporting director Ray Saari said in an interview last Thursday.
A major overhaul is more likely. Roster turnover is a way of life in USL1, with most players on one-year contracts with the club having an option to renew. In 2025, Portland re-signed just 12 of 25 players when their contacts expired in November, and that was after going 12-8-12 and ending one goal shy of reaching the championship game.
The Portland Press Herald predicts that at most 11 of the current 28 players will be back (see below).
WHAT IS THE CLUB LOOKING FOR?
Saari said some players are already signed for 2027 but would not identify them. Sources have said Felipe Rodriguez Gentile, who just turned 20, signed for 2027 when he left a club in England and joined the Hearts in August. Gentile scored two goals in 10 matches.
Saari did say he’s looking to add veterans of United States leagues “down the spine” of the field with proven ability to manage late-game situations.
“I’ve found in my experience in the USL, there’s no metric that outlasts good character and being on a winning team consistently,” Saari said.
After the win Saturday, Murphy noted he needs to evaluate “all policies and procedures,” in part to try to determine why so many Hearts of Pine players suffered injuries this season.
“Do we have to revamp what we do preseason? (The) offseason? Everything is under the microscope because the fans deserve to have a home playoff game,” Murphy said.
Saari, Murphy and rest of the Hearts of Pine must make their decisions by Nov. 15.
WHO WILL BE BACK: ONE WRITER’S OPINION
No player on the 2026 Hearts of Pine was so outstanding that he absolutely must be retained. There are seven we think are “Very Likely to Return”: injured standouts Masashi Wada and Ollie Wright, goalkeeper Hunter Morse, midfielders Matteo Kidd, Diego Letayf Escutia, and Rodriguez Gentile, and striker Aboubacar Camara.
Wada suffered a lower-leg fracture on April 11 in the home opener. Wright had late September surgery to repair the torn ACL in his right knee. Wada might be ready when the 2027 season begins in March. Wright is out until the end of June/early July, possibly longer.
Both Wada and Wright were all-USL1 players in 2025. That’s the main reason to extend their contract, if it wasn’t already guaranteed.
There is also a public relations reason. The Hearts of Pine have promoted and proven by their actions that they care about their players. Releasing Wada or Wright is a bad look for a club that carefully curates its image.
Camara is an impressive finisher, scoring 10 USL1 goals on 33 shots, with the potential to improve. Kidd, a player Murphy trusts, was the team’s most consistent, tenacious player and versatile. Letayf Escutia might seem like an odd choice, but he went from college, to pre-professional USL2, to practice player, to Portland starter in a matter of months. He is a tough defender who adds depth, likely at the league minimum salary.
Morse comes with a caveat. He’s led the league in saves two years running, a function of being exposed to counter-attacks because of Murphy’s preferred pressing system. It doesn’t seem unreasonable that Morse might desire a different, more defense-first system.
MAYBE PORTLAND, MAYBE NOT
Six players are in this group. Up to four could return.
Portland gave up the fourth-most goals in USL1. That doesn’t bode well for the three main center backs,, Brecc Evans, Kemali Green and Serigne Faye. It’s difficult to think more than one returns.
Faye had the best tackle (76.2%) and duel (62.9%) rates but played the least. Green had the worst stats of the three. Evans was Portland’s pivotal offseason acquisition after his second-team all-USL1 with FC Naples in 2025, but did not perform to that standard.
Right back Mo Mohamed is most likely to return from this group. The only reason he’s not in the “Very Likely to Return” group is he was released last November, only to be re-signed in the preseason. Mohamed was Portland’s most consistent back four performer. His confidence only went up after a September call-up to the Somalia national team. In the Africa Nations Cup, Mohamed successfully went toe-to-toe for a half with Yan Diomande of Ivory Coast. Diomande had recently signed a seven-year contract with Real Madrid.
Kamara (4 goals, 6 assists in 2026) can be a game-changer with his offensive skills. Portland likes having him as a strong, hard-running target at the top of the offense. That injuries limited him to seven games makes his return uncertain.
SAYING GOODBYE TO PORTLAND
Lopez has already said his farewell to the game. That leaves 14 more players unlikely to return.
Midfielder Diego Gonzalez impressed with nine goals and two assists in 21 games but was on loan from Houston Dynamo.
Michel Poon-Angeron and Diogo Barbosa were two regulars in Portland’s midfield. There just wasn’t enough ball-winning in that portion of the field. Similarly, midseason acquisitions Eiji Hata and Josh Drack played a lot at outside back but were not difference makers.
Several other players, whether because of injury, ability or a combination of both, failed to grab consistent playing time on a struggling team. Backup keeper Kash Oladapo; defenders Jaden Jones-Riley, Zion Scarlett and Esteban Espinosa; midfielders Khalid Hersi of Lewiston, Konstantinos Georgallides and Bowdoin College grad Tyler Huck; and forwards Walter Varela and Lagos Kunga were unable to make a compelling case to be retained.

title: Woman accused of driving under the influence, using son as shield after school bus chase
text:
Police: Woman uses son as shield after school bus chase
A South Carolina woman who led authorities on a chase in a school bus is accused of using her young son as a shield when she eventually stopped for authorities.
The North Charleston Police Department said on Thursday, officials received an alert that a school bus was traveling along Palmetto Commerce Parkway in an erratic manner. The incident was reported around 3:30 p.m. 
The bus reportedly almost crashed into another vehicle, with the driver believed to be impaired.
Related video: ATM theft suspect on video throws cash out the window during police chase
Officials identified the driver as Shakira Jones.
Authorities were able to locate the bus, which was traveling 65 miles per hour in a posted 45 miles per hour zone. Jones was also said to be making erratic lane changes.
Jones failed to stop when police made an attempt to pull her over.
She was said to have accelerated into a parking lot where school staff had to take cover and run from the bus, police stated.
Bus eventually stops
After the bus came to a final stop, officers continued issuing commands, but Jones refused to exit, according to police.
Police said Jones placed a child in front of her in an apparent attempt to shield herself from officers. Officers safely removed the child and tried to take Jones into custody. After a brief struggle, she was arrested, authorities said.
Investigators later determined that the child aboard the bus was Jones' son. He was eventually turned over to a relative.
During the investigation, officers also reportedly found a bottle of prescribed amphetamines among Jones' personal belongings within arm's reach of the driver's seat.
Police said Jones consented to standardized field sobriety tests, and the officer who administered them concluded that there was probable cause that she had been driving while impaired.
Jones was taken to the Al Cannon Detention Center and charged with failure to stop for emergency responders, driving under the influence, and child endangerment.

title: Former Lisbon lettuce grower Springworks Farm sold for $1.1 million at auction
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LISBON — Springworks Farm was sold at auction Friday to an anonymous private investor from Lisbon for $1.1 million.
The investor, who declined to disclose his name, said he didn’t have any immediate plans for the property.
Springworks Farm was a thriving aquaponics farm in Lisbon that sold to a host of grocery stores and schools, and was the exclusive supplier of organic and other lettuce to Hannaford from 2021 until earlier this year.
The auction was for the farm of 168 acres, two abutting lots, 117,000 square feet of greenhouse growing space, 56,000 square feet of light industrial buildings, and all related equipment.
The auctioneer opened bidding at $6 million. After a silence, one of the few bidders in the room offered $500,000. Auction principles gathered in another room and returned with the auctioneer announcing that the one bidder had agreed to raise his bid to $1 million.
Bidding then picked up between the initial bidder and the anonymous private investor, who eventually won with a bid of $1.1 million.
“The town of Lisbon has been wonderful to deal with through this whole scenario,” said Mike Carey, co-owner of Tranzon Auction Properties, which handled the auction. “They care about what happens in their community. We’re happy to see that property go to a third-party and there will be continued use here.”
Springworks founder Trevor Kenkel purchased the land for the farm in June 2014 for $457,500. Efforts to reach him were unsuccessful.
At its peak, the farm supplied all 184 Hannaford stores with baby romaine lettuce and Boston bibb, plus an assortment of pre-cut products in select stores, including single cut romaine, single cut Boston bibb, and salad mix.
The farm also sold products to Whole Foods, Roche Bros. Supermarkets, Food City, Sysco of Northern New England, Lisbon K-12 schools, and other local institutions.

title: Yucktober: Todd, Alyssa, & Joy try spruce gum
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The WABI morning crew has stumbled upon a few interesting food combinations for this year’s Yucktober edition.
Their latest adventure, spruce gum, came from a viewer.
Joy, Todd, and Alyssa had no knowledge of this treat, and so, they called on former colleague Wayne Harvey to help them out.
Spruce gum is the hardened resin harvested from spruce trees, particularly black and red spruce, that was traditionally chewed as a natural chewing gum in New England and Atlantic Canada.
Indigenous peoples and early settlers collected the amber-colored resin as it oozed from bark cuts, letting it harden before chewing for its piney, slightly bitter flavor. It became commercially popular in Maine in the 19th century before being largely replaced by manufactured chicle-based gum.

title: Lawrence McCutcheon, 5-time Pro Bowl running back for Los Angeles Rams, dies at 76
text:
Lawrence McCutcheon, 5-time Pro Bowl running back for Los Angeles Rams, dies at 76
Lawrence McCutcheon, a five-time Pro Bowl running back for the Los Angeles Rams who went on to a long career in the team's front office, died Friday. He was 76.
McCutcheon's family announced his death through the Rams. In a statement, the family said McCutcheon had "a long, courageous battle with Parkinson's disease."
McCutcheon played his first eight NFL seasons for the Rams, who drafted him out of Colorado State in 1972. The native of Plainview, Texas, quickly emerged as one of the most dynamic running backs of the 1970s, earning a Pro Bowl selection and leading the Rams in rushing each year from 1973 to 1977 in coach Chuck Knox's productive offense.
McCutcheon, nicknamed "Clutch," was a second-team AP All-Pro selection in 1974.
He appeared in 11 postseason games for the Rams. In the Super Bowl in January 1980, he even threw a touchdown pass to Ron Smith to put Los Angeles ahead before the Pittsburgh Steelers rallied to win the championship.
McCutcheon was the Rams' career rushing leader when he left in 1980. After he finished his playing career with stops in Denver, Seattle and Buffalo over two seasons, McCutcheon became an executive for the Rams, eventually spending more than three decades in their front office.
McCutcheon rose to become the St. Louis Rams' director of player personnel from 2003 until his retirement in 2016, shortly before the team moved home to Los Angeles.
"Through a decade-long playing career and another 32 years in the Rams' front office, Clutch earned the respect and admiration of teammates, opposing players, colleagues and fans alike," McCutcheon's family said in its statement. "Clutch will be missed and remembered forever."
McCutcheon's son, Daylon, was a cornerback for the Cleveland Browns from 1999 to 2006. Lawrence McCutcheon's grandson, Dyson, is a defensive back at Middle Tennessee.

title: Microsoft offers 60,000 employees voluntary buyouts as AI spending accelerates
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - Microsoft has offered 60,000 employees, or about 27% of its global workforce, voluntary buyouts as the software giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence.
The company’s voluntary exit offer was available to eligible employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States, the company’s Chief People Officer Amy Coleman wrote in a blog post Monday.
“The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us,” Coleman wrote. “We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft.”
The company, which releases its quarterly financial results Wednesday, had approximately 223,000 full-time employees at the end of June.
Shares of Microsoft Corp., based in Redmond, Washington, hit an all-time high this month. The stock rose about 1% on Monday.
In May, Microsoft planned to offer buyouts to about 8,750 people, or 7% of its U.S. workforce, according to two people familiar with the plan who were not authorized to speak about it publicly. In July, the company said it was cutting 4,800 jobs, about 2.1% of its global workforce, including a large number of workers at its Xbox video game business.
The gusher of investment in data centers — likely topping $700 billion this year — to power artificial intelligence has made memory chips, computer processors and other equipment, as well as electricity, more expensive. Economists expect it will continue to push up inflation at least through the end of this year.
Microsoft has been ramping up its AI capabilities for several years. In 2024 the company revealed a new class of AI-imbued personal computers that centered on fusing its AI assistant, called Copilot, into the Windows operating system for PCs, where Microsoft already has the eyes of millions of consumers.
And in October 2025 Microsoft introduced a new artificial intelligence character called Mico, a floating cartoon face shaped like a blob or flame that embodies the software giant’s Copilot virtual assistant.

title: Jennifer Navarro will represent Brunswick taxpayers, not needless projects

text:
Brunswick’s out-of-control spending practices and zoning changes are forever changing the character of our town. The town manager has admitted there are no plans to address this. Quite the opposite — town government is spending more while wages never catch up and the cost of living rises.
Expensive projects like the recreation department facility, a new public works building and extravagant attributes that are completely elective for the Jordan Avenue rebuild, etc. — all with no regard for the taxpayer. This must stop now.
Brunswick needs a leader who’ll ensure transparency in every aspect of town government; someone who will respond to residents — not ignore inquiries for weeks or not at all. We need a fellow, concerned taxpayer, who’ll end needless spending. That person is Jennifer Navarro of Brunswick. She has a vested interested in our town and will make decisions affecting the taxpayers.
Return town spending to a concern of the elected. Vote Jennifer Navarro.
Mark Riendeau
Brunswick

title: This Maine field hockey star is one of the country’s top scorers at BU
text:
She was speaking over the phone, but Sarah Shute’s voice lit up when asked to describe Lucy Johnson’s game.
“The way that she plays is so exciting to watch,” said Shute, the first-year Boston University field hockey coach. “She’s very creative and she’s so fast. And she can shoot from anywhere, which makes her really dangerous.”
What the Maine high school field hockey scene watched unfold for four years at Cheverus is now playing out at the national level. Johnson, a sophomore forward for the Terriers, is among the top scorers in the country, tied for 12th nationally with 13 goals for a team with an 8-8 record and one regular-season game remaining.
She has been near the top of the leaderboard all season, and in mid-October was third in goals. She scored in five of BU’s first six victories.
“It’s definitely very rewarding, and really feels like all the work that I’ve done to get here has paid off,” said Johnson, a Portland native. “For a few games I was a little nervous coming into the season, seeing how it was going to go. Seeing my name in the starting lineup was definitely a little nerve-wracking at first.
“But once I settled in and just played a few games and got some more minutes in me, I was like ‘I can do everything. I’m capable of being successful.'”
Johnson has been on scoring leaderboards since arriving at Cheverus. She scored 28 goals as a freshman for a Class A championship team, set the state record with 49 goals as a sophomore, and set another Maine mark with 152 goals for her career.
But being at the top of a national list at the Division I level? Even Johnson acknowledged some surprise.
“After the Bucknell game, one of my teammates’ dads was on the phone and he was like, ‘Yeah, the announcer just said you’re second in the country.’ I was like ‘Wait, what?'” she said. “I got chills. I was very proud of myself in the moment.”
Johnson said she thinks about her teammates when she sees her name near the top of the list — teammates like her sister Lily, a junior midfielder who, like Lucy, was a Miss Maine Field Hockey winner at Cheverus, and who has played in nine games for the Terriers and started five.
“Another thought that (comes) to my head is ‘Wow, I play with such amazing people,'” Lucy Johnson said. “We all set each other up for success.”
That kind of success wasn’t there for Johnson as a freshman with the Terriers, when she played 19 games but didn’t register a point.
“It was more of a struggle with confidence. In high school it was a lot easier to be that star player, but also be a leader,” she said. “When you come to a different level where you’re playing with girls that are at the same level as you … everyone’s good. It’s kind of hard.”
Johnson said it was “motivating” to see where she needed to bring her abilities to make an impact with the Terriers. Last summer she stayed sharp by playing in weekly games at Bowdoin and Boston College. She and Lily simulated the running tests they would have to do at BU, further boosting their conditioning.
“We would either go to the gym and run on the treadmill, or we would go to the turf and do our run tests … or do repeats, just running up and down the field, or do sprint circuits,” Johnson said. “We would do some sort of running every single day. … We would run our mile test, the exact test, at least once a week or twice.”
Shute said that work paid off.
“She came into preseason really fit, so her ability to perform at a high level for a long period of time is really stellar,” she said. “At our level, it’s really unheard of to play (forward) for an entire game and not be subbed off, but she has the ability to be effective for the full 60 minutes.”
That’s given her plenty of chances to show all the skills that made her the state’s most prolific scorer. She opened the season with a pair of goals in each of the first two games against Merrimack and Providence, and added four goals in a 7-2 win over Bucknell.
“When she’s on the ball, she’s so explosive,” Shute said. “If she gets a half-step on somebody, she can cut the ball back and take it to the top of the circle and take a shot, or she keeps going. She has the ability to eliminate at a really high speed, which I think is hard to do.”
Maine saw it for years. Now the rest of the country is getting its chance.
“In our first few games, I (realized) I’m a Division I athlete also, and I’m playing against these Division I athletes,” Johnson said. “I’m fit to be here.”

title: Portland council postpones vote on warming shelter plan
text:
PORTLAND — The City Council on Monday postponed until Nov. 2 a vote on allocating funding for a winter warming shelter, putting off a decision after discussing alternative options in executive session.
Officials did not comment on the reasons for postponing, and public comment was not taken.
The council’s decision followed a lengthy closed-door session to discuss the potential acquisition of real estate and consult with its attorney regarding the shelter, which officials hope to stand up by mid-November.
While the city had initially settled on a nonprofit provider and downtown location for a shelter, a combination of zoning regulations on the property and neighborhood concern left officials scrambling to find a replacement.
The emergency meeting Monday was called so the council to consider spending $900,000 in opioid settlement funds toward a nightly shelter operation at 166 Riverside Industrial Parkway, the site of the city-run shelter last winter.
The proposal would require a lease agreement and transportation plan for shuttling people on and off the peninsula, and is estimated to cost $1.2 million — a $500,000 increase from the downtown option.
While no public comment was taken, homeless advocates earlier Monday shared concerns over the location and for using $900,000 in opioid settlement funds that they argue should be reserved for more targeted substance use and recovery programs.
“These limited funds are urgently needed for prevention programming, recovery centers, substance use treatment, and many other critical services,” the nonprofit Preble Street wrote on social media. “Our hope is that if opioid settlement funds are needed to bridge gaps in funding for a warming shelter, they are used responsibly and only as needed, and that the city provides full transparency of how the funds are used.”
Preble Street also pressed officials to secure a warming shelter option as soon as possible, and shared a preference that it be located on the peninsula for better accessibility.
Under the initial shelter plan, Biddeford nonprofit Seeds of Hope was to host between 45-50 individuals per night in the basement of Preble Street’s Elena’s Way shelter on Portland Street.
However, earlier this month, staff said zoning requirements in place on the building — including stipulations that the sleeping area be limited to the upper level and a maximum of 40 shelter guests be allowed at one time — made the plan unfeasible.
Further complicating the issue was a recent city inspection of Preble Street’s operation, which found that the organization is not following parts of its management plan, leading to neighborhood concern.
According to a council memo, Seeds of Hope informed staff that it is no longer willing to operate an emergency shelter at Elena’s Way “due to community resistance and regulatory challenges,” and Preble Street also declined to operate it.
Prior to going into executive session Monday, city staff said the Riverside Industrial Parkway option is currently the “strongest, most substantive location” but said officials would be presented with alternatives.
The $361,000 MaineHousing recently awarded to Portland’s initial shelter plan at Elena’s Way has been built into the budget for the Riverside proposal. The city would also need to update its contract with Seeds of Hope to operate it.

title: Couple arrested after children found living in what sheriff called a ‘house of horrors’
text:
EVANS, W.Va (WDTV/Gray News) - A couple was arrested after three children reported years of abuse in what a sheriff called a “house of horrors” in West Virginia.
Erica Lynn Sayre and her husband, Clifford Gale Sayre, are charged with child neglect and child abuse, according to the Jackson County Sheriff’s Office.
Jackson County Sheriff RH Mellinger detailed the abuse and called the children’s living environment a “house of horrors.”
The investigation uncovered years of “disturbing” maltreatment, including the children being repeatedly hit, strangled, deprived of food and water, denied bathroom privileges, having soiled cat litter dumped in their beds and dog feces on personal items, and being forced to run barefoot on a gravel driveway as a means of punishment for any conflicts with Erica Sayre, according to authorities.
The children were allegedly hit with household objects, causing excessive bleeding injuries, forced to place a soiled sock in their mouths and forcibly had their hair cut, according to authorities. One child described being hit in the head with an electronic device, which caused a “bleeding injury for which she was denied medical treatment.” Another child was threatened to be killed if she contacted child protective services, according to authorities.
The children also reported being tormented and harassed about their biological parents who are dead, according to authorities.
During interviews with police, one of the children became “visibly emotional” and said, “I can’t go back to that home.” Another child described years of alleged abuse and said she “just wants a normal life,” the sheriff said.
Deputies said Clifford Sayre witnessed the abuse and failed to intervene.
One child said Clifford Sayre physically restrained her hands while Erica Sayre forcibly cut her hair with a razor blade, resulting in an injury. The child allegedly told authorities, “mom hits us and Gale lets her.”
The investigation revealed physical evidence, including documented scars consistent with the children’s accounts, and the children’s statements corroborated one another, according to Mellinger.
Erica Sayre faces three counts of child abuse resulting in bodily injury and three counts of child neglect creating risk of injury. Clifford Sayre faces three counts of child neglect resulting in bodily injury and three counts of child neglect creating risk of injury.
Both are out on bond. Erica Sayre’s preliminary hearing is set for Nov. 20. Clifford Sayre’s preliminary hearing is Monday.

title: A 10-year-old boy and his teacher drowned on a school trip. Here’s what officials say happened
text:
JOHNSON COUNTY, Iowa (KCRG/Gray News) - Officials in Iowa have revealed what happened just before a 10-year-old boy and his teacher drowned on a school field trip.
Hannah Jorgensen, a 24-year-old teacher at Borlaug Elementary, led a group of 14 students on a School of the Wild trip Sept. 22 at Lake Macbride State Park, according to the Johnson County Sheriff’s Office.
The woodland hike ended near the shore of the Coralville Reservoir, where the fifth grade students – including 10-year-old Ahmed Osman – stopped to eat lunch around noon.
During the lunch break, investigators say Ahmed stepped into the water flowing down the spillway. He slipped on the rocks and fell into the water.
Jorgensen jumped in the water to rescue Ahmed. She left her phone on the shore but told her students to call 911.
One student was able to make the call, and the others alerted a bystander. The bystander jumped into the water to rescue Ahmed and his teacher but was unable to do so.
First responders later recovered both Ahmed and Jorgensen’s bodies from the lake. The 10-year-old’s family has called Jorgensen a hero for trying to save him.
The bystander, who safely made it out of the water, stayed on the scene with the students and spoke with the investigators. The students were also interviewed as part of the investigation.
The investigation into the incident is ongoing.

title: Burnham woman back in court on new Montana animal cruelty charges
text:
BELFAST, Maine (WABI) - A Burnham woman with multiple animal cruelty convictions was back in court Monday on new, out-of-state allegations.
Alexis Ingraham, 41, was convicted of animal cruelty in August, with a prior conviction in 2011.
She was sentenced to two years in prison and two years of probation, plus a lifetime ban on owning animals, but that sentence is on hold pending appeal.
Ingraham appeared virtually in a Belfast courtroom Monday afternoon after being taken into custody on four new misdemeanor counts of animal cruelty out of Montana.
According to court documents, investigators allege Ingraham boarded two mares and two foals for months on a Montana property, where they were found emaciated in May with no feed and no water.
Despite being sent photos of their decline as early as March, she allegedly failed to intervene. All four horses were seized and taken to an equine medical center.
Ingraham waived extradition to Montana, saying she is not running from the charges.
She is currently in the Waldo County Jail awaiting transfer to Montana.

title: Meet the 83-year-old marina keeper preserving hundreds of years of Vermont history
text:
ORWELL, Vt. (Aging Untold) — At one of the narrowest points on Lake Champlain, a piece of Vermont’s maritime past is still standing — and still in use.
For more than 30 years, 83-year-old Pat Ullom and her son have run Chipman Point Marina.
Chipman Point was once where “all the goods landed,” Ullom said.
A landing point for 1800s commerce
In the 1800s, the area was a busy maritime community close to New York state.
The marina’s main stone building was built in 1810 and quarried from the property itself. Boats once unloaded cargo directly into the building through its doorways, and the second floor functioned “more like a grocery store.”
Ullom said the beams inside are original to the building.
“Yeah, yeah, I do that a lot,” Ullom said, when asked if she ever looks out at the water and imagines what the property looked like in 1810.
A store that’s kept its character for a century
Next to the 1810 stone building stands a structure built in 1824 that has operated as a store for almost 100 years.
Pat Ullom keeps the candy on the counter and the coffee, still priced at 25 cents a cup, flowing.
Part of the original floor remains intact. Ullom said a previous owner who had the property for 50 years used to chew tobacco, leaving marks still visible in the wood today.
With boating season underway, the marina is picking up activity again.
Living above the history she preserves
Ullom lives on the third floor of the 1824 building. She said she doesn’t see herself as the building’s owner, but as someone passing through it.
“I don’t feel that I own it,” Ullom said. “I feel that I’ve been lucky enough to live here.”
