'Crash ur row only': United flight turned around after passenger allegedly said he'd 'hijack' plane
text:
'Crash ur row only': United flight turned around after passenger allegedly said he'd 'hijack' plane
An airplane passenger was arrested for allegedly writing a message while midair that he was going to “hijack” the plane, forcing the United flight to be diverted back to Las Vegas shortly after takeoff Saturday.
Related previous video above: Flights stopped at Washington, D.C., airport after unauthorized drone appeared over runway
The 25-year-old allegedly communicated that he was “gonna hijack this” plane — although he used an expletive — and “crash ur row only,” according to a copy of the criminal complaint. The document doesn't specify exactly how the message was sent or to whom it was directed.
Las Vegas police said they detained the man after a report of a person making “terroristic threats” on the Saturday night flight that had been headed to Newark, New Jersey. He was arrested on charges of making a threat or providing false information regarding an act of terrorism, which carries a possible sentence of 1 to 20 years in prison.
An attorney listed for the man did not immediately return a request for comment. His initial court appearance is scheduled for Tuesday.
The scheduled redeye flight returned to the airport less than an hour after departing, according to Flightradar24 data.
United confirmed that the flight with 150 passengers on board returned safely to Las Vegas to address a “potential security concern.” The flight was delayed overnight and departed for Newark on Sunday morning.
The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed it will investigate the incident and said in an email to The Associated Press there have been over 1,400 unruly passenger incidents so far in 2026.
Associated Press writer Rio Yamat contributed to this report.

title: Men’s ice hockey defeats Colgate 3-0 over homecoming weekend
text:
ORONO, Maine — It was homecoming weekend in Orono, and the festivities began with a packed house at Alfond Arena on Friday, Oct. 23. The Maine hockey team took on Colgate University in a sold-out arena.
The game plan coming into this game was to shut down the opposing offense and establish pressure on the offensive side of the ice. The Black Bears wanted to make an impression on power plays and control the game from start to finish to bring the fans a win for homecoming weekend.
The first period started back and forth as both teams vied for the puck, but quickly turned to the Maine attack as they put a few shots on goal during an early stretch of pressure. The attack did not result in a goal but established the pressure that would lead to a power play later in the first period.
That power play led to the first goal of the game, scored by Maine’s fourth-year forward Tanner Klempke on the advantage. The goal was assisted by both graduate student forward Owen Fowler and fourth-year forward Sully Scholle. This goal would garner the lead that the Black Bears coasted on all the way through the end of the first period.
Stout defense was the name of the game for that first block of play, as third-year goalie Petter Wickström Stumer recorded multiple saves to keep the Maine goal clean throughout the early contest.
That sentiment continued throughout the game. The second period began with more shutdown defense as Wickström Stumer recorded more saves to keep the Maine net empty. Immediately following those saves, Maine shot the puck down the ice and put the pressure right back into full gear, pressure that would lead straight into the second goal of the evening for Maine. Second-year defenseman Loic Usereau would net the second goal for the Black Bears, with an assist from Tanner Klempke to put them ahead 2-0. The assist brought Klempke’s point total to two.
The rest of the second period consisted of more stifling defense and pressure from the Maine squad. Wickström Stumer recorded even more saves and pushed the Black Bears into the third period with a 2-0 lead.
The third period began, and the plan was simple: Hold on to the lead and cruise to a homecoming victory.
That is exactly what UMaine did. The team only gave up two shots in the first four minutes, and before that, the unit held pressure on Colgate’s goalie for the entire first wave of the last period.
About 10 minutes into the last period of play, third-year forward Lee Parks and the Black Bears would net a third goal to propel the team up by three and light the fans on fire. Alfond Arena was rocking, and the team was playing its best hockey of the season.
From there, the team cleaned up nicely and skated to the end of the game with its 3-0 lead to kick off a great weekend for students and alumni attending the game.
The game’s most impactful player was goalie Petter Wickström Stumer, who tallied a ridiculous 24-save shutout to lead Maine to its victory.
UMaine is back in action on Saturday night against Colgate once again, and next week the team will travel to Boston for a conference matchup against Boston University with momentum.

title: Family says 7-year-old girl injured in Bend school shooting moved out of ICU
text:
BEND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - The 7-year-old girl who survived a shooting at a Bend elementary school earlier this month has been moved out of the intensive care unit, her family said in a statement Monday.
In the statement, the family of Saylor Graham-Poarch said she was in critical condition after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary but is now stable. Her family said while she has been moved out of ICU, she has a long recovery ahead of her.
Saylor’s family said in the statement:
“Even as we’re grateful for Saylor’s progress, our hearts are broken for the families of the three children and the teacher who were killed. We are holding them close, and we grieve with them.
Thank you to everyone who has reached out, prayed for Saylor, sent messages, and shown our family so much love during the hardest time of our lives. We can’t respond to everyone individually, but please know that every kind word, prayer, and act of support means more to us than we can say.
Many of you have asked how you can help. Along with everything else, our family is facing the costs of Saylor’s recovery and the time we need to spend with her. We’ve included a GoFundMe link below for anyone who would like to give. Any donation, share, or continued support is deeply appreciated.
Above all, please keep Saylor in your thoughts and prayers as she heals. We are beyond grateful that she is still here with us.
Thank you for standing with Saylor and our family."
Police said a 16-year-old former student went into Silver Rail Elementary School on Oct. 15 and shot into a special needs classroom. Teacher Megan Lambert, 25, was killed along with students Rhoam Summer, 5, and two other children, ages 8 and 11. The shooter was also killed.
Another teacher, Becky Drury, also survived the shooting and needed surgery on her left arm and right hand. She released a statement about what happened that day last week.
A memorial service was held for Lambert on Saturday at Caldera High School in Bend.
Silver Rail Elementary remains closed through at least this week. Bend-La Pine Schools announced that crews are making progress cleaning and repairing the school after the shooting.
The district also shared a list of resources for Silver Rail families, including childcare options with the Boys & Girls Clubs and the Bend FC Timbers, and grab-and-go free school meals.

title: How daylight saving time changes affect you and what you can do about it
text:
How daylight saving time changes affect you and what you can do about it
An extra hour of sleep is on the way for most Americans, though the "fall back" to standard time will bring darker afternoons, too.
One tip: Try to get outside for some morning sun — it'll help your body clock reset faster.
Daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, which means you should set your clock back an hour before you go to bed. Standard time will last until March 14, when we will again "spring forward" with the return of daylight saving time.
There's a lot of grumbling about the twice-a-year time changes. An AP-NORC poll last year found that only 12% of American adults were in favor of it, while almost half opposed it. Lawmakers in Washington took up the issue yet again over the summer.
Related video above: Sleep consultant advises parents on adjusting sleep schedules for daylight savings?
People often find the spring switch harder, losing that hour of sleep we allegedly recover in the fall. But many people also mourn fall's end of daylight saving time, when days already are getting shorter and moving the clocks can mean less daylight after school or work for exercise or outdoor fun. The poll found that, if forced to choose, most Americans would prefer to keep that extra hour of daylight in the evening.
But health groups, including the American Medical Association and American Academy of Sleep Medicine, have long urged adopting standard time year-round. That's because it aligns more with the sun, which rises later in the winter. Brighter mornings and less light at night are key to keeping that circadian rhythm on track, making it easier to wake up on time and stick with healthy sleep patterns.
Most countries do not observe daylight saving time. For those that do — mostly in North America and Europe — the date that clocks are changed varies. In the U.S., Hawaii and most of Arizona don't change and stay on standard time.
Here's what to know about the twice-yearly ritual.
The brain has a master clock that is set by exposure to sunlight and darkness. This circadian rhythm is a roughly 24-hour cycle that determines when we become sleepy and when we're more alert. The patterns change with age, one reason that early-to-rise youngsters evolve into hard-to-wake teens.
Morning light is key to synchronizing that internal clock. By evening, levels of a hormone called melatonin begin to surge, triggering drowsiness. Too much light in the evening — whether it's from later time outdoors during daylight saving time or from artificial light like computer screens — delays that surge and the cycle gets out of sync.
And that circadian clock affects more than sleep, also influencing things like heart rate, blood pressure, stress hormones and metabolism.
Even an hour's change on the clock can throw off sleep schedules because even though the clocks change, work and school start times stay the same.
Right after the spring change, darker mornings and lighter evenings make it harder to fall asleep on time. Those first few days have been linked to increases in car crashes and even an uptick in heart attacks.
During the fall and winter, some people with seasonal affective disorder, a type of depression usually linked to the shorter days and less sunlight, often struggle.
Many people easily adjust to the clock switch, as they do when they recover from jet lag after traveling. But a time change can add pressure on shift workers whose schedules already are out of sync with the sun, or those regularly sleep-deprived for other reasons.
About 1 in 3 U.S. adults sleep less than the recommended seven-plus hours nightly, and more than half of U.S. teens don't get the recommended eight-plus hours on weeknights.
Chronic sleep deprivation is linked to heart disease, cognitive decline, obesity and numerous other problems.
In both fall and spring, changing bedtimes by as little as 15 minutes a night in the days before the change can help ease into the time change.
But sunshine in the morning is critical to helping reset your circadian rhythm for healthful sleep. If you can't get outdoors, sit by windows.
Every year, there's talk about ending the time change. The nation even tried it in the 1970s, but it lasted less than a year after a public outcry.
The latest attempt came in July, when the U.S. House of Representatives overwhelmingly passed the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent. President Donald Trump backs the idea and is pressuring reluctant senators to support it, even posting the cellphone number of Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, an opponent, on social media.

title: A cat was tied up in a plastic bag and thrown into a Maine dumpster
text:
More than a century ago, New Englander H.P. Lovecraft wrote of the city of Ulthar, where the law forbade the killing of cats and woe came to those who did.
Much like Edgar Allan Poe before him, he saw something detestable in maiming cats, a purring companion once admired as divine and perhaps the only animal to domesticate themselves. The edict of Ulthar lives on online, where sleuths seek justice for afflicted felines.
But not all cats can find refuge in Ulthar.
In Bingham recently, a cat was tied up in a plastic bag and thrown into a dumpster at the local transfer station.
The vigilant transfer station staff found the cat before its situation became more tragic, the town said Sunday morning.
Under the care of Bingham’s animal control officer, the cat is doing well despite the “horrific ordeal.”
The town acknowledged that financial strain can push people to make hard choices, but said “there is no excuse for animal cruelty.”
“Human decency and basic compassion should have guided you to a completely different choice,” the town castigated.
Anyone struggling to care for an animal can contact their local animal shelter, animal control officer or town office to connect with someone for help finding a new home for a pet.
“Please do the right thing next time. Our community is better than this, and we will continue to look out for those who cannot speak for themselves,” the town said.
As in Ulthar, no one may harm or kill a cat in Bingham.

title: Officials ask for help identifying unauthorized fire truck
text:

title: Obama rebukes Ramaswamy ad using rival’s estranged mother: ‘No line he will not cross’
text:
DETROIT (AP) — Former President Barack Obama on Saturday seized on what he described as cruelty and indecency coming from President Donald Trump and his Republican allies, stepping into one of the nation’s ugliest midterm fights as he worked to rally Democratic voters in two Midwestern battlegrounds.
First in Ohio, Obama took aim at Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an advertising campaign featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have also defended the ad, even as Republican leaders across Ohio, including Gov. Mike DeWine, have called for its removal.
“In recent days, we’ve seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to,” Obama said of Ramaswamy, noting that Acton has “spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she’s experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness.”
Later in Michigan, Obama condemned critics of Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, suggesting that they’re using his name or his faith to tear him down.
“We have seen this movie before. I starred in it,” Obama told a packed high school gym in Detroit. “I’ve got a long-form birth certificate to prove it.”
“Abdul is as Michigan as it gets,” he added.
Obama, 65, remains the Democratic Party’s best motivator nearly a decade after leaving the White House. And he’s taking his star power on the road in the final days of the midterm elections, which will help determine the balance of power in American politics on Nov. 3.
Trump cast his own ballot on Saturday in Florida, where he defended the Ramaswamy ad, which has emerged as a national flashpoint a little more than a week before Election Day.
“The mother said that Amy Acton is a liar, and she’s no good,” Trump said. ”And you know what? I don’t think you can get a better reference on that.”
The Ramaswamy campaign video features Acton’s birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her “a liar” and insinuating she has mental health issues.
Acton, Ohio’s COVID-19-era health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur’s husband, was indicted on a charge of rape involving Acton.
The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur failed to show for a court appearance and became a fugitive. Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death in 2004.
Appearing before Obama, Acton spoke as if addressing Ramaswamy directly.
“My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his stumbling campaign, but it’s not going to work,” she said. “Decency still matters.” She added: “Mr. Ramaswamy, you are not just out of touch, you are out for yourself and you are a danger to my state. Apparently there is no low to which you won’t stoop.”
Although Ohio has become more reliably Republican, it’s been a hotly contested battleground this year. Trump and Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to drum up support for Sen. Jon Husted and Ramaswamy. And the controversy over Ramaswamy’s ad has ratcheted up the already high temperature.
Michigan, too, is a critical state this midterm season, with high-stakes contests for the Senate and governor.
While Obama addressed both races, he offered a passionate defense of El-Sayed, a former public health official running against former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican.
The former president pushed back against those who call El-Sayed a radical, declaring that “Abdul shares my values.” He also acknowledged that El-Sayed was critical of him after his 2012 reelection for not following through on all of his progressive campaign promises.
El-Sayed wrote that Obama “was not the right choice — he just wasn’t the wrong one.”
“Some of these folks say, well, you know, Abdul didn’t like some of the things you did as president,” Obama said in Detroit, wearing a blue shirt with no tie, his sleeves rolled up. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama. Michelle Obama, about five times a day.”
Democrats hoped that Obama’s appearance in the city, which is three-quarters Black, could bolster support for El-Sayed among Black voters. In the primary, his opponent Haley Stevens won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by about 6 percentage points. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian vice president, campaigned for El-Sayed in September.
Cheryl McWilliams, 67, said Obama’s speech “pumps you up to vote,” and she’s hoping to see high turnout in the midterms.
“If Detroit doesn’t vote, whoever’s running is going to lose, period,” McWilliams said. “I’m just hoping we can reach voters that don’t vote. They think it doesn’t matter, and it does.”
Chunnika Hodges, who lives in Detroit and canvassed for El-Sayed on Saturday, said some Black voters are supporting Rogers because they don’t think anything has changed after years of voting for Democrats. Some are also wary of El-Sayed because of his progressive policies, Hodges said.
“We don’t lean to the conservative, but we have seen that within our community,” Hodges said. “There are conservative Blacks, conservative Democrats.”
While Obama talked up Democratic candidates in Ohio and Michigan, he also spoke at length about Trump.
He accused the Republican president and his family of rampant corruption and called out his inability to lower costs, noting that Trump has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn.
“I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation,” Obama quipped. “He should be on HGTV.” He went on: “There’s gold everywhere. He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”
The former Democratic president acknowledged that the nation has Trump for another two years, until his term ends. But voters are not stuck with Trump’s allies, he said.
“We’re not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are handling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people,” Obama said. “After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence … you get a chance to say enough is enough.”
Obama will headline a rally in Georgia next week with Sen. Jon Ossoff and candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Trump, campaigning in Perry, Georgia, on Saturday evening with their Republican rivals, made several references to Obama’s Michigan event, insisting “the place was empty.”
___
Peoples reported from New York. AP writer Jill Colvin in New York contributed. GaNun is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Rumford Police Respond To Double Stabbing And Axe Attack In Separate Incidents
text:
It was a violent Sunday in Rumford, where knives and an axe were used in separate cases.
Rumford, Maine Police Encounter 2 Violent Calls in One Day
Police officers never know what types of situations they will encounter.
On Sunday, October 25, 2026, Rumford saw an especially busy day, with two violent calls back-to-back.
Three people now face charges for alleged attacks on three people.
Rumford, Maine Police Say 2 People Were Stabbed on Sunday and 2 Others Arrested
Rumford Police were called to 209 Waldo Street at approximately 8:48 am on Sunday, after 911 callers reported assaults involving two victims and two suspects who had fled on foot.
Police officers and Oxford County Sheriff's deputies arrived within minutes of the calls and found two victims suffering from stab wounds.
A 44-year-old man had a knife wound to his back, with significant bleeding, and a 37-year-old woman sustained a knife wound to the side of her abdomen. Both victims are from Rumford.
They were transported to Rumford Hospital for emergency treatment and are expected to survive their injuries.
While officers tended to the victims, other officers and deputies located the suspects, who took off on foot in different directions.
Tips from residents helped the police quickly apprehend the two suspects and take them into custody.
Jazya D. Swan, 19, of Lewiston, is charged with criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon and refusing to submit to arrest or detention.
A 15-year-old female from Lisbon, Maine, is charged with elevated aggravated assault, criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon, and refusing to submit to arrest or detention.
Rumford, Maine Police Report an Axe Attack Over a Motorcycle
In an unrelated call, Rumford Police Officers responded to a 911 call reporting a woman was attacking a resident of Madison's condos with an axe during an argument at approximately 11:57 am.
An investigation determined the 44-year-old male victim had arranged through social media for a Massachusetts woman to transport his red 1984 Honda GL 1200 motorcycle from his former home in Northborough, Massachusetts, to Rumford.
When Luciane Dezan, 46, of Medford, Massachusetts, arrived with the bike, the victim discovered damage he believed occurred in transit and told the woman he wouldn't pay the full agreed-upon fee.
The two argued, and Dezan allegedly retrieved an axe from her van and began repeatedly striking the motorcycle, causing extensive damage.
When the man attempted to stop her, she allegedly swung the axe at his head, narrowly missing him.
Police estimate the bike sustained approximately $2,000 in damage during the attack.
Dezan was charged with attempted elevated aggravated assault and aggravated criminal mischief and transported to the Oxford County Jail.

title: $5.6M grant will help Maine train 500 workers for skilled jobs
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine has secured nearly $5.6 million in federal funding to train 500 workers for in-demand careers and help employers fill skilled jobs in defense shipbuilding, advanced manufacturing, construction and related trades.
“Employers need skilled workers to keep Maine’s key industries moving forward,” said Maine Department of Labor Commissioner Laura Fortman. “This grant will help connect people with the training, skills and credentials employers are looking for, while opening doors to new careers in high-wage, in-demand jobs.”
The grant will provide career planning, short-term training, industry-recognized credentials and paid work-based learning opportunities, including apprenticeships. The goal is to help participants find employment or start structured training within six months.
Staff at Maine Career Centers, operated by the Maine Department of Labor, will also connect participants with workforce resources, including Maine’s Competitive Skills Scholarship Program and construction training programs offered by the AFL-CIO Maine and the Associated General Contractors of Maine.
The award is part of a $95.5 million U.S. Department of Labor investment supporting initiatives across 17 states to accelerate reemployment and meet workforce needs in growing industries.

title: 13 students taken to hospital after Mississippi school bus collision
text:
RIDGELAND, Miss. (WLBT/Gray News) - Multiple students were taken to a hospital after a Mississippi school bus was involved in a collision Monday morning, authorities said.
According to the Madison County School District, police and emergency medical personnel responded to the scene around 8:30 a.m.
Ridgeland Police Chief Brian Myers said that the collision happened at the intersection of Colony Park Boulevard and Highway 51.
Thirteen students were taken to a local hospital for evaluation and treatment. More were taken by parents, the district said. The severity of the injuries is unclear at this time.
Chief Myers said 32 people total were on the bus; thirty-one of those were students.
No injuries were reported with the other vehicle involved, Chief Myers said.
District personnel are currently working to reunite students with their parents and guardians. The district is contacting parents of students on the bus directly.
“The safety and security of our students is our utmost concern, and we are working closely with first responders and families. We will continue to share information as it becomes available,” the school district said.

title: Maine Featured Prominently As Part of Reimagined Disney World Ride
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For many people throughout the state of Maine, a trip to Walt Disney World in Florida can be a once-in-a-lifetime destination experience.
For Mainers that make that trip, there usually isn't many signs of home in central Florida short of some retirees and the spotting of a Maine license plate on occasion.
But if you're planning on visiting Epcot Center as part of Walt Disney World in the near future, there's an unmistakable piece of Maine prominently featured as part of a reimagined attraction.
Maine Lighthouse Featured in Soarin' Ride at Walt Disney World's Epcot
When Soarin' first opened at Epcot back in 2005, it was instantly one of the most popular attractions at Walt Disney World.
The concept behind the ride is simple. Visitors hop aboard a simulated aircraft and get flown around the globe to some of the world's most stunning landmarks and breathtaking places.
One of the wrinkles that made the Soarin' ride so unique is that the attraction would feed scents in for certain locations to enhance the sense of being there.
In May of 2026, the Soarin' attraction was reimagined at Epcot to celebrate the history and beauty of America.
As part of the opening minute, Portland Head Light is prominently featured for 'flyers'. On the ride, you'll soar directly over the most famed lighthouse in Maine.
Maine was one of only a handful of states and Portland Head Light one of the few landmarks featured as part of the celebration of America.
Maine Beer is Featured Elsewhere at Walt Disney World
Without even leaving Epcot, you'll find another piece of Maine available at the park.
That would be Allagash beer. As part of the Epcot 2026 Food and Wine Festival, the Haunted House Hoppy Dark Ale from Allagash is one of the featured beers at the American pavilion.

title: 20 Maine concerts to catch before the end of the year
text:
As we head into the final stretch of 2026, it’s a good idea to get a handle on some of the concerts around the state that you can still make plans to see before year’s end.
Maine might be a small state, but we make up for it with a lot of musical venues and national and local acts gracing our stages. Here are 20 of them you can mark on your calendar.
7:30 p.m. Nov. 5. Johnson Hall Opera House, 280 Water St., Gardiner, $69.24. johnsonhall.org.
Black Violin is the Grammy-nominated classical-meets-hip-hop duo of Wil Baptiste and Kev Marcus. The Be Free tour melds blazing strings with big beats and a heartbeat of pure authenticity. Individuality, creativity and connection will be boldly celebrated, and you can be part of it.
7:30 p.m. Nov. 6. The Dance Hall, 7 Walker St., Kittery, $20 in advance, $25 day of show, $12 students. thedancehallkittery.org.
Tanasi is a “worldgrass” trio out of Asheville, North Carolina. Their sounds captures global folk traditions with close harmonies. The Appalachian string band features Billy Cardine on dobro and slide instruments, Anya Hinkle on vocals and guitar and Mary Lucey on vocals, upright bass and clawhammer banjo.
7 p.m. Nov. 6. The Hill Arts, 76 Congress St., Portland, $25 in advance, $30 at the door, $15 students and seniors in advance, $20 at the door. thehillarts.me.
The music of late folk singer and five-time Grammy winner John Prine lives on through tribute act Highway Kind. Hear songs you’ve known and loved for decades, and sing along when the spirit moves you. Prine died in 2020 at the age of 73. His debut album came out in 1971, and over the course of his storied career he released 18 studio albums along with several live ones.
8 p.m. Nov. 6. Aura, 121 Center St., Portland, $40.50-$51.25, 18-plus. auramaine.com.
Come ready to dance the night away when you see New York City’s hypnotic dance music duo The Knocks. James Patterson and Ben Ruttner are known for epic DJ sets and live electronic performances. Streaming numbers are in the low billions, and popular tracks include “Fireworks” and “Ride or Die.”
8 p.m. Nov. 8. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $35 in advance, $40 day of show. statetheatreportland.com.
Grammy-nominated singer-songwriter Eric D. Johnson, who performs under the moniker Fruit Bats, is on the road with his band in support of “The Landfill,” released in June. Johnson describes the album as an “emotional companion piece” to “Baby Man” from 2025. Americana singer-songwriter Sarah King opens the show.
7 p.m. Nov. 11. Cross Insurance Center, 515 Main St., Bangor, $62.75-$124.50. waterfrontconcerts.com.
Sugarland is the country duo of singer-songwriters Jennifer Nettles (acoustic guitar, lead vocals) and Kristian Bush (guitar, mandolin, backing vocals). The band’s Ride or Die tour celebrates the 20th anniversary of their hit album “Enjoy the Ride,” home to Billboard Hot Country Top Ten singles “Settlin'” and “Want To.”
8 p.m. Nov. 13. Stone Mountain Arts Center, 695 Dugway Road, Brownfield, $40. stonemountainartscenter.com.
Alejandro Escovedo has spent his entire musical life with a foot in several genres, including punk, rock, country and roots. With boundless energy and surrounded by top-notch musicians, a live Escovedo performance is always a riveting experience.
7:30 p.m. Nov. 14. Westbrook Performing Arts Center, 471 Stroudwater St., Westbrook, $42-$70.75. waterfrontconcerts.com.
If you love Canadian rock band Rush and missed the recent Boston shows, or need another dose of their music, grab a ticket to see the Rush Tribute Project in Westbrook. The band will be performing the entire 1981 “Moving Pictures” album, which means you’ll hear tunes like “Tom Sawyer,” “Red Barchetta” and “Limelight.” The set will also feature other Rush songs including deep cuts like “La Villa Strangiato” and “Entre Nous” played on vintage instruments. The show features multi-camera projection, lasers and spectacular lighting.
8 p.m. Nov. 15. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $30-$45. statetheatreportland.com.
Married singer-songwriters Michael and Tanya Trotter record and perform under the name The War and Treaty. Their fusion of Americana, soul, blues, folk, county and gospel translates to a captivating live show. They have released seven albums since 2016, including “The Story of Michael and Tanya,” from earlier this year.
8 p.m. Friday and Saturday, 4 p.m. Sunday. Nov. 27-29. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $28 in advance, $33 day of show, $56 two-day pass,$90 four pack. statetheatreportland.com.
A longtime Thanksgiving weekend tradition is local musician Spencer Albee and his band The Walrus performing Beatles songs. Hear a whole bunch of Fab Four tunes at one – or all – of the State Theatre shows. The Walrus will also be performing Dec. 11 at The Criterion Theatre in Bar Harbor. Those tickets start at $30.78 at criteriontheatre.org.
7:30 p.m. Dec. 3. Jonathan’s, 92 Bourne Lane, Ogunquit, $70-$111. jonathansogunquit.com.
Singer-songwriter Joan Osborne will perform her mid-’90s album “Relish” in its entirety as she celebrates its 30th anniversary. Top to bottom, starting with “St. Teresa” and ending with “Lumina,” the album stands the test of time with a roots, blues, rock and soul sound. “Relish” is home to Osborne’s biggest song, “One of Us,” written by Eric Bazilian. The tune is a staple of the ’90s, and hasn’t lost any of its gutsy luster.
8 p.m. Dec. 5. Live at Madrid’s, 144 Fore St., Portland, $25 in advance, $30 day of show. statetheatreportland.com.
You can attend one show and check multiple boxes of genres and sounds. Pink Talking Phish is a combination of the music of Pink Floyd, Talking Heads and Phish. If that’s not enough, the show will be opened by Say You Love Me playing the music of Fleetwood Mac.
8 p.m. Dec. 5. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $25 in advance, $30 day of show. statetheatreportland.com.
Maine’s Mallett Brothers Band will bring their roots and Americana music to the State Theatre. The band is brothers Will (guitar, harmonica, vocals) and Luke Mallett (guitar and vocals), Nick Leen (bass), Andrew Martelle (fiddle, synth, backup vocals) and Brian Higgins (drums, percussion, backup vocals).
8 p.m. Dec. 12. Portland House of Music, 25 Temple St., Portland, $29.50 in advance, $35 day of show, 21-plus. statetheatreportland.com.
Indie folk band The Ballroom Thieves is the Maine-based duo of Calin Peters (vocals, cello and bass) and Martin Earley (guitar and vocals). With a discography that began in 2015 with “A Wolf in the Doorway,” The Ballroom Thieves have released several albums and EPs. They’ve also toured extensively, including a slot on the main stage at the prestigious Newport Folk Festival.
7:30 p.m. Dec. 17. Johnson Hall Opera House, 280 Water St., Gardiner, $55. johnsonhall.org.
7:30 p.m. Dec. 18-19. Jonathan’s, 92 Bourne Lane, Ogunquit, $90-$131. jonathansogunquit.com.
Singer Judy Collins is winding down her time as a live performer by spending several months on the Sweet Judy Blue Eyes farewell tour. Collins’ recording of Joni Mitchell’s “Both Sides Now” from the 1967 “Wildflowers” album earned a place in the Grammy Hall of Fame. In 1975, Collins won a Grammy for her interpretation of Stephen Sondheim’s “Send in the Clowns.” Never one to rest on her laurels, the prolific Collins has authored several books and released the 2023 album “Spellbound,” featuring all original songs.
8 p.m. Dec. 18. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $25 in advance, $30 day of show. statetheatreportland.com.
Talking Heads tribute band Start Making Sense has come through Maine several times and always draws a huge crowd. That’s because they’re an elite tier act that put their heart and soul into creating a Talking Heads experience that will have you on your feet the entire time. Watch out, you might get what you’re after!
8 p.m. Dec. 18-19. Stone Mountain Arts Center, 695 Dugway Road, Brownfield, $105. stonemountainartscenter.com.
You have two chances to see singer-songwriter Rickie Lee Jones at the intimate Stone Mountain Arts Center in Brownfield. Known for her descriptive songwriting and jazzy, quirky vocal style, Jones is highly respected by her peers and loyal fans. Her live shows are riveting, while also comfortably casual as Jones has a uniquely engaging stage presence.
3 p.m. Dec. 20. Waterville Opera House, 1 Common St., Waterville, $45-$55. watervillecreates.org.
Big band legend Tommy Dorsey’s impact continues with the Tommy Dorsey Orchestra, under the direction of trombonist Jeff Bush. The orchestra will play quintessential tunes like “Opus One,” “Song of India” and “Marie.” You’ll be treated to fresh arrangements of the swinging sound that made Dorsey’s contributions timeless.
8 p.m. Dec. 26-27. One Longfellow Square, 181 State St., Portland, $30 in advance, $35 day of show, $120 for table with two seats, $54 premium balcony. onelongfellowsquare.com.
For the past few years, local singer Katie Matzell and her band have been knocking the socks off audiences with their homage to Bonnie Raitt. Give yourself something to talk about by grabbing a ticket one of the shows. You’ll hear hits and deep cuts from Raitt’s decades-long career.
9 p.m. Dec. 31. Portland House of Music, 25 Temple St., $30 in advance, $40 day of show, 21-plus. statetheatreportland.com.
They call Portland home, but rock trio Weakened Friends spend most of their time touring around the country. Sonia Sturino, Annie Hoffman and Adam Hand have three blistering albums worth of songs to choose from, so expect an electrifying night of music. For a preview, listen to “Live From Hell,” released earlier this year.

title: One Dead in Mapleton Crash
text:
MAPLETON, Maine (WAGM) -One man has died following a crash in Mapleton over the weekend.
Around 8 p.m. on Saturday, October 24th, the Aroostook County Sheriff’s Office responded to a single-vehicle crash on Main Street in Mapleton. The driver involved was 53-year-old Christopher Putnam of Mapleton, who was driving a 2008 Kia Sedona at the time. Putnam was ejected from the vehicle during the crash and later died of his injuries. The Presque Isle Fire department says the street was shut down while crews worked, and traffic was diverted around Pelkey Road to Grendell Road. The Sheriff’s Office was assisted by the Mapleton Fire Department and the Presque Isle Police Department. No other details were released as the crash remains under investigation.

The team's effort was led by Kulani Granholm, who finished in second place overall with a time of 18:54.88, nearly 30 seconds faster than her finishing time at PVC's a week before. title: Susan Collins’ response to foul attack ad is part of a pattern
text:
Sen. Susan Collins is again trying to take credit for reducing harm she caused.
What Collins’ spokesperson left out in saying the disgusting attack ad against Troy Jackson should be pulled, was that Collins herself put the issue in the spotlight in early September. In an interview with Jonathan Martin of Politico, Collins presented details about Jackson’s family, while saying she wasn’t going to bring it up, to which Martin replied, “I think you just mentioned it.”
Sen. Collins is always having to have it both ways. She advanced the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, with its big healthcare cuts, before trying to take credit for a rural hospital fund that restores $1 for every $75 cut. Collins said she’d only back pro-choice justices, then voted for Brett Kavanaugh; she introduced a weak abortion bill that couldn’t pass and voted against a much stronger reproductive rights bill that had far more votes. Aren’t we sick of this?
Amy Fried
Bangor

title: Thousands of observers are expected to descend on polling places to monitor the vote on Election Day
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Democrats and outside watchdogs are planning a massive presence at the polls on Election Day driven by concerns that President Donald Trump will further leverage the vast resources of the federal government to interfere with a midterm that could hobble his final two years in office.
They won’t be the only ones there. A sprawling election protection effort on the left that is expected to deploy tens of thousands of monitors will be met by the largest-ever monitoring program by the Justice Department and still more observers from Republican-aligned groups. The result could be unlike anything seen at the polls in modern times.
The effort among Democratic and nonprofit groups includes training volunteers to stand watch outside polling places and report activities they consider concerning. The network includes traditional government watchdogs such as Common Cause and the American Civil Liberties Union plus a flood of volunteers assembled by state Democratic parties, congressional leaders, national activist groups and organizations focused on protecting democracy.
The Democratic National Committee’s Association of State Democratic Committees created a first-of-its-kind cybersecurity unit staffed by former CIA and FBI officials to monitor and report online misinformation, including artificial intelligence deepfakes, said Jane Kleeb, vice chair of the DNC.
That’s as Democratic mayors, attorneys general and secretaries of state host tabletop exercises simulating worst-case scenarios, such as a surge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials at voting locations or the seizure of ballots and voting equipment.
On Capitol Hill, Democratic leaders have assembled a legal team that rivals that of any presidential campaign.
“We’ve never done this before,” Kleeb said of the party’s sweeping efforts. But “we’ve never had to deal with the president of the United States saying that he may seize ballots, put ICE agents outside polling locations and other kinds of very clear direct threats to the voting process.”
The Department of Justice has already filed lawsuits in California and Alaska that could affect ballot counting or certification.
While Trump continues to make baseless allegations of cheating in the election, administration and military officials have said they have no plans to deploy immigration agents or troops to polling sites.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis blamed “radical Democrats” for creating fears about election security by refusing to enact voter ID requirements and other Republican-backed measures.
“President Trump has done more than any other president to ensure we have free and fair elections,” Bis said.
Tens of thousands of volunteers trained to observe
State Democratic parties have trained an estimated 10,000 volunteers to observe polling places and report anything potentially concerning they might see from federal agents. Common Cause has trained roughly 16,000 more volunteers to stand watch at voting precincts, said Suzanne Almeida, vice president of states for the group.
She said a broader Election Protection coalition involving 300 other groups has trained tens of thousands more.
Smaller pockets of volunteers from other groups also are preparing to show up, including roughly 100 organized by Senate Democrats and hundreds more from a Democratic-allied group called Save America, which is training clergy members, veterans, teachers and other local community members. National groups such as Indivisible and MoveOn are activating their own expansive networks.
There are so many organizations working to protect the voting process — including many that cannot legally coordinate with each other — that some officials involved worry about unintentionally creating chaos outside polling locations.
Almeida said Election Day confusion is possible in some precincts but the nature of the threat requires a collective effort.
“It will actually take all of us if some of the threats we are most worried about come to pass,” she said.
Trump administration sends its own team
Harmeet Dhillon, a Trump appointee who leads the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, was asked on CBS’ “60 Minutes” whether the Republican administration is planning to send ICE agents to polling places.
“There is no plan to do that,” she responded.
Still, the Justice Department is planning its largest-ever election monitoring effort, with about 1,000 department staff expected to observe voting and ensure federal laws are being followed, spokesperson Kiersten Pels said. That comes after a primary season in which the department said it deployed more than 100 election monitors across hundreds of polling locations.
At least one of those placements sparked tensions with local officials. Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon, a Republican, said the behavior of two monitors during that state’s primary was “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.” A Laramie County clerk said the Justice Department monitors arrived at the polls intending to interview voters, but her office didn’t allow it.
The department disagrees that the monitors did anything improper, Pels said. She added that the monitors are trained to comply with federal law governing conduct at polling places and won’t “interfere with the voting process.”
Democratic lawmakers and voting rights advocates have raised concerns that the Trump administration’s monitors could intimidate voters or abandon the duty they’ve had for decades to protect against civil rights violations.
The department plans to send them to every state, focusing on high-population areas, jurisdictions that have had problems in the past and districts with close elections, according to a senior department official who briefed reporters on the condition of anonymity under terms set by the department.
The Republican National Committee said its operation involves deploying “election integrity deputy state directors” in 22 states, among them Arizona, Michigan, Georgia and North Carolina.
Those workers are the “eyes and the ears of the RNC in the field” who recruit volunteers and organize trainings, said Ally Triolo, the RNC’s election integrity communications director. Their mission is to surface anything that seems unlawful.
At the same time, the RNC has enlisted nearly 22,000 poll workers and is recruiting poll-watching volunteers for competitive districts. The poll watchers will “observe the process and help ensure election rules are followed in accordance with the law,” Triolo said.
Local election officials prepare for increased attention
While federal monitors have quietly observed elections for decades, largely without incident, some election officials are taking precautions.
Chris Swope, the city clerk in Lansing, Michigan, said he preemptively contacted law enforcement and his attorney in case federal monitors violate election law, although he expects them to abide by the rules.
The Democratic Mayors Association issued guidance to local Democratic officials with detailed instructions about what to do if federal agents appear at polling locations.
It notes that federal law prohibits the presence of federal immigration agents, the FBI or other investigative personnel. It also issued a reminder that federal agents are not allowed to be armed at the polls, nor are they allowed to interact with voters or handle ballots or election equipment.
Justice Department officials have said their monitors won’t be armed and will not interfere with voting. Asked about department monitors being sent to Georgia, Trump told a reporter recently: “They’re not going to do anything other than watch.”
Some of the poll observations have already begun. Mary Corcoran, Save America’s executive director, said her group’s volunteers have been monitoring precincts during early voting in Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina and Ohio to help give voters a sense of security.
“The fear is the point, and we must do something about it,” she said. “Left unanswered, fear does the work of keeping people home without a single agent setting foot at a polling place.”
___ Associated Press writers Jacqueline GaNun in Lansing, Mich., Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington and Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed to this report.

title: The Player Involved in Cooper Flagg's Injury Once Played in Maine
text:
The Player Involved in Cooper Flagg’s Injury Once Played in Maine
While injuries are part of the game, the player who was assessed a flagrant foul on the play that led to the Newport native’s injury has a Maine connection.
👇 KEEP READING: Here Are All the Awards Maine's Cooper Flagg Won at Duke 👇
Cooper Flagg injured his left shoulder Friday, Oct. 23, when Indiana’s Aaron Nesmith fouled him from behind during a dunk attempt shortly before halftime, causing him to land awkwardly under the basket.
Nesmith received a flagrant 1 foul, and Flagg missed the remainder of Dallas’ 121-105 victory before an MRI revealed a mild left shoulder sprain. The Mavericks said he would be reevaluated this week but did not specify a day or what that evaluation would involve.
Nesmith spent a brief stint with the Maine Celtics during the 2021-22 season while on assignment from the Boston Celtics to their NBA G League affiliate in Portland.
In his G League debut on Jan. 9, 2022, he recorded 21 points, nine rebounds, and five assists in Maine’s 117-89 victory over the Wisconsin Herd at the Portland Expo.
And there you have it! The play that sidelined one of Maine’s biggest basketball stars involved a player who once suited up for the state’s NBA G League team.

title: 5 new releases from Maine musicians worth a listen
text:
Maine-based musicians have been very busy these past few months, and I’m excited to share that there is a bunch of new music you should know about.
Here are five acts that I’m shining a light on. Be sure to follow them so that you know when they’re playing live.
Name of release: “The Art of Getting By” (album)
Notes: Xander Nelson’s debut full-length album is a power pop gem. He spent four years working on it, and the efforts have paid off. Eleven tracks take listeners on a satisfying ride through upbeat rock landscapes with songs like “Hear Me Out,” “What Are You Waiting For” and the sensational title track. Nelson also shows a tender side on “Walk With Me” and “Calling Your Name.” In an artist statement, Nelson said the album is about the roller coaster of ups and downs he’s experienced over the last few years. “In that time, I played the biggest shows of my life so far, and faced a deep depression and existential crisis,” he wrote.
Release: “Vegas” (album)
Notes: The heart and soul of Dead Gowns is singer-songwriter Geneviève Beaudoin. The exquisite album “Vegas” was released on Friday, a follow-up to last year’s debut “It’s Summer, I Love You, and I’m Surrounded by Snow.” On “Vegas,” Beaudoin continues on her path of crafting songs that are quietly lush, including “Everything You Wanted” and “Salt Destroyer,” while also creating fully-formed and complex offerings like the track “No Longer Contacted.” The band just launched a string of tour dates that end at Oxbow Brewing Company in Portland on Nov. 21. Dead Gowns has been releasing music since 2018, and there’s never been a misstep. Once you’ve come up for air from “Vegas,” be sure to work your way backwards all the way to the “New Spine” EP.
Name of release: “Let’s Hear it for the Monster Squad” (single)
Notes: Lynda Mandolyn’s favorite holiday is Halloween, and her throwback tune “Let’s Hear It for the Monster Squad” name-drops Dracula, Frankenstein and Wolfman, among other creepy creatures. “Here they come in the night, here they come to take your life,” Mandolyn sings in a catchy, jangly tune that sounds like a time machine to the psychedelic ’60s. Mandolyn consistently releases fantastic music, as evidenced in songs like “Silver Day,” and her dreamy cover of early ’60s hit “I Love How You Love Me.”
Release: “The End” (single)
Notes: Lest anyone think I don’t appreciate a full-blown rock song, I give you “The End,” the new single from indie rock act Grand Hotel. The track is on the album “Red Flags,” which you can buy on vinyl, and is the only album song available on streaming. Head to grandhotel.bandcamp.com where you can purchase a download of “The End” and order the vinyl of the album. “The End” was produced and engineered by James Bridges (Fall Out Boy, Mike Gordan) and Chris McLaughlin (Beyonce, Jay-Z, Kanye West). Grand Hotel is Kyle Gervais (guitar and lead vocals), Glen Capen (guitar), Jason Elvin (bass) and Aaron LaChance (drums). The song is a propulsive and enthralling tune that does drop some profanity. Grand Hotel formed in 2008, released three albums in rapid succession, then went on hiatus. Occasionally they re-form. This is one of those times.
JEFF BADGER
Release: “Dig ‘Em Up” (single)
Notes: Singer-songwriter Jeff Badger is gearing up to release his next album, and its second single “Dig ‘Em Up” is a jaunty, piano-driven tune with a playful bounce and offbeat rhythm. Badger said it’s about digging up old ideas. “All your dead ideas are never really dead. They’re in a shallow grave out back behind the shed. So get yourself a shovel, get yourself a pick. Put your back into it now, it’s time to dig,” sings Badger. Badger initially won me over six years ago with “No Corona,” a hopeful song released in April 2020.

title: 14 County Standouts Make the Week Eight Athlete of the Week Ballot
text:
Postseason Performances Take Over the Week Eight Athlete of the Week Ballot
The postseason is underway, and the Fall Week Eight Athlete of the Week ballot reflects just how big the performances have become.
Regional championship races, tournament soccer victories, shutouts, game-winning goals and standout individual efforts helped produce this week's field of 14 Aroostook County athletes.
Seven boys and seven girls have made the final ballot.
Voting is open now, and you can vote once per hour in both polls through Thursday at 3 p.m.
Here are the Fall Week Eight nominees.
Boys Athlete of the Week Nominees
Peyton Gorneault, Caribou, Cross Country
Gorneault delivered a huge performance at the Class B North Regional Championship. The Caribou freshman finished fourth overall in 17:12.04, helping the Vikings capture the Northern Maine team championship and advance to states.
Brayden Drake, Houlton/GHCA, Cross Country
Drake helped Houlton/GHCA put together a dominant regional championship performance, finishing third in Class C North in 16:59.00.
His finish helped Houlton/GHCA capture its second consecutive regional championship.
Paxton Darrell, Presque Isle, Cross Country
Darrell led the Wildcats at the Class B North Regional Championship, placing fifth overall in 17:15.20.
His performance helped Presque Isle finish third as a team and earn a spot in the state championship meet.
Dominic Burgess, Van Buren, Soccer
Burgess stepped up in tournament play for the Crusaders, scoring a goal in Van Buren's 3-1 preliminary-round victory over Schenck.
The win kept Van Buren's season alive and sent the Crusaders into the next round.
Brayden Barnard, Washburn, Soccer
Barnard earned his nomination after scoring 2 goals in Washburn's victory over Hodgdon, helping the Beavers pick up a big late-season win.
Gage Phillips, Katahdin, Soccer
Phillips put together a strong week in net for the Cougars.
He made 7 saves while recording a shutout against Van Buren, then followed it with 7 more saves in Katahdin's tournament game against Lee Academy.
That gave Phillips 14 saves across two games with one clean sheet.
Kyle Waye, Washburn
Waye was nominated for the way he represents his team on and off the field.
His nomination highlighted his effort, encouragement of teammates and sportsmanship, including his willingness to check on opposing players when they are injured.
Girls Athlete of the Week Nominees
Samantha Argraves, Presque Isle, Soccer
Argraves continued a strong season in goal by recording another shutout in Presque Isle's 4-0 victory over Fort Kent.
The clean sheet was her seventh shutout of the season during her first year as the Wildcats' full-time varsity goalkeeper.
Madelyn Marquis, Van Buren, Soccer
Marquis produced a big offensive performance for the Crusaders, scoring 2 goals and adding an assist in Van Buren's 3-0 victory over Easton.
Dani Pelletier, Madawaska, Soccer
Pelletier delivered one of the biggest moments of the week.
The eighth-grader scored just 57 seconds into the second overtime, giving Madawaska a dramatic 1-0 victory over Washburn.
Jenna Strid, Caribou, Cross Country
Strid delivered a strong postseason run for the Vikings, finishing eighth at the Class B North Regional Championship in 20:07.58.
Her top-10 finish helped Caribou place third as a team and qualify for the state championship meet.
Annamarie Blanchard, Presque Isle, Soccer
Blanchard found the back of the net during Presque Isle's 4-0 victory over Fort Kent, helping the Wildcats finish the regular season with another strong performance.
Trinity Daigle, Fort Kent, Soccer
Daigle came through in goal when Fort Kent entered tournament play.
She recorded the shutout in the Warriors' 3-0 quarterfinal victory over MCI, helping Fort Kent advance deeper into the Class C North tournament.
Charlotte Estabrook, Houlton/GHCA, Cross Country
Estabrook earned an individual trip to the state championships with a strong Class C North regional performance.
She finished 19th overall in 24:25.61, earning one of the individual qualifying spots for Houlton/GHCA.
Time to Pick the Week Eight Winners
Week Eight gives voters a little bit of everything.
There are regional championship performances, team titles, individual state qualifiers, playoff goals, a double-overtime game-winner and goalkeepers who delivered shutouts when their teams needed them.
Now it is up to the voters.
Vote once per hour in both the boys and girls polls through Thursday at 3 p.m.
The Fall Week Eight Athletes of the Week will be announced Friday morning.

title: ProPublica fails to support its insinuations about Susan Collins
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Timothy C. Woodcock is a Bangor attorney. He was on Sen. Bill Cohen’s personal and committee staffs. From 1983 to 1987, he was an assistant U.S. attorney for the District of Maine, and, in 1987, he was an associate counsel on the Senate Iran-Contra Committee. He is married to Carol Woodcock, Sen. Susan Collins’ Bangor State Office representative.
In late September, several Maine newspapers ran a ProPublica story claiming FBI public integrity agents were “circling” Sen. Susan Collins until President Donald Trump “got in the way.” The story promises revelations, but upon close examination, it delivers nothing.
The story’s central figure is Martin Kao, former CEO of Navatek, a long-established Hawaii-based naval engineering firm. In July and August 2019, Kao and two associates funneled money to relatives, who then contributed to Collins’ 2020 campaign. Federal law prohibits these “conduit contributions.” In December 2019, Kao also used a shell company he created to give $150,000 in company funds to a super PAC supporting Collins.
Kao’s crimes went beyond just campaign contributions. In 2022, he pleaded guilty to defrauding the Paycheck Protection Program of more $12.5 million, money meant to help businesses shuttered by COVID. He is also accused of defrauding a bank of $3 million to buy an opulent Hawaii home.
Kao pleaded guilty in separate federal cases involving campaign contributions and financial fraud, and he is now in federal prison.
The majority of the ProPublica piece focuses on Kao’s illicit 2019 campaign contributions, but the story obscures the fact that none of this is “new” news. The federal indictment of Kao proves this point. In February 2022, a District of Columbia grand jury returned a five-count indictment against Kao and his associates. It detailed both the conduit contributions and the shell company contribution.
The December 2019 meeting at a Corner Bakery, which the story repeatedly highlights as though ProPublica had discovered it, appears in the indictment at paragraph 49, though without naming the bakery. Readers should understand that this meeting and the illegal contributions were not only documented, they were formally charged and prosecuted to conviction four years before ProPublica’s headline.
Significantly, the indictment does not identify either the Collins campaign committee or the super PAC. Instead, they are consistently referred to only as “Campaign Committee A” and “Political Committee A.” Prosecutors employ such masking terms to shield innocent parties from the unfairness of being besmirched by association with the accused. Omitting the identities of such parties from an indictment is always a deliberate decision.
The omission of the committees’ identities from the Kao indictment objectively demonstrates that the Biden Justice Department, headed by then-Attorney General Merrick Garland, decided that Collins and the committees deserved that protection. The omission of the committees’ identities also squares with the FBI’s recent statement that its investigation of Kao had “found nothing implicating Senator Collins or Senator Collins’ campaign.” A simple internet search will yield the Kao indictment. Readers are encouraged to review it for themselves.
Then there are the FBI agents. By ProPublica’s own account, they were highly skilled and pored over “thousands” of Kao’s records, including emails with Collins’ “inner circle.” What does ProPublica contend these experienced agents missed? The story doesn’t clearly say.
That leaves a 50-page memo that Kao, himself, wrote in September 2024 in an unsuccessful attempt to reduce his sentence by implicating “dozens” of people on Capitol Hill. The story never says the memo even names Collins. And, in 2024, two years after his guilty plea, what could Kao have told the agents about Collins that they wouldn’t already have known? Once again, ProPublica doesn’t make that clear.
ProPublica’s omissions are not limited to the FBI investigation. In an Oct. 17 letter to the editor published by the Portland Press Herald, former Federal Election Commissioner Sean Cooksey explained a three-year FEC investigation found no evidence of wrongdoing by Collins, her campaign or the super PAC. How did ProPublica’s reporters miss this?
ProPublica itself carefully avoids accusing Collins of wrongdoing. It trades instead on the transparently self-serving claims of a convicted fraudster, its assurances to readers of its own professionalism, and the corrosive power of insinuation. Readers deserve better. ProPublica should be held to account.

title: Flood warning lingers in Four Corners as soaked towns face sewage-tainted waters. 1 death reported
text:
Parts of the Southwest’s Four Corners region remained under a flood warning Monday as some saturated neighborhoods began cleaning up, assessing damage and watching out for water that could be contaminated with chemicals and raw sewage.
Flooding caused by excessive rainfall happened Monday along the San Juan River in parts of the Four Corners region, the meeting point of Utah, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico. The area has experienced unusually heavy rain since Wednesday that caused rivers to surge, flooding homes and forcing water rescues. Storms led to a tornado that touched down in Santa Fe, New Mexico, on Saturday night.
One flooding-related death was reported in Santa Fe on Saturday during a water rescue of a family that had attempted to cross a flooded arroyo in their vehicle, the county sheriff’s office said. A father and child were able to get onto land, but a female passenger was swept away by the current and was found dead a mile away, the office said.
Rising river has led to evacuations in Utah and Colorado
By Monday morning, the San Juan River was 1 1/2 feet (45.7 centimeters) above the flood stage of 23 feet (7 meters), the National Weather Service said. It was expected to crest to 31 feet (9.4 meters) later Monday, then fall below flood stage by Tuesday morning.
This compares to Sept. 10, 1927, when the river crested at 32 feet (9.7 meters), the weather service said.
Some residents in one community along the river, Bluff, Utah, were evacuated over the weekend but were allowed to return early Monday.
Returning residents and businesses should use caution as several properties were still flooded, county officials said.
“Stay out of the San Juan River,” the weather service said. “Water levels remain elevated, and possible sewage contamination poses additional health risks.”
Farmington area deals with evacuations and power outage
In the Farmington area of New Mexico, local officials said swollen rivers were receding, but that many people remained evacuated and hundreds were without power.
San Juan County, New Mexico, did not have official figures on the number of homes damaged or how many people were evacuated, spokesperson Devin Neeley told The Associated Press.
“It’s a pretty active disaster zone,” he said.
Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham and Major General Miguel Aguilar of the New Mexico National Guard planned to visit the county Monday to survey damage and meet with affected residents.
Floodwaters could be contaminated with chemicals and raw sewage
Officials in the hard-hit counties urged patience and caution. Water could be contaminated with chemicals and raw sewage, and gas and propane lines could be broken, among other hazards.
“The public is anxious to get back in,” San Juan County Fire & Rescue Chief David Vega acknowledged at a news conference Sunday. “But I want the public to know there are still hazards out there.”
Undersheriff Cory Tanner said officials were going from house to house to check for hazards — a process that could take days to complete.
Zach and Abigail Flatt started putting together go-bags after receiving evacuation orders on their phones Thursday evening. Their home in Bloomfield, New Mexico, sits on the San Juan River.
“In 30 or 40 minutes it had jumped about 4 feet,” Zach recalled Sunday. “After I saw that big jump, and how close it was to going over the banks, I said we’ve got to get out.”
By the time the family was loaded into the car, water was coming up over the tires. They found a hotel room with their two children, ages 2 and 4, and watched via webcams as at least 18 inches (.45 meters) of water inundated their property, washing away 22 of their 24 chickens.
“We watched stuff just float away, off the porch into the front yard,” Zach said.
Authorities are assessing damage in the Navajo Nation and in a Colorado county
In the Shiprock, New Mexico, area of the Navajo Nation, wastewater facilities and water holding ponds were damaged by flooding, causing sewage releases into the San Juan River, according to Navajo Tribal Utility Authority Shiprock District Manager Wilfred Franklin Jr.
New Mexico’s congressional delegation on Sunday urged President Donald Trump to declare an emergency for the state to release federal assistance funding.
In Colorado, teams created maps of some counties to help identify affected roads, road closures, impacted areas and evacuation zones.
The flooding is just the latest from two months of on-and-off heavy rain in the region caused by tropical moisture coming ashore from the Pacific. After months of drought, other recent deadly flooding struck the Grand Canyon and other areas of New Mexico.
Forecasters said El Niño, the natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific, was likely to blame for the latest storm’s unusually heavy rainfall.
___
Associated Press writers Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, Anna Wilder in Austin, Texas, and Christopher Weber in Los Angeles contributed.

title: Monday Five and Five: The Postseason Is Heating Up
text:
Monday Five and Five: Tournament Wins and Regional Championships
Tournament time is here, and it didn't take long for things to get interesting.
We had penalty kicks, six-goal playoff performances and a pair of big regional championship days for County cross country.
Now the soccer field is getting smaller, the games are getting bigger, and our runners are headed to Augusta with state championships on the line.
Here are my five from last week and five things I'm looking forward to this week.
Five From Last Week
5. Fort Kent Girls Move On
Fort Kent opened tournament play exactly the way the top seed wanted to.
The Lady Warriors shut out Maine Central Institute 3-0 and moved into the Class C North semifinals. Fort Kent has been one of the strongest girls teams in the area all season, and now the Warriors are one step closer to playing for a regional championship.
4. Caribou Scores Six to Stay Alive
Caribou's boys came into the Class B tournament needing a win, and the Vikings delivered plenty of offense.
Louie Hebert, Declan Miller and Carter St. Pierre each scored twice as Caribou defeated Medomak Valley 6-2.
Three players. Two goals apiece. Six goals in a tournament game.
That's a pretty good way to earn another one.
3. Houlton Survives a Penalty-Kick Thriller
Sometimes you just have to survive and advance.
Houlton and Penquis went through regulation and overtime without a goal before the Shires finally pulled it out in penalty kicks.
Houlton won the shootout 3-2 and kept its season alive, earning a spot in the eight-player quarterfinals.
2. Caribou and County Runners Have a Huge Class B Regional
Saturday was a big one for County cross country.
Caribou's boys won the Class B North regional championship with 61 points, while Pierce Gorneault won the individual boys title in 16:01.03.
Emma Graves made it an individual sweep for Caribou, winning the girls championship in 18:44.40.
Presque Isle's girls finished second, Caribou's girls were third and Presque Isle's boys placed third, sending all four County Class B teams to the state championships.
1. Houlton/GHCA Goes Back-to-Back
Winning one regional championship is tough enough.
Houlton/GHCA made it two in a row Saturday.
The Shires won the Class C North boys championship with just 30 points, placing four runners among the first five finishers.
Malachi Witmer was second in 16:52.80, Brayden Drake finished third, Wyatt Quint was fourth and Logan Witmer placed fifth.
The Houlton girls didn't qualify as a team, but Charlotte Estabrook and Isabella McCarthy advanced individually, along with Washburn's Eleanora Streeter and MSSM's Sadie Wigmore.
That's another regional championship for Houlton and another big group of County runners headed to states.
Five to Watch This Week
5. Caribou Gets a Shot at No. 1
Caribou's reward for scoring six goals Saturday?
A date with undefeated John Bapst.
The eighth-seeded Vikings travel to face the top-seeded Crusaders Tuesday in the Class B North quarterfinals.
John Bapst finished the regular season 13-0-1, so Caribou knows exactly what kind of challenge is waiting. But after putting six on the board in the prelims, the Vikings get the opportunity to see what they can do against the top team in the region.
4. Plenty of County Flavor in Eight-Player Soccer
There are still several County teams to follow in the eight-player tournament.
Wisdom's boys host Lee Academy Tuesday after the Pandas knocked Katahdin out in the preliminary round.
Houlton gets the biggest test possible after surviving Penquis, moving on to face top-seeded Mattanawcook Academy.
Wisdom's girls are also still alive after earning the No. 2 seed in the North.
At this point, every game means somebody's season continues and somebody's season ends.
3. Presque Isle Girls Begin Their Tournament Run
After earning a first-round bye, Presque Isle finally gets into tournament action Tuesday.
The third-seeded Wildcats host No. 6 Skowhegan in a Class B North quarterfinal.
Presque Isle finished the regular season 9-3-2 and now gets the opportunity to begin its postseason run at home.
2. County Runners Head to States
Saturday brings one more trip south, and this time it's for a state championship.
The state cross country championships will be held at Cony High School in Augusta, beginning with the Class B boys at 11 a.m.
Caribou's boys head down as regional champions, while Presque Isle's boys, Presque Isle's girls and Caribou's girls all qualified as teams.
Houlton/GHCA will represent The County in the Class C boys race after winning its second straight regional title.
And there will be several individual qualifiers to watch as well.
It's one more chance for County runners to bring some hardware back north.
1. Class D North Is Full of County Matchups
If you're looking for the busiest part of the soccer tournament this week, Class D North is the place to start.
On the boys side Tuesday:
No. 5 Easton at No. 4 Hodgdon
No. 6 Washburn at No. 3 Fort Fairfield
No. 7 Penobscot Valley at No. 2 Central Aroostook
No. 8 MSSM at No. 1 Madawaska
That means three of the four quarterfinals guarantee a County team will advance.
The girls bracket gives us even more head-to-head County soccer:
No. 5 Madawaska at No. 4 Ashland
No. 6 Van Buren at No. 3 Central Aroostook
No. 7 Washburn at No. 2 Fort Fairfield
Top-seeded Penobscot Valley hosts Schenck/Stearns in the other quarterfinal.
By Saturday, we could have a whole lot of Aroostook County representation left in the Class D North semifinals.
Now It Gets Fun
We're officially at the point where there are no easy do-overs.
Soccer seasons are on the line every time teams take the field, and our cross country runners get one final shot Saturday with state championships at stake.
There should be plenty to talk about by the time next Monday rolls around.
