title: Nicki Minaj joins Trump on Air Force One: Who else is flying with the president?
text:
ABOARD AIR FORCE ONE (AP) — President Donald Trump has clocked about 70 hours aboard Air Force One so far this month, racing from rally to rally across the United States to try to bolster his Republican Party in the midterm elections.
Also along for the ride: an entourage ranging from aging boxing champions to Cabinet members to relatively unknown aides who help craft Trump’s words and ideas. The passenger list for Trump’s marathon through the sky signals who has the ear of the president.
“It can say what his priorities are,” said David Cohen, a professor of political science at the University of Akron. “Who he surrounds himself with are the people he is going to be listening to. They’re the ones who are going to be whispering in his ear and talking softly in private quarters to the president of the United States.”
Here’s a look at who has had access to power in the confines of Trump’s plane this month.
The inner circle
White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who recently finished treatment for breast cancer, is a frequent flyer. Trump has called Wiles, who co-managed his 2024 campaign, the “most powerful woman in the world.” As Air Force One ascended from Greenville, North Carolina, after Trump’s 15th rally in 20 days, Wiles gave reporters her take on how it went as she walked up the aisle.
“Great,” she said. “They’ve all been great, honestly.”
Other insiders who’ve made the manifest: special envoy Steve Witkoff, who has been trying to negotiate an end to the Iran war that has weighed on Republicans’ midterm fortunes; deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, the architect of Trump’s immigration crackdown; Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner; Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins.
The most frequent Cabinet member aboard has been Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a billionaire who previously ran the financial services firm Cantor Fitzgerald. A Trump buddy going back to the 1990s, Lutnick can often be heard laughing at the president’s jokes. His role at Trump’s rallies has been to highlight new factory investments that Trump uses to try to convince his supporters that the economy is doing well.
Punching above their weight
Bill Pulte has joined Trump for at least five legs of the midterm marathon so far, a sign that his status inside the administration is far higher than his title — director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency — would suggest.
The scion of a homebuilding company, Pulte is a Trump pal who was for a brief period also the acting director of national intelligence and oversaw layoffs in that office. He has led pressure campaigns on Federal Reserve officials such as Jerome Powell and Lisa Cook. Pulte has also passed along policy ideas such as changing the 30-year mortgage to 50 years, an idea that has since been abandoned.
Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr has also flown with the president, notably on Oct. 13 and Oct. 14 on a lengthy West Coast swing. Carr has sought to use his regulatory powers over broadcast networks to chastise them over their coverage of the president.
Personal aides who keep Trump going
Chief among the retinue of assistants around the president is Natalie Harp, an executive assistant who is on most of Trump’s trips. Walt Nauta, the director of Oval Office Operations, is not far behind her in air miles. Chamberlain Harris, Nauta’s deputy, is another frequent traveler. She also serves as a member of the Commission of Fine Arts, one of the government bodies with a role in reviewing the White House ballroom and other Trump construction projects.
Although Trump likes to ad-lib, the speechwriting director, Ross Worthington, has joined him repeatedly on the plane this month. The president’s stump speech features a promise of $5,000 checks if Republicans keep their House and Senate majorities after the Nov. 3 election. He also tends to highlight new factory projects and investments in the communities he visits.
Margo Martin, a communications adviser who posts videos of Trump on social media, has joined the tour, as has White House communications director Steven Cheung. Katie Zacharia, who was the White House press secretary for five days, spent two of them with the president on a trip to Alaska, Nevada, Arizona and Montana.
Plenty of political strategists
Trump is surrounded on these trips by White House and external consultants making strategic choices for the midterms, including Matt Brasseaux, his political director, who previously worked at the Republican National Committee.
Johnny DeStefano, who was a top aide in Trump’s first term, temporarily rejoined the White House this summer to work on midterm strategy and has been seen on Air Force One, as has former White House deputy chief of staff James Blair.
Celebrities hitch a ride
Going into what could be some rough midterm races, Trump has brought aboard with him some of the biggest names in boxing: Mike Tyson, Floyd Mayweather Jr. and Evander Holyfield. In a 1997 heavyweight championship bout, Tyson bit off a piece of Holyfield’s right ear. They did not fly on Air Force One at the same time.
Towson University professor Martha Kumar said that presidential travel during a campaign can be intense and that presidents often have passengers who can keep the environment relaxed even as the work continues. “You want to have people around you that make you feel comfortable,” Kumar said. “When you think about it, it is really stressful. You want some relief.”
On Sunday, Cheung posted a video in which he was interviewing the rapper Nicki Minaj aboard Air Force One as it took Trump to Michigan for a campaign rally. Minaj praised the president, and the White House’s goal is to have Trump wrap up his midterm blitz by having a celebrity with him at each stop.
Who else has hitched a ride with Trump? Retired NASCAR champion Richard Petty went to North Carolina, former NFL coach Jon Gruden to Ohio, and retired NFL running back Todd Gurley to Georgia. Influencer-turned-boxer Jake Paul also traveled with the president. The celebrities have had cameos in Trump’s rallies.
Congress gets onboard
The goal of Trump’s travel over the past month has been to help Republicans keep control of Congress.
As the White House’s liaison with the House, Jeff Freeland has been on Air Force One with multiple lawmakers. Rep. William Timmons of South Carolina flew with the president, as have multiple Texas House members, including Reps. Beth Van Duyne and Brandon Gill, as well as Reps. Brian Jack of Georgia, Tim Moore of North Carolina and Anna Paulina Luna of Florida.
John Barrasso of Wyoming, the second-ranking Republican senator, has flown multiple times with the president this month, as has Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who is considering a presidential bid in 2028.

title: Billion-dollar sick day: US productivity expected to take a hit with release of 'GTA VI'
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Billion-dollar sick day: US productivity expected to take a hit with release of 'GTA VI'
The box office may have been lit up by talking space rocks, Greek legends, wall-crawling superheroes and unhealthy relationships this year, but the biggest media release of 2026 — and maybe any year — is still to come. And it won't be at the movie theater.
Related video above: Soldiers incentivized to reenlist with time off to play Grand Theft Auto VI
Rockstar Games' long-awaited "Grand Theft Auto VI" will finally release worldwide on Nov. 19, and early projections estimate it could make $1 billion within its first couple of days. It's expected to accrue upwards of $10 billion in gross lifetime revenue. The game has already secured almost $600 million from preorders alone.
Strauss Zelnick, CEO of Rockstar Games' owner, Take-Two Interactive, told shareholders the company expects more than $1 billion in operating cash flow this fiscal year, largely on the back of "GTA 6." To date, the game's predecessor has accrued nearly $11 billion in gross revenue since its release.
But that money has to come from somewhere.
Analysts say when the latest entry in the "Grand Theft Auto" video game series launches on Nov. 19, the U.S. stands to lose around $1 billion in productivity.
According to a report from the International Business Times, José García Montalvo, an economics professor at Pompeu Fabra University in Barcelona, said this is just an academic projection, but there is substantial evidence to support it.
For starters, it's happened before.
When the previous entry in the series, "Grand Theft Auto V," was released in 2013, an IGN survey of 11,000 readers revealed 46% had called off from work ahead of time, while 20% said they planned to call out sick the morning of the game's launch. About 6% of workers aged 18 to 35 in major metropolitan areas such as Los Angeles and New York City took time off for the release.
In a similar IGN survey for this go-around, 42% of the 10,400 readers polled said they have already requested off for Nov. 19, while 9% said they're planning to call off sick.
For the release of "Grand Theft Auto VI," an estimated 1.5 million Americans are expected to call off sick on Nov. 19, leading to a potential $1 billion loss of U.S. output in a single day.
This follows a trend set by the day after the Super Bowl, also known as "Super Sick Monday." In 2026, 26.2 million U.S. employees had planned to miss work that day, according to UKG's annual Super Bowl Absenteeism Survey, leading to an estimated $5 billion loss in productivity. UKG also reported a potential $17 billion loss in global productivity from the 2026 FIFA World Cup.
Montalvo bases this estimate on an average annual output of $70,000 per U.S. worker and a short-term productivity dip of 2%. An additional dip in productivity is expected from workers who don't call off sick but still stay up late playing the game — or work remotely on release day. The bulk of employees expected to call out sick are men ages 18 to 30, with most of them expected to be from the tech world.
So, if the office is feeling emptier than usual on Nov. 19, there's a good chance it's because your colleagues are committing crimes — at least virtually.

title: Police say ax-swinging woman attacked motorcycle, then man in Rumford
text:
RUMFORD — A Massachusetts woman was arrested on Sunday after allegedly attacking a local man’s motorcycle with an ax before swinging the tool at the man’s head.
Luciane Dezan, 46, of Medford, was charged with attempted elevated aggravated assault and aggravated criminal mischief. She was taken to the Oxford County Jail in Paris where she remained on Monday.
According to police reports, Dezan began swinging her ax when a dispute arose over her transport of the victim’s motorcycle from Massachusetts to Maine.
The local man, 44, whose name is being withheld by police, had hired Dezan to haul his 1984 Honda GL1200 motorcycle from his former residence in Northborough, Massachusetts, to Rumford.
When the pair met at a business on U.S. Route 2 in Rumford, the meeting quickly devolved into violence, police said.
“When Dezan arrived with the motorcycle, the victim discovered damage that he believed had occurred during transportation,” according to a Rumford police news release. “After confronting Dezan about the damage and indicating that he was unwilling to pay the full agreed-upon transportation fee, an argument ensued.”
The argument proceeded until Dezan began taking her frustrations out first on the local man’s motorcycle, according to the report.
“The investigation revealed that Dezan retrieved an axe from her van and began repeatedly striking the motorcycle, causing extensive damage,” according to the press release. “When the victim attempted to intervene and stop the destruction, Dezan allegedly swung the axe toward his head, narrowly missing him.”
Police said the victim avoided a serious head injury only by ducking out of the path of the ax swung by Dezan.
His motorcycle did not fare as well. Police estimated damage from repeated blows from the ax at $2,000.
Police said the confrontation was captured by surveillance cameras. The video was not available on Monday.
Dezan was being held on $10,000 cash bail.
Police were assisted at the scene by the Oxford County Sheriff’s Department.

title: Pres. Trump to rally GOP voters in dual TX rallies Tuesday
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump is set to return to Texas on Tuesday to rally GOP voters in Lubbock and Corpus Christi.
The rallies come one week before Election Day and are being held to encourage Republican voters to get out to the polls.
Recent polls have shown that some Texas midterm matchups are particularly competitive, with much attention focused on the U.S. Senate race between State Rep. James Talarico (D) and Attorney General Ken Paxton (R). Several political analyses currently rate the Senate race as a toss-up.
Joshua Blank, research director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, said the impact of Trump’s visits to the state remain unclear.
“The president’s focus on Texas has been a big topic of discussion, in particular, whether or not it helps or hurts Republican candidates in tight races. Ultimately, the president has decided that his efforts in Texas will be helpful,” Blank said.
Trump is scheduled to speak at 2 p.m. Central time in Corpus Christi and at 6 p.m. Central time in Lubbock.

Parts of Portland's Commercial Street reduced to one lane as city upgrades storm drain system
Starting Monday, the stretch of Commercial Street between Center Street and Maple Street will be reduced to alternating one-way traffic during the day while the city of Portland continues its work to upgrade the storm drain system
Parts of Portland's Commercial Street reduced to one lane as city upgrades storm drain system
Starting Monday, the stretch of Commercial Street between Center Street and Maple Street will be reduced to alternating one-way traffic during the day while the city of Portland continues its work to upgrade the storm drain system
Starting Monday, Oct. 26, the stretch of Commercial Street between Center Street and Maple Street will be reduced to alternating one-way traffic during the daytime while the city of Portland continues its work to upgrade the storm drain system.
The city says that stretch of Commercial Street will be reduced to one lane from 9 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. every weekday. Then, in mid-November, it will be permanently reduced to one lane until the project is completed.
Parking will also be reduced on Commercial Street during the project.
The city says the storm drain project is meant to help mitigate flooding issues the area sees, especially during storms.
Workers will be installing 1,000 feet of 42-inch storm drain piping beneath Commercial Street to replace the 18-inch pipes that are currently there. Work has already started on the Portland Fish Pier, where the city is constructing a new 42-inch separated storm drain outfall.
The city says the new system will include tidal backwater valves to reduce tidal backflow and improve performance during high tides. The upgraded storm drain is designed to handle a 25-year storm.
The project received a $3.6 million grant as part of the Maine DOT's Maine Infrastructure Adaptation Fund.
The city of Portland is asking drivers to avoid the area if possible to avoid traffic congestion.

title: Former hairstylist and nail tech battles lung cancer after decades of chemical exposure
text:
RICHMOND, Va. (Aging Untold) — For 35 years, Jeorgi Golden knew the ins and outs of the salon, working as a Black hairstylist where coworkers and clients became family.
“I started in the late 70s, early 80s,” Golden said. “It was more like being a social worker or a counselor because we talked about everything.”
With the exception of Mondays, Golden spent long hours at the salon seeing client after client. These days, she misses the comfort it once brought her.
“Smelling the natural hair when you press it, it’s nostalgia,” Golden said. “It makes me think of my grandmother who did my hair when I was a kid.”
For years, Golden would do at least 10 ladies’ hair each day. By the end of the week, she would have seen approximately 40 to 50 clients.
Some of those women asked for everything from press and curls to hair relaxers or a Jheri Curl, a popular hairstyle at the time that gave coarse hair a curly, wet look.
She remembers when relaxers were her biggest seller, not just for women, but also for men.
“The salon would be filled, especially if you had a salon that had 10 to 15 people in there working. And everybody’s doing that,” Golden said.
For Golden, it was about making her customers happy and getting the job done. But the chemicals she breathed in daily may have cost her dearly.
The only protection was gloves
Golden said salon workers in those days received minimal safety guidance about those products and how they should be applied.
“The only thing you was told was, ‘Oh you can put on gloves cause you’re dealing with lye.’ That was it. There was no other protection,” she said. “So, we went in blindly, thinking that the products that was sold to us and said, ‘Hey this is gonna make you beautiful.’ They didn’t tell us that it was gonna definitely hurt us at the end.”
She said no one ever mentioned the dangers, even though formaldehyde was an ingredient found in those products.
Formaldehyde is classified as a carcinogen by the EPA.
For Golden and other hairstylists, they trusted the products and never questioned potential health risks.
Golden was diagnosed with lung cancer in April 2024 after a routine tuberculosis test revealed something alarming. She says she never smoked or drank, making her cancer diagnosis particularly puzzling until she began connecting it to her decades of salon work.
“I was like, ‘I didn’t do anything. How did this happen?’” Golden said. “And then I started going back through the times. Yeah, I did nails... formaldehyde, it was right there. And that was before they made it a nicer-smelling product.”
Golden’s health concerns began decades earlier. At age 26, she had a hysterectomy after developing polyps.
“I was still doing hair and the pain was just excruciating,” Golden said. “I passed out at work, and [the doctor] said I have to have a hysterectomy.”
The physician told her they found polyps, but they never explicitly said it was cancer at the time.
“I think a lot of women who was in the industry have a lot of medical issues that they don’t connect,” she said. “You think it’s something that’s isolated, but I think if you have more than 10 women having the same thing who did the same job...then it’s related.”
Chemical exposure concerns widespread
Her concerns reflect those of other hairstylists.
InvestigateTV analyzed complaints submitted to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) over the past five years about formaldehyde dangers affecting hair salon owners and workers across the country.
We found dozens of complaints filed by salon owners and employees about the lack of ventilation within their salons and concerns about not having safety data sheets about the chemicals they’d be working with.
One complaint from a New York salon stated, “Brazilian blowout treatments are done in a very small space in the salon with little ventilation. The formaldehyde vapors from the procedure impacts staff health, such as respiratory irritation.”
Another complaint noted, “The use of hair products and color agents are exposing employees to chemical hazards...the chemicals are ammonia, formaldehyde, toluene and acetone...no ventilation system is being utilized to control the airborne hazard.”
An additional complaint said that “employees are experiencing headaches, breathing issues, burning throats and eyes due to the exposure of formaldehyde during Brazilian Blowout treatments.”
That same complaint goes on to say that the salon wasn’t providing proper ventilation and personal protection equipment and safety goggles and gloves.
In 2010, OSHA investigated a series of specific Brazilian blowout products finding some were listed as formaldehyde-free but on-site testing showed they “found formaldehyde in the air” after questions and complaints were made by hair salon owners and workers.
Inspectors missed the dangers, stylist says
Golden recalls that those same experiences reflect what she says she personally saw in her salon when inspectors visited years ago. She said when the inspector walked in, they would see there was some ventilation available, and not once did they question the toxins in the air further.
A 2022 National Institutes of Health study called the “Sister Study” found a correlation between formaldehyde and uterine cancer after following 33,000 women for 11 years.
The study also found that Black women are disproportionately more affected because of their higher use of those chemicals.
When that study emerged, Golden began thinking about how those chemicals might have affected her own health.
“My first thought was, ‘Hmm, that really couldn’t be us,’” Golden said. “And then as I started reading more and we as women who were in the salon and we’re talking and saying ‘Well, you know, so and so got cancer.’”
She said she and her colleagues who had gotten sick began connecting the dots.
Lawmakers push for action
The health concerns Golden and other salon workers face have caught the attention of federal lawmakers.
U.S. Rep. Shontel Brown of Ohio, who developed uterine fibroids and had a hysterectomy, is among lawmakers calling on the FDA to ban chemical hair products containing formaldehyde.
“These chemicals and these hair relaxers have proven to be dangerous,” the Democrat lawmaker said. “Eighty percent of Black women are going to be diagnosed with fibroids. And I am a person who has survived uterine fibroids.”
Brown and other lawmakers are pushing for additional legislation to study uterine cancer and other illnesses related to chemical hair straighteners.
“The bottom line is we want people to feel safe,” Brown said. “We want people to be able to beautify themselves, without worrying about if this is going to give me any adverse health effects.”
Fellow Democrat, Rep. Alma Adams of North Carolina, noted that currently, there is no federal funding allocated to research uterine cancer.
On a state level, California, Washington, and Maryland have banned or restricted formaldehyde in cosmetics.
Despite national concern, the FDA has not banned the ingredients and has missed its fifth deadline to propose a ban on formaldehyde products.
“When you think about the United States of America, this should not be a partisan issue,” Brown said. “We have women in every state, right? And so we make up 51% of the population.”
The Cost of Beauty
Back at home now, Jeorgi Golden is retired and doing her best to stay healthy. She said that she doesn’t regret her life in the salon. She hopes other stylists will remember to put their health and well-being first.
“I tell any woman, any woman, if you hear that whisper and wake up in the middle of the night go to the doctor,” Golden said. “Because we as women put everything off. We take care of everybody but ourselves.”
She mentions that there is a cost to beauty.
“We, as women of color, we want to have the image that they have said we should have, and as they say, beauty costs and we are paying the costs for that beauty.”

title: Former Buxton police officer pleads guilty to criminal charge for using BMV data to find ex-partner
text:
BIDDEFORD — A former Buxton police officer has pleaded guilty to one misdemeanor count of criminal invasion of computer privacy after a prosecutor for the state said he used law enforcement data to find out where his ex-partner lived.
Andrew Ward changed his plea Monday morning, when he had been scheduled to begin a jury-waived bench trial in York County Superior Court.
The state agreed to dismiss three other misdemeanor counts against Ward, including one count each of domestic violence stalking, stalking and official oppression. He was ordered to pay a $500 fine and will surrender his certification to be a law enforcement officer in Maine.
Attorneys on both sides spent several hours with Superior Court Justice Richard Mulhern before they came to the agreement, and Ward’s attorney argued in earlier court records that the domestic violence allegations were unsupported because Ward’s ex-partner had also been initiating contact with him.
Mulhern said in court that he had given the lawyers an “indication” before the hearing of where he believed the case would end up, based on the evidence he had reviewed ahead of trial.
As Ward left the courtroom, his attorney Michael Cunniff said the dismissal of the three counts speaks to the quality of the state’s case. Ward pleaded not guilty and denied the state’s characterizations when he was charged in 2025.
Prosecutor Paul Cavanaugh said Monday that prosecuting the case shows the state’s willingness to hold its law enforcement officers accountable.
“The system has to monitor itself and be willing to deal with people in the system that misuse the system,” Cavanaugh said after the hearing. “Otherwise, the public is going to have trust issues with the system.”
In court records, Cavanaugh argued that Ward searched repeatedly for the addresses of both his ex and her new partner using a Bureau of Motor Vehicles database that only certain government employees have access to.
Cunniff had asked that the computer privacy charge be dismissed earlier this year, arguing that home addresses are available in the public domain; Cavanaugh said it’s how Ward accessed the information that troubled him. The BMV database includes driver’s license and registration data, some of which is not public.
“He had too much access to too much information to allow him to use it in this manner,” Cavanaugh said.
Ward resigned from the Buxton Police Department in October 2024, the chief previously told a reporter, before the department could finish an internal investigation. He had previously worked for Cumberland County, Saco and the town of Harrison, according to an employment history provided by the Public Employee Retirement System.

title: The Somerset Hall Band: Keeping Orono’s music scene alive
text:
Without its live music scene, the University of Maine in Orono would be missing an absolutely vital element of what makes this campus feel alive. In my time here, many great bands have come out of the woodwork and built up an audience. Yet four years is rarely enough time for a band to come together, find its sound and make an impact. Most musicians don’t find their group or their groove until they’ve spent some time getting the lay of the land. That’s what makes the Somerset Hall Band an exciting exception. Formed by first-year Somerset residents Ben Redfield, Nate Lee, Evan Cummings and Harlow Keener, and second-year student Declan Nichols, the Somerset Hall Band is trying to alleviate concerns about the fading music scene.
Many people fret about the future of Orono’s live music scene as some of the great names from the past couple of years prepare to walk the commencement stage and start their lives. I had the pleasure of seeing the Somerset folk play this past week, and they offer a promising rebuttal to this fear. Playing a variety of grunge, punk and contemporary covers, the Somerset Hall Band performs with an engaging energy.
Shortly after seeing their show, I interviewed the Somerset Hall Band to get a sense of how this group came to be and what the future holds for them.
When asked about their origins, Ben had this to say: “It was orientation. Oh yeah, it was orientation. I just started talking to [Evan Cummings]. I was like, ‘You play any music? I’m looking for some people to play with.’ And he’s like, ‘Yeah.’”
Nate and Ben, the co-founders, met through the UMaine roommate search portal.
“I met Nate online in March. It was like the, ‘to meet a roommate’ app, yeah, you know what I’m talking about? I met him on that, and then we’re just like, ‘Yo, you want to start a band?’ And then it was just like history.”
Harlow found her way into the band through an equally quintessential freshman experience.
“Two friends of Nate and Ben were with me when I sang karaoke on the quad one night, and they thought that they should introduce me to Ben and Nate because they play music. And so I knocked on their door, their dorm, and they accepted me.”
The Somerset Hall Band embraces the elements of being a freshman ensemble. There is a hard-to-capture energy that comes with being a first-year student on campus, and it’s great to see elements of that coming through in the music scene, with the band even adopting the freshman dorm hall as its namesake. Though Ben explained it wasn’t their first pick.
“That was like, the eighth idea. Yeah, that was an awfully nice idea. Yeah, I don’t even know what the thought process was. I think we just liked the name, and yeah, we chose it for the band.”
You can keep an eye out for any upcoming shows through their Instagram, @somersethall.band.

title: MaineCare expansion has helped vulnerable Mainers
text:
Jordan Rhodes is the director of research and policy analysis within the Commissioner’s Office at the Maine Department of Health and Human Services. His research centers around policies and interventions that improve access to care, affordability and health outcomes among Mainers.
In January 2019, Maine expanded MaineCare eligibility, the state’s Medicaid program, to adults with incomes up to 138% of the federal poverty level. This equates to an annual salary of roughly $22,000 for a one-person household and $30,000 for a two-person household.
While this represented a significant policy change, and one that voters approved and advocates had supported for years, assessing the effects of expanded MaineCare eligibility has been challenging, due to overlapping events and policy changes during this time.
Notably, MaineCare expansion was implemented just one year prior to the disruptions in coverage and access to care that accompanied the COVID-19 pandemic.
In a new study published in Maine Policy Review, my colleague and I applied a careful empirical analysis to examine the impact of MaineCare expansion on coverage and access to care. Our analysis focuses on low-income childless adults, the population most likely to have gained coverage through this policy change.
We also looked at the potential implications of upcoming Medicaid work requirements that will take effect in January 2027. Our analysis included a comparison of characteristics and outcomes corresponding to Maine’s low-income childless population and their counterparts in other states.
We found the following:
- Maine’s low-income childless adult population faces significant health challenges
relative to both other adults in the state and to their counterparts in other states. This includes higher rates of chronic and acute conditions, such as arthritis, asthma and cancer, as well as significant behavioral health challenges, with over 1 in 2 low-income childless adults in Maine reporting a diagnosis of depressive disorder. These conditions require consistent access to care to ensure proper disease management.
- In the years following Maine’s 2019 coverage expansion, the state’s low-income childless adult population was more likely to have health insurance coverage, less likely to delay medical care due to costs and more likely to receive an annual check-up. The fact that changes of the same magnitude are not observed among low-income childless adults in states that did not expand Medicaid indicates a link between MaineCare expansion and gains in coverage and access to care.
- While Medicaid work requirements will be implemented nationally beginning in January, low-income childless adults in Maine may face unique hurdles in complying with these requirements. We find that, relative to their counterparts in other Medicaid expansion states, Maine’s low-income childless adult population is more likely to reside in a rural area, to be the only adult in their household and to report being unable to work. These characteristics are not necessarily predictive of coverage losses. They do, however, identify potential challenges in meeting the new requirements, through factors such as longer drive times to eligibility offices, greater healthcare needs and lack of household support in navigating the new eligibility rules.
Our findings suggest that the 2019 MaineCare expansion contributed to gains in coverage and access to care among Mainers facing significant economic and health challenges. The coverage gains from MaineCare expansion coincided with the lowest uninsured rate in the state’s history, including substantial gains across the state’s most rural communities.
At the same time, our analysis sheds light on potential barriers to maintaining or accessing coverage and care that may accompany upcoming Medicaid work requirements. We hope that our findings are informative to policy makers throughout the state as they continue to debate the future of the MaineCare program.

title: 35-year-old bull rider identified after fatal accident at a rodeo in Ohio
text:
35-year-old bull rider identified after fatal accident at rodeo in Ohio
Authorities say that a bull rider has died after he sustained injuries during a rodeo in southwestern Ohio on Saturday evening.
According to the Clearcreek Township Police Department, first responders were dispatched to the incident at the Fox Hollow Rodeo along State Route 73 in Warren County, Ohio, at approximately 7:41 p.m.
As officers arrived, they reported finding a man who had suffered a traumatic chest injury caused by a bull after it appeared to have either kicked or stepped on him in the rodeo's bullpen.
The rider, identified as 35-year-old Jason Blake Saylor, was then transported to Atrium Medical Center, where he was later pronounced dead.
On Sunday, Fox Hollow Rodeo released a statement that extended condolences to Saylor's family.
"Our hearts are absolutely broken following the tragic loss of one of our bull riders and brothers in Christ, last night at Fox Hollow Rodeo," the rodeo wrote in a Facebook post. "There are no words to express the sadness we are feeling. Our thoughts and prayers are with his family, friends, and everyone affected by this heartbreaking tragedy. We ask that everyone please respect the privacy of his family and loved ones during this incredibly difficult time. Please keep an eye on our Facebook page over the next few days for any further announcements or updates. Thank you to everyone for your love, prayers, and support during this difficult time."
Clearcreek Township police say that they are continuing to investigate the incident. Those with additional information or video of the accident are urged to contact Warren County police dispatch at 513-695-2525 or Clearcreek Township police at 937-748-1267 during business hours.
Located north of Cincinnati, Clearcreek Township is located around 19 miles outside of Dayton, Ohio.

title: Amy Acton addresses Ramaswamy ad in one-on-one interview: 'There’s no low'
text:
Amy Acton addresses Ramaswamy ad in one-on-one interview: 'There’s no low'
The Ohio governor's race between Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat Dr. Amy Acton is in the national spotlight following the release of a campaign ad featuring Acton's estranged mother.
The ad, created by Ramaswamy's campaign, shows Acton's mother calling her a liar.
"Amy has a serious problem. She is a liar. She lies about her past," Donna Arthur said in the ad, which was funded by Ramaswamy's campaign.
Acton responded to the ad during her first one-on-one interview since the controversy began.
"Obviously it's a very sad situation to see my mother. Last time I saw her, I was 12 years old in a courthouse where she and her husband were indicted before they skipped town as fugitives from the law with a warrant against their arrest. And it didn't surprise me because I know there's no low that my opponent won't go to. He knows his campaign is struggling," Acton said.
Acton explained that she has not seen her mother since the late 1970s because her mother stayed married to a man who Acton accuses of sexually abusing her when she was 12 years old.
The ad continues to run as the race for Ohio governor approaches Election Day, which is now just eight days away.
"To stoop this low to someone. It's clear my mother is not well. We've learned more, I'm learning things that I didn't know, I was obviously a child when this happened, I'm 60 years old now. I just think no office is worth this. No goal or striving in life, my opponent will do or say anything to get ahead," Acton said.
Ramaswamy has responded to pushback on the ad, saying, "I would love for this race, and this election, to be about the substantive issues that impact Ohioans," Ramaswamy said. "Amy Acton has been hiding from those issues."
A statement from Ramaswamy's spokesperson Connie Luck said, "We don't know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke out about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor."
Luck went on to bring up the topic of live debates, reiterating Ramaswamy has accepted debate offers while Acton has not.
"If Amy disagrees with these criticisms, she should stand before the people of Ohio, answer the questions, and let voters decide for themselves. The fact that she won’t, and Vivek will, should tell you everything about who’s really lying," Luck stated.
The debate comment stems from Ramaswamy accepting debate invites, while Acton chose not to accept.
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have backed Ramaswamy, with Vance saying, "Politics is a tough business" and Trump denouncing Gov. Mike DeWine who called the ad "deeply troubling."
"The ad on its face is deeply, deeply troubling. But when you know the rest of the story when you know the back story when you know that the husband of the mom was indicted by a grand jury after hearing testimony. When you know that, it just to me makes it more serious. It makes it just more wrong," DeWine told reporters.
Trump responded with a lengthy post to Truth Social.
"He strongly suggested that Vivek should, “take down the Ad.” He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn’t want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing," the post reads.
The full one on one sit down with Amy Acton will air Tuesday at 6 p.m. You can watch WLWT's full one-on-one with Ramaswamy here.

title: Nathan Fielder's Early Comedy Has a Surprising Connection to Bangor
text:
Nathan Fielder’s Early Comedy Has a Surprising Connection to Bangor
The “You Can See Everything” director has had a long career in comedy, and one of his earliest skits had a Pine Tree State connection.
👇 KEEP READING: 23 Famous People You Probably Didn't Know Were Born In Maine 👇
“You Can See Everything” is an A24 documentary directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim that opened in theaters Oct. 16, 2026.
It follows Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and her family, beginning 34 days before she reported to prison for defrauding investors.
Fielder is a Canadian comedian, writer and director best known for “Nathan for You,” “The Rehearsal” and “The Curse.”
He became involved after learning Holmes wanted to participate in a documentary, and she and her partner, Billy Evans, invited him into their home to document their lives.
Early in his career, Fielder posted comedy sketches on his YouTube channel, including “Even the Best,” a short he made with comedian Katie Crown.
Set to Howie Day’s “Collide,” the video parodies the sentimental romantic scenes common in mid-2000s teen dramas, with the pair sharing an awkward moment.
Day was born in Bangor, grew up in neighboring Brewer, and graduated from Brewer High School.
He began playing piano at age 5 and guitar at 12, then started writing music and performing across New England at 15, launching his career while still living in Maine.
And there you have it! One of Fielder’s early comedy sketches has an unexpected Maine connection through the music of Bangor-born Howie Day.

title: The SS United States is scheduled for sinking to become the world’s largest artificial reef
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
DESTIN, Fla. (AP) — A historic ocean liner is a step closer to becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.
Officials in Florida’s Okaloosa County expect to sink the SS United States off the Gulf Coast during the second week of November. The exact dates could change because of weather.
The ship will be sunk about 22 nautical miles (41 kilometers) southwest of Destin.
“This is an exciting move forward to create a one-of-a-kind resource for the environment and for our tourism industry,” county officials wrote in a news release.
The nearly 1,000-foot (305-meter) vessel shattered the trans-Atlantic speed record on its maiden voyage in 1952. Preservation groups tried to save the ship but were hindered by high costs.
Supporters hope that sinking the ship will make it a barnacle-encrusted star among more than 500 artificial reefs and a signature diving attraction, helping to generate millions of dollars a year in local tourism spending for scuba shops, charter fishing boats and hotels.

title: Maine's public advocate warns community solar farms of 'misleading' appeals to low-income customers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Office of Public Advocate is warning community solar companies against making “misleading” appeals to people who receive benefits from the state’s low-income assistance program for electricity.
Public Advocate Heather Sanborn said at least one company is offering 20% electric bill discounts to electric customers if they subscribe in a community solar program.
But after a change to the Low Income Assistance Program this year, those customers could receive up to 80% off their monthly bill based on income eligibility, Sanborn said. The way that community solar billing works, those people could lose out on the full benefits they might receive if they remained ordinary electric customers, Sanborn added.
“We want to make sure that if folks … target marketing to low-income customers, they are actually providing a better offer for those customers than what those customers would have received if they hadn’t signed up,” Sanborn said.
In a letter to about a dozen community solar companies, Sanborn said they should stop advertising to people enrolled in low-income program unless they could provide a discount at least equal to what the program provides.
The marketing may constitute an unfair trade practice prohibited under state utility rules, and if companies fail to comply, the public advocate may seek enforcement action at the Maine Public Utilities Commission, Sanborn said in the letter.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Australian judge rejects prisoner’s claim that access to Vegemite spread is a human right
text:
Australian judge rejects prisoner’s claim that access to the nation's beloved toast spread is a human right
A prisoner on Monday lost his challenge to an Australian state’s ban on inmates eating Vegemite after he argued in court that withholding the polarizing yeast-based spread breached his human right to “enjoy his culture as an Australian.”
Andre McKechnie, 55, who is serving a life sentence for murder, took his battle for the salty, sticky, black-brown byproduct of brewing beer to the Supreme Court of the state of Victoria last year.
He had argued being refused Vegemite denied him his right under the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act to “enjoy his culture as an Australian in the community with other persons of Australian background,” court documents showed.
Justice Claire Harris accepted prison authorities’ refusal to allow McKechnie Vegemite “limited his cultural rights” under the charter.
But she found the ban was justified in meeting authorities’ goals of removing illicit drugs and alcohol from the prison system.
“The limitation on Mr. McKechnie’s ability to enjoy Vegemite in community with other persons of Australian background is primarily that he is a prisoner,” Harris wrote in her 47-page judgment.
Prison officials testify Vegemite could impair drug sniffer dogs and be used to make alcohol
Prison officials testified at a trial in July that Vegemite had been banned throughout the state’s 12 prisons for the past 20 years because it could potentially impair sniffer dogs’ ability to detect narcotics and could be used to brew alcohol because of its yeast content.
McKechnie, who represented himself in court by video link from maximum security Barwon Prison west of Melbourne, argued that the fact that neighboring New South Wales state did not ban Vegemite from its prisons was evidence that there were “less restrictive means reasonably available” to achieve such drug and alcohol outcomes.
Most Australians revere Vegemite as an unfairly maligned culinary icon, and more than 80% of Australian households are estimated to have a jar in their pantries. Vegemite is typically considered an acquired taste at best by those who weren't raised on it.
The last U.S. president to visit Australia, Barack Obama, once said: “It’s horrible.”
Prisoner argues Vegemite ban contributed to vitamin deficiency
McKechnie had initially testified that the lack of Vegemite had contributed to his thiamine deficiency.
He said both Vegemite and pork were sources of thiamine, also known as vitamin B1. As a Jew who observed kosher law, he told the court he couldn’t eat pork either and took daily doses of the vitamin.
Vegemite has long been marketed as a source of B vitamins thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3) and folate (B9), which are promoted as healthy additions to the diets of growing children.
But McKechnie dropped the thiamine issue as “not important,” after lawyers for the prison authorities objected to his evidence.
Prisoner said Vegemite ban left him feeling ‘deprived, sad and disconnected’
McKechnie said not eating Vegemite made him feel “deprived of being able to practice my Australian culture, sad and disconnected from my family and community.”
The judge responded that “it is difficult to accept that the inability to consume Vegemite, rather than the fact of his imprisonment, is a material cause of his sadness and disconnection from his family and community.”
McKechnie cited an article published in the food studies journal “Gastronomica” in 2003 that said, “Vegemite may be the best predictor of national identity of any food in the world.”
The article, based on research by Australia’s Queensland University in 1995, found that a “taste for the spread strongly correlates with early exposure and to Australian birth and ancestry.”
McKechnie also referred to the Australian Olympic Committee overturning a Chinese import ban on Vegemite ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing.
He cited Australian band Men at Work's 1980s international hit “Down Under” that mentions a “Vegemite sandwich.”
On the effectiveness of smearing contraband with Vegemite, McKechnie cited a Melbourne newspaper article from 2017 that reported a man’s unsuccessful attempt to use the odor of the spread to conceal illicit drugs that he attempted to smuggle into a music festival in Victoria. The attempt was thwarted by police sniffer dogs.
Judge rejects evidence that Vegemite doesn't interfere with drug sniffer dogs
The judge upheld prison authorities’ argument that McKechnie had failed to provide any proper foundations for his opinion that Vegemite does not interfere with drug sniffer dogs.
McKechnie also argued that Vegemite contained “no live yeast” and that any piece of fruit would be more useful in making alcohol than the spread.
A state prison department manager, Kevin White, cited publicly available research that said Vegemite helped home-brewed beer ferment more quickly.
Vegemite's owner, Bega Group, did not respond to a request for comment on Monday.

title: UMaine faculty and students condemn proposed cuts at charged town hall
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
More than 100 University of Maine students, faculty and staff members packed a town hall meeting Monday, voicing their disapproval of looming layoffs with union chants, requests to administrators and calls to vote for pro-union candidates across the state.
The emergency town hall, which was held in Donald P. Corbett Hall on UMaine’s campus, was an extension of letters and requests that staff, faculty and union members have sent to university administrators after a $19 million budget shortfall that will require layoffs and retrenchment was announced by administrators in September.
Faculty and staff members have asked for more transparency and input in creating the university’s budget. Administrators have shared plans to close the budget gap, which many universities and colleges across the country are facing, to $3 million and said they are searching for ways to limit layoffs. Plans have not included information about where layoffs will occur in academic departments.
All of the eight speakers who took the podium Monday condemned the cuts, saying that they are not for the betterment of learning or working at the university. One of the speakers, Faculty Senate President Brian McGill, repeated requests the senate have made for involvement and shared governance in the upcoming budget.
With the cuts to faculty positions and student academics still unknown, the UMaine faculty senate passed a resolution to request more input in the budget and sent 36 questions to the administration. The questions, which ask how the budget shortfall was caused and what actions will be taken to ensure cuts do not happen for multiple years, should be answered so the campus community and Mainers better understand what’s going on, McGill said.
“They seem like questions every taxpayer in the state should be asking right now about this university, and we’re working our best to try and get the information,” he said.
Administrators responded to the request for more input last week, saying that faculty have a consulting role and not a deliberative position. Suggestions for cuts from UMaine’s dean’s office have been rejected because of “potential adverse consequences for students and faculty,” according to the response.
Rep. Amy Roeder, D-Bangor and Sen. Mike Tipping, D-Orono said state appropriated funds that have not kept pace with inflation are at least partially to blame for the university’s budget shortfall.
Appropriated funds from the Maine State Legislature accounted for more than 70% of UMaine’s total revenue in previous decades, but now equates to roughly 40%, Tipping said. Student tuition and fees have replaced that revenue.
While student fees and tuition now make up nearly half of the University of Maine System’s revenue, looming cuts may take away from what students are offered, Roeder said.
“What exactly are the students supposed to get less of?” she said.
While an announcement of the Universities of Maine Professional Staff Association launching a UMaine chapter, calls to vote for Roader, Tipping and Democratic U.S. Senate Candidate Troy Jackson, and chants ignited the crowd, the largest reaction came when speakers mentioned the university system’s contract with Open AI.
The University of Maine System entered a two-year contract with the artificial intelligence giant in May. The contract gives every faculty and staff member and student access to a specialized version of its chatbot called ChatGPT Edu.
Every mention of the contract was met with loud boos and jeers from the crowd.
One of the speakers who mentioned the contract, Andrii Obertas, a graduate student from Ukraine, said the program’s integration is showing that the university is not prioritizing faculty positions.
“It is an acknowledgement by universities’ leadership that UMaine can no longer fulfill its mission of advancing learning and discovery through excellence and innovation,” Obertas said. “It signals a level of financial mismanagement that risks trapping the university in a vicious cycle of layoffs, declining enrollment, worsening financial scrutiny, and even more layoffs afterwards.”

title: Letter: We deserve a senator who is greater than Susan Collins
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
I long ago decided never to vote for Susan Collins, and my resolve is unchanged. My decision not to vote for her isn’t simply about what I see as her subservience to President Donald Trump’s agenda of vengeance and disdain for the rule of law. My decision rests on my thinking about the role of a U.S. senator.
We’ve had some great senators from Maine during my long years of voting here: Ed Muskie; Bill Cohen; George Mitchell; and in one important moment, Margaret Chase Smith. All were distinguished, I believe, not just by their loyalty and love for Maine but by a deeply felt awareness of the broader concerns of our country and even its place in the world.
Senators should be accountable to us as citizens of their home state, and we should feel that they’re the people to turn to when we’re up against local conditions and urgent personal needs. But beyond the local and immediate concerns, what about Collins’ votes on healthcare impacts across the country?
I don’t know whether Troy Jackson will develop into the kind of senator we were fortunate to have representing us when Bill Cohen came from Bangor and kept us in mind while he went onto the national and international stage. Perhaps Jackson has it in him to grow into that kind of wisdom.
I believe that Collins isn’t and has never been that kind of senator. We need our senators to look outward, as I believe Angus King does, while staying in close touch with us. We need and deserve someone greater than Susan Collins has ever been.
Ruth Nadelhaft 
Bangor

title: Family says 7-year-old girl injured in Bend school shooting moved out of ICU
text:
BEND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - The 7-year-old girl who survived a shooting at a Bend elementary school earlier this month has been moved out of the intensive care unit, her family said in a statement Monday.
In the statement, the family of Saylor Graham-Poarch said she was in critical condition after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary but is now stable. Her family said while she has been moved out of ICU, she has a long recovery ahead of her.
Saylor’s family said in the statement:
“Even as we’re grateful for Saylor’s progress, our hearts are broken for the families of the three children and the teacher who were killed. We are holding them close, and we grieve with them.
Thank you to everyone who has reached out, prayed for Saylor, sent messages, and shown our family so much love during the hardest time of our lives. We can’t respond to everyone individually, but please know that every kind word, prayer, and act of support means more to us than we can say.
Many of you have asked how you can help. Along with everything else, our family is facing the costs of Saylor’s recovery and the time we need to spend with her. We’ve included a GoFundMe link below for anyone who would like to give. Any donation, share, or continued support is deeply appreciated.
Above all, please keep Saylor in your thoughts and prayers as she heals. We are beyond grateful that she is still here with us.
Thank you for standing with Saylor and our family."
Police said a 16-year-old former student went into Silver Rail Elementary School on Oct. 15 and shot into a special needs classroom. Teacher Megan Lambert, 25, was killed along with students Rhoam Summer, 5, and two other children, ages 8 and 11. The shooter was also killed.
Another teacher, Becky Drury, also survived the shooting and needed surgery on her left arm and right hand. She released a statement about what happened that day last week.
A memorial service was held for Lambert on Saturday at Caldera High School in Bend.
Silver Rail Elementary remains closed through at least this week. Bend-La Pine Schools announced that crews are making progress cleaning and repairing the school after the shooting.
The district also shared a list of resources for Silver Rail families, including childcare options with the Boys & Girls Clubs and the Bend FC Timbers, and grab-and-go free school meals.

title: Trump administration attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey again
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is attempting to prosecute James Comey for what it calls a decade-old leak of classified information, an effort the former FBI director’s lawyers immediately dismissed as legally invalid and outside the legal time limit for when the Justice Department can file a criminal indictment.
The allegations from the Justice Department were revealed Monday in newly unsealed court documents that shed light on a closed-door fight that represents an unmistakable escalation in the administration’s targeting of Comey, a longtime critic and foe of President Donald Trump who has faced two other criminal cases since the Republican returned to the White House last year.
The effort to prosecute Comey is also part of a series of politically charged investigative actions the department has undertaken in the run-up to next week’s midterm elections.
“Well, they’re back — again,” Comey said in a video statement Monday. “It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice — one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing’s changed with me; I’m still innocent, I’m still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary.”
The Justice Department said it had filed what’s known as a “criminal information” to extend the statute of limitations for charges in the case.
“Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further,” a department spokesperson said.
Asked about the Comey case, Trump told reporters upon arriving back to Joint Base Andrews in Maryland late Monday following his rally in Mississippi that “I don’t know much about it. I just heard about it.”
He added, “He’s a dirty cop, James Comey. But I know nothing about it.”
An information can be filed without the approval of a judge or a grand jury’s finding of probable cause to a court. Comey’s lawyers made clear that they intend to fight the charges as invalid because the Justice Department did not file an indictment, which must be voted on by a grand jury, inside the 10-year statute of limitations required under the law.
“For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence,” his attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement.
The allegation was previously investigated
The latest allegation concerns an October 2016 New York Times story related to a secret court order that required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. The story cited two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity about the order from a judge on the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court that Yahoo was barred from publicly disclosing.
Federal authorities, including prosecutor John Durham, began investigating the disclosure in early 2017. Durham, who later investigated the FBI’s conduct as it scrutinized potential ties between Russia and Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, wrote a classified memo in December 2018 recommending no criminal charges against anyone in connection with the disclosure, Comey’s attorneys said in a recent court filing.
In January 2019, the U.S. Attorney’s office for the District of Columbia opened a second investigation of the same matter under the code name “Tropical Vortex.” But that investigation was closed without any charges filed in February 2020.
“Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone. Now, ten years after the article was published, the Government filed an “Information” against Mr. Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit,” Fitzgerald said.
Prosecutors in a newly unsealed filing said investigators found evidence that Comey “sought to correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before” that New York Times story was published, directed his staff to speak to a journalist at the newspaper related to accuracy concerns “and thereby illegally transferred classified information.”
The criminal information was filed under seal on Oct. 5, 10 years after the 2016 story was published. “But,” Comey’s lawyers said, “the applicable statute of limitations explicitly demands an indictment within 10 years of the offense; an information does not suffice.”
They have asked a judge to dismiss the information, a request that is still pending.
Trump and Comey have a long and uneasy history
The first criminal case against Comey, filed in federal court in Virginia, accused him of having lied to Congress in 2020 but was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who brought the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47,” a case Comey has sought to dismiss.
The prosecutions are part of a Trump retribution campaign that has even extended to Comey’s daughter, Maurene, who was fired from her job as a Justice Department prosecutor in New York last year in a termination that a federal judge on Monday ruled was illegal.
Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush’s Republican administration.
But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president -- an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum.
Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump’s campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, found that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration.
The two men have been bitterly at odds ever since Comey’s firing.
Comey in 2018 published a memoir, “A Higher Loyalty,” that painted Trump in deeply unflattering ways, likening him to a mafia don and characterizing him as “untethered to truth.” Trump, for his part, has repeatedly claimed that Comey should face charges for “treason” — an accusation Comey dismissed as “dumb lies” — and called him an “untruthful slime ball.”
The Justice Department has made a series of splashy moves in recent weeks , including a criminal complaint last Friday charging two former FBI officials with lying to Congress about their participation in investigations concerning Hunter Biden, and the search by federal agents of the Washington home of Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.
___
Associated Press writer Will Weissert contributed to this report.

title: Ghostly walking tours return to downtown Bangor ahead of Halloween
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - From haunted buildings to ghost sightings, Bangor is chalk full of scary stories you can learn about.
The Bangor Historical Society will be hosting its Ghostly Bangor Walking Tours on Tuesday and Friday.
The downtown tours explore landmark buildings and how their history has spawned local ghost stories and urban legends.
Stops include the Thomas A. Hill House, the Penobscot Theater, and the Freese’s Assisted Living apartment building.
Historical Society Curator Matt Bishop says the tours help to shed a grain of truth on Bangor’s past while tying into the spirit of Halloween.
“It’s a great way to get historical context, and everybody absorbs history in different ways. So many people love ghost stories and spookiness and Halloween, but there’s just so many facts that go along with these stories. It’s just great to be able to connect some of these facts in a different way and kind of keeping up with the season so everybody’s able to enjoy it,” said Bishop.
This will also be the last set of tours before the Historical Society closes for holiday preparations.
The Ghostly Bangor Walking Tours will run October 27th and October 30th from 7:00pm to 8:30pm, beginning at 159 Union Street.

title: Dozens forced from their homes after Auburn apartment building fire
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUBURN, Maine (WMTW) - Dozens of people need another place to stay right now after a fire at a large apartment building in Auburn on Sunday evening.
The Auburn Fire Department said a kitchen fire at 74 Lake Auburn Avenue, next to Washburn Elementary School, triggered the sprinkler system in the 86-unit apartment building. While the flames were contained, there was some significant water damage.
That is the Lake Auburn Towne House, a public housing project owned by the Auburn Housing Authority for people age 62 and older and those with disabilities. The six-story building includes 32 efficiency units and 54 one-bedroom apartments.
Red Cross officials say 76 people were initially displaced by the fire.
The Red Cross said many people were able to return to their apartments or found another place to stay, about 18 people were not able to find another place on their own.
The city of Auburn asked the Red Cross to open an emergency shelter to help those people unable to find housing, and eight Red Cross disaster volunteers responded to help open that shelter at the Auburn Drop-In Center on Mill Street.
The shelter opened at 11 p.m. on Sunday.
Anyone affected by this incident who needs help can contact the Red Cross at 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733-2767).
“Losing access to your home without warning is incredibly stressful,” said Sophie Piconi, executive director, Red Cross Central and Mid Coast Maine Chapter. ”Our priority is ensuring that every resident affected has a safe place to go and the support they need. Red Cross volunteers are on the ground providing shelter, comfort and hope. We will continue working alongside the city, emergency management and community partners to help these residents begin their recovery journey.”

title: Woman arrested after trying to attack man with axe
text:
RUMFORD, Maine (WMTW) - A Massachusetts woman was arrested in Rumford after trying to attack a man with an axe.
Investigators say the 44-year-old man had arranged for 46-year-old Luciane Dezan of Medford, Massachusetts, to take his motorcycle from Northborough, Massachusetts, to Rumford.
When the motorcycle arrived, he found damage he believed happened during the trip. He told Dezan he would not pay the full fee they had agreed upon. After confronting her, the two began arguing. Investigators say that is when Dezan got an axe from her van and began hitting the motorcycle, causing extensive damage. They say he tried to get her to stop, and she swung the axe at his head, narrowly missing him. Police say there was around $2,000 in damage done to the motorcycle.
Dezan was arrested by Rumford Police and faces attempted elevated aggravated assault and aggravated criminal mischief charges. She was taken to Oxford County Jail, and her bail was set at $10,000 cash.

title: Fair trade | Letters To Editor
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
To the Editor,
Here’s something you don’t often hear in letters like this: Canada has not always played fair with Maine.
Ottawa protects its dairy farmers with over-quota tariffs above 200%, and last year Canada’s Parliament barred its own negotiators from opening that market further. Canadian governments have also backed their lobster industry at every link in the chain, which is a big part of why so much of Maine’s catch is processed across the border. Those are real grievances.
But a 50% tariff on $20 billion of Canadian goods, answered by Canadian tariffs in return, doesn’t fix any of that. It just sends the bill to Maine.
No state is more tied to Canada than ours. In 2024, Canada supplied about 70% of Maine’s imports and bought roughly $1.3 billion of our exports. Much of what comes south is the fuel that heats our homes and runs our trucks. Senator Susan Collins estimates that about $170 million in Maine goods landed on Canada’s retaliation list, most of it forest products.
I owned and ran the Union River Lobster Pot, and I served in the Maine Senate. Small-business owners can plan around a bad season or a jump in costs. What they can’t plan around is a rulebook that changes every few weeks. When you don’t know what fuel, packaging or equipment will cost next month, you hold off on hiring and skip the investment that would make you stronger.
I want more lobster processed in Maine. I want Canada to honor the dairy access it agreed to. Those goals are worth fighting for at the negotiating table with real enforcement. They aren’t won by blanket tariffs that tax Maine families and small businesses for problems they didn’t create.
Right now the two countries aren’t even talking. Senator Collins has urged both governments to return to the table and reach a fair agreement. She’s right, and our delegation should keep pushing.
Brian Langley
Ellsworth

title: Candlelight vigil held in honor of those killed in Lewiston mass shooting
text:
LEWISTON, Maine (WMTW) - On the three-year anniversary of a Lewiston mass shooting that killed 18 people and injured 13 others, the community held a candlelight vigil to honor the victims and stand alongside the survivors.
The event was hosted and organized by the Maine Resiliency Center, an organization created weeks after the shooting to provide support and services to the victims’ families, survivors and anybody impacted by the tragedy.
“Eighteen of them were killed. Tonight, we gather to remember those 18 people who were killed,” announced Maine Resiliency Center associate director Meredith Stack.
Dozens filled the hill at Lewiston’s Simard-Payne Park for the ceremony before a reading of the names of the 18 victims.
“It isn’t only the lives that ended on October 25th. It’s all the life that should have been lived since,” said Maine Resiliency Center director Danielle Parent.
One of the names that was read was Arthur Strout. Strout’s father, Arthur Barnard, attended the ceremony.
“I’ve come to grips that it’s unavoidable,” said Barnard. “The feelings and the things and emotions that happen today, it’s just unavoidable.”
Barnard said that this morning, he took time to recall the last time he spent with his son, three years ago.
“This morning, just waking up, and thinking about how it unfolded, everything that day. And I think it happens for all of us. The things we say to each other before this all happened,” commented Barnard. “I guess the only thing, I really, I was fortunate I spent the last 2.5 hours of his life with him, and he was happy.”
The ceremony closed as the group walked together to the Longley Bridge to release flower petals.

title: Federal relief for federal pain – again
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I just finished reading the recent report about “a groundbreaking $8 billion bailout” (“Federal fuel relief offered to Maine farmers and fishermen,” Oct. 21). It sure rang a familiar, costly bell.
In 2018, USDA made $12 billion available for agricultural tariff relief aid. Due to retaliatory tariffs imposed on U.S. agricultural products, our exports became immediately more expensive compared to global options. To wit, between 2017 and 2024, U.S. soybean exports yearly averages were below 2016 levels.
In mid-2019, Trump’s administration authorized an additional $16 billion farm aid package to offset farmers’ tariff-induced losses.
During Trump’s current term, U.S. soy exports to China fell 73% in 2025, from 2024 levels, while Brazilian soybean exports to China are up 88% since 2016. Mercurial executive orders have long-term effects that are not easily undone.
In December 2025, the USDA made $12 billion available for farm losses from “unfair market disruptions.” And now an additional $8 billion in aid is going to agricultural workers due to high diesel costs directly tied to Trump’s unilateral actions.
How much and for how long does the country have to pay for Trump’s “Art of the Deal” failures before our kids’ future is relegated to the same fate as his bankrupt casinos?
Mike Del Tergo
Falmouth

Driver suffers possible life-threatening injuries in head-on crash in Gray
The Cumberland County Sheriff's Office says speed may have been a contributing factor in the crash, the investigation is ongoing
A driver was hospitalized with possible life-threatening injuries following a head-on crash in Gray on Monday evening, according to the Cumberland County Sheriff's Office.
Deputies and Gray firefighters responded to the area of Maine Wildlife Parkway around 5:10 p.m. for a reported two-vehicle collision.
Investigators said a maroon Nissan Rogue driven by Pamela Larracey of Mechanic Falls crossed the center line and struck a black 2023 GMC Yukon driven by Christina Lush of Lewiston.
The Yukon was also carrying four juvenile passengers. All five occupants sustained non-life-threatening injuries, according to deputies.

Investigators said speed appears to have contributed to the crash.

title: Six Flags says it will install seat belts on Georgia roller coaster after rider's death
text:
Six Flags says it will install seat belts on Georgia roller coaster after rider's death
The chief executive of Six Flags says the company will install seat belts on the Georgia roller coaster from which a rider fell to his death earlier this month. The company's rides with similar restraints will also get the safety upgrade.
The theme park operator announced the extra safeguard less than two weeks after 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem of Atlanta died after being ejected from his seat on the Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia.
“We are reinforcing safety precautions at our parks and taking additional measures, including adding seat belts on Goliath and other coasters with a similar restraint,” John Reilly, president and CEO of Six Flags Entertainment Corporation, said in a statement Friday.
Goliath remains shut down while state and local officials investigate the Oct. 12 death.
Related video above: Mako reopens at SeaWorld Orlando after precautionary closure following death of Georgia Six Flags guest
Reilly didn't specify which other Six Flags coasters will get seat belts. But it has temporarily closed eight additional roller coasters at five other parks in the U.S. and Canada. Those rides all share the same manufacturer and a similar restraint system.
Six Flags hasn't said when those coasters are expected to reopen. Reilly's statement said Six Flags has enlisted independent engineers and inspectors to review safety procedures for all rides at its theme parks.
Investigators haven't said what went wrong on the Georgia coaster. Witnesses said they saw Kariem rise up out of his seat and fall headfirst back into the cart before being ejected. Some people who rode Goliath before him that day said they had concerns about its restraints.
All nine of the Six Flags coasters taken offline were manufactured by the Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard. They also feature similar clamshell restraints that sit at the top of a vertical bar between each rider's knees. The bar locks a padded restraint into place over the rider's lap and upper legs.
The U.S. patent granted to Bolliger & Mabillard for the restraint system in 2001 says it's designed to make each rider feel “that he is seated on a flying carpet or that he is at the controls of a kind of flying scooter, while still guaranteeing optimum security.”
Following the death in Georgia, non-Six Flags theme parks SeaWorld Orlando in Florida and La Ronde in Montreal, Canada, also temporarily closed one roller coaster apiece that uses clamshell restraints.
SeaWorld reopened its Mako coaster Tuesday after it had been offline for a week. The Associated Press emailed the company Saturday asking if seat belts or other safety upgrades were planned for the coaster.
The AP also emailed a spokesperson for La Ronde seeking an update on its shuttered coaster.
In addition to Goliath in Georgia, eight coasters remain closed at Six Flags parks in Gurnee, Illinois; Jackson Township, New Jersey; Charlotte, North Carolina; Mason, Ohio; and Vaughan, Ontario.
