title: Habitat York County breaks ground on its largest-ever affordable housing project
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Habitat for Humanity York County is developing its largest-ever affordable housing project — a five-home neighborhood on Island Avenue in Sanford.
A ceremonial groundbreaking was held Saturday and construction will start in November. The project is expected to expand access to affordable homeownership for five local families.
Homeowners have been selected for two of the homes, and applications are open for the remaining three. Habitat homebuyers who between 50% and 80% of area median income can purchase their homes with affordable mortgages and partner with Habitat throughout the process, including helping build their homes.
The application deadline is Oct. 30. For more information, visit Habitat York County’s website.
$1.6M project
The project’s working budget is $1.6 million, Nancy Lowenberg, the organization’s director of development and community relations, told Mainebiz.
Primary funding sources include a $500,000 U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development community development block grant awarded by the city of Sanford’s Office of Community Development, a forgivable loan of $400,000 from MaineHousing and $100,000 in grants and gifts from foundations, local businesses and individuals. It’s expected that home sales will generate another $600,000 to reinvest into the project.
The development will use pre-manufactured models purchased from Sanford modular home building Canbury Homes Inc. The general contractor is Habitat’s staff construction manager, Matt Cronin, assisted by a daily construction volunteer crew and corporate workday teams.
Construction is expected to begin in November 2027 and continue through late winter that year.
The nonprofit would welcome support from York County businesses, Lowenberg added.
Maine’s second-most expensive county
The two- and three-bedroom energy-efficient homes will have heat pumps, stainless-steel appliances, and full basements.
The homes will have a maximum price of $378,000. Monthly mortgage payments will be capped at 29% to 30% of household income, and could be as low as $1,250 per month, according to a news release.
In York County, rising housing costs and limited availability have made homeownership increasingly out of reach for many working adults, according to Habitat’s prospectus.
York County has Maine’s second-highest median home sales price, at $566,500, according to Maine Listings. Maine’s overall median sales price is $420,000.
About Habitat for Humanity
Since its founding in 1985, Habitat for Humanity York County has built 40 homes.
Habitat for Humanity acquires land through donations and purchases.
Applicants agree to collaborate on the construction of their home; that includes performing 200 to 400 hours of “sweat equity” volunteering on the build site or at the Kennebunk ReStore.

title: Sophie Warren for Maine State Senate
text:
I am writing to endorse Sophie Warren for the Maine State Senate. While I am often overwhelmed by the way we can treat each other in this country, I must remind myself: community is the antidote to anxiety, and there are people fighting for a kinder America — an America that protects those historically unprotected and thus protects us all.
I see Sophie as this woman. She comes at politics with a human-first approach, and her desire for peace seeps into her government work. Sophie takes the time to be in the community; we will find her going door-to-door, greeting voters at the polls and even replying to social media messages.
When I think about the future I want for our country, I envision leaders like Sophie Warren, leaders who see all people as people and push for legislation that reflects that.
Alexandra Archambault
Scarborough

title: Payton Pritchard scores 28 in Celtics’ win over Bulls
text:
BOSTON — Payton Pritchard made all five of his 3-point attempts during Boston’s big third quarter and finished with 28 points, to lead the Celtics to a 134-99 victory over the Chicago Bulls on Monday night.
Jayson Tatum had 23 points, seven rebounds and six assists, and Paul George scored 16 points for Boston (2-1), which outscored the Bulls 39-21 in the third when Prichard scored 19.
Norman Powell led the Bulls (1-3) with 20 points.
Boston never trailed, opening a 16-point lead early in the second, led by 12 at halftime and 30 after three. Tatum had 19 of his points in the first half, including a buzzer-beating drive at the end of the first and long 3-pointer with .8 left in the second.
The Celtics had been off since winning their home opener against the defending champion Knicks on Friday when Tatum carried them with 36 points.
George, Pritchard and Sam Hauser each nailed a 3 during a 93-second stretch that pushed Boston ahead 89-70 late in the third.
Pritchard made consecutive 3s two minutes later, making it 101-73. The Celtics were 8 for 13 from 3-point range in the third.
The Bulls, who entered with the league’s worst 3-point shooting percentage at 22.6%, missed 15 of their initial 19 attempts from beyond the arc and finished 12 of 44.
Chicago lost its home opener in its last game on Saturday. In a scheduling quirk, the teams met in Boston again Friday.
Up next
Bulls: Host New York on Wednesday night.
Celtics: Host Brooklyn on Tuesday night.

title: Mild today, cooler tomorrow. Quiet stretch continues
text:
Mild today, cooler tomorrow. Quiet stretch continues
Temperatures climb nicely into the 60s to around 70 degrees Monday afternoon with a light southwest breeze. An approaching cold front kicks off a few isolated showers inland. Otherwise, mostly sunny and dry, with mainly clear skies expected overnight.
Tuesday won't be as warm in the wake of the cold front, with highs in the upper 40s and lower 50s in the afternoon. Plentiful sunshine is expected with a breeze from the northwest gusting to 15 to 20 mph. Lighter winds and similar temperatures are expected on Wednesday.
By Thursday, temperatures start to climb again with highs in the 60s. Friday looks even warmer, with highs in the 60s and low 70s in the afternoon. A front crosses, kicking off a few isolated showers, but still no meaningful rain is expected through the weekend.

title: Influencer embraces hair loss from alopecia, encourages other women
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (Aging Untold) — A Charlotte influencer who lost her hair to alopecia is using her platform to encourage other women facing the condition.
Alopecia is an autoimmune disease that causes patchy hair loss and affects nearly 7 million people in the U.S. It is the second-leading cause of hair loss in the country.
For nine years, Angela Agnew was proud of her long, flowing hair before she noticed it thinning.
“Then I finally went to a specialist, and I asked her, I said, ‘Hey, what’s going on here?’” Agnew said.
Agnew said she had to accept a reality she couldn’t control.
“To realize there was nothing else I could do, that this was something that I had to accept, it was hard,” Agnew said.
From hiding to going public
Agnew lived in silence, hiding under wigs, until she saw another woman being bullied online for thinning hair. She then shaved her head on camera.
Aging Untold expert Amy O’Rourke said the emotional weight of hair loss is something many women carry alone.
“So, for men and women, losing your hair can be a big deal. Loss of identity,” O’Rourke said.
“First, I think of how heavy it would be to be hiding that, and then you lift it out and get rid of it, and how much lighter you can handle your life. It gives you so much more energy not having to clamp down on this issue that you’ve been struggling with,” O’Rourke said.
Agnew’s hair loss is permanent, but her impact is growing.
“Angela just saying I’m going to embrace this thing, I’m going to come out, I’m going to be proud I’m going to be who I am. I was struck with how beautiful she is,” O’Rourke said.
“The positive for me that has come from this is the encouraging of other women,” Agnew said.
Agnew is now an advocate against bullying and a voice for other women dealing with hair loss.

title: Archaeologists just found the oldest dwelling in the Western Hemisphere
text:
Archaeologists just found the oldest dwelling in the Western Hemisphere
Archaeologists just found the oldest dwelling in the Western Hemisphere
Archaeologists uncovered something more than a hunting stopover just east of the Bering Land Bridge. Far more. An excavation team at Shég’ Xdaltth’í’ — in what is now Alaska, roughly 34 miles southeast of Fairbanks — discovered the earliest known Nenana Complex occupation east of the Bering Land Bridge. It isn’t the oldest archaeological evidence of humans in the Western Hemisphere, but it may be the oldest spot where people actually settled in. It also delivered some intriguing news about domesticated dogs.
In a new study published in the journal Science Advances, the authors date the early base camp to 13,800 years ago, when it was inhabited by the Late Pleistocene people of Alaska.
Related video above: Archaeologists were searching for a lost sanctuary—and rediscovered a treasure trove of ancient statues
While researchers believe human dispersal across the Bering Land Bridge helped populate the Americas, we still don’t fully understand the region’s archaeological record, in part because most known Beringian sites are scattered remains of small seasonal hunting camps. The Shég’ Xdaltth’í’ site in interior Alaska — a name that translates as “They Were There” — offers a rare focal point. The study’s authors wrote that the oldest array of cultural remains found there includes a “unique hafted-biface form, osseous tools, diverse fauna, and well-preserved activity areas, a record unparalleled for this age in Beringia.” The findings may all be a part of what is ultimately a historic discovery.
“The complex feature at Shég’ Xdaltth’í’ represents the earliest potential case of a habitation structure in North America,” the authors wrote. “Early Alaskans knew their surroundings well.”
Even though Shég’ Xdaltth’í’ has been studied for more than a decade, the experts weren’t expecting to unearth tens of thousands of artifacts. But that’s exactly what they found, highlighted by stone tools, bone needles, and an antler pendant — along with a hearth, a small pit, and a soil stain marking where a wooden post once stood, likely the remains of a lean-to or early tent. Nearby, the team also uncovered an earth oven filled with charcoal and animal bones, probably used to slow-cook meat for a large family group.
Hunting camps aren’t uncommon in the region, but this is something far beyond that, instead showing people “settling in” to a location they returned to intermittently over roughly 1,000 years. “I expected we’d find hunting tools and knapping [stone tool making] debris surrounding a hearth or two, but I had no idea that we’d stumble into a base camp with tens of thousands of artifacts,” Kelly Graf, the study’s first author and an archaeologist at the University of Kansas, told Live Science. “It was a total surprise.”
The latest archaeological and genetic research has the ancestors of today’s Indigenous Americans entering the continent around 21,000 years ago, so finding an occupied site in eastern Beringia — the Alaskan half of the landmass that joined northeast Asia and northwest North America during the last ice age — with cultural links running both west and south fits the narrative.
Those westward links show up in the stone and the stone sources. The team said the obsidian artifacts match a geological fingerprint hundreds of miles to the northwest, meaning people carried the volcanic rock a long way to the site. The hafted bifaces, meanwhile, were knapped from rhyolite and basalt into a distinctive diamond shape unique to central Alaska, yet they closely resemble tools from sites far to the west in Beringia, in present-day northern Siberia.
Then there are the finds that point south instead. Eight bone needle fragments tie the camp to sites farther south in North America, where the only other eyed needles had previously been recovered, making the Shég’ Xdaltth’í’ needles the oldest discovered in the Western Hemisphere. The antler pendant, with a hole drilled at one end and a point at the other, resembles personal adornments found elsewhere in North America as well.
“The co-occurrence of these cultural features at the single site of Shég’ Xdaltth’í’ is truly notable,” the team wrote, adding that the finds “highlight the strong cultural connection between early Beringians and Americans.”
Whether the residents themselves made those journeys remains unclear. “It would be hard to pin down whether or not they were moving back and forth during a lifetime,” Graf said, “but at least we can say there is a connection.”
The research uncovered one additional surprise. While bones from more than a dozen wolf-like animals create additional links to Asia, an analysis of one animal’s jaw showed it came from neither a dire wolf nor a Pleistocene gray wolf, but from a population of wolf-like canids unique to central Alaska. Because current genetic evidence suggests early domesticated dogs in North America descended from Siberian wolves, the site’s timing and location offer circumstantial evidence that these people may have been dog owners.
Still, further work is needed, both at Shég’ Xdaltth’í’ and elsewhere, to understand the dispersal and timing of population shifts east of the land bridge. “Alaska is a big place and so remote,” Graf said, “so there are really just a few small areas that have been intensively investigated.”

title: AI is starting to look rural, and it needs to stop
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
OPINION: As the artificial intelligence (AI) bubble continues to grow, we are starting to see multiple major corporations set their sights on rural neighborhoods. With concerns about the environmental impacts and how surging electric rates may affect some communities, many worry about what this shift by AI companies will mean for them and their families.
There are more than 3,000 operational data centers in the United States alone. That number is expected to rise sharply over the next few years, with more than 1,500 data centers in various stages of development. Of those 1,500 data centers, 67% of them are expected to be built in rural areas, per the Pew Research Center.
The main issue with this is that there are so many unknowns that come into play when it comes to this move. Research shows that around 60% of rural Americans are very worried about how AI data centers will impact their electric costs. Another 40% are worried about data centers’ overuse of water.
These concerns are for a good reason. AI data centers use a massive amount of electricity to function. Because they are connected to the same power grid as multiple houses, the extra demand begins to affect everybody in the system, leading to higher prices.
“Right now, in most cases, those costs don’t just go to the companies running the data centers. Instead, they’re spread across everyone who uses the grid. That’s because electricity rates have not been uniformly adjusted to require data center companies to pay for all the costs they impose on the grid,” stated Hannah Wiseman, a professor of law at Penn State. “One way to think about this phenomenon is like a growing town where a large new facility moves in and needs a lot of power. The local infrastructure must improve and expand, and the cost of those upgrades is shared across the community, without a careful redesign of rates and fees.”
Other concerns outline AI impacts on farmland and how it will affect local producers. While AI can help farmers grow and harvest crops more precisely, it further exacerbates economic inequality in this field, as that equipment is very expensive and only affordable by bigger and more established farms. This puts smaller farms at the risk of getting kicked out of the industry.
Furthermore, automated technology such as robots and drones have been known to lead to pollution. Misuse of chemicals and improper water management have been known to be issues with these AI systems that cause environmental degradation.
These concerns grow when AI data centers move into rural communities because they share local infrastructure with rural farms and lead to more business between the two. Additionally, AI data centers are just buying agricultural land outright as well, turning important environmentally fertile land into a massive computing facility and further putting strain on this essential industry.
I think it’s important to note that AI data centers certainly do have some positive benefits such as job creation, local tax revenue and technological advancements. These are things that many suggest are reasons AI data centers are vital to bringing growth to rural communities.
However, I’d argue that there are just too many unknown, potentially harmful effects that come from bringing data centers to rural communities. Furthermore, based on backlash and concerns from people all over the country, I believe it is just too early to allow AI data centers into our neighborhoods. Until all the logistics and kinks are worked out regarding how data centers affect the cost of living and the environment of rural communities, we need to say no to bringing them into towns.

title: Presque Isle police intervene in threatened suicide
text:
To reach a suicide prevention hotline, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.
Presque Isle police intervened to stop a threatened suicide on Friday.
The Presque Isle Police Department received a call at about 5:20 p.m. that an armed man was threatening to take his own life, city spokesperson Kim Smith said.
Safety personnel evacuated the area as a precaution, according to Police Chief Chris Hayes.
Staff with the Presque Isle department and the Houlton Regional Communications Center worked with the man for approximately an hour. The man eventually dropped the firearm, Hayes said.
Police placed him in protective custody. No one was injured.
The department will not release information about the man’s identity, health or personal circumstances out of respect for his privacy, the chief said.
There is no threat to the public, Smith said.

title: Man serving a life sentence for murder slips through a fence and escapes a Tennessee prison
text:
Man serving a life sentence for murder slips through a fence and escapes a Tennessee prison
A man serving a life sentence for killing his co-worker four years ago has escaped from a prison in northwest Tennessee by slipping through a fence, authorities said.
Officials realized Jacob Morley, 28, was unaccounted for around 11:30 p.m. Sunday at the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, the Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement.
Investigators looked at security cameras and saw Morley escaped while wearing his prison uniform, officials said. They did not release any other details, including how Morley got through the fence.
Prison officials offered a reward of up to $2,500 for Morley's arrest. They said law enforcement throughout the area has searched buildings and other structures near the prison about 90 miles (145 kilometers) north of Memphis.
Morley is 5-foot-11 (1.8 meters) and 240 pounds (109 kilograms). He has brown hair and green eyes.
Morley was sentenced to life for killing co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield's body was found in a box under Morley's Carter County home after he had been missing for a few weeks.
Along with first-degree murder, Morley was also convicted of aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest. When Morley saw deputies at his home in 2022, he led police on a chase that ended in North Carolina, authorities said.
Several violent attacks between inmates and by employees have been reported in recent years at Northwest Correctional Complex. A grand jury in July returned dozens of indictments for five inmate murders, assaults against staff and inmates and other violence.
Northwest Correctional Complex can house 1,776 men and can house minors who have been convicted as adults, according to the Department of Correction. In 2023, an audit of Tennessee prisons found that the department was struggling to fill open positions at the prison and had a 61% vacancy rate for correctional officers in that fiscal year.

High pressure builds in for Tuesday. Expect lots of sunshine with a slight northwest breeze gusting 20-25 mph at times.
Afternoon highs will be much cooler than Monday mainly mid to upper 40s, with low 50s possible in central and southern Maine.
It turns cold Tuesday night with teens and 20s for lows.

Winds turn lighter and temperatures warm into the upper 40s to mid 50s.

title: Delegations meet in Iran with Mideast region on edge over potential for renewed fighting
text:
Delegations meet in Iran with Mideast region on edge over potential for renewed fighting
High-level delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey were in Tehran on Monday for meetings with Iranian authorities to try to avert renewed fighting between Iran and Israel and the United States, Iran's Foreign Ministry said.
The talks come as many in Iran are anxious about a possible return to all-out war. Israeli and American leaders have been sharpening their threats ahead of elections in both countries, while Iranian leaders have remained defiant.
Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Ibrahim Kalin, the head of Turkey’s intelligence service, were to meet with Iran’s top security officials and negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington.
Related video: Trump and Obama share dueling messages in final stretch of midterm elections
The war in Yemen and strikes by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi Arabia were also topics of the talks, according to two regional officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei told reporters in the Iranian capital that the agenda for the meeting was not set, but the talks would “undoubtedly address the most pressing threats to regional security.”
Saudi Arabia said in a statement that the delegations hoped to find “ways to de-escalate tensions, enhance regional security and promote its stability.”
Qatari mediators also traveled to Tehran on Sunday, working in coordination with the U.S., as part of efforts to de-escalate regional tensions, according to a regional official speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the talks.
Pakistan and Qatar helped broker an agreement in June aimed at having Iran fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, ending a U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and opening negotiations on a broader settlement addressing Iran’s nuclear program. The deal unraveled quickly, however, as both sides renewed attacks.
Iran and Israel trade accusations
With worries about renewed fighting ahead of Israel's election on Tuesday and the Nov. 3 midterm elections in the U.S., Baghaei on the weekend said Tehran had not closed the window of diplomacy and that messages were being passed to the U.S. via intermediaries.
With negotiations long stalled, he said that the U.S. appears to be persisting in unilateral demands and that President Donald Trump and U.S. officials repeatedly use the phrase “complete surrender,” which Baghaei said no Iranian accepts.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, meantime, repeated his warning on Sunday that Iran or its proxies could attack ahead of the close elections to disrupt the vote, citing intelligence.
“The (military) is ready both to defend and to strike,” he said in a video statement, adding: “You will suffer disproportionate blows far greater than you can imagine.”
Israel’s Channel 12 reported Sunday night that Netanyahu and his military chief of staff clashed over an instruction by Netanyahu to carry out an “action” that the army believes could quickly trigger a resumption of the conflict with Iran.
Netanyahu’s office later described the report as “fake news.” In a post on X, Defense Minister Israel Katz said that reports about “rifts between the political leadership and the IDF concerning Iran are completely baseless and false.”
“I state unequivocally that there has been no intention by Israel of initiating an attack on Iran before the elections in Israel,” Katz said. “We made it clear that should Iran attack Israel, we would respond with great force.”
In Tehran, when asked whether Iran was planning attacks, Baghaei on Monday only said that “the Israeli regime is highly skilled at carrying out false-flag operations.”
"The Islamic Republic of Iran will not hesitate to exercise its inherent right to self-defense to protect Iran’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, and independence,” he said.
Front in the Iran war widens
Yemen has become a widening front in the Iran war that began in February, with the Houthis increasingly launching attacks on Saudi Arabia because it supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government battling the rebels.
The conflict has intensified since forces from the internationally recognized government and the Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on Houthi-held Sanaa International Airport in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that largely stopped the fighting in the country’s civil war.
Early Monday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the rebel group had fired ballistic missiles at military gatherings and weapons depots belonging to the Saudi-backed government forces in Aden and Lahj provinces. He claimed the attacks destroyed military equipment and caused casualties but did not provide evidence. The Associated Press couldn’t independently verify the claims.
Meantime, residents in Houthi-held Sanaa and on the Red Sea coast reported a series of explosions.
Houthi media said airstrikes targeted a solar power system and a water well in Sanaa, but offered no proof. In the port city of Mokha, recently seized by the Houthis, residents said rockets hit several buildings including a hospital.
Houthi-run al-Masirah channel also reported strikes in Saada, in northern Yemen, and in southwestern Taiz province, where the rebels and Saudi-backed government forces have been fighting for weeks.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said an operation in Houthi-controlled territory destroyed five tunnels used for storing ballistic missiles, four ballistic missile launchers and another missile storage.
___
Associated Press journalists Victoria Eastwood and Fatma Khaled in Cairo, Natalie Melzer in Tel Aviv, Israel, Munir Ahmed in Islamabad, Ahmed al-Haj in Aden, Yemen, and David Rising in Bangkok contributed to this report.

title: Understanding the importance of pelvic floor therapy for women
text:
LAKE OSWEGO, Ore. (InvestigateTV) - It’s a condition that can affect women at any age whether they’ve had children or not.
Doctors say one in three women experience a pelvic floor disorder in their lifetime, but getting treatment can drastically improve their quality of life.
With every throw, jump and stretch, Mackenzie Devine is strengthening muscles, including important ones that aren’t visible.
It’s exercise, physical therapy and personal time all rolled into one. For her, it’s a top priority.
“For me pelvic floor therapy is non-negotiable for my time and schedule,” Mackenzie Devine said.
Devine has quite the schedule. She’s a mother of five, including two sets of twins.
“I’ve got two sets of twins. One set is 10 months old, the other set just turned four. And then a 5-and-a-half-year-old,” Devine said.
She said pelvic floor therapy has been a helpful tool throughout all of her postpartum journeys. Pelvic floor therapy is a treatment for the group of muscles in the pelvic girdle.
“I think it’s huge with regard to your overall confidence in motherhood. For example, if you don’t know how to engage your pelvic floor, just putting your baby into the crib can be painful,” Devine said.
Dr. Jessica Hund, founder of The Floor PDX in Lake Oswego, works with women of all ages and stages who come to her seeking relief from common ailments that are not commonly spoken of, even among close friends.
“It’s not normal to be like hey, let’s go grab lattes and tell you about how sex has been killing me for 10 years,” Hund said. “Or I don’t feel confident in anything down below my waistband since having a kiddo, or perimenopause is wrecking me and this part of me is not what I knew it to be before.”
Hund said many people have the wrong idea about pelvic floor therapy.
“I think there has been a long-held misconception that if something is leaking or broken that you need to do Kegels or pelvic floor contractions and that’s all you need to do. The problem with that is your pelvic floor is a dynamic system that’s supposed to involuntarily react to the tasks you’re doing,” Hund said.
When patients come in for the first time, Hund said it usually starts with a quick internal assessment.
“We can feel all these muscles and see how are they resting, are they acting really guarded, are they able to move, are we touching pain points you’ve never experienced before,” Hund said.
But patients actually spend most of their time strength training.
“That’s why we’re in the gym because that’s how life is being lived, with the load that’s being passed to you when you’re jumping and landing and going back to the things you’re doing in real life, which is our greatest goal,” Hund said.
Whether someone is five months postpartum or five years, Hund said it’s never too late.
Hund said there’s a close connection between pelvic floor health and mental health.
“This area of your body also matters, and it’s so closely tied to mental health presentation of I don’t feel worthy, I’m not meeting exercise goals I want, my relationship is struggle because I can’t connect on an intimate level I want to,” Hund said.
Rachael Adair also reached out for help after giving birth to her baby boy, Finnegan.
“He entered the world in a bit of a dramatic fashion, and I found myself needing pelvic floor therapy,” Adair said.
Adair said a weakened pelvic floor played into a weakened sense of self-esteem. For a new mother already facing changes, she knew she didn’t want to face it alone.
“I left the hospital in shambles and tears — and the shift to motherhood has been a big one for me, but having the support from this team and being able to understand my body better and who I am has built a lot of confidence and love for myself which has changed a lot for me,” Adair said.
Pelvic floor therapy is often covered by insurance.

title: Couple arrested after children found living in what sheriff called a ‘house of horrors’
text:
EVANS, W.Va (WDTV/Gray News) - A couple was arrested after three children reported years of abuse in what a sheriff called a “house of horrors” in West Virginia.
Erica Lynn Sayre and her husband, Clifford Gale Sayre, are charged with child neglect and child abuse, according to the Jackson County Sheriff’s Office.
Jackson County Sheriff RH Mellinger detailed the abuse and called the children’s living environment a “house of horrors.”
The investigation uncovered years of “disturbing” maltreatment, including the children being repeatedly hit, strangled, deprived of food and water, denied bathroom privileges, having soiled cat litter dumped in their beds and dog feces on personal items, and being forced to run barefoot on a gravel driveway as a means of punishment for any conflicts with Erica Sayre, according to authorities.
The children were allegedly hit with household objects, causing excessive bleeding injuries, forced to place a soiled sock in their mouths and forcibly had their hair cut, according to authorities. One child described being hit in the head with an electronic device, which caused a “bleeding injury for which she was denied medical treatment.” Another child was threatened to be killed if she contacted child protective services, according to authorities.
The children also reported being tormented and harassed about their biological parents who are dead, according to authorities.
During interviews with police, one of the children became “visibly emotional” and said, “I can’t go back to that home.” Another child described years of alleged abuse and said she “just wants a normal life,” the sheriff said.
Deputies said Clifford Sayre witnessed the abuse and failed to intervene.
One child said Clifford Sayre physically restrained her hands while Erica Sayre forcibly cut her hair with a razor blade, resulting in an injury. The child allegedly told authorities, “mom hits us and Gale lets her.”
The investigation revealed physical evidence, including documented scars consistent with the children’s accounts, and the children’s statements corroborated one another, according to Mellinger.
Erica Sayre faces three counts of child abuse resulting in bodily injury and three counts of child neglect creating risk of injury. Clifford Sayre faces three counts of child neglect resulting in bodily injury and three counts of child neglect creating risk of injury.
Both are out on bond. Erica Sayre’s preliminary hearing is set for Nov. 20. Clifford Sayre’s preliminary hearing is Monday.

title: How much was a Halloween costume decades ago? Test your knowledge
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How much was a Halloween costume decades ago? Test your knowledge
Do you think you know how much the cost of Halloween costumes has changed?
On average, adults plan to spend $59.29 this year on costumes, according to a survey from the Halloween and Costume Association.
Total Halloween spending has increased over the years, reaching $13.5 billion in the U.S., according to the National Retail Federation. About $4.4 billion is expected to be spent on costumes this year.
The NRF's annual Halloween survey also found that many shoppers have reported feeling like prices are higher this year, with 79% of people expecting prices to be higher due to tariffs.
The Get the Facts Data Team built a quiz to test your knowledge about the cost of Halloween costumes. Match the values below to the correct costume.
We identified three popular Halloween costumes that were advertised in newspapers in the 1960s, '70s and '80s. Spider-Man was featured back then and, in 2026, was the most popular children's costume, according to the NRF.
The data team then calculated what the cost of each costume would be in 2026 dollars using the Consumer Price Index. The actual cost was also identified using prices from Spirit Halloween's online website.
Because there are so many more variants of costumes available now, the data team used the most basic version of a costume available.
The Spiderman costume was advertised in a 1974 advertisement as being $2.94. Adjusted for inflation, that's $19.39 in 2026 dollars. Spirit Halloween sells a children's Spiderman costume for $49.99, as of October 2026.

title: 14 County Standouts Make the Week Eight Athlete of the Week Ballot
text:
Postseason Performances Take Over the Week Eight Athlete of the Week Ballot
The postseason is underway, and the Fall Week Eight Athlete of the Week ballot reflects just how big the performances have become.
Regional championship races, tournament soccer victories, shutouts, game-winning goals and standout individual efforts helped produce this week's field of 14 Aroostook County athletes.
Seven boys and seven girls have made the final ballot.
Voting is open now, and you can vote once per hour in both polls through Thursday at 3 p.m.
Here are the Fall Week Eight nominees.
Boys Athlete of the Week Nominees
Peyton Gorneault, Caribou, Cross Country
Gorneault delivered a huge performance at the Class B North Regional Championship. The Caribou freshman finished fourth overall in 17:12.04, helping the Vikings capture the Northern Maine team championship and advance to states.
Brayden Drake, Houlton/GHCA, Cross Country
Drake helped Houlton/GHCA put together a dominant regional championship performance, finishing third in Class C North in 16:59.00.
His finish helped Houlton/GHCA capture its second consecutive regional championship.
Paxton Darrell, Presque Isle, Cross Country
Darrell led the Wildcats at the Class B North Regional Championship, placing fifth overall in 17:15.20.
His performance helped Presque Isle finish third as a team and earn a spot in the state championship meet.
Dominic Burgess, Van Buren, Soccer
Burgess stepped up in tournament play for the Crusaders, scoring a goal in Van Buren's 3-1 preliminary-round victory over Schenck.
The win kept Van Buren's season alive and sent the Crusaders into the next round.
Brayden Barnard, Washburn, Soccer
Barnard earned his nomination after scoring 2 goals in Washburn's victory over Hodgdon, helping the Beavers pick up a big late-season win.
Gage Phillips, Katahdin, Soccer
Phillips put together a strong week in net for the Cougars.
He made 7 saves while recording a shutout against Van Buren, then followed it with 7 more saves in Katahdin's tournament game against Lee Academy.
That gave Phillips 14 saves across two games with one clean sheet.
Kyle Waye, Washburn
Waye was nominated for the way he represents his team on and off the field.
His nomination highlighted his effort, encouragement of teammates and sportsmanship, including his willingness to check on opposing players when they are injured.
Girls Athlete of the Week Nominees
Samantha Argraves, Presque Isle, Soccer
Argraves continued a strong season in goal by recording another shutout in Presque Isle's 4-0 victory over Fort Kent.
The clean sheet was her seventh shutout of the season during her first year as the Wildcats' full-time varsity goalkeeper.
Madelyn Marquis, Van Buren, Soccer
Marquis produced a big offensive performance for the Crusaders, scoring 2 goals and adding an assist in Van Buren's 3-0 victory over Easton.
Dani Pelletier, Madawaska, Soccer
Pelletier delivered one of the biggest moments of the week.
The eighth-grader scored just 57 seconds into the second overtime, giving Madawaska a dramatic 1-0 victory over Washburn.
Jenna Strid, Caribou, Cross Country
Strid delivered a strong postseason run for the Vikings, finishing eighth at the Class B North Regional Championship in 20:07.58.
Her top-10 finish helped Caribou place third as a team and qualify for the state championship meet.
Annamarie Blanchard, Presque Isle, Soccer
Blanchard found the back of the net during Presque Isle's 4-0 victory over Fort Kent, helping the Wildcats finish the regular season with another strong performance.
Trinity Daigle, Fort Kent, Soccer
Daigle came through in goal when Fort Kent entered tournament play.
She recorded the shutout in the Warriors' 3-0 quarterfinal victory over MCI, helping Fort Kent advance deeper into the Class C North tournament.
Charlotte Estabrook, Houlton/GHCA, Cross Country
Estabrook earned an individual trip to the state championships with a strong Class C North regional performance.
She finished 19th overall in 24:25.61, earning one of the individual qualifying spots for Houlton/GHCA.
Time to Pick the Week Eight Winners
Week Eight gives voters a little bit of everything.
There are regional championship performances, team titles, individual state qualifiers, playoff goals, a double-overtime game-winner and goalkeepers who delivered shutouts when their teams needed them.

title: Boy dies 5 years after being hit by crossfire in quadruple shooting
text:
CINCINNATI, Ohio (WXIX/Gray News) — A 13-year-old boy has died five years after he was shot in a quadruple shooting, according to police in Cincinnati, Ohio.
The Hamilton County Coroner’s Office identified the boy as Marcellus Whitehead.
2021 shooting left 4 injured
Marcellus was 8 years old when gunfire erupted around 6:15 p.m. on a Saturday near the McHenry and Cavanaugh Avenue intersection in Cincinnati’s Westwood neighborhood. He and three others, including a 6-year-old child and two adults, were hit by bullets.
At the time of the shooting, then-Cincinnati Police Lt. Col. Mike John said the 8-year-old was left in “very, very bad shape” after being caught in the crossfire while hanging out in a nearby lot.
“I believe the children were just hanging out in that lot, and it’s just a tragic, tragic situation. It’s awful,” John said at the time. “Thoughts and prayers go out to the families in an incident like this. I mean, you can’t explain it. It’s a Saturday evening in the summer. It’s just a terrible situation.”
Doctors at Cincinnati Children’s Hospital Medical Center placed Marcellus in a medically induced coma a day after the shooting.
At the time, the 6-year-old was in critical condition as well, according to John. The two adult victims suffered non-life-threatening injuries, John said.
2 men arrested in connection with shooting
Cincinnati police arrested Darius Harris Jr., now 24, who was initially charged with seven counts of felonious assault, Hamilton County court records show. Five of those counts were dismissed, court records show.
According to the Ohio Department of Corrections, Harris Jr. is now serving a prison sentence on charges of carrying a concealed weapon, having a weapon while under disability and two counts of felonious assault.
Javari Walker, now 23, was also arrested in connection with the shooting, court records show. Walker was sentenced to jail in 2023 and convicted of having weapons while under disability, according to court records.

title: 3 people, including teen, arrested after botched robbery shooting leaves 15-year-old dead
text:
GULFPORT, Miss. (WLOX/Gray News) — Three people, including a teenager, are in custody after a shooting early Saturday left a 15-year-old dead, authorities said.
Officials said Elijah Markell Parham, 18, Elliona Yari-Cheri Goffney, 18, and a 17-year-old are each charged in connection with the shooting death of Jonte Payton, 15.
Investigators said around 2 a.m. Saturday, a botched robbery led to a fight that ended with Jonte being shot in front of a home on Commerce Street in Gulfport, Mississippi. Officers were able to identify a suspect vehicle after pulling footage from nearby surveillance cameras.
Officers later found the vehicle with the 17-year-old and Goffney at Cypress Lanes Apartments, where they were arrested. Parham later turned himself in at the Gulfport Police Department.
Parham and the 17-year-old are charged with capital murder and armed robbery. Goffney is charged with accessory after the fact.
All three were taken to the Harrison County Adult Detention Center to be held pending bond after processing and interviews.

title: Nicki Minaj joins Trump on Air Force One: Who else is flying with the president?
text:
ABOARD AIR FORCE ONE (AP) — President Donald Trump has clocked about 70 hours aboard Air Force One so far this month, racing from rally to rally across the United States to try to bolster his Republican Party in the midterm elections.
Also along for the ride: an entourage ranging from aging boxing champions to Cabinet members to relatively unknown aides who help craft Trump’s words and ideas. The passenger list for Trump’s marathon through the sky signals who has the ear of the president.
“It can say what his priorities are,” said David Cohen, a professor of political science at the University of Akron. “Who he surrounds himself with are the people he is going to be listening to. They’re the ones who are going to be whispering in his ear and talking softly in private quarters to the president of the United States.”
Here’s a look at who has had access to power in the confines of Trump’s plane this month.
The inner circle
White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who recently finished treatment for breast cancer, is a frequent flyer. Trump has called Wiles, who co-managed his 2024 campaign, the “most powerful woman in the world.” As Air Force One ascended from Greenville, North Carolina, after Trump’s 15th rally in 20 days, Wiles gave reporters her take on how it went as she walked up the aisle.
“Great,” she said. “They’ve all been great, honestly.”
Other insiders who’ve made the manifest: special envoy Steve Witkoff, who has been trying to negotiate an end to the Iran war that has weighed on Republicans’ midterm fortunes; deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, the architect of Trump’s immigration crackdown; Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner; Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins.
The most frequent Cabinet member aboard has been Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a billionaire who previously ran the financial services firm Cantor Fitzgerald. A Trump buddy going back to the 1990s, Lutnick can often be heard laughing at the president’s jokes. His role at Trump’s rallies has been to highlight new factory investments that Trump uses to try to convince his supporters that the economy is doing well.
Punching above their weight
Bill Pulte has joined Trump for at least five legs of the midterm marathon so far, a sign that his status inside the administration is far higher than his title — director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency — would suggest.
The scion of a homebuilding company, Pulte is a Trump pal who was for a brief period also the acting director of national intelligence and oversaw layoffs in that office. He has led pressure campaigns on Federal Reserve officials such as Jerome Powell and Lisa Cook. Pulte has also passed along policy ideas such as changing the 30-year mortgage to 50 years, an idea that has since been abandoned.
Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr has also flown with the president, notably on Oct. 13 and Oct. 14 on a lengthy West Coast swing. Carr has sought to use his regulatory powers over broadcast networks to chastise them over their coverage of the president.
Personal aides who keep Trump going
Chief among the retinue of assistants around the president is Natalie Harp, an executive assistant who is on most of Trump’s trips. Walt Nauta, the director of Oval Office Operations, is not far behind her in air miles. Chamberlain Harris, Nauta’s deputy, is another frequent traveler. She also serves as a member of the Commission of Fine Arts, one of the government bodies with a role in reviewing the White House ballroom and other Trump construction projects.
Although Trump likes to ad-lib, the speechwriting director, Ross Worthington, has joined him repeatedly on the plane this month. The president’s stump speech features a promise of $5,000 checks if Republicans keep their House and Senate majorities after the Nov. 3 election. He also tends to highlight new factory projects and investments in the communities he visits.
Margo Martin, a communications adviser who posts videos of Trump on social media, has joined the tour, as has White House communications director Steven Cheung. Katie Zacharia, who was the White House press secretary for five days, spent two of them with the president on a trip to Alaska, Nevada, Arizona and Montana.
Plenty of political strategists
Trump is surrounded on these trips by White House and external consultants making strategic choices for the midterms, including Matt Brasseaux, his political director, who previously worked at the Republican National Committee.
Johnny DeStefano, who was a top aide in Trump’s first term, temporarily rejoined the White House this summer to work on midterm strategy and has been seen on Air Force One, as has former White House deputy chief of staff James Blair.
Celebrities hitch a ride
Going into what could be some rough midterm races, Trump has brought aboard with him some of the biggest names in boxing: Mike Tyson, Floyd Mayweather Jr. and Evander Holyfield. In a 1997 heavyweight championship bout, Tyson bit off a piece of Holyfield’s right ear. They did not fly on Air Force One at the same time.
Towson University professor Martha Kumar said that presidential travel during a campaign can be intense and that presidents often have passengers who can keep the environment relaxed even as the work continues. “You want to have people around you that make you feel comfortable,” Kumar said. “When you think about it, it is really stressful. You want some relief.”
On Sunday, Cheung posted a video in which he was interviewing the rapper Nicki Minaj aboard Air Force One as it took Trump to Michigan for a campaign rally. Minaj praised the president, and the White House’s goal is to have Trump wrap up his midterm blitz by having a celebrity with him at each stop.
Who else has hitched a ride with Trump? Retired NASCAR champion Richard Petty went to North Carolina, former NFL coach Jon Gruden to Ohio, and retired NFL running back Todd Gurley to Georgia. Influencer-turned-boxer Jake Paul also traveled with the president. The celebrities have had cameos in Trump’s rallies.
Congress gets onboard
The goal of Trump’s travel over the past month has been to help Republicans keep control of Congress.
As the White House’s liaison with the House, Jeff Freeland has been on Air Force One with multiple lawmakers. Rep. William Timmons of South Carolina flew with the president, as have multiple Texas House members, including Reps. Beth Van Duyne and Brandon Gill, as well as Reps. Brian Jack of Georgia, Tim Moore of North Carolina and Anna Paulina Luna of Florida.
John Barrasso of Wyoming, the second-ranking Republican senator, has flown multiple times with the president this month, as has Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who is considering a presidential bid in 2028.

title: Maine climber rescued after getting stuck on granite cliff
text:
A Portland man was rescued Sunday morning after he got stuck while climbing a granite cliff in New Hampshire.
The 30-year-old was climbing alone and unroped on the Sliding Board route up Whitehorse Ledge in Hale’s Location, a small township north of Conway, about 8 a.m. when he realized he could not climb any higher or climb back down, according to New Hampshire Fish and Game.
The climber, who was about 500 feet from the ground, managed to get to a secure spot and called for help, Fish and Game said Monday morning.
Nine climbers made their way up to him, fixing ropes from the ground up to the Portlander.
They brought him to the cliff’s base, which they reached about 10 a.m.

title: Eric Bauza, modern voice of Looney Tunes characters, dies at 46
text:
Eric Bauza, the award-winning voice actor whose performances of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and many more characters made him the modern voice of Looney Tunes, has died. He was 46.
Bauza died suddenly late Sunday, his family said in a statement. The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner reported that he died at his home from hypertensive cardiovascular disease.
Beginning in 2001, Bauza amassed more than 400 voice acting credits in a career that gave voice to beloved characters in animated Looney Tunes series including “Puss in Boots,” “Muppet Babies,” “Avatar: The Last Airbender,” and countless others. He won three Children’s and Family Emmy Awards, from 2022 to 2025.
“Looney Tunes will always have a special place in my heart,” Bauza said in an interview with The Associated Press this year. “I watched them on Saturday mornings originally. It’s not just the voice but the overall aesthetic has influenced me as an artist.”
Raised in Scarborough, Ontario by Filipino immigrant parents, Bauza found his passion for voice acting as a teenager. In high school, he would deliver the P.A. system morning announcements in various cartoon voices.
In voicing Looney Tunes characters, Bauza faithfully and reverentially channeled Mel Blanc. So great was his affection for Blanc that, in conversation, he would even toss out an impression of Blanc outside the recording booth. Bauza last year told The New York Times: “Mel Blanc is like the voice of God for me.”
Bauza’s Looney Tunes work included such feature films as “Space Jam: A New Legacy” (2021), “The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie” (2024) and this year’s “Coyote vs. Acme.” That film, in which Wile E. Coyote takes the Acme Corporation to court for its defective products, became a modest cause célèbre after Warner Bros. opted not to release it.
After an outcry from fans, partly stoked by Bauza, the film eventually found a distributor in Ketchup Entertainment and surpassed $100 million at the worldwide box office. While the film was in limbo, Bauza argued for its release at the 2024 Annie Awards, in the voice of Daffy Duck.
“He’s the go-to cartoon character above anyone else when it comes to begging and pleading,” Bauza explained. “It seemed appropriate.”
As a voice acting professional, Bauza sometimes chafed at celebrities brought in to replace him in bigger-budgeted productions. Bauza occasionally voice-matched for stars including Bill Hader on “Bob’s Burgers” and Antonio Banderas as Puss in Boots.
“From my experience working several times in the feature film format, there’s always the reminder that it is ‘temporary dialogue’ and ‘Chris Pratt will be voicing all the Looney Tunes in this feature film’ — no, just kidding,” Bauza told The AP.
But even in productions where A-list stars took the spotlight, Bauza said there was still room for “nine-to-fivers like me” to color in the scenery. Bauza, who seldom went more than a few minutes without slipping into the voice of Bugs or Daffy or some other character, was rarely anything but grateful at being part of the Looney Tunes legacy.
“The Looney Tunes were here before I was born and they’re definitely going to be here long after I leave this realm,” he said shortly before the release of “Coyote vs. Acme.” “I just feel like the luckiest guy.”

title: Kitten rescued from transfer station dumpster in Somerset County
text:
BINGHAM, Maine (WABI) - This past weekend, a roughly three month old kitten was found in a tied plastic bag at a transfer station in Concord Township, just outside Bingham in Somerset County.
The kitten is alive and being cared for, thanks to the vigilance of an employee.
“I kept hearing a kitten meowing, and then I kept looking, and I see a bag moving,” said Peter Abraham, the transfer station manager for the town of Bingham. “So, I went back to the garage, and I got my pick pole, and I pulled the bag apart, and the kitten was in the bag.”
That was when he called Tina Tibbetts, Bingham’s new animal control officer.
“It upset me a lot. It upset a lot of people in Bingham, knowing that someone couldn’t just bring him to the Humane Society. You don’t have to throw an animal into the dump,” said Tibbetts.
Tibbetts and other town officials say this incident shows the crucial need for animal welfare resources in Maine.
A candlemaker by trade, Tibbetts has no history of working with animals, but she stepped up when she saw a need in her rural community.
“I saw the sign. I love animals, and I knew Bingham needed an animal control officer. Nobody wanted the job,” said Tibbetts.
The kitten, now named “Dumpster,” is one of more than 70 animals Tibbetts has helped relocate in just two weeks of working for the town as ACO out of her own home. She’s hoping to raise money for a small, heated animal shelter in Bingham, as well as an animal food pantry.
Donation boxes are being left at local businesses. Anyone from outside the area looking to donate can call Tibbetts at 995-1196 or message Tina Marie Tibbetts on Facebook.
As for Dumpster, Tibbetts says he may have found a forever home with her and her family, and seems to be in good shape—except for some fleas.
If you have any information regarding how the kitten ended up in the transfer station dumpster, you’re asked to contact the Somerset County Sheriff’s Office.
The Town of Bingham also urges anyone who finds themselves unable or unwilling to care for an animal there to call their local animal shelter, ACO, town office, or even your local dispatch center’s non-emergency line.

title: UMaine celebrates decades of athletic excellence with Hall of Fame inductions
text:
Fifty years after playing on the national stage, the 1976 University of Maine baseball team received one of the program’s highest honors. Alongside basketball standout Blanca Millan and hockey champion Cory Larose, the team was inducted into the UMaine Sports Hall of Fame on Oct. 16, celebrating decades of achievement across three different sports.
The three inductees represent different eras of Black Bear athletics, but they all share a determination to compete at the highest level and leave a lasting impact on the university.
The 1976 baseball team established itself as one of the most successful squads in UMaine history, finishing the season with a 29-9 record and earning a trip to the College World Series in Omaha, Nebraska.
Led by head coach John Winkin, the Black Bears won the Yankee Conference and Eastern Collegiate Athletic Conference titles before sweeping through the NCAA Northeast Regional. The team won seven consecutive postseason games to secure its place among the nation’s top college baseball programs.
Maine continued its impressive run in Omaha. After dropping its opening game to Eastern Michigan University, the Black Bears bounced back with a dramatic 9-8 victory over Auburn University and followed it with a 6-3 win against Washington State. Their run ended against Arizona State University, but the team had already cemented its place in program history.
Pitcher Bert Roberge was a key contributor, finishing the season with a 9-2 record, a 2.06 earned run average and 60 strikeouts in his senior season. Tony DiBiase, an all-conference first baseman that year, led the offense with a .339 batting average. Jack Leggett and John Dumont also played major roles in the team’s success, both having the program’s highest career hits at 104.
The team achieved more than just a winning record and accolades. Its success helped establish UMaine as a nationally competitive baseball program and set the foundation for future teams. Winkin went on to bring six more teams to the College World Series, further strengthening his legacy at the university.
Blanca Millan brought a different kind of excellence to UMaine, becoming one of the most accomplished players in the history of the women’s basketball program.
A three-time All-America East first-team selection, Millan finished her college career with 1,974 points and 324 steals. Her ability to score while disrupting opposing offenses made her one of the conference’s most difficult players to defend.
Millan made history by becoming the first player in America East women’s basketball history to earn both Player of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year honors twice. She helped lead the Black Bears to America East championships and NCAA Tournament appearances in 2018 and 2019.
Millan helped set the standard for the program, showing how high-level defense and offense combine to achieve success. Her induction honors a career that strengthened UMaine women’s basketball and established a lasting legacy for generations of players to follow.
For Cory Larose, the defining moment of his UMaine career came on college hockey’s biggest stage.
Larose was a member of the 1998-99 Black Bears team that captured the NCAA Division I national championship. Maine defeated New Hampshire 3-2 in overtime, completing a memorable championship run and securing its second national title.
Larose was a key player throughout his time at Maine. In 1999-2000, he led Maine with 36 assists and 51 points, earning first-team All-Hockey East recognition and second-team All-American honors. He finished his college career with 180 points, including 61 goals and 119 assists.
After graduating, Larose played professional hockey before moving to the athletic footwear industry. He worked for companies including Nike, Reebok and Saucony. His success demonstrates how the skills developed through college athletics can translate into success beyond competition.
The induction of the 1976 baseball team, Millan and Larose highlights UMaine’s long-lasting athletic excellence. From a historic run in Omaha to dominance on the basketball court and a national championship on the ice, each story shows the commitment required to compete and succeed.
Their induction is more than a celebration; it is a reminder of the athletes who helped shape the Black Bear identity and the legacy that future generations will continue to build.

title: Growing up with, and apart from, Susan Collins
text:
Peter Nalli has lived in southern Maine for 25 years. He is an independent consultant who has worked in education, policy, politics and economic and community development.
It’s hard to change your mind about someone you once respected. When I hear Sen. Susan Collins speak, some part of my brain (or heart) still wants to believe the 30-year-old pitch of a humble and hard-working County girl devoted to public service.
Susan Collins became a United States senator when I was in sixth grade at North
Yarmouth Memorial School. As an 11-year-old, I recall a vague sense of pride that our state
had sent two women to the Senate (someday, there might be a woman president!).
There was also a feeling that Sen. Collins might march down the trail blazed by Margaret Chase Smith, who ranks with Stephen King, Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain and Miss Rumphius in the pantheon of Pine State heroes.
Arriving at college in 2003, the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan roared away. Surprisingly few of my new classmates had heard of Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain or Miss Rumphius. By now, I was a registered Democrat, but my general pitch about the glory of my home state focused on Mainers’ independence of thought and spirit, evidenced by two women senators who seemed to think for themselves.
My first political rally was a pro-choice march in Washington, D.C., where I joined dozens of classmates outraged by infringements of Roe v. Wade. I kept noting to friends (probably obnoxiously) that Maine’s senators would always protect a woman’s right to choose.
In 2006, my parents paid me to paint their bedroom a shade of mauve. From a radio balanced on the stepstool, I listened to all the hearings for Samuel Alito’s nomination to the Supreme Court. He called Roe v. Wade “important precedent” that “required considerable respect” and Sen. Collins voted to confirm him.
Twelve years later, now 33 years old, I pulled my car over on Route 2 in Mexico, shocked.
The Androscoggin glinted through fall foliage as I listened to Dr. Christine Blasey Ford carefully and credibly describe how Brett Kavanaugh had pinned her down and sexually assaulted her. Days later, listening to the radio at camp, my jaw dropped again as an unhinged Brett Kavanaugh pitched a fit to the Senate Judiciary Committee, a childish and noxious display that surely disqualified him for the nation’s highest court.
A week later, back in Portland, a friend called to say that Susan Collins was voting to confirm Kavanaugh and I thought they were joking. The following summer, Collins attended a fundraiser at the Northeast Harbor mansion of Leonard Leo, a D.C. architect of the plan to create a MAGA Supreme Court.
When I was 37 years old, the Supreme Court that Susan Collins created voted to overturn Roe v. Wade, ending a woman’s federal right to access an abortion if she needs one. Justices Kavanaugh and Alito joined the majority and Collins expressed dismay.
The Supreme Court that Susan Collins created has ruled that lawlessness by a president is legal because he is president, that protections for clean air and water should be gutted, that the Voting Rights Act is irrelevant and that a tax and economic system prioritizing corporations and billionaires is sacrosanct. It’s a Supreme Court and a set of rulings for Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and Leonard Leo, not for the people of Aroostook County, York County or many Mainers in between.
In the system that Susan Collins helped create, healthcare is more expensive, workers have fewer rights and the most powerful and richest are a protected class with policies designed to make them richer. She still gets money for projects in Maine and occasionally votes against her party. Just enough to keep us on the hook.
I was 40 years old when ICE surged in Maine and masked federal agents abducted a civil engineer with a work visa at the Top of the Old Port parking lot in Portland. He was snatched by government agents with his car left running, the driver’s side window smashed, his phone on the ground, his bag and keys on the passenger seat. Stories of others abducted from their schooling, jobs and neighborhoods spread quickly. Masked agents threatened peaceful protesters, drove to their homes and told them they were now in a federal registry.
Susan Collins could have curtailed ICE funding, demanded new conditions on enforcement,
investigated the thuggish behavior or exercised her supposed power. Instead, she called her
colleague, then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, and asked them just to stop. She didn’t solve the
problem, she hit snooze. Six months later, ICE agents gunned down an innocent man in
Biddeford.
Susan Collins keeps boasting about her power in Washington, but a senseless war in Iran is raging, unregulated artificial intelligence is about to wreak havoc on our economy and well-
being and health insurance, housing and fuel costs are soaring. The Supreme Court she built is shredding the foundations of our constitutional order and, according to reports, there will likely be another Supreme Court vacancy next year.
I stopped bragging long ago that Maine has a moderate or independent-minded senator. I’m now 41 years old and we need change.

title: Appeals court declines to rule on federal bid to set aside California ballots of alleged noncitizens
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — An appeals court on Monday declined to rule on whether California elections officials can count roughly 20,000 ballots that the Justice Department alleges belong to noncitizen voters.
The decision sets the federal government and state officials up for another legal showdown on the matter on Tuesday in front of a federal district judge, giving the federal government a very short window to compel California to sequester votes before the Nov. 3 elections.
The Republican administration sued election officials in the heavily Democratic state in mid-October, accusing them of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a list of 20,000 people it alleged were likely noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls. The administration asked the judge to stop the state from counting those ballots until immigration status checks could be completed.
After a district judge had scheduled an Oct. 27 hearing on the issue, the federal government appealed to the 9th Circuit Court, arguing that a faster decision was needed to prevent the further counting of votes.
But two of the three 9th Circuit Court judges rejected that argument on Monday, writing that the federal government “failed to allow the district court adequate opportunity to consider” their initial request to sequester the ballots in question.
The Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to an emailed inquiry.

title: Border crossing reopens with tighter checks for flesh-eating screwworm
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Border crossing reopens with tighter checks for flesh-eating screwworm
With the all-clear from U.S. agriculture inspectors, Mexican cattle began moving on Monday through a border crossing in New Mexico that had been closed for nearly two years as both nations work to stop the flesh-eating New World screwworm from spreading.
The screwworm — actually a fly larva that burrows into the flesh of livestock, pets and even humans — has threatened the $113 billion U.S. cattle industry. Containment efforts have cost jobs and trade in border communities, and they cut off a source of cattle as the U.S. struggles to rebuild drought-depleted herds. Reopening crossings could help ease that squeeze, although experts caution that shoppers shouldn't expect quick relief on beef prices.
The port at Columbus, New Mexico, is the third to resume Mexican cattle imports under new safeguards, which include tests, shots and inspections that happen before an animal even gets close to the border.
Related video above: US resumes Mexican cattle imports after screwworm outbreak
Officials and ranchers in the two countries say layers of treatment and inspection give them confidence that imported livestock won't carry screwworm through the ports. But flies can buzz across the border on their own, meaning ranchers, hunters and pet owners should remain vigilant.
The parasite was an annual livestock scourge before being largely eradicated in the U.S. in the 1960s. It reappeared in Mexico in 2024, and the first confirmed U.S. case was in Texas in June.
More than 60 cases have been confirmed in Texas and New Mexico, with infestations of cattle, sheep, goats, horses and dogs. Last week, the first case in U.S. wildlife was confirmed after a hunter found screwworm in an elk.
Before the current outbreak, the U.S. was importing about 1 million head of cattle per year. It will take time to get back to that number while keeping a sharp eye on the risks to animal health, said Dudley Hoskins, undersecretary for the Department of Agriculture.
“As long as we can manage and mitigate that risk at an acceptable level, we will continue to process the safe and legal movement of cattle through these ports,” he said, watching as cattle lined up in the chutes at Columbus.
New Mexico is key for cattle imports
About a third of all Mexican cattle imported to the U.S. each year pass through Columbus and the Santa Teresa port near El Paso, Texas. Gerardo Fierro, executive director of the New Mexico Border Authority, pegged the value of the cattle trade for the area at $1 billion.
Fierro said the community watched as jobs, cattle sales and even tax revenue from the diesel fuel used to transport the animals evaporated due to the closures. Ranchers were no longer crossing into New Mexico and spending money on supplies, lodging and food, and farmers had no customers for their alfalfa and grain.
“This means a lot,” he said of the reopening.
Another border crossing for cattle in Arizona is due to open in late November.
Layers of safeguards ensure cows are clean
New Mexico state veterinarian Samantha Holeck said the rigorous process for getting cattle ready starts at their home ranches, where private veterinarians check for tuberculosis and other diseases and deliver medications that prevent screwworm.
At the next stop, veterinarians accredited by the Mexican government look for open wounds, signs of illness or other injuries. Then a head-to-tail inspection is done by the USDA while still in Mexico.
The last hurdle? Dipping — as it's commonly known — involves the cows being immersed in vats of insecticide to get rid of any missed parasites.
Flies have lots of ways to move around
Holeck said the protocols developed over recent years helped to buy more time, and the USDA is using fly traps and drones to survey areas.
The government has a longstanding program to breed sterile male flies and drop swarms of them from planes to mate with wild females, causing the flies to die out. The government is building a $610 million factory in Texas that can produce 300 million sterile flies per week. That will augment production at facilities in Mexico and Panama.
“That’s our sharpest tool,” Hoskins said.
Beef prices are a bigger problem
Mexican ranchers once again have a market for their feeder cattle, but experts say it will take time for U.S. ranchers to rebuild herds that have dwindled to record lows due to years of persistent drought. Constrained supplies have pushed prices higher.
Tom Paterson, president of the New Mexico Cattle Growers' Association, was among those who met with U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins last week in Columbus.
“I agree with the secretary,” he said, “when she says that food security is national security.”

title: Portland police shoot pepper balls into McDonald's bathroom after Bangor woman won’t come out
text:
A Bangor woman was arrested in Portland on Monday after allegedly locking herself in a McDonald’s bathroom and claiming to have a gun, leading to a standoff with police.
The incident started shortly before 11:30 a.m. when emergency medical personnel were called to the McDonald’s at 332 St. John St. for a report of a woman in the bathroom who was allegedly consuming drugs and requesting emergency medical services, according to the Portland Police Department.
When the medics arrived, the woman, later identified as Erin Baker, 44, of Bangor, told them that she had a gun. Portland police were called in and started negotiating with the woman, who remained inside the bathroom for nearly 30 minutes, according to police.
Officers “deployed pepperball rounds” into the bathroom, and Baker was “exited” and taken into custody without further incident.
She was taken to Cumberland County Jail and charged with creating a police standoff, terrorizing, refusing to submit, and criminal trespass, police said.
Police did not find a gun at the scene.

title: Candlelight vigil held in honor of those killed in Lewiston mass shooting
text:
LEWISTON, Maine (WMTW) - On the three-year anniversary of a Lewiston mass shooting that killed 18 people and injured 13 others, the community held a candlelight vigil to honor the victims and stand alongside the survivors.
The event was hosted and organized by the Maine Resiliency Center, an organization created weeks after the shooting to provide support and services to the victims’ families, survivors and anybody impacted by the tragedy.
“Eighteen of them were killed. Tonight, we gather to remember those 18 people who were killed,” announced Maine Resiliency Center associate director Meredith Stack.
Dozens filled the hill at Lewiston’s Simard-Payne Park for the ceremony before a reading of the names of the 18 victims.
“It isn’t only the lives that ended on October 25th. It’s all the life that should have been lived since,” said Maine Resiliency Center director Danielle Parent.
One of the names that was read was Arthur Strout. Strout’s father, Arthur Barnard, attended the ceremony.
“I’ve come to grips that it’s unavoidable,” said Barnard. “The feelings and the things and emotions that happen today, it’s just unavoidable.”
Barnard said that this morning, he took time to recall the last time he spent with his son, three years ago.
“This morning, just waking up, and thinking about how it unfolded, everything that day. And I think it happens for all of us. The things we say to each other before this all happened,” commented Barnard. “I guess the only thing, I really, I was fortunate I spent the last 2.5 hours of his life with him, and he was happy.”
The ceremony closed as the group walked together to the Longley Bridge to release flower petals.

title: United flight turned around after report of passenger making a terroristic threat
text:
LAS VEGAS (AP) — A United Airlines flight was diverted back to Las Vegas shortly after takeoff over the weekend due to what police said was a report of a passenger making a terroristic threat.
Las Vegas police said they detained a 25-year-old passenger after the report on the Saturday night flight headed to Newark, New Jersey. The man was arrested on charges of making a threat or providing false information regarding an act of terrorism.
Police did not immediately provide more details on what the man is accused of doing or saying. The Federal Aviation Administration said the flight crew had reported a “passenger disturbance” on the flight.
An attorney listed for the man did not immediately return a request for comment. His initial court appearance is scheduled for Tuesday.
The scheduled redeye flight returned to the airport less than an hour after departing, according to Flightradar24 data.
United confirmed that the flight with 150 passengers on board returned safely to Las Vegas to address a “potential security concern.” The flight was delayed overnight and departed for Newark on Sunday morning.
The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed it will investigate the incident and said in an email to The Associated Press there have been over 1,400 unruly passenger incidents so far in 2026.
