title: Former hairstylist and nail tech battles lung cancer after decades of chemical exposure
text:
RICHMOND, Va. (Aging Untold) — For 35 years, Jeorgi Golden knew the ins and outs of the salon, working as a Black hairstylist where coworkers and clients became family.
“I started in the late 70s, early 80s,” Golden said. “It was more like being a social worker or a counselor because we talked about everything.”
With the exception of Mondays, Golden spent long hours at the salon seeing client after client. These days, she misses the comfort it once brought her.
“Smelling the natural hair when you press it, it’s nostalgia,” Golden said. “It makes me think of my grandmother who did my hair when I was a kid.”
For years, Golden would do at least 10 ladies’ hair each day. By the end of the week, she would have seen approximately 40 to 50 clients.
Some of those women asked for everything from press and curls to hair relaxers or a Jheri Curl, a popular hairstyle at the time that gave coarse hair a curly, wet look.
She remembers when relaxers were her biggest seller, not just for women, but also for men.
“The salon would be filled, especially if you had a salon that had 10 to 15 people in there working. And everybody’s doing that,” Golden said.
For Golden, it was about making her customers happy and getting the job done. But the chemicals she breathed in daily may have cost her dearly.
The only protection was gloves
Golden said salon workers in those days received minimal safety guidance about those products and how they should be applied.
“The only thing you was told was, ‘Oh you can put on gloves cause you’re dealing with lye.’ That was it. There was no other protection,” she said. “So, we went in blindly, thinking that the products that was sold to us and said, ‘Hey this is gonna make you beautiful.’ They didn’t tell us that it was gonna definitely hurt us at the end.”
She said no one ever mentioned the dangers, even though formaldehyde was an ingredient found in those products.
Formaldehyde is classified as a carcinogen by the EPA.
For Golden and other hairstylists, they trusted the products and never questioned potential health risks.
Studies now show that toxic gas poses serious health risks to both consumers and salon workers, linking exposure to eye problems, respiratory issues, and even certain types of cancer.
Golden was diagnosed with lung cancer in April 2024 after a routine tuberculosis test revealed something alarming. She says she never smoked or drank, making her cancer diagnosis particularly puzzling until she began connecting it to her decades of salon work.
“I was like, ‘I didn’t do anything. How did this happen?’” Golden said. “And then I started going back through the times. Yeah, I did nails... formaldehyde, it was right there. And that was before they made it a nicer-smelling product.”
Golden’s health concerns began decades earlier. At age 26, she had a hysterectomy after developing polyps.
“I was still doing hair and the pain was just excruciating,” Golden said. “I passed out at work, and [the doctor] said I have to have a hysterectomy.”
The physician told her they found polyps, but they never explicitly said it was cancer at the time.
“I think a lot of women who was in the industry have a lot of medical issues that they don’t connect,” she said. “You think it’s something that’s isolated, but I think if you have more than 10 women having the same thing who did the same job...then it’s related.”
Chemical exposure concerns widespread
Her concerns reflect those of other hairstylists.
InvestigateTV analyzed complaints submitted to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) over the past five years about formaldehyde dangers affecting hair salon owners and workers across the country.
We found dozens of complaints filed by salon owners and employees about the lack of ventilation within their salons and concerns about not having safety data sheets about the chemicals they’d be working with.
One complaint from a New York salon stated, “Brazilian blowout treatments are done in a very small space in the salon with little ventilation. The formaldehyde vapors from the procedure impacts staff health, such as respiratory irritation.”
Another complaint noted, “The use of hair products and color agents are exposing employees to chemical hazards...the chemicals are ammonia, formaldehyde, toluene and acetone...no ventilation system is being utilized to control the airborne hazard.”
An additional complaint said that “employees are experiencing headaches, breathing issues, burning throats and eyes due to the exposure of formaldehyde during Brazilian Blowout treatments.”
That same complaint goes on to say that the salon wasn’t providing proper ventilation and personal protection equipment and safety goggles and gloves.
In 2010, OSHA investigated a series of specific Brazilian blowout products finding some were listed as formaldehyde-free but on-site testing showed they “found formaldehyde in the air” after questions and complaints were made by hair salon owners and workers.
Inspectors missed the dangers, stylist says
Golden recalls that those same experiences reflect what she says she personally saw in her salon when inspectors visited years ago. She said when the inspector walked in, they would see there was some ventilation available, and not once did they question the toxins in the air further.
A 2022 National Institutes of Health study called the “Sister Study” found a correlation between formaldehyde and uterine cancer after following 33,000 women for 11 years.
The study also found that Black women are disproportionately more affected because of their higher use of those chemicals.
When that study emerged, Golden began thinking about how those chemicals might have affected her own health.
“My first thought was, ‘Hmm, that really couldn’t be us,’” Golden said. “And then as I started reading more and we as women who were in the salon and we’re talking and saying ‘Well, you know, so and so got cancer.’”
She said she and her colleagues who had gotten sick began connecting the dots.
Lawmakers push for action
The health concerns Golden and other salon workers face have caught the attention of federal lawmakers.
U.S. Rep. Shontel Brown of Ohio, who developed uterine fibroids and had a hysterectomy, is among lawmakers calling on the FDA to ban chemical hair products containing formaldehyde.
“These chemicals and these hair relaxers have proven to be dangerous,” the Democrat lawmaker said. “Eighty percent of Black women are going to be diagnosed with fibroids. And I am a person who has survived uterine fibroids.”
Brown and other lawmakers are pushing for additional legislation to study uterine cancer and other illnesses related to chemical hair straighteners.
“The bottom line is we want people to feel safe,” Brown said. “We want people to be able to beautify themselves, without worrying about if this is going to give me any adverse health effects.”
Fellow Democrat, Rep. Alma Adams of North Carolina, noted that currently, there is no federal funding allocated to research uterine cancer.
On a state level, California, Washington, and Maryland have banned or restricted formaldehyde in cosmetics.
Despite national concern, the FDA has not banned the ingredients and has missed its fifth deadline to propose a ban on formaldehyde products.
“When you think about the United States of America, this should not be a partisan issue,” Brown said. “We have women in every state, right? And so we make up 51% of the population.”
The Cost of Beauty
Back at home now, Jeorgi Golden is retired and doing her best to stay healthy. She said that she doesn’t regret her life in the salon. She hopes other stylists will remember to put their health and well-being first.
“I tell any woman, any woman, if you hear that whisper and wake up in the middle of the night go to the doctor,” Golden said. “Because we as women put everything off. We take care of everybody but ourselves.”
She mentions that there is a cost to beauty.
“We, as women of color, we want to have the image that they have said we should have, and as they say, beauty costs and we are paying the costs for that beauty.”

title: Is It Really Illegal To Drive in the Left Lane On I-95?
text:
Is It Really Illegal To Drive in the Left Lane On the I-95 in Maine?
If you spend a lot of time driving the I-95 through Maine there is a good chance that you have broken the law without even realizing it.
Is It Illegal To Drive In The Left Lane On The I-95?
Without hashing out the specifics of how fast you drive, I think we can all agree that many of us frequently drive faster than the posted speed limit. A lot of times this happens when we're on the highway. This often causes us to drive faster than the flow of traffic. When that happens we tend to camp in the left lane of the highway.
Is it legal to do this? Technically, no.
According to the Maine Legislature website:
An operator driving on a limited-access way with a speed limit of 65 or more miles per hour is restricted in ordinary operation to the right-hand lane and may use adjacent lanes for overtaking and passing another vehicle, but must return to the right-hand lane at the earliest opportunity. This requirement does not apply to an authorized emergency vehicle, or to a vehicle otherwise directed by posted signs, a law enforcement officer or a highway maintenance crew.
So, will you get pulled over for riding in the left lane? As long as you are actively passing a line of cars, probably not. But, you're going to want to slip back into that right lane as soon as you can.
If you do get pulled over for camping in the left lane you could be facing a $152 ticket!
You can read more about the laws HERE.
It is just another reminder to always be aware of the rules of the road in the states where you travel.

title: Illinois man charged with mailing white powder to members of Congress
text:
SPRINGFIELD, Ill. (AP) — A 37-year-old Illinois man is charged with sending threatening letters to members of Congress containing a white powder, including one with a note reading “HAH enjoy the gift,” according to federal court records.
The criminal complaint unsealed Monday claims Matthew Ungelsbee sent at least four plain white envelopes with a powdery substance to elected officials in Chicago. They were postmarked in Springfield, Illinois, on Oct. 19 and had Unglesbee’s name handwritten in the return address section.
Unglesbee, of Quincy in southwestern Illinois, is charged with mailing threatening communications and perpetrating a hoax. He was scheduled to appear in court Monday afternoon. Court records did not list a defense attorney, and a phone number for Unglesbee could not be found. A Facebook message to a Matthew Unglesbee in Quincy was not immediately returned.
FBI agents interviewed Unglesbee at his home on Sunday and he told them all the letters contained salt, court records show. He claimed he’d sent the letters after hearing someone talk about similar mailings in the news earlier this month.
Testing confirmed the white substance was not dangerous. The records did not identify the substance.
A motive was unclear. But Unglesbee said he knew the congress members would “take it serious” because the powder might be perceived as anthrax, which he knew was dangerous and could prompt a response by hazmat teams, according to the complaint.
“Unglesbee claimed he was joking but recognized the recipients would not know he was joking and could perceive it as a threat,” the complaint stated.
Investigators said none of the recipients opened the letters. The most recent envelope was received Oct. 23 at the office of a U.S. senator, records show. It contained a white powdery substance and a handwritten note reading “HAH enjoy the gift,” according to the documents.
The investigation began after an anonymous tipster reported overhearing Unglesbee in a restaurant talking about mailing a suspicious substance to members of Congress. The tip was received Oct. 16, and the FBI tracked Ungelsbee down after the envelopes arrived at the congressional offices days later.
The recipients of the mailings were not named. Authorities searched Unglesbee’s home and found a fifth envelope addressed to another congress member’s Washington, D.C., office, the records show.
Earlier this month, federal authorities said they were investigating letters with “suspicious substances” that had been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide. That investigation by the FBI, the U.S. Postal Inspection Service and U.S. Capitol Police was first disclosed in a message from the Senate Sergeant at Arms obtained Oct. 15 by The Associated Press.
Unglesbee denied involvement in those mailings.

title: Maine Democrats have switched from defense to offense
text:
Devon Murphy-Anderson is the executive director of the Maine Democratic Party. She is from Harpswell and lives in Portland.
Most people think elections are won or lost on Election Day. But any good operative knows elections are often decided long before the first Tuesday in November.
Two years ago, I sat in a coffee shop in Bath reviewing polling about a referendum Republicans had qualified for Maine’s 2025 ballot. As I read about the attacks on absentee voting, I saw it for what it was: Republicans were using voter suppression tactics from other states in an attempt to give Sen. Susan Collins a more favorable electorate in 2026, in a year when fewer voters would be paying attention.
That’s when I decided to apply to be executive director of the Maine Democratic Party. If Republicans were campaigning for November 2026 two years early, Democrats needed to get in the fight.
When Republicans realized they were on track to lose, they regrouped by using dark money from an out-of-state billionaire to collect signatures for a referendum in 2026 targeting LGBTQ youth in our state. Their strategy was clear: create a wedge issue to mobilize their base and help Collins stay in office.
Once again, Maine Democrats and nonprofit groups united to meet them on the field. Turns out, the fraud Republicans are always yelling about was happening in their own operation. We challenged their signatures, uncovered widespread fraud and got their referendum disqualified.
We ended up saving absentee voting in Maine by defeating that referendum by nearly 30 points.
I’m proud of the Mainers we defended and the voting rights we protected. But now, as thousands of Mainers cast ballots every day, what I’m most proud of is that these wins have allowed us to go on offense.
Maine Democrats have built an organizing operation reaching all 16 counties. We’ve opened 25 field offices, hired dozens of organizers and brought thousands of volunteers into the effort to elect Democrats up and down the ballot.
And we’re doing this on a compressed timeline with our full ticket. In just 12 weeks, our coordinated campaign has surpassed 1 million voter contact attempts, including more than 230,000 door attempts and 790,000 calls.
I share those numbers because people should understand how much work is happening across Maine. But they don’t tell the whole story. Behind every number is someone giving their time to something they believe in.
Some are longtime volunteers. Others are getting involved for the first time. They’re students, retirees, parents and people who have already worked a full day but still find time to make calls or knock on doors.
Spending time with our organizers and volunteers has been one of the best parts of my job. Last week, I spent five hours with a volunteer named Molly. Together, we packed supplies, scripts, turf lists, literature, signs and water for more than 55 canvass launch locations.
While labeling boxes and getting too many papercuts, Molly and I talked about music, our community, our fears for our country and our hope for this election.
Her commitment to fostering that hope through volunteering is something I’ve seen across Maine. People are showing up because they’re concerned about their communities and want to do something about it.
With just over a week until Election Day, there’s still work ahead. Nothing is guaranteed, and we’re not taking a single vote for granted. Many legislative races will be decided by handfuls of votes. And our race to elect Troy Jackson and finally retire Collins remains a toss-up.
If you’ve been waiting for a moment to get involved, this is it. Sign up to knock on doors, make calls or volunteer in your community.
The work we’ve done has brought us this far. Now it’s time to bring it home.
Whatever happens Nov. 3, thousands of Mainers have already shown what we can accomplish when we come together. That’s something worth being proud of.

title: Cyclist fights off muggers with her Winnie the Pooh Stanley cup: ‘I was always a fighter’
text:
NEW YORK (WABC) - A New York woman fought off three men who tried to rob her while she was cycling in Central Park. She says her helmet, bag and Winnie the Pooh-themed Stanley cup helped her survive the attack.
Katherine Marroquin, 32, was riding her bike just before 10 p.m. last Sunday on her after-work commute through Central Park. She stopped after dropping her AirPods, and three men suddenly appeared from behind some bushes.
“They were hiding somewhere. It was really dark, and they waited for me to lean down and wait, and then, they appeared,” Marroquin said. “I think they were trying to steal phones, maybe, and they just saw me, saw the bike. They were like, ‘Oh, money.’”
Marroquin says the men struck her in the head, surrounded her and started going through her belongings. One of the men threw her stainless steel Stanley cup, which has a Winnie the Pooh design, on the ground in front of her.
Marroquin says she grabbed the tumbler from the ground and used it to defend herself.
“It’s three people by myself. I got to defend myself. I didn’t think about money or anything. I thought about my life and seeing my mom again. So, I grabbed the cup, and I hit one of the guys in the head,” she said.
The men soon ran off, taking her book bag with them.
Marroquin’s only injury was a cut next to her eye that was already there but reopened during the fight. She says her bag and helmet absorbed much of the attack.
Reflecting on the confrontation, Marroquin says she was determined not to surrender what she had worked for.
“I was always a fighter since I was little, you know? So, I feel like it’s unfair for people to come in and think that they could take whatever you work for. You know, I feel like it’s not fair,” she said.
The irony of all this is that Marroquin just started biking to work last year because she thought that would be safer than taking the subway.
“This is the reason why I started riding the bike because the subway was very dangerous,” she said.
The New York Police Department has released surveillance images of the people who are wanted in connection to the robbery. So far, there have been no arrests.

title: Alleged drunk driver crashes into large group of cyclists in California, killing 2
text:
Alleged drunk driver crashes into large group of cyclists in California, killing 2
A Halloween-themed group bicycle ride in California ended in tragedy Saturday night after an allegedly drunk driver plowed into several riders, killing two, authorities said.
According to the Montclair Police Department, the crash was reported in the area of Kingsley Street and Tudor Avenue at about 10:39 p.m., KCAL reported. Investigations revealed that about 30 bicyclists, as part of a self-coordinated Halloween ride, were riding when a driver collided with several individuals.
The driver fled the scene immediately following the collisions.
Police said one bicyclist was pronounced dead at the scene. An additional rider, identified only as a woman, died at a local hospital.
Another person was hospitalized with major injuries. They remain in stable condition. An additional rider suffered minor injuries and declined treatment, police said.
Law enforcement later identified the driver and found him at his home about a mile from the crash scene. The man, identified as 38-year-old Valentin Alberto Rodriguez, was arrested at about 2:40 a.m. Sunday on suspicion of DUI causing injury or death, felony hit-and-run involving death and gross vehicular manslaughter while intoxicated.
He was booked into the West Valley Detention Center in California.
A memorial of flowers and balloons marked the corner where the collision happened, with family members of the victims stopping to pay their respects throughout the day Sunday.

title: Take a risk and make this year’s Halloween costume memorable
text:
OPINION: Halloween is the best holiday, and I will die on that hill. Halloween in Orono is even better because everyone is ready to party without shame. You can be a character from your favorite movie, a historical figure, a celebrity, or something that does not even exist. Yet, recently, Halloween seems to be a competition to see who can wear the same five costumes as everyone else. There is nothing wrong with a classic costume, but Halloween is the perfect opportunity to get creative, so why settle for the most basic option?
Walk into almost any Halloween party, and you are bound to see the usual suspects. There will be vampires, witches, Jokers and nurses. You might also run into a handful of cowboys, devils, angels and superheroes. These costumes are classics for a reason. They are recognizable, easy to put together and usually do not require much planning. However, when half the room looks like it came from the same costume rack, it becomes difficult to stand out.
The problem is not that these costumes are bad. In fact, some of the best costumes are simple ones. The problem is that people sometimes stop at the first idea that comes to mind instead of putting their own spin on it. A vampire can be more than a cape and fake blood. A cowboy can be more than a hat and boots. Even a ghost can be something other than a white sheet with eyeholes cut into it. A little imagination can turn an ordinary costume into something memorable.
Creativity also does not have to mean spending a fortune. Some of the best Halloween costumes come from clothes already sitting in your closet, items borrowed from friends or a quick trip to a thrift store. A costume based on an obscure movie character, a ridiculous internet meme or an everyday object can be more entertaining than an expensive outfit bought straight off a shelf. Sometimes the most popular costumes are the ones that make people stop and ask, “Wait, what are you supposed to be?”
There is also something satisfying about coming up with an idea yourself. Halloween gives people a chance to show off their personalities, interests and sense of humor in ways they normally would not. A creative costume can become a conversation starter, an inside joke or the highlight of someone’s night. It gives people a reason to remember your costume instead of forgetting it by the time they get home.
Of course, not everyone wants to spend hours planning an outfit, and nobody should feel pressured to turn Halloween into a major artistic production. Sometimes, a simple costume is all someone needs to have a good time. The goal is not to criticize people for dressing as witches or vampires, but to encourage everyone to think outside the box before choosing the same outfit they wore three years ago.
At the end of the day, Halloween should be about having fun and expressing yourself. Take a chance and give people something to talk about. That does not mean your costume has to be super niche, impossible to understand or so complicated that you need to explain it to everyone. Just get creative, and have a happy Halloween!

Woman arrested after standoff with police at a McDonald's in Portland
text:
Bangor woman arrested after standoff with police at a McDonald's in Portland
A Maine woman is facing multiple charges after police said she was involved in a standoff with officers while inside a bathroom at a McDonald's in Portland.
Erin Baker, 44, of Bangor, was arrested Monday and charged with creating a police standoff, terrorizing, refusing to submit and criminal trespass.
The Portland Police Department said emergency medical personnel responded to the McDonald's at 332 St. John St. at about 11:22 a.m. after someone reported that a woman in the bathroom, who was later identified as Baker, was using drugs and requesting emergency medical services.
Police said that when emergency medical personnel arrived at the McDonald's, Baker told them that she had a gun. Portland police officers then responded to the McDonald's and began negotiations with Baker, who remained inside the bathroom for nearly 30 minutes.
Officers eventually deployed pepperball rounds into the bathroom, at which point Baker came out and was taken into custody without further incident.
Police said no firearm was recovered from the scene.
Baker was taken to the Cumberland County Jail following her arrest.
Investigators are asking anyone who has information that may assist in this case to call 207-874-8575 or text the keyword "PPDME" and their message to 847411.

title: Peace Ridge Sanctuary now caring for 16 horses rescued from Burnham farm
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FREEDOM, Maine (WABI) - Sixteen horses seized from a Burnham farm where their owner was convicted of animal cruelty are now living at Northeast Equine Sanctuary, a 642-acre facility in Freedom.
Alexis Ingraham was sentenced in October to two years in prison on four counts of animal cruelty, including two aggravated felony charges. During her trial in August, jurors heard details of severe neglect to horses and other animals on her farm.
Northeast Equine Sanctuary owner Daniella Tessier said she was aware of Ingraham for 15 years before her arrest.
Sanctuary owner describes rescue effort
“A lot of people in the community will be able to think back to Fair Play Farm,” Tessier said. “Obviously as a shelter, getting a lot of phone calls from people who are really concerned because they’re driving by and seeing the bad conditions of the animals.”
In March 2025, Tessier learned an animal control officer was removing cats and dogs from Ingraham’s farm in Burnham. Because of that, Ingraham had reportedly sold her horses to avoid having them seized as well.
“One thing that we don’t do is buy animals,” Tessier said.
In this case, Tessier said she took extraordinary measures to save 16 lives.
“So we purchased all of the animals that she had secreted away, um all of the animals that we could find,” Tessier said. “And the minute we had them in our possession, we called the animal welfare program. So that’s when the case was finally opened.”
Horses adjusting after neglect
Ingraham’s horses now live at the Freedom sanctuary.
“We had to start all over with desensitizing them to touch,” Tessier said. “Because they were quite a few of those horses that were just like-they expected the worst from us.”
Tessier said one horse was one of Ingraham’s main breeders and was pregnant when she arrived at the sanctuary.
“Honey actually gave birth to a son pretty soon after we got them in from that case,” Tessier said. “I’m always really happy when a mother animal gets to come in and have her baby and doesn’t have to experience any trauma.”
Tessier says the non-profit spent more than $100,000 just on Ingraham’s horses. “It was a lot of horses to take in all at once, and a lot of rehab to do. It was very expensive.“
All 45 horses have a story
All 45 horses at the rescue have a story, including one named Dusty. Tessier said she received a call from a local animal control officer about a horse that was down in a field.
“And when I saw the pictures, he was in like end stage muscle wasting,” Tessier said.
Tessier and her crew began an intensive re-feeding program for Dusty. He didn’t just survive, he’s now thriving at the horse sanctuary.
“Another example of a horse that deserved much better,” Tessier said.
Dusty is also the inspiration for legislation soon to be proposed by Tessier, in cases involving long-term animal starvation.
“When animals are shown to have been depleted because of long term starvation, we would like to have special considering for changes,” Tessier said. “We’d like to call it Dusty’s Law.”
Sanctuary faces high costs, limited space
Tessier said it costs about $30,000 a month to run the program at Northeast Equine Sanctuary. The sanctuary goes through more than 1,000 bales of hay and about 1,000 pounds of grain per month, along with medical costs.
Right now, the sanctuary is at maximum capacity. And Tessier says, winter is typically when they get the majority of calls for help.
“And that’s why we’ve started this active adoption program, where we’re really hoping that we might be able to start adopting horses out to people that really embrace like, the force-free model for companion horses,” Tessier said.
The sanctuary has about 150 acres it would like to use for the horses, but the land needs to be fenced in first. The sanctuary is looking for a company to sponsor the fencing project.

title: Walter Koenig, Chekov on ‘Star Trek,’ Dies at 90
text:
Walter Koenig, ‘Star Trek’s Chekov, Dies at 90
Another member of the original Star Trek cast has died, just a few weeks after the franchise celebrated the 60th anniversary of its debut on television.
Walter Koenig, best known as Ensign Chekov on Star Trek television shows and movies, has passed away. He was 90 years old.
He death was confirmed by his representatives, who shared this statement...
Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world. He passed of old age at home in North Hollywood last night surrounded by his daughter and niece.
Koenig was born in Chicago, and then studied psychology college, where a professor encouraged him to try acting. Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry actually cast Koenig in a role in his earlier TV series The Lieutenant. He joined the cast of Star Trek as Ensign Pavel Chekov at the start of the show’s second season, where his youthful looks and resemblance to Davy Jones of the Monkees helped him in the land the role, supposedly because Roddenberry was hoping to diversify the cast to appeal to more young viewers.
Although he wasn’t among the initial Star Trek cast, Chekov became a fixture in almost every subsequent production featuring the first crew of the U.S.S. Enterprise. (Chekov wasn’t included among the cast of the animated Star Trek series of the 1970s, but Koenig wound up working on the show as a writer instead.) He co-starred in every Star Trek film from 1979’s The Motion Picture to 1994’s Star Trek Generations, which handed off the big-screen Trek franchise from the original stars to the cast of the recently concluded sequel TV series Star Trek: The Next Generation.
While Koenig was a sturdy presence in all of the Trek films, his most famous and best-remembered moment in the series is surely in Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home (1986), when the time-displaced Enterprise crew are searching for a way back to the future and Chekov asks the locals for help locating some nuclear vessels — which, in his thick Russian accent, sounds like “nuclear wessels.”
READ MORE: The Coolest Star Trek Movies That Were Never Made
Outside of Star Trek, Koenig appeared in television series like Ironside, The Questor Tapes, and Babylon 5. He also wrote for the original TV series of Land of the Lost and also penned numerous books, including an autobiography of his life and career, and several comics and graphic novels. And, of course, he was a beloved fixture at Star Trek conventions for decades.
With Koenig’s passing, that leaves just two original Star Trek cast members alive. William Shatner, the Enterprise’s Captain Kirk, is now 95 years old, while George Takei (AKA Lieutenant Sulu) is 89.

title: At 81, the ‘Bike Man’ keeps rolling along
text:
LYNDONVILLE, Vt. (InvestigateTV) - In Lyndonville, Vermont, Gordon Thresher is known as “The Bike Man.”
“I strip bicycles to fix bicycles,” Thresher said.
Down in the basement is where Thresher spends much of the winter, fixing up donated bikes.
“Even have some of them delivered to me. They want them out of their yards, usually a total mess, that’s okay,” he said.
It usually takes two to three hours to make them street worthy.
“I’ve never bought a chain for a bicycle, because I take these apart,” Thresher said. “I put tags on them, because tomorrow I’ll forget what I’m doing today.”
On this day, he’s working on a mountain bike. Bikes have been his passion since he was a kid. “I only had one bike, a Western Auto bike. I got it for $10, and I thought it was monstrous, the best thing I had.”
And it helped him make money in younger years in central Vermont. He’d tow a lawnmower behind his bike.
“And at first, I had one lawn, then I was up to 14 lawns, and then they had me work in the cemetery,” he said.
When the temps warm up, the 81-year-old brings up the bikes to his garage. It’s a bit of a struggle. “My back is not perfect, but it’s usable, that’s all that matters.”
He peddles the bikes for $25 to $50, but money is not really a concern. “Sell ‘em, give them away, I don’t care.”
“I remember one little girl came along and she said, ‘Daddy, can I ride that bike?’” He says, ‘Well, she’s going to want it.’ That’s okay because I want her to ride it home. It pleases me because another bike goes down the road."
The former electrician has working man’s hands, rough from years of hard work.
He said working on the bikes keeps his fingers flexible. And the riding? “My back doesn’t hurt when I ride a bike.”
As for slowing down, that’s not in the cards for Thresher.
“I don’t plan on stopping at all,” he said.

title: Hospice Awareness: Plan Early, Ease Pain
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Talking about end-of-life care can be one of the hardest conversations a family has to face. But healthcare professionals say discussing hospice care early on can help loved ones understand a patient’s wishes and focus on comfort and support.
November is Home Care, Hospice, and Caregiver Awareness Month and Northern Light Home Care & Hospice is shining a light on end-of-life care in Aroostook. Hospice care is for those who have a life expectancy of 6 months or less and at the Aroostook House of Comfort, healthcare professionals work to make life a little easier for those nearing the end of their life.
Lisa Roop, an RN for Northern Light Home Care & Hospice says: “People often times wait until the very end, until the last minute, before they get involved with hospice. So, I think getting in touch with hospice is really important sooner rather than later. It’s better to have an evaluation earlier on in your disease process because you might not be ready. It’s better to discuss and have an idea of what your loved one wants than to have things just kind of show up out of nowhere. The other thing I say is that death and dying is like the weather. You can’t control it, but you can prepare for it.”
Roop says there are some common misconceptions about hospice care. “Hospice isn’t only death care. It’s end of life care because death is just a moment and there’s a dying process and there’s a whole end of life time period. So, it really is care for people at end of life. It can be really a beautiful period for families to just kind of come together and figure out what’s important to them as a family and figure out what’s important to the patient as an individual. So no, it’s not sad all the time. In fact, it’s only sad in little moments.”
Northern Light Home Care & Hospice offers care services for patients at the House of Comfort and in home, but they also comfort families after a loved one passes. “We have nursing care. We have home health aides like a CNA, and they come in and help with personal care. We also have social workers, and bereavement coordinators, and spiritual counselors, home makers, volunteers. We try to take care of the whole person and the whole family. We have bereavement support and that goes on for 13 months after the patient has passed. So, you have the first everything with bereavement support. So, you have like the first weekend without your loved one. You have the first holiday season. You have your loved one’s first birthday,” continued Roop.
Roop says families shouldn’t wait to discuss hospice. Locals should have the conversation now, while everyone can be part of it. For more information on hospice services visit northernlighthealth.org/homecare-hospice.

title: Trainer fined, suspended after horse’s leg breaks through trailer floor on way to Windsor Fairgrounds
text:
WINDSOR, Maine (WABI) - Transport of a race horse that led to a euthanization has led to penalties.
A Maine State Harness Racing Commission investigation found that on Aug. 31, Stanley Whittemore’s horse, Vogue Blue Chip, had his right hind leg fall through the floor of Whittemore’s trailer during transport to the Windsor Fairgrounds, dragging on the road for several miles.
“I stopped a couple times because he wasn’t riding well, and he didn’t ship well. I had discussed it with my wife. We just qualified the horse at Skowhegan Fair the week prior to race, and he shipped badly then. I said, ‘maybe I should just put something on his front feet so that he couldn’t paw and cause so much damage as he did. But, it really wasn’t nearly as bad as he shipped the day on the way to Windsor,” said Whittemore.
The MSHRC report submitted by its state steward, Greg Kirby, stated that a vehicle followed Whittemore with the driver honking the horn for more than two miles to try to get Whittemore to stop before his arrival at the fairgrounds. Kirby conducted interviews with witnesses. He was in the judge’s booth during the incident.
“I apologize to the guy who flashed his lights to get me to stop. I had absolutely no knowledge of that. I did not see that at all. I apologized to him, and I appreciated his trying to help, but I had no idea that there was any such thing. (When I got to the fairgrounds), I went to the back of my truck, and I found a shovel. I was foolishly thinking that I could pry it apart with an aluminum shovel. The shovel was used to pry the boards apart and free the horse’s leg,” said Whittemore.
Vogue Blue Chip’s lateral aspect of his distal cannon bone was exposed and fractured, according to veterinarian-on-scene Dr. Casey Whitehouse. He was euthanized.
“It’s a fatal injury. We knew that once she got there. I would never try to lessen my guilt if there is any guilt to be borne. This is in the 61 years in the horse business, absolutely the worst thing that ever happened,” said Whittemore.
Kirby served as judge at Whittemore’s MSHRC hearing on Sept. 4.
Kirby found that Whittemore violated the commission’s rules with regard to improper conduct, any act or conduct that is detrimental to the sport, and any conduct, while in the view of the public, which in any way tarnishes the image of the sport.
Whittemore received the commission’s maximum penalty of a $1,000 fine and a one-year suspension that runs through Sept. 7, 2027.
“He’s been fair with me, and that’s why I accepted his penalty. My sincerest apologies to the horse No. 1, to Windsor Fair, to the Maine racing commission, and the whole racing community. The people who saw it, I’m very sorry that you had to view it,” said Whittemore.
Jim Britt is the Director of Communications for the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry. He confirmed that “Animal Welfare has concluded its investigation and will take no further action at this time. Any action by the Maine State Harness Racing Commission is separate.”
“The buck stops here. I’m totally 100 percent responsible,” said Whittemore.
Kirby added in the hearing that Whittemore’s trailer “was not sufficient to be hauling a thousand-pound animal around.”
Whittemore said he had inspected the trailer underneath beforehand, but he moved the interior’s center partition to give the horse more room.
He wondered if that allowed Vogue Blue Chip to have more room to damage the floor.
Whittemore said he’s unsure if he will return to horse racing after his suspension.

title: Looking for a Scare? Check Out These 20 Haunted Attractions
text:
20 Terrifying Haunted Attractions in Maine, New Hampshire, & Massachusetts
With the exception of a very few people, everyone seems to love 'spooky season'.
When we say that, obviously, we are talking about that period of time between Labor Day and November 1st. Yes, we know that Halloween is on October 31st, but the season is too fun to just limit to one day, right?
While the holiday mostly focused on kids back in the 80s and 90s it has become more and more adult over the last few decades.
In addition to nearly every bar and nightclub throwing a Halloween party, we are seeing more and more haunted attractions. Back in the day we would have called these haunted houses, but these days they go way beyond that. Now, these haunted attractions take over trails, old factories, ski areas, and even amusement parks.
If getting the crap scared out of you is your idea of fun, we have you covered. We've put together a list of some of the best haunted attractions throughout Maine, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire.
20 of the Best Haunted Attractions in New England in 2026
As you can see, we dug deep to find the best haunted attractions throughout our part of New England. We made sure that, no matter where you are, one of these attractions is not far.
Maineiac Manor in the Bangor Mall is one of our favorites because, at least in the past, they have done a Holiday version of the haunt to coincide with Christmas. Canobie Lake Park's Screeemfest is one of a kind, too. And, we always love the United Volunteers of Maine haunted house in Augusta because it gives local nonprofits a chance to raise money for their organizations.

title: Characters of the County: Joan Drappeau Tells the Story
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Dresden resident Joan Drappeau has a lifelong love of storytelling she is taking to the next level.
The Northern Minnesota native is balancing running a bakery with her digital marketing start-up, along with a part-time waitressing position, her work as a landlord, and help she provides her father for his job.
Drappeau grew up a middle child of 13 siblings. The majority of her time was spent outdoors “on the range,” which Drappeau said inspired an appreciation for spending time in nature, including hiking and water skiing.
Early on, Drappeau felt a desire to travel. She pursued a bachelor’s degree in business administration, management, and operations from Metro State University in Minneapolis and immediately began saving to travel.
“I would work and save money and then travel and then run out of money,” Drappeau said.
Drappeau explored Florida, California, Colorado, and Alaska. Between travels, Drappeau said she worked 70-80 hours a week as a waitress. Eventually, she saved enough money to travel further, first to Europe then to other parts of the world.
“The reward is so magic, to be able to meet other people and see other beautiful things in the world,” Drappeau said. “It’s not just our little corner of the beauty here that is intriguing, although this is the place, the best place.”
Traveling on a budget forced Drappeau to adapt, she said. Whether it was finding places to sleep or going without comforts, she learned how to overcome difficulties.
“You learn about other places going, but you also learn about yourself even more so than that, which is kind of surprising for people, because you grow internally, being out in the stresses of life on the road,” Drappeau said.
While abroad, she met her husband, Benoit Drappeau. The two continued traveling, often cycling or eating rice and beans to save money. Their travels often took them through the rural parts of countries, including China when it first opened to tourists.
“They didn’t really quite know what to do with us, because all the foreigners at that time were going to the big cities, and we were a little bit against the grain,” Drappeau said.
Travel inspired Drappeau’s passion for telling stories and her awareness of how a decision can impact a life somewhere across the world, she said. She saw a fisherman whose waters were drained for strip mining and children in China making fireworks.
“That’s I think where the whole idea started, try to be as conscious about your decisions and purchasing patterns as you can,” Drappeau said.
After years of travel, Drappeau now has 10,000 slides from her trips. On one of those trips, Drappeau discovered something that would change the course of her life.
“We took a bus to Venice then the north part of Greece, these little hills were just kicking my (expletive),” Drappeau said. “I go, ‘What is wrong?’ Well, I was pregnant.”
The Drappeaus moved to Maine in 2002, to be close to the lakes and ocean. The baby would be the first her three children.
While her children attended Dresden Elementary School, a staffing shortage led to Drappeau baking bread. Drappeau baked and sold loaves and gave the proceeds to the school to help save positions. The high amount of competition made baking bread unprofitable, so Drappeau shifted to a different market, she said.
“My friend is celiac, so I started making gluten-free breads for her, she was my tester,” Drappeau said. “And I’m like ‘I made another hockey puck today.’”
Eventually, Drappeau solved the problem and began selling her gluten-free bread to nearby restaurants and the Rising Tide Co-op in Damariscotta under the name Bread Lady Bakery. Through this, she gained a following, she said.
“I mistakenly had my address on some of the marketing materials, and I would have them drive down the dirt road looking for me, ‘Is this Bread Lady Bakery?’” Drappeau said.
Selling bread was not Drappeau’s goal, she said. Six years ago, she and her husband founded Slicpix, a digital marketing startup company that includes the Interactivity Studio. The studio allows companies to separate individual items from an image and add more information about them.
“We wanted to use stories to promote good,” Drappeau said. “We always wanted to help businesses tell their story to differentiate their products and make a difference.”
The technology has evolved since Drappeau first had the idea and now utilizes artificial intelligence to select items from images. To keep up with the rapidly-changing industry, Drappeau brings on interns and encourages them to share ideas.
“We always say, there’s never a bad idea, so everybody brings ideas,” Drappeau said. “Just rule out the ones that don’t quite make sense.”
So far, people are able to use the platform for free. Drappeau said the platform’s payment gate will go out on Friday, Nov. 27.
While she tries to grow her digital marketing business, Drappeau is balancing additional business. Drappeau also works as a waitress at Sea Dog Brewing Co. in Topsham on weekends, helps her 91-year-old father with email campaigns for his work, and rents out her house to tenants, who she calls her “mini-family.”
“I’m giving it all,” Drappeau said. “I’m giving it 120%.”
Her lifelong love of travel has not ended, Drappeau said. Once she gets her business off the ground, Drappeau said she hopes to travel to Africa and work for a nonprofit drilling wells.
“The more that you go, the more that you want to see and do,” Drappeau said. “I will travel again.”
For more information about Slicpix, go to slicpix.com, or find the business on Instagram at @interactivity.studio.

title: Mild Temps Stick Around Today, Then Breezy & Colder Tuesday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A cold front will drop southward through the state this afternoon. Other than a slight chance for a few isolated light rain showers... the front will pass through mainly dry. We’ll see a partly to mostly cloudy sky for the remainder of the day with high temperatures in the mid-50s to around 60° across the north and low to mid-60s elsewhere. Skies will clear out tonight. Colder air will move in behind the front with lows dropping to the upper 20s to mid-30s. It’ll be a bit breezy too with a northwest wind gusting to 20-25 MPH at times.
The northwest wind will continue to usher colder air into the region for Tuesday. High pressure will build in for our Tuesday providing us with lots of sunshine and temperatures in the 40s to near 50°. High pressure continues to bring sunny and cool weather for Wednesday. title: 2-year-old suffers catastrophic brain injury after exposure to 7-OH
text:
AUBURN, Ind. (WPTA/Gray News) - An Indiana 2-year-old suffered catastrophic brain injury after police say he was exposed to a drug called 7-OH.
Police charged 20-year-old Kole Schwarz with neglect of a dependent resulting in catastrophic injury. Court records say Schwarz was the mother’s live-in boyfriend at the time.
Family members say the toddler was rushed to a hospital in DeKalb County on Sept. 6, where the affidavit says he was “unresponsive and placed in a medically induced coma.”
The child was later transferred to Riley Hospital in Indianapolis.
Court papers say a specialized lab test later found kratom-related drugs in his blood.
Investigators say the child’s mother told them she believed Schwarz used “7-OHs” and she was concerned the toddler may have ingested one.
Detectives say Schwarz admitted buying tablets sold as “7-OH” under the counter through a contact in Fort Wayne.
The detective calls that product the likely source of the exposure. Schwarz told police the tablets stayed sealed in his pocket.
Court papers say the child had an “unknown green substance around his mouth” and a doctor found MRI evidence that met the criteria for catastrophic injury.
Auburn police say the mother of the child is not a suspect in the case and has cooperated throughout the investigation.
The toddler’s grandmother, Josie Casebere, says she spent six weeks in the hospital with her grandson.
“It’s been the hardest thing in my life. I mean, I’ve lost parents and friends, and this is... I know we didn’t lose him, but it’s still been the hardest thing I’ve ever went through,” she said. “He’s got a wheelchair order that’s supposed to fit him until he’s six. If that tells you anything. They don’t know that he’ll ever walk again or anything.”
The FDA calls 7-OH a potent opioid concentrated from kratom, warning of a “concerning proliferation of concentrated 7-OH products that are sold over the counter and online.”
“This public health threat is troubling and requires immediate and impactful policies to educate consumers and take regulatory action that limits access to 7-OH-containing products,” the FDA’s report says.
It is illegal in Indiana, but in Michigan, it is sold as gummies, drinks and pills.
Berrien County health officials warned last week that kratom-related hospitalizations are rising. Michigan has no statewide age limit.
“Kratom contains a chemical called 7-OH (7-hydroxymitragynine), which acts like an opioid and can cause severe withdrawal symptoms. Kratom is an increasingly popular substance among teens and is sold at gas stations and smoke shops as candy-flavored gummies, drinks, pills and more,” the county’s health warning says. “While advertised as an energy booster, mood lifter, pain reliever and remedy for symptoms of quitting opioids, kratom can cause serious health issues, such as seizures, liver toxicity and substance use disorder. It also can lead to an overdose.”
Casebere says she spoke out to raise awareness about 7-OH.
“They’re labeling it however they want to because it’s not regulated, and they’re selling it to our kids,” she said.

title: Boy dies 5 years after being hit by crossfire in quadruple shooting
text:
CINCINNATI, Ohio (WXIX/Gray News) — A 13-year-old boy has died five years after he was shot in a quadruple shooting, according to police in Cincinnati, Ohio.
The Hamilton County Coroner’s Office identified the boy as Marcellus Whitehead.
2021 shooting left 4 injured
Marcellus was 8 years old when gunfire erupted around 6:15 p.m. on a Saturday near the McHenry and Cavanaugh Avenue intersection in Cincinnati’s Westwood neighborhood. He and three others, including a 6-year-old child and two adults, were hit by bullets.
At the time of the shooting, then-Cincinnati Police Lt. Col. Mike John said the 8-year-old was left in “very, very bad shape” after being caught in the crossfire while hanging out in a nearby lot.
“I believe the children were just hanging out in that lot, and it’s just a tragic, tragic situation. It’s awful,” John said at the time. “Thoughts and prayers go out to the families in an incident like this. I mean, you can’t explain it. It’s a Saturday evening in the summer. It’s just a terrible situation.”
Doctors at Cincinnati Children’s Hospital Medical Center placed Marcellus in a medically induced coma a day after the shooting.
At the time, the 6-year-old was in critical condition as well, according to John. The two adult victims suffered non-life-threatening injuries, John said.
2 men arrested in connection with shooting
Cincinnati police arrested Darius Harris Jr., now 24, who was initially charged with seven counts of felonious assault, Hamilton County court records show. Five of those counts were dismissed, court records show.
According to the Ohio Department of Corrections, Harris Jr. is now serving a prison sentence on charges of carrying a concealed weapon, having a weapon while under disability and two counts of felonious assault.
Javari Walker, now 23, was also arrested in connection with the shooting, court records show. Walker was sentenced to jail in 2023 and convicted of having weapons while under disability, according to court records.

title: Will two Dan Sullivans on the ballot for Alaska's Senate seat confuse voters?
text:
Will two Dan Sullivans running for Alaska's Senate seat confuse voters?
The Department of Justice filed a lawsuit aiming to block the certification of Alaska's U.S. Senate race if the Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses to the Democratic candidate.
The Republicans are concerned Dan J. Sullivan, who's running as an Independent, will confuse voters.
Over the weekend, Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the lawsuit, claiming this is an effort to put guardrails in place if there's voter confusion.
"If it's clear that there was confusion and that confusion led to an unjust, improper result that is not the will of the Alaskan voters, we want to make sure that the Alaskan system and the Alaskan state courts and the Alaskan electoral process can understand that in a way that lets them do the right thing," Blanche said.
Last week, Mary Peltola, Alaska's Democratic Senate candidate, called out the lawsuit.
"This is the corruption AK is fed up with, and it's why I'm in this race. Sullivan has enriched himself at our expense for 12 years. Now he's using his DC allies to try to keep himself in power and put his own interests ahead of Alaskans."
Alaska's Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski criticized the legal action, saying the Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit.
"Alaskans don't need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year's ballot," Murkowski said.

title: Candlelight vigil held in honor of those killed in Lewiston mass shooting
text:
Candlelight vigil held in honor of those killed in Lewiston mass shooting
On the three-year anniversary of a Lewiston mass shooting that killed 18 people and injured 13 others, the community held a candlelight vigil to honor the victims and stand alongside the survivors.
The event was hosted and organized by the Maine Resiliency Center, an organization created weeks after the shooting to provide support and services to the victims' families, survivors and anybody impacted by the tragedy.
"Eighteen of them were killed. Tonight, we gather to remember those 18 people who were killed," announced Maine Resiliency Center associate director Meredith Stack.
Dozens filled the hill at Lewiston's Simard-Payne Park for the ceremony before a reading of the names of the 18 victims.
"It isn't only the lives that ended on October 25th. It's all the life that should have been lived since," said Maine Resiliency Center director Danielle Parent.
One of the names that was read was Arthur Strout. Strout's father, Arthur Barnard, attended the ceremony.
"I've come to grips that it's unavoidable," said Barnard. "The feelings and the things and emotions that happen today, it's just unavoidable."
Barnard said that this morning, he took time to recall the last time he spent with his son, three years ago.
"This morning, just waking up, and thinking about how it unfolded, everything that day. And I think it happens for all of us. The things we say to each other before this all happened," commented Barnard. "I guess the only thing, I really, I was fortunate I spent the last 2.5 hours of his life with him, and he was happy."
The ceremony closed as the group walked together to the Longley Bridge to release flower petals.

title: Man serving a life sentence for murder slips through a fence and escapes a Tennessee prison
text:
TIPTONVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — A man serving a life sentence for killing his co-worker four years ago has escaped from a prison in northwest Tennessee by slipping through a fence, authorities said.
Officials realized Jacob Morley, 28, was unaccounted for around 11:30 p.m. Sunday at the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, the Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement.
Investigators looked at security cameras and saw Morley escaped while wearing his prison uniform, officials said. They did not release any other details, including how Morley got through the fence.
Prison officials offered a reward of up to $2,500 for Morley’s arrest. They said law enforcement throughout the area has searched buildings and other structures near the prison about 90 miles (145 kilometers) north of Memphis in an isolated, rural area of flat land tucked near a bend in the Mississippi River near Missouri.
Morley is 5-foot-11 (1.8 meters) and 240 pounds (109 kilograms). He has brown hair and green eyes.
Morley was sentenced to life for killing co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield’s body was found in a box under Morley’s Carter County home after he had been missing for a few weeks.
Along with first-degree murder, Morley was also convicted of aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest. When Morley saw deputies at his home in 2022, he led police on a chase that ended in North Carolina, authorities said.
Several violent attacks between inmates and by employees have been reported in recent years at Northwest Correctional Complex. A grand jury in July returned dozens of indictments for five inmate murders, assaults against staff and inmates and other violence.
Northwest Correctional Complex can house 1,776 men and can house minors who have been convicted as adults, according to the Department of Correction. In 2023, an audit of Tennessee prisons found that the department was struggling to fill open positions at the prison and had a 61% vacancy rate for correctional officers in that fiscal year.

title: Two suspects arrested after stabbings in Rumford
text:
RUMFORD, Maine (WMTW) - Two suspects are in custody after stabbings in Rumford.
Rumford Police say officers responded to an apartment on Waldo Street after a 911 call reporting an assault involving two suspects who had run away. Authorities say while officers were responding, another 911 caller reported a stabbing, the sound of breaking glass, and a man yelling that someone was trying to kill him.
Officials found two victims suffering from stab wounds. A 44-year-old man had a knife wound on his back with significant bleeding, and a 37-year-old woman had a knife wound on the side of her abdomen. Authorities say both victims are from Rumford. Both were taken to the hospital. Officials say they are both expected to survive.
Police say they found two suspects matching descriptions given to them, who ran away when officers ordered them to stop. Officials are also thanking several neighbors who they say helped law enforcement by providing information about the suspects’ movements and possible hiding locations.
Authorities say the two suspects, a 19-year-old man from Lewiston and a 15-year-old girl from Lisbon, are now in custody. The 19-year-old has been identified as Jazya D. Swan, who police describe as a transient. Both face charges of elevated aggravated assault, criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon, and refusing to submit to arrest or detention. The 19-year-old is now at Oxford County Jail. His bail is set at $20,000 cash. The 15-year-old was taken to Long Creek Youth Development Center.
Investigators believe the people involved were known to one another and that alcohol and marijuana may have been contributing factors. They also believe the incident is connected to the shots-fired investigation at the same apartment on Oct. 14.

title: Exciting whitewater and kayaking adventures continue at West Forks
text:
After two days of exciting outdoor adventures in the West Forks area as part of the Penobscot Paddle and Chowder Society’s annual three-day event called Fall Supper Weekend, one day remained. A continuation of whitewater paddling and mountain hiking trips were planned.
West Forks is home to some of the most exceptional whitewater in New England, so it was a given that exhilarating paddling would be part of the agenda. Two whitewater trips on the Kennebec River were scheduled.
The first, a Class III whitewater trip down the Kennebec Gorge, began early in the morning a few miles north of West Forks at Harris Dam at the outlet of Indian Pond. Chowderheads with the PPCS carried their boats down the long, steep stairs to the put-in immediately below the dam and launched in a low water release called “fish flow.” Paddling the fish flow has become a popular club outing that allows participants to descend the intimidating gorge at a more benign level than the much higher normal rafting release.
Boaters enjoyed a technical paddle through iconic rapids named Taster, Rock Garden, Big Mama, Alley Way, Z-Turn and Magic Falls. One mishap that resulted in a short swim in the Alley Way was quickly remedied. At the bottom of Magic Falls, the crew halted to await the increased rafting release and members of the second club trip.
Back at Harris Dam, another group of Chowderheads in kayaks and inflatables were beginning to embark on the rafting release, a feisty 5,000 cubic feet per second. A solid Class IV trip, paddlers navigated through or around such famous river features as Disappearing Wave, Big Mama Wave, Good-bye Hole, Whitewasher Hole, Big Kahuna Wave and Magic Falls Hole. Everyone had a successful descent.
At the end of the gorge, they joined the fish flow group. Exciting big volume, Class III whitewater ensued to Carry Brook, the first takeout below the gorge. Some paddlers carried their boats up the steep stairs to waiting vehicles, while others continued paddling easier whitewater for 9 miles to West Forks.
While whitewater adventures were taking place on the Kennebec River, my son, Adam, coordinated a mountain hike on Number Five Mountain. Located in a remote area west of the Forks, the 3,186-foot peak seemed like a good opportunity to jumpstart my fall hiking game, so I joined the group.
Getting to Number Five is a challenge. We drove north on Route 201 from West Forks for about 12 miles to Hardscrabble Road on the left. From there, we followed the sometimes rough dirt road for about 17 miles to an obscure right turn where a sign points to the trailhead. The remainder of the drive is on a narrow road in poor condition and a high clearance vehicle is advisable.
We began hiking gradually on an overgrown, old logging road. After a short distance, the trail turned right and we entered a sparse mixed-hardwood and conifer forest.
The trail meandered steadily upward with occasional steep ledges. While stopping for a break, we were surprised when a young family with three children passed us. We hadn’t expected to meet other hikers, let alone children, on the remote, isolated mountain.
After leveling off and passing through a damp area with some well-placed log walkways, the path angled precipitously upward. Shortly beyond, we emerged onto an expansive ledge with excellent views south.
The winds were gusting and storm clouds forming as we ascended abrupt, extended ledges past the closed fire tower to the summit. Views north of Attean and Sally Mountains and virtually the entire, famed Moose River Bow Trip were phenomenal. Frigid wind chills and fears of a rainstorm forced a hasty retreat.
During our hurried descent, we were astonished to encounter a mountain biker pushing his bike up the trail. I’ve watched videos of mountain bikers performing incredible feats, but descending the narrow, ledge-filled trail seemed foolhardy. He seemed confident and no related accidents were subsequently reported in the news, so I assume he made it safely down.
We finished the hike just before the rain began, thereby completing the last of the Fall Supper Weekend outings. Since many outstanding trips were experienced during the three-day event, we’ll probably return to West Forks again next year.
Read about many more exceptional mountain hikes and whitewater trips in my book “Maine Al Fresco: The Fifty Finest Outdoor Adventures in Maine.”
The author of “The Great Mars Hill Bank Robbery” and “Mountains for Mortals – New England,” Ron Chase resides in Topsham. His latest book, “Maine Al Fresco: The Fifty Finest Outdoor Adventures in Maine” is available at North Country Press and through online retailers. title: Family steps in, detains man who tried to kidnap girl at gunpoint outside her home, sheriff says
text:
SALEM, Ind. (WDRB+WAVE/Gray News) — A family in Indiana is being credited with saving a girl from being kidnapped at gunpoint.
According to the Washington County Sheriff’s Department, deputies responded at 4:30 p.m. to a home after receiving a report of a man attempting to abduct a girl at gunpoint.
Police said Jeffrey Mauck, 53, approached the girl outside her home and attempted to force her into his vehicle.
The girl told police that Mauck grabbed her and threatened her with a gun.
Police said she screamed for help and struggled to break free. The struggle caught the attention of her family members, who came outside and detained Mauck until police arrived.
Mauck had a revolver, ammunition, handcuffs and two folding knives, according to police.
“This is an extremely disturbing incident, and we are thankful this young girl was able to get away and that her family acted quickly,” Washington County Sheriff Brent Miller said in a news release. “Anyone who attempts to harm or abduct a child in Washington County will be met with the full force of law enforcement. Protecting our children and keeping our families safe will always be among our highest priorities.”
Mauck was arrested and charged with attempted kidnapping, criminal confinement, aggravated battery, pointing a firearm and operating a vehicle while intoxicated.

title: What it means when you see purple paint on a tree
text:
This story was originally published in November 2019.
Have you ever been out in the woods and found a tree with a purple stripe painted on it? And if so, what did you do after that?
The correct answer, it turns out, is to turn around and exit the area. In recent years, the use of purple paint as a way to designate areas where access to land is limited to those who’ve received advance permission from the landowner has become quite prevalent.
According to Mark Latti, the communications director for the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, the state’s “purple paint law” went into effect in 2011. Before that, the use of silver paint was the standard.
And not too many years ago, the customary way for a Maine landowner to post their property and let others know about any access restrictions was to nail signs to trees.
The DIF&W explained in a recent email blast that one vertical OSHA safety purple stripe that’s at least one inch wide and at least eight inches long is to be translated as “access by permission only” in the state of Maine. And that paint doesn’t have to be on a tree. It may also be on posts and stones, as long as the stripes are between three and five feet off the ground.
According to state law, the signs must be no more than 100 feet apart at locations that are readily visible to people approaching the property, as well as at all vehicular access points off a public road.
Hardware stores sell special paint for use in marking properties. The Lowe’s store in Brewer, for instance, sells a purple Krylon spray paint that’s labeled “No Hunting, Purple Marking for Boundaries.”
While Maine hunters enjoy a liberal access policy and often use the land of others without permission, many believe that in many cases, responsible hunters ought to ask before hunting on land they don’t own.
