title: Keep dogs safe during Maine’s trapping season
text:
Keep dogs safe during Maine’s trapping season
Keep dogs safe during Maine’s trapping season
Regulated wildlife trapping in Maine helps protect habitats by managing abundant wildlife populations and reducing disease, starvation, and conflicts with humans. Padded traps are designed to hold animals without causing injury. However, in areas open to approved trapping, unleashed dogs face a small risk of becoming caught.
Trappers must set traps responsibly and ensure that they do not pose an unreasonable risk to people. Traps are generally placed away from public paths, trails, and other areas frequently used by people and pets. Although the likelihood of a dog being caught is low, knowing how to help your pet can help you act safely.
If your dog is caught in a padded foothold trap, remain calm. If possible, ask another person to help. Cover the dog’s mouth with a jacket or create a barrier to reduce the risk of being bitten. Even a normally calm dog may bite when frightened or in pain.
Pull the trap’s chain tight from its anchor point and try to place the trap flat on the ground. This will make it easier to open. Locate the levers on either side of the trap’s jaws, then press them down with your hands or feet to release the tension. Carefully remove the dog’s foot and check it for injuries.
If you believe a trap has been placed unlawfully or in a dangerous location, do not move or disturb it. It is unlawful to interfere with a legally set trap, disturb an animal caught in a trap, or take an animal from someone else’s trap. Instead, contact the landowner or a Maine game warden to report your concern and confirm whether the trap was set legally.
Trapping in Maine is managed by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, and trapping laws are enforced by Maine game wardens.
The best way to prevent an incident is to keep your dog leashed in areas open to trapping. Traps may be placed near road intersections and other travel corridors in remote areas. If you hunt with a dog, stay alert and be aware of trapping activity where you hunt.

title: Police arrest 15-year-old after 11 shot near football stadium in Florida
text:
Police arrest 15-year-old after 11 shot near Florida A&M University stadium | 1 other hurt
A 15-year-old was arrested and faces 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent in connection with a mass shooting Saturday night that left 11 people wounded, Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said Monday morning.
The investigation suggests a physical altercation took place among “individuals known to one another” before shots were fired near the Florida A&M football stadium, Revell said.
“At this stage of the investigation, none of the victims appear to have been the intended targets,” the police chief said.
Watch previous video in the playfinder above
The investigation remains active and additional arrests are possible, Revell said.
Six juveniles, including an 11-year-old, are among the injured, Revell said late Saturday. No deaths have been reported.
The off-campus shooting took place hours after a homecoming football game at Bragg Memorial Stadium, where the Golden Lions of the University of Arkansas-Pine Bluff beat the Florida A&M Rattlers 31-28. It’s unclear whether the shooting was connected to the game.
In addition to those shot, a victim’s grandmother was injured while fleeing.
As of Sunday morning, five people had been released from the hospital, while six remained hospitalized, Tallahassee police said. Of those still being treated, one was in critical condition, police said.
There have been at least 383 mass shootings in the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which, like CNN, defines a mass shooting as one in which four or more people are shot, not including the shooter.
Homecoming events at Florida A&M, a historically Black university with nearly 10,000 students, took place throughout the past week and were scheduled to conclude Sunday, according to the university’s homecoming schedule.
Saturday night’s shooting on Perry Street likely stemmed from a fight between two to three people, the police chief said, and the department’s Violent Crimes Unit will lead the investigation.
Tallahassee police detectives have reviewed digital evidence and canvassed the area, police said in a statement Sunday.
“We need our community’s help. No detail is too small, and no piece of information should go unreported,” the statement said. “If you know something, please share it with our detectives. Your information could be the key to holding those responsible accountable.”
Investigators established a tip hotline and a link for people to submit evidence.
“As our detectives work to determine exactly what happened and identify those responsible, we remain committed to getting answers for these families.”
Florida A&M President Marva Johnson encouraged anyone with information to call the tip line, saying the Tallahassee police are leading the investigation.
“To our Rattler family and our surrounding Tallahassee community, I share your outrage and profound sadness at the senseless and despicable shooting that took place near our FAMU campus last night,” Johnson said in a statement Sunday evening.
“To all the victims, please know that we are with you and we are praying for your recovery in body, mind and spirit,” she said. “We have reached out to the members of our FAMU family who were injured in this tragic incident to offer our care and support.”
Tallahassee Mayor John Dailey called the incident a “truly horrific and heartbreaking tragedy.”
“Tonight and in the days ahead, the FAMU family is not alone. Our entire community stands with you,” Dailey wrote on X.
Stephanie Walters, who was selling HBCU apparel during homecoming, said she also heard shots.
“People are just scared,” she told CNN affiliate WCTV. “If you were out here, you heard the gunshots. It was a lot of them. There was no doubt in my mind that somebody was injured.”
Raymond Isham said he had just left campus when the shooting happened, and he was concerned about his daughter, who was in the area where the shooting occurred.
“She’s obviously going to have to process through this,” Isham told WCTV, “and we’re going to be there with her to walk through this.”
This story has been updated with additional information.

title: ‘I get very angry’: Mother speaks out after 10-year-old shot by another child
text:
VALDOSTA, Ga. (WALB/Gray News) — The mother of a 10-year-old boy shot in the face by a 9-year-old in September says she has not been told of a court date in the case, and that the mother of the boy involved still lives a few houses down from her.
Marshania English’s son, Javion, was shot at Brittany Woods Apartments on Monday, Sept. 7, according to the Valdosta Police Department. Police said the boy and a 9-year-old were playing with a gun when it went off.
Javion has since returned home and is not back in school full time with his usual activities, according to English.
“For the first few days, you know, it was very emotional. It was a lot going on,” English said. “And now that we’re home and he’s just not going back to school, he had his days with his ups and downs.”
English said she now watches her son more closely.
“And now, like, I have to pay a lot more attention to him,” English said.
Mother, 9-year-old facing charges
Police said detectives obtained arrest warrants on Sept. 9 for 46-year-old Andrea McClendon, the mother of the 9-year-old and the owner of the firearm. McClendon is charged with second-degree cruelty to children and reckless conduct. Police said she turned herself in at the Lowndes County Jail on Sept. 14.
Through the Department of Juvenile Justice, detectives also charged the 9-year-old with reckless conduct and possession of a firearm by a minor.
Mother describes neighbor living nearby
English said McClendon still lives a few houses down from her.
“I think that’s my biggest thing, because she still lives down from me, a couple houses down from me,” English said. “You know, I see them every day, which I don’t allow J.B. on to come outside, only when I’m outside. But when I’m out the door, I see them, and it’s just, I get angry.”
English said she feels no justice has been served.
“I feel like my son has been shot, and no justice has been served,” English said. “Like, they’re still able to go out, grocery shop, and still live their life. But my son is here, having to tell people, oh, what happened to his teeth, or the mark on his neck. And I don’t think it’s right, to be honest. I really don’t.”
Javion back in school
English said Javion is back in school. He is not currently participating in PE activities.
Asked how he is adjusting, Javion said, “Good.”
Javion described sitting outside as peaceful.
“It’s really peaceful, because I really just sit down,” Javion said.
PREVIOUS COVERAGE: 10-year-old shot in the face by 9-year-old while playing with a gun in Valdosta, police say
Recounting the shooting
Javion said the other boy asked whether Javion wanted to see his mother’s gun.
“Then, when I came inside, he asked me did I want to see his mama gun,” Javion said. “Then I said, ‘Yeah, just don’t point it at me. Turn that gun. I don’t want no bullets at me.’ He did the opposite. Then pointed at me and put bullets in it. Then he cocked it back. Then he locked the door.”
Javion said he tried to get the gun away before the shooting.
“Then I ran. Then I pushed the gun down to try to take it. He pointed it at me, and I really didn’t know. I locked the door. And then I stayed in there for some minutes,” Javion said. “Then it got quiet. So I went to the door... And then I got shot.”
Mother describes being overwhelmed
When asked how important his mother is to him, Javion said, “A hundred percent. Important to me.”
English said she is overwhelmed by what her son now has to go through.
“I’m overwhelmed. I really am. I’m overwhelmed,” English said. “You know, because now he has to start therapy. And it’s just something that he has to deal with for the rest of his life.”
Mother wants distance from suspect’s family
English said she would feel more at peace with distance between the two families.
“I probably would feel more at peace is either I moved or they moved,” English said.
English said she believes the legal system failed her after McClendon was released from custody quickly.
She said she has not been told of any court date in the case.
“To be honest, I haven’t heard anything about a court date or anything like that,” English said.
GoFundMe set up for dental work
English said a GoFundMe has been set up to help pay for Javion’s dental costs.
“People can support our GoFundMe so that Javion can get his teeth fixed,” English said. “It would go towards his teeth cosmetics, which we would try to get him some veneers.”

title: As Greely High School addresses inequity in boys and girls sports, some parents say not enough has been done
text:
Holly Wallace noticed differences in what her daughter’s softball team and the boys baseball team received through Greely High School’s athletic department.
An active supporter of Cumberland-North Yarmouth school district’s softball team, the Cumberland resident said female players had a lower-quality batting cage and practice field than their male counterparts. When she raised the issue, Wallace was told the differences were out of the district’s control as the fields were on town property, and she moved on.
Last June, as Wallace’s daughter pitched her final game of high school softball before graduating, the district revealed an external investigation found that discrepancies between boys and girls teams at Greely High School — including the batting cages — violated federal laws against sex-based discrimination.
“If I’d known it was a Title IX violation, I wonder if I would have changed how loud I got years and years ago about the facility. I wonder if other parents would, too,” said Wallace.
As Maine School Administrative District 51 staff respond to these findings this fall, the community is hearing how the athletic department is remedying the deficiencies — and asking what’s being done to ensure equity in high school sports.
TITLE IX VIOLATIONS
Title IX is a federal civil rights law that prohibits sex-based discrimination in education and other activities that receive federal funding. The 1972 statute requires schools to provide equivalent opportunities, benefits and treatments for male and female athletes. This includes equitable equipment, practice and game time, and access to facilities and private funds.
MSAD 51 received five complaints about Title IX violations from September 2023 to June 2026, according to district records. The complaints from parents and coaches included instances in which the boys alpine ski team received travel and lodging for a state race while the girls team had to find their own, the girls lacrosse team didn’t get game music while the boys team did, and practice equipment provided to the boys baseball team not being equally provided to the girls softball team.
In an internal review, the district determined that all five complaints included at least one Title IX violation and assured they were being remediated.
Following these complaints, last fall, the school district voluntarily hired the law firm Drummond Woodsum to audit gender equity across the Greely High School athletic program.
The review determined there was less preference for some girls teams.
Broadly, the scheduling of facilities for practices and games disadvantaged girls teams, who more frequently had lower-quality outdoor fields and inconvenient practice and game time slots. Some sport-specific findings included the girls softball team having less access to training aids and better fields, the girls hockey team not having a locker room at Family Ice Center in Falmouth, and fundraised money disproportionately enhancing the boys teams.
At an Oct. 1 school board meeting, MSAD 51 Athletic Director David Shapiro outlined how the athletic department has was addressing the findings. Shapiro promised the scheduling of facilities and practice times would involve more collaboration. The hockey teams would take turns using the single ice rink locker room. The allocation of booster funding would receive more oversight, and the softball team would get a better batting cage.
While the consensus was that these fixes were positive, several members of the school board asked Shapiro to take broader accountability for the culture that allowed these inequalitiesin the first place.
“Equity initiatives can’t be based on responses to problems all the time. We have to take leadership in this area,” said school board member Sara Staples.
Others put their response to the presentation more bluntly.
“This is embarrassing,” said Greely parent Matt Grondin.
During public comment, junior varsity girls basketball coach and district parent Jamie Clark said she was “deeply disappointed” by how Title IX violations had been handled. She also said she had not spoken up during the Drummond Woodsum investigation because she feared retaliation.
Clark also said she has spoken with other parents and coaches about gender equity concerns who have not come forward also out of fear of retaliation and because they have the impression that “nothing will change.” Other parents said they have heard from other district employees or coaches who feel similarly.
Shapiro directed all requests for comment to the superintendent. Porter said complaints regarding retaliation are addressed by the district.
PLAY BALL
Some community members later expressed their frustration with the school district’s response to the external audit.
“The tone felt very much like, ‘Oh, we’re great. We made a few mistakes, we fixed them. We’ve got no big issue,’” said Jessica Grondin, whose daughter plays soccer and softball at Greely High School and whose husband spoke during public comment. “That was super disappointing for me, and I think others as well.”
Grondin has not filed a formal Title IX complaint, but had emailed the athletic department about smaller things she and other parents had noticed abou lesser resources for her daughter’s teams. She felt dejected by the limited response, she said.
Several parents said they were not worried about how the district addresses official Title IX complaints, which has a set procedure, but how staff respond to smaller differences between the treatment of boys and girls teams that contribute to a culture of inequality. Responding to the audit’s findings with issue-specific solutions instead of a more widespread change was a reflection of this approach, they said.
“My impression was that it was an immediate downplay of the systematic inadequacies as to why these violations occurred,” said Jim Faunce, who has daughters in eighth and 11th grade who play school sports. “It gave me the impression that there’s no real plan to change.”
Parents said their daughters only sometimes noticed the less preferential treatment of their teams. Wallace said she felt “embarrassed” for not recognizing that what she saw was a Title IX violation, worrying she let her daughter’s team down.
Northeastern University law professor Martha Davis, an expert in the field of women’s rights and constitutional law, said it doesn’t rest with participants to report Title IX violations. Instead, school staff should be equipped to abide by the federal statute.
“It’s really a matter of training, to understand when these things should be reported,” said Davis.
Davis also said Title IX violations are not uncommon in public education, as disparities often go unrecognized or accepted as natural. But small inequalities in the treatment of the sexes in schools undermine our constitutional values of equality, she said.
“If things are not equivalent or equal, it communicates to the participants on the losing end that their participation is not as important, their achievements are not as important, which isn’t true,” said Davis.
On Oct. 22 in his regular superintendent’s report to the school board, Porter supplemented Shapiro’s Oct. 1 presentation in response to community feedback.
“We have a Title IX problem in our athletic program that needs attention,” said Porter. “We can do better and be better.”
Porter shared how the district is taking new steps to remedy the culture around gender equity. He said all staff will receive comprehensive Title IX training over the next two months. Coaches for the winter season, which starts in two weeks, will also have mandatory training.
He also said there would be a regular assessment of Title IX compliance across athletic programs, the mode of which yet to be determined, and that the athletic director would consult with the district’s equity committee.
“We shouldn’t even have violations on the physical side,” said Porter. “But culture and climate, that will be more challenging to look at.”

title: Trump administration attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey again
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is attempting to prosecute James Comey for what it calls a decade-old leak of classified information, an effort the former FBI director’s lawyers immediately dismissed as legally invalid and outside the legal time limit for when the Justice Department can file a criminal indictment.
The allegations from the Justice Department were revealed Monday in newly unsealed court documents that shed light on a closed-door fight that represents an unmistakable escalation in the administration’s targeting of Comey, a longtime critic and foe of President Donald Trump who has faced two other criminal cases since the Republican returned to the White House last year.
The effort to prosecute Comey is also part of a series of politically charged investigative actions the department has undertaken in the run-up to next week’s midterm elections.
“Well, they’re back — again,” Comey said in a video statement Monday. “It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice — one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing’s changed with me; I’m still innocent, I’m still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary.”
The Justice Department said it had filed what’s known as a “criminal information” to extend the statute of limitations for charges in the case.
“Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further,” a department spokesperson said.
Asked about the Comey case, Trump told reporters upon arriving back to Joint Base Andrews in Maryland late Monday following his rally in Mississippi that “I don’t know much about it. I just heard about it.”
He added, “He’s a dirty cop, James Comey. But I know nothing about it.”
An information can be filed without the approval of a judge or a grand jury’s finding of probable cause to a court. Comey’s lawyers made clear that they intend to fight the charges as invalid because the Justice Department did not file an indictment, which must be voted on by a grand jury, inside the 10-year statute of limitations required under the law.
“For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence,” his attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement.
The allegation was previously investigated
The latest allegation concerns an October 2016 New York Times story related to a secret court order that required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. The story cited two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity about the order from a judge on the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court that Yahoo was barred from publicly disclosing.
Federal authorities, including prosecutor John Durham, began investigating the disclosure in early 2017. Durham, who later investigated the FBI’s conduct as it scrutinized potential ties between Russia and Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, wrote a classified memo in December 2018 recommending no criminal charges against anyone in connection with the disclosure, Comey’s attorneys said in a recent court filing.
In January 2019, the U.S. Attorney’s office for the District of Columbia opened a second investigation of the same matter under the code name “Tropical Vortex.” But that investigation was closed without any charges filed in February 2020.
“Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone. Now, ten years after the article was published, the Government filed an “Information” against Mr. Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit,” Fitzgerald said.
Prosecutors in a newly unsealed filing said investigators found evidence that Comey “sought to correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before” that New York Times story was published, directed his staff to speak to a journalist at the newspaper related to accuracy concerns “and thereby illegally transferred classified information.”
The criminal information was filed under seal on Oct. 5, 10 years after the 2016 story was published. “But,” Comey’s lawyers said, “the applicable statute of limitations explicitly demands an indictment within 10 years of the offense; an information does not suffice.”
They have asked a judge to dismiss the information, a request that is still pending.
Trump and Comey have a long and uneasy history
The first criminal case against Comey, filed in federal court in Virginia, accused him of having lied to Congress in 2020 but was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who brought the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47,” a case Comey has sought to dismiss.
The prosecutions are part of a Trump retribution campaign that has even extended to Comey’s daughter, Maurene, who was fired from her job as a Justice Department prosecutor in New York last year in a termination that a federal judge on Monday ruled was illegal.
Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush’s Republican administration.
But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president -- an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum.
Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump’s campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, found that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration.
The two men have been bitterly at odds ever since Comey’s firing.
Comey in 2018 published a memoir, “A Higher Loyalty,” that painted Trump in deeply unflattering ways, likening him to a mafia don and characterizing him as “untethered to truth.” Trump, for his part, has repeatedly claimed that Comey should face charges for “treason” — an accusation Comey dismissed as “dumb lies” — and called him an “untruthful slime ball.”
The Justice Department has made a series of splashy moves in recent weeks , including a criminal complaint last Friday charging two former FBI officials with lying to Congress about their participation in investigations concerning Hunter Biden, and the search by federal agents of the Washington home of Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.
___
Associated Press writer Will Weissert contributed to this report.

title: Influencer embraces hair loss from alopecia, encourages other women
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (Aging Untold) — A Charlotte influencer who lost her hair to alopecia is using her platform to encourage other women facing the condition.
Alopecia is an autoimmune disease that causes patchy hair loss and affects nearly 7 million people in the U.S. It is the second-leading cause of hair loss in the country.
For nine years, Angela Agnew was proud of her long, flowing hair before she noticed it thinning.
“Then I finally went to a specialist, and I asked her, I said, ‘Hey, what’s going on here?’” Agnew said.
Agnew said she had to accept a reality she couldn’t control.
“To realize there was nothing else I could do, that this was something that I had to accept, it was hard,” Agnew said.
From hiding to going public
Agnew lived in silence, hiding under wigs, until she saw another woman being bullied online for thinning hair. She then shaved her head on camera.
Aging Untold expert Amy O’Rourke said the emotional weight of hair loss is something many women carry alone.
“So, for men and women, losing your hair can be a big deal. Loss of identity,” O’Rourke said.
“First, I think of how heavy it would be to be hiding that, and then you lift it out and get rid of it, and how much lighter you can handle your life. It gives you so much more energy not having to clamp down on this issue that you’ve been struggling with,” O’Rourke said.
Agnew’s hair loss is permanent, but her impact is growing.
“Angela just saying I’m going to embrace this thing, I’m going to come out, I’m going to be proud I’m going to be who I am. I was struck with how beautiful she is,” O’Rourke said.
“The positive for me that has come from this is the encouraging of other women,” Agnew said.
Agnew is now an advocate against bullying and a voice for other women dealing with hair loss.

title: The science of being scared: What happens to your brain, body when fear strikes?
text:
The science of being scared: What happens to your brain and body when fear strikes?
From racing hearts to adrenaline rushes, a trip through haunted attractions reveals why our bodies react to fear, and why some people enjoy it.
The science of being scared: What happens to your brain and body when fear strikes?
From racing hearts to adrenaline rushes, a trip through haunted attractions reveals why our bodies react to fear, and why some people enjoy it.
Screams, chainsaws and terrifying characters are all part of the experience at Halloween haunted attractions, but what actually happens inside our bodies when we get scared?
Sister station KETV's reporter Connor Schmidt put that question to the test, wearing a smartwatch to track his heart rate while walking through three haunted attractions.
At Scary Acres in Omaha, Neb., creating fear is part of the experience from the moment visitors arrive. Schmidt's heart rate was around 85 beats per minute before entering the haunted attraction.
"It's an immersive experience," said Angela, owner of Scary Acres. "So, from the moment that you walk through the gates until the time that you exit the park, we're looking to transport you into kind of a horror-genre frame of mind."
Scare actor and acting coach Lucas Williams says one method is especially effective.
"You can't beat a chainsaw," Williams said. "Grab the chainsaw. Just, it's the easiest thing to scare you."
But why do human bodies react so quickly?
"Whenever there's a stressful situation, our brain responds to it instantaneously," said Dr. Harmit Singh with the Creighton University School of Medicine. "Our brain is wired for our stress response, because it's our alarm system."
He said that the adrenaline one experiences when the body responds to stress helps prepare it for action: responses include the heart racing and muscles getting tense. Despite those reactions, Singh says people can enjoy being scared when they know they're in a controlled environment.
Schmidt's watch registered at least 115 beats per minute inside the Haunted Castle, 124 inside House on the Hill and 119 in the Haunted Forest.

title: At 81, the ‘Bike Man’ keeps rolling along
text:
LYNDONVILLE, Vt. (InvestigateTV) - In Lyndonville, Vermont, Gordon Thresher is known as “The Bike Man.”
“I strip bicycles to fix bicycles,” Thresher said.
Down in the basement is where Thresher spends much of the winter, fixing up donated bikes.
“Even have some of them delivered to me. They want them out of their yards, usually a total mess, that’s okay,” he said.
It usually takes two to three hours to make them street worthy.
“I’ve never bought a chain for a bicycle, because I take these apart,” Thresher said. “I put tags on them, because tomorrow I’ll forget what I’m doing today.”
On this day, he’s working on a mountain bike. Bikes have been his passion since he was a kid. “I only had one bike, a Western Auto bike. I got it for $10, and I thought it was monstrous, the best thing I had.”
And it helped him make money in younger years in central Vermont. He’d tow a lawnmower behind his bike.
“And at first, I had one lawn, then I was up to 14 lawns, and then they had me work in the cemetery,” he said.
When the temps warm up, the 81-year-old brings up the bikes to his garage. It’s a bit of a struggle. “My back is not perfect, but it’s usable, that’s all that matters.”
He peddles the bikes for $25 to $50, but money is not really a concern. “Sell ‘em, give them away, I don’t care.”
“I remember one little girl came along and she said, ‘Daddy, can I ride that bike?’” He says, ‘Well, she’s going to want it.’ That’s okay because I want her to ride it home. It pleases me because another bike goes down the road."
The former electrician has working man’s hands, rough from years of hard work.
He said working on the bikes keeps his fingers flexible. And the riding? “My back doesn’t hurt when I ride a bike.”
As for slowing down, that’s not in the cards for Thresher.
“I don’t plan on stopping at all,” he said.

title: How going outside in nature could ease stress
text:
(Aging Untold) — There is something about nature that makes us feel instantly connected.
For the Tomlinson family, spending time outdoors is a daily routine.
“Nature makes me feel happy and excited when I always get around it because it makes me feel like I’m at home,” said Gibbs Tomlinson, who enjoys spending time in nature.
“See the sun come through the trees and being able to put a shadow on a leaf, the fish glistening in the creek, and it just makes you feel wholesome,” Brent Tomlinson, Gibbs’ father, said.
Reconnecting with the outdoors
Research shows nature could ease symptoms of depression, stress and ADHD.
Aging Untold expert and gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said human history was not built around pavement or concrete.
“Human history wasn’t built in a concrete jungle. It wasn’t built around pavement. It was built around nature. And we are natural beings that need to connect back to fresh air, to the earth, to having nature around us,” Cradduck said.
Cradduck said being outside is one of the most powerful treatments for what she described as the “mental exhaustion” of the digital age.
“We’re living in a world that’s constantly throwing information our way - we’re in information overload, and we’re not getting back to just the basics and the roots of society, you know, grounding getting in there and just being part of the community that you live in, not having everything thrown at you all the time,” Cradduck said.
Benefits without a hike
Cradduck said people do not need extensive access to wilderness to benefit from nature.
“Not everybody has the opportunity to walk over to Central Park in the middle of their city. Not everybody has the opportunity to go for a walk in nature and go for a hike in the mountains, but everybody has an opportunity to go outside, get that sunlight, let your rhythms reset, let your body understand that there is a great outdoors. We know how valuable it is for our own health,” Cradduck said.

title: Man completes 12,000-mile walk across America’s four corners in Lubec for mental health awareness
text:
LUBEC, Maine (WABI) — A Florida man who traveled across the United States to raise money and awareness for mental health completed his historic journey in Washington County over the weekend.
Kyndal Ray Edwards, a mental health coach from Jacksonville, Florida, crossed the finish line at West Quoddy Head Lighthouse in Lubec on Sunday afternoon after visiting all four corners of the contiguous United States.
For Edwards, walking across America was a dream years in the making following his own battles with depression and addiction.
“I got arrested August 9, 2017, and then April 12, 2019, while I was in prison, I made a conscious decision that I didn’t want to be the person that I was anymore,” Edwards said.
Inspired by a story of a local who traveled coast to coast, Edwards began his walk across America on Jan. 1, 2022. Along the way, he raised funds for the nonprofit Never Alone Recovery while carrying “A Walking Testimony”—a dedication honoring 180 people who lost their lives to drug overdose or suicide.
Edwards documented every step of his trek on social media, building a following of hundreds of thousands of followers. On Sunday, supporters, friends, and family traveled from across the country to greet him at the easternmost point of the Lower 48.
“I found Kyndal’s story on Facebook through my algorithm. Ever since discovering him, he’s been a huge inspiration to me. I’m somebody who’s colossally passionate about mental health and advocacy, and I just incredibly appreciate the work that he’s doing,” said Heather Rotman of Massachusetts.
“I think his whole premise is very admirable. We’ve been following him and we wanted to be here to congratulate him,” said Laurie Schoen of Connecticut.
“I get people reaching out to me all the time who have either lost children or have adult children who are struggling with addiction themselves. And so just the fact that he’s made an impact in people’s lives—for us as parents, that’s incredible,” said Kyndal’s mom.
In total, Edwards spent nearly five years on the road, walking for 1,022 of those days and logging 12,144 miles.
“Words could never express just how grateful and thankful I am for the support,” Edwards said. “For people to come out here and make human connection, it’s important because there’s not enough unity in community. There are not enough people in their communities actually getting together... We need more hugs, handshakes, and high-fives in the world.”
Looking back on more than 12,000 miles on foot, Edwards said one memory stands out above all the rest.
“Any time that somebody has pulled over on the side of the road saying that they were on their way home to take their life, and the ‘You Matter’ sign was the sign that they needed to still be here,” Edwards said. “That’s definitely going to be the number one.”
To learn more about Edwards’ mission, visit kyndalray.com or follow the Kyndal Ray Edwards Facebook page.

Did Maine potato farms get over $11 million in federal subsidies in 2026?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Yes.
Maine potato growers have received $10.3 million in direct federal assistance and another $8.4 million in subsidies for crop insurance premiums this year, for a combined $18.7 million.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Assistance for Specialty Crop Farmers dashboard shows $10.3 million in payments to Maine potato producers. The one-time program, meant to help farmers facing higher production costs and market disruptions, paid eligible potato growers $225 per acre planted in 2025, with a limit of $250,000 per farm.
Separately, the USDA’s 2026 crop insurance data shows $8.4 million in federal subsidies for Maine potato insurance premiums as of Oct. 19. The premiums cost $12.1 million overall, with farmers responsible for the unsubsidized portion. Insurance subsidies reduce growers’ costs rather than providing direct cash payments.
Maine farmers harvested 51,900 acres of potatoes in 2025. The USDA valued that crop at $253.5 million, down from $271.2 million in 2024.

title: Plein Air Painters of Acadia and Jayne Dwyer Jewelry on display at the library
text:
SOUTHWEST HARBOR — Visit the Southwest Harbor Public Library Nov. 3-28 to view an exhibit by the Plein Air Painters of Acadia and Paper Moon polymer clay jewelry by Jayne Dwyer. Join for a reception on Friday, Nov. 6 from 5-6:30 p.m. to celebrate the love of painting out-of-doors. Meet artists and ask them about their work and adventures while enjoying light refreshments.
Dwyer’s nature- and coastal Maine-inspired jewelry, each one a handcrafted miniature works of art, make perfect gifts for the holiday season. The millefiore, or caning process used to create her designs, involves no painting. Dwyer sculpts her designs from colorful logs of polymer clay, creating detailed canes similar to patterned cookie dough slices. Though they appear painted, each image is entirely hand-sculpted.

title: Ethics panel fines Bobby Charles nearly $23K over illegal contributions
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
AUGUSTA, Maine — Regulators fined Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles nearly $23,000 on Monday for accepting dozens of contributions over state limits, rejecting his campaign’s request to decide after Election Day.
The penalty is half of the roughly $45,000 that donors gave Charles’ campaign beyond the cap for the general election, and double the minimum that was recommended by staff of the Maine Ethics Commission last week.
Charles drew the fine eight days before Election Day, entering the final stretch as an underdog to Democrat Hannah Pingree. It is also apparently the first penalty of its kind. In a memo, commission staff said they had no record of assessing fines to candidates for over-the-limit contributions because such errors are usually small enough for campaigns to fix alone.
The case started with an Oct. 1 complaint from the Maine Democratic Party. It flagged dozens of excess contributions on Charles’ September campaign finance report and asked the commission to investigate whether he took them knowingly, which would be a crime.
Ethics staff don’t believe the campaign took the money on purpose. The Charles campaign’s treasurer, Bill Riley, told staff the problem came after a new compliance consultant took over from the person who handled the primary.
Charles’ campaign has since returned all of the excess money and amended its reports. Its lawyers asked the commission to put off a decision until Nov. 18 and impose no penalty, citing the campaign’s cooperation and the short notice on the staff’s recommendation.
But the refunds did not erase the violation, commissioners said at a Monday meeting in Augusta. A motion to hold another pre-election meeting to give the campaign more time to explain itself failed. Commissioner Sarah LeClaire, a Democrat, said the campaign took no action between its September filing and the complaint.
“Every penny has been returned, but it’s the acceptances of the overages and the failure to do anything about it on their own that weigh on me,” LeClaire said.
Commissioners assessed the fine in a 4-1 vote. The dissenter was Republican Dennis Keschl, a former state representative from Belgrade who said he wanted to know more about what the campaign did to prevent more overages after its first report.
Commissioner Brooke Bailey, a Democrat who chairs the body, said the penalty had to be large enough to deter other candidates.
“I think, at base, we want to be sending a message out to other campaigns,” Bailey said. “I think it sends that message, and I think it completes the interest of disposing of this matter prior to the election.”

title: Maine fire department sounds alarm about private vehicle using sirens and lights
text:
Maine fire department sounds alarm about private vehicle using sirens and lights
The Limerick Fire Department says a fire truck that has been driving around the Lake Arrowhead area with lights and sirens activated is not an official emergency response vehicle.
The fire department shared a video clip on Sunday showing the truck passing by. Officials say the vehicle is not associated in any way with the Limerick Fire Department or any surrounding town. Officials said they believe the vehicle is privately owned.
At the time the video was taken, there was no emergency response happening.
Anyone with information or pictures or videos of the vehicle should contact Maine State Police.
Under Maine state law, using sirens on a private vehicle is illegal in Maine and flashing red or red and white lights is only allowed for authorized volunteer firefighters or EMS personnel under strict conditions.

title: The Telling Room launches $1M fundraising campaign to expand its space
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Telling Room has moved into a larger home on Portland’s Washington Avenue, gaining 50% more space for its youth writing programs, as the nonprofit launches a three-year, $1 million fundraising campaign to support its growth.
The Portland-based nonprofit writing center moved in September from its longtime home on Commercial Street in the Old Port to 55 Washington Ave. The new space will allow the organization to expand programming for young writers, hire and retain staff and host more community events, including author readings and book launches.
The Telling Room helps youth and teens develop their storytelling skills which in turns helps build self-confidence and self-expression.
Students from between 100 and 135 Maine communities participate in its workshops annually.
In 2015, The Telling Room won the National Arts and Humanities Youth Program Award for its Young Writers & Leaders program, and several of its staff members and students visited the White House and met with first lady Michelle Obama.
Founded in 2004, The Telling Room rented space on Commercial Street for more than two decades before organizers decided they needed a larger, more cohesive space that would be easier for students to access.
“Once we were coming up on 20 years, we had to reevaluate and think about what’s the next vision for the organization,” said Telling Room Executive Director Kristina Powell.
About a year ago, Powell and Program Coordinator Nick Whiston toured available space at 55 Washington Ave. on the Portland peninsula owned by The Dayton Group.
“One of the wonderful things about our new space is that you walk in and you really feel like you’ve arrived in a singular place, and that’s something that’s not that easy to find,” Whiston said. “So I’m really excited.”
Powell is also happy to join the popular Washington Avenue corridor, which is busy with restaurants, small businesses and other nonprofits, including the housing-focused Project Home at 75 Washington Ave. and The Root Cellar, which offers food assistance, youth mentoring and English-language learning, at 94 Washington Ave.
To help support the move, as well as attract and retain staff that will help expand its programming, The Telling Room recently launched a three-year, $1 million campaign called Grow.Write.Now.
More than $300,000 has already been raised.
Powell said she feels positive about the future of the organization. “It’s been really lovely with pinch myself moments that have felt so good. It’s been a long run in the making.”
To learn more about The Telling Room and the Grow.Write.Now. campaign, go to tellingroom.org.

title: Join thousands of others at the opera — in a Maine movie theater
text:
At a time when movie-going is on the rise thanks to summer blockbusters like “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey,” and even more recent phenomena such as the documentary “You Can See Everything,” a trip to the movies for an opera might be the perfect Saturday afternoon counterprogramming.
Although it might not draw as many people as it used to, the Metropolitan Opera has continued to entertain fans at the Strand Theatre in Rockland through its MET: Live in HD series. For the last 20 years, these livestreams – referred to as “simulcasts” because they are broadcast to thousands of theaters across the globe at the same time – have given Midcoast Mainers a chance to get up close to the elaborate sets and breathtaking arias of an art form traditionally confined to patrons with the budget for pricey theater tickets. No opera glasses required.
For Brian Harden, 79, who’s been a season ticket holder at the Strand for 10 years, the MET Live in HD series made him a fan of opera because of one’s proximity to the sets and performers. He said the series allows him to see the best of the art form without the high price tag.
“I could never afford to sit where I sit at the Strand,” said Harden, whose favorite seat at the Strand is the balcony’s front row. “If I went to an opera house to see a live opera, I’d be up in the second balcony.”
This season’s program includes old favorites, such as special encores of Bizet’s “Carmen” or Mozart’s “The Magic Flute” — just in time for the Christmas holiday — alongside live transmissions of revivals, new stagings of old productions, and even the MET premiere of Kevin Puts and Mark Campbell’s “Silent Night” — an opera about a World War 1 Christmastime truce.
The 2026-27 MET: Live in HD series began in September and will run through June. The season has six more live performances alongside two special encores of recordings of iconic productions from years past. Each performance is accompanied by English subtitles as well as a 30- to 40-minute intermission that includes behind-the-scenes footage and interviews with cast and crew.
But if you happen to miss the initial livestream, don’t worry. The Strand also offers an encore presentation of each performance at a later date and time.
Strand patrons can watch the performance on a 25-foot screen from either the floor or the balcony of the restored 350-seat art house theater; visitors can expect comfortable seating alongside high-tech sound and visuals. For those seeking a snack to go along with the show, the Strand has a concession stand that includes a variety of local baked goods.
“We’re trying to really honor the movie palaces of the past but then have the modern amenities,” said Jana Herbener, marketing director at the Strand Theatre.
Strand Theatre, 345 Main St., Rockland. Seating is reserved and tickets can be purchased online at rocklandstrand.com or at the box office, which opens an hour ahead of the showtime. General admission is $32 for live performances and $27 for an encore presentation; discounts are available for Strand members and students. For opera superfans, the Strand offers season tickets for $330.
What’s playing this season?
The MET: Live in HD season has already begun, but there are many shows yet to air. Note that encore dates and times may vary by theater. All performances have one intermission unless otherwise noted. Here’s the schedule for the rest of the season at the Strand:
Special Met Encore: “Carmen,” 1 p.m. Nov. 21, Georges Bizet’s classic opera, recording of the MET’s 2010 production by Richard Eyre, 180 minutes.
“Samson et Dalila,” noon Dec. 5, Darko Tresnjak’s revival of Camille Saint-Saëns’ opera based on the biblical story of Samson and Delilah, 235 minutes with two intermissions.
“Samson et Dalila (encore),” 5 p.m. Dec. 17.
“Special Met Holiday Encore: The Magic Flute,” 1 p.m. Dec. 23, a 2006 recording of Julie Taymor’s production of Mozart’s classic opera, 115 minutes.
“La Fanciulla del West,” 1 p.m. Jan. 23, Richard Jones’ new production of Puccini’s Wild West-set opera, 195 minutes.
“La Fanciulla del West (encore),” 5 p.m. Feb. 4.
“Silent Night,” 1 p.m. March 20, Met premiere of Kevin Puts and Mark Campbell’s opera about the 1914 war-time Christmas truce, 180 minutes.
“Silent Night (encore),” 5 p.m. April 1.
“Manon,” noon April 3, revival of Jules Massenet’s opera, production by Laurent Pelly, 265 minutes with two intermissons.
“Manon (encore),” 5 p.m. April 15.
“Otello,” 1 p.m. April 24, revival of Giuseppe Verdi’s opera based on the Shakespearan tragedy, production by Bartlett Sher, 200 minutes.
“Otello (encore),” 5 p.m. April 29.

title: Here's how many in Maine have voted by mail so far
text:
Here's how many people in Maine have voted by mail ahead of the 2026 midterm election
The Hearst Get the Facts Data Team is tracking early ballots ahead of Election Day, Nov. 3.
Here's how many people in Maine have voted by mail ahead of the 2026 midterm election
The Hearst Get the Facts Data Team is tracking early ballots ahead of Election Day, Nov. 3.
The Hearst Get the Facts Data Team is tracking early and mail-in ballots that have been cast ahead of the 2026 midterm election.
The data comes from the University of Florida Election Lab, which has tracked early voting data since 2008 and also aggregates turnout and results data. Early voting counts are compiled directly from state and regional sources.
As of 9:45 a.m. Tuesday, more than 196,100 mail-in ballots have been returned in Maine. The UF Election Lab does not have data from Maine when it comes to early in-person voting.
The Maine Secretary of State's Office said that it had issued 237,365 absentee ballots as of 3 p.m. Friday, which includes ballots that are given to people who vote early in person. A total of 252,135 absentee ballots were issued in Maine for the 2022 election.
Use the map above to see how many early votes have been cast in each state, including mail-in ballots accepted and early votes. The data does not show election results, just the number of votes that have been cast.
Voters in Maine, 30 other states and Washington, D.C., can register under a party affiliation.
According to the data, 49.7% of the mail-in ballots that have been received in Maine have been cast by registered Democrats, while 21.4% have been cast by Republicans. The remaining 28.9% of mail-in ballots were cast by unenrolled voters.
Information about early voting in Maine
In the lead-up to Election Day, which is Nov. 3, Maine election officials encouraged voters to make their absentee ballot request early in order to allow enough time for the ballot to be mailed to them. Voters who were planning to use the U.S. mail to receive their absentee ballot should have made the request no later than 15 days prior to Election Day, which was Monday, Oct. 19, for this election.
Maine voters can also request an absentee ballot online until 5 p.m. on the third business day prior to the election, which this year is Thursday, Oct. 29.
Absentee ballots can be delivered via mail or dropped off either in person or via absentee ballot drop box at a municipal clerk's office.
Voters who wish to send their absentee ballots back by U.S. mail are advised to send their ballot no later than seven days before Election Day, which is Tuesday, Oct. 27, for the Nov. 3 election. The Secretary of State's Office said the U.S. Postal Service has assured that all absentee ballots that are put in the mail at least a week before Election Day are guaranteed to be delivered in time to be cast and counted in the election.
In order to be counted, absentee ballots must be received by a municipal clerk by 8 p.m. on Election Day, Nov. 3.
Maine has an absentee ballot tracking system that shows voters the date their application was accepted by their municipal clerk, the date their clerk mailed out their absentee ballot and the date the clerk received the ballot. Click here to check the status of your absentee ballot.
Since Oct. 5, Maine voters have been able to vote early in person. The deadline for absentee voting in the presence of a municipal clerk is 5 p.m. on the Thursday before the election, which is Oct. 29 for the general election — unless special circumstances exist.
More information about this election is available in our Maine voter guide.

title: Portland Press Herald asks to unseal records in database lawsuit against DHS
text:
The Portland Press Herald is asking to intervene in a federal lawsuit that four Maine residents have filed against the Department of Homeland Security, for the purpose of unsealing court records.
The Press Herald is asking that dozens of court filings be unsealed, including excerpts of depositions with federal agents and documents detailing the government’s activities in Maine during the January U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement surge. The paper is also challenging the redactions of federal agents’ names.
Four Maine residents who observed federal agents during the surge have accused the agency of illegally adding people to a law enforcement database, and driving by observers’ homes, as retaliation for what they have said is activity protected by the First Amendment.
“The Press Herald has reported extensively on this case and the underlying government surveillance practices at issue, but its reporters’ ability to do so fully and accurately is impaired by their inability to access judicial records at the center of the case,” attorneys for the Press Herald and from the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press wrote in a motion filed Friday.
Motions justifying the government’s request for the redactions and sealing were also filed under seal.
The plaintiffs have asked the court in the motion to issue an injunction before trial, barring agents from retaliating against observers with threats of a database and other tactics, like driving by protesters’ homes or calling them. The government is asking that the lawsuit be dismissed, arguing that the actions alleged were committed only by a couple of random agents during an isolated time frame in January.
Redacted filings in the lawsuit last month confirmed at least one plaintiff was added to a database. As a result, the plaintiffs state, she was held at the Canadian border for at least an hour in March before she was allowed to enter the United States.

title: Eight days until the midterms: Where the president is rallying support before Election Day
text:
Eight days until the midterms: Where is the president rallying support before Election Day?
President Donald Trump is ramping up campaign efforts ahead of the midterm elections, holding rallies in Georgia and Michigan and planning visits to Mississippi, Texas, and Ohio.
Eight days until the midterms: Where is the president rallying support before Election Day?
President Donald Trump is ramping up campaign efforts ahead of the midterm elections, holding rallies in Georgia and Michigan and planning visits to Mississippi, Texas, and Ohio.
President Donald Trump is intensifying his campaign efforts ahead of the midterm elections, urging supporters to vote during rallies in Georgia and Michigan over the weekend.
Trump told his supporters to vote as if he were on the ballot.
"When I'm not on the ballot, people don't show up. Please show up and vote because essentially we are all on the ballot because they'll take away everything," Trump said.
While speaking in Michigan, Trump criticized Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, questioning his loyalty to the United States and using anti-Muslim rhetoric while describing him. El-Sayed is running against Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman.
"I'm here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States Senator, and that's the fact. We're not going to let that happen," Trump said.
El-Sayed has called Trump's previous attacks shameful and has repeatedly denied any ties to extremist groups.
Michigan's Senate race is drawing attention, as the outcome could symbolize the future of the Democratic Party potentially moving further to the left.
Former President Barack Obama also campaigned over the weekend, visiting Ohio and Michigan. Obama accused Trump and his family of corruption and criticized the administration's tariffs and its approach to Iran.
"Our current president loves tariffs, loves them. Now there's one economic policy: tariffs. They're going to be great, the greatest tariffs ever, and he was warned at the time, when you impose tariffs, consumers pay the tab," Obama said. "In a place like Michigan and the auto industry, you've got integrated systems between Canada, the United States, and so each car requires a whole bunch of parts from a whole bunch of places. So, he was warned this will drive prices up."
Trump returned to the White House after the weekend rallies, but with the midterms approaching, he is scheduled to visit Mississippi, Texas, and Ohio in the coming days as part of his campaign efforts.

title: Restoring the National Poetry Foundation at UMaine
text:
“I’m looking at one now that says, ‘Voices of the Lady: Collected Poems’ and it says Stewart Z. and another name. And when I look through these files, I see the correspondence of these authors,” said Gabbie Needham, a fourth-year secondary education student with an English concentration, who described her job in 400 Neville Hall, also known as the National Poetry Foundation.
Unfortunately, the name is not so indicative of the significance of the foundation, as Jennifer Moxley, an English professor and published poet who joined the university in the year 2000, explained it is more “bravado,” and that “it’s not technically a foundation either.” While there are lost gems of information inside the filing cabinets Needham is exploring, the work is not always so glamorous.
“Some of the stuff that I see is not very interesting,” Needham said. “Maybe it’s a photocopy of the NPF contract or a list of apartments for a visiting author to stay at.” The reason her help is needed is because the task of cataloging is not straightforward. Needham explained how each individual folder is related to one central project, but that inside, the papers are “pretty much just thrown in there,” and that, “the next folder after it might be like five years later.”
“It used to be a working space where books were being made, but the production kind of slowed down to a trickle and now we’re just doing the one magazine and the occasional book,” Moxley recalled. She cited the primary reason for this as a lack of funding. “Those offices had a typesetter and a financial person for years. One retired and then the other is only at a quarter time with the center.” As funds fall, it can be harder to keep people in the room working.
The walls are lined with tens of books written primarily by Carroll F. Terrell (founder of the Terrell House) and Burton Hatlen. Moxley remembered how, “the founders, Terry and Burt, would have a few students involved. Like an intern or an assistant, one or two grad students. But in all the years I’ve been teaching here, I’ll ask my poetry workshops, ‘do you know about this’ and it seems that students never had much interest.” By ‘this’ she does not just mean the happenings in the NPF, but the rich history of poetry and poetics at the University of Maine.
The books are cowritten alongside professors and experts far outside of Maine. The main product to come out of the space was the ‘Man/Woman and Poet’ series. In these books, interviews with renowned writers, transcriptions of lectures and scholarly study tried to characterize and interrogate the style of famous poets.
“I had met Burton at a conference,” Moxley said, “And he had read my work. Part of the reason I wanted to come here as a professor was because of this center and this history of poetics at UMaine.” It seems unfortunate then that a tradition rich enough to draw professors here would be out of mind for the student body.
“The vision of the space now is, how do we make students feel ownership of it and make them aware of the history that they are walking into? Our dream is to clean it all up, you know, fresh and paint, and then on one wall have floor-to-ceiling bookshelves with a big poetry library,” said Moxley.
The goal, as Moxley explained, is to have a space where students will stay and where books can be produced again. As there is nowhere else on campus specifically for poetics, the concentration of books, materials and students is hoped to attract more ideas, energy and excitement.
“Even though my major is so close to English — like it’s ‘Secondary Education, comma, English’ — I felt so removed from English majors. I didn’t feel a sense of community and connection and I guess the hope is that people will,” Needham spoke to her own experience.
Both Moxley and Needham said that they took a chance for this project; Moxley with the offer, and Needham with accepting the internship. Out of this leap of faith, the ball has begun rolling with the potential to bring English majors closer to their history at the University of Maine, and to each other.

title: What is ‘moneymaxxing’ and how can it help your budget?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — “Moneymaxxing” is a viral social media trend focused on making the most out of every dollar already being earned.
Clay Cooper, a wealth management advisor with Northwestern Mutual, said the concept covers things like moving money to a higher-yield savings account, maximizing credit card rewards or cutting unused recurring subscriptions.
Cooper said the trend is essentially a positive spin on traditional financial planning, and it starts with a thorough budget review. He recommends pulling bank and credit card statements from the past year and closely examining spending patterns.
Cooper said one of the most valuable steps is identifying unused subscriptions.
“The other thing I think is great to do while you’re looking at your bank statements is go through it with a fine-tooth comb and go, ‘What subscriptions am I paying for that I don’t even know, or I’m not using?’” Cooper said. “I am embarrassed to say my wife and I just did this at the beginning of the year — we cut out 12 subscriptions.”
Cooper said credit card rewards should only be viewed as a bonus on planned spending, not a motivation to spend more.
“Normal expense — automate the cash back and pay the full balance every single month,” Cooper said. “If you’re buying something just to earn credit card points, you’re no longer moneymaxxing, in my opinion.”
Cooper said the goal of moneymaxxing should not come at the cost of overall well-being. When optimizing credit cards or squeezing extra interest out of savings, the effort needs to be worth it and sustainable over time. He said the goal is progress, not perfection.

title: Maine Featured Prominently As Part of Reimagined Disney World Ride
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For many people throughout the state of Maine, a trip to Walt Disney World in Florida can be a once-in-a-lifetime destination experience.
For Mainers that make that trip, there usually isn't many signs of home in central Florida short of some retirees and the spotting of a Maine license plate on occasion.
But if you're planning on visiting Epcot Center as part of Walt Disney World in the near future, there's an unmistakable piece of Maine prominently featured as part of a reimagined attraction.
Maine Lighthouse Featured in Soarin' Ride at Walt Disney World's Epcot
When Soarin' first opened at Epcot back in 2005, it was instantly one of the most popular attractions at Walt Disney World.
The concept behind the ride is simple. Visitors hop aboard a simulated aircraft and get flown around the globe to some of the world's most stunning landmarks and breathtaking places.
One of the wrinkles that made the Soarin' ride so unique is that the attraction would feed scents in for certain locations to enhance the sense of being there.
In May of 2026, the Soarin' attraction was reimagined at Epcot to celebrate the history and beauty of America.
As part of the opening minute, Portland Head Light is prominently featured for 'flyers'. On the ride, you'll soar directly over the most famed lighthouse in Maine.
Maine was one of only a handful of states and Portland Head Light one of the few landmarks featured as part of the celebration of America.
Maine Beer is Featured Elsewhere at Walt Disney World
Without even leaving Epcot, you'll find another piece of Maine available at the park.
That would be Allagash beer. As part of the Epcot 2026 Food and Wine Festival, the Haunted House Hoppy Dark Ale from Allagash is one of the featured beers at the American pavilion.

title: 13 students taken to hospital after Mississippi school bus collision
text:
RIDGELAND, Miss. (WLBT/Gray News) - Multiple students were taken to a hospital after a Mississippi school bus was involved in a collision Monday morning, authorities said.
According to the Madison County School District, police and emergency medical personnel responded to the scene around 8:30 a.m.
Ridgeland Police Chief Brian Myers said that the collision happened at the intersection of Colony Park Boulevard and Highway 51.
Thirteen students were taken to a local hospital for evaluation and treatment. More were taken by parents, the district said. The severity of the injuries is unclear at this time.
Chief Myers said 32 people total were on the bus; thirty-one of those were students.
No injuries were reported with the other vehicle involved, Chief Myers said.
District personnel are currently working to reunite students with their parents and guardians. The district is contacting parents of students on the bus directly.
“The safety and security of our students is our utmost concern, and we are working closely with first responders and families. We will continue to share information as it becomes available,” the school district said.

title: Netanyahu denies reports about escalation with Iran in last day before election
text:
Netanyahu denies reports about escalation with Iran in last day before election
Israelis entered the final 24 hours of an intense election season on Monday, as reports circulated that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have clashed with the Israeli military over initiating a possible escalation with Iran immediately before elections.
Tensions flared over reports that Netanyahu and his military chief of staff clashed over an instruction by the prime minister to carry out an “action” the army worried could reignite the conflict with Iran. Netanyahu’s office denied the report, first published by Israel’s Channel 12, as “fake news.”
Defense Minister Israel Katz also quickly denied the report. “I state unequivocally that there has been no intention by Israel of initiating an attack on Iran before the elections in Israel,” Katz wrote on X on Monday, calling reports of rifts between political and military leaders “completely baseless and false.” However, he stressed that Israel would respond forcefully if Iran attacks first.
Related video: Eight days until the midterms: Where is the president holding rallies before election day?
Israel’s opposition candidates slammed the reports, accusing Netanyahu of endangering regional stability for his political preservation. Netanyahu’s main rival, former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, warned Netanyahu not to “dare to place your own political interests above the security of the state.” He posted on X, “Netanyahu, my eyes are on you.”
Avigdor Lieberman, head of the hawkish Yisrael Beytenu party, part of the opposition bloc, sent a letter to Israel’s attorney general demanding a criminal investigation into possible treason by Netanyahu’s “attempts to drag Israel into a war on the eve of elections, including a willingness to sacrifice (Israeli) soldiers out of fear of losing the election.”
Although Israelis are breathlessly approaching the election as one of the most crucial in years, people across the Middle East not expecting dramatic changes regardless of the victor. Both Netanyahu and his main rivals have similar approaches to Israel’s regional security in both Gaza and Iran.
In southern Gaza, Jamal Abu Deeb, who was displaced from Khan Younis, said that no matter who is elected, it won't be good news for the Palestinians. “It is all war and destruction,” he said, adding that there are still strikes every day that kill people and children across Gaza. “Do you think whoever gets elected will give us a better life? Quite the opposite.”
“They all have the same playbook, they have no mercy — death and destruction for everyone,” said Ibrahim Qeshta, who was displaced from Rafah. “Eisenkot is like Netanyahu, he will be the same. Our people die everyday, for nothing.”
Iran also watched the last-minute electioneering warily. “It makes no difference to us who ultimately takes the helm of a regime whose track record shows that it has brought nothing to our region but violence and bloodshed,” Esmail Baghaei, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, said in his weekly media briefing on Monday.
Associated Press writer Wafaa Shurafa contributed from Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip.

title: 3 people, including teen, arrested after botched robbery shooting leaves 15-year-old dead
text:
GULFPORT, Miss. (WLOX/Gray News) — Three people, including a teenager, are in custody after a shooting early Saturday left a 15-year-old dead, authorities said.
Officials said Elijah Markell Parham, 18, Elliona Yari-Cheri Goffney, 18, and a 17-year-old are each charged in connection with the shooting death of Jonte Payton, 15.
Investigators said around 2 a.m. Saturday, a botched robbery led to a fight that ended with Jonte being shot in front of a home on Commerce Street in Gulfport, Mississippi. Officers were able to identify a suspect vehicle after pulling footage from nearby surveillance cameras.
Officers later found the vehicle with the 17-year-old and Goffney at Cypress Lanes Apartments, where they were arrested. Parham later turned himself in at the Gulfport Police Department.
Parham and the 17-year-old are charged with capital murder and armed robbery. Goffney is charged with accessory after the fact.
All three were taken to the Harrison County Adult Detention Center to be held pending bond after processing and interviews.

title: NASCAR race at Talladega stopped after Joey Logano’s car goes airborne in scary 15-car wreck
text:
TALLADEGA, Ala. (AP) — The NASCAR Chase race at Talladega Superspeedway was stopped under the red flag with five laps remaining after a scary wreck involving three-time Cup Series champion Joey Logano, whose car went airborne and landed on its roof.
Safety crews needed several minutes to turn Logano’s No. 22 Ford back over on its wheels, and Logano was able to climb from the car to cheers from the crowd.
Logano was running in fourth when he lost control off a push by Carson Hocevar and started a 15-car pileup on the frontstretch that also included Chase Briscoe, Brad Keselowski, Austin Cindric, Josh Berry and Riley Herbst, who appeared to lose the brakes in his No. 35 Toyota before hitting the inside wall at virtually full speed.
“I just got a push in the wrong spot there,” Logano said. “It was very much a ‘Talladega Nights,’ Oh no, I’m upside down, this is not good’ moment. I can’t thank the safety crew enough. They did an amazing job flipping that thing over.”
Herbst, who missed the Daytona race in August with a concussion from a crash at New Hampshire Motor Speedway, was able to exit his car with help from safety workers. He took a moment to lean against his car before removing his helmet.
In a postrace interview with USA Sports, Herbst had a soft cast on his left hand and a wrap around his wrist and forearm.
“I’m OK; it was a big one,” Herbst said. “But just thank you to 2311 Racing and Toyota for the support. It’s been an up-and-down year, to say the least. I thought we had a shot at it there at the end. We got shuffled out a little bit, but came back and ultimately just got caught up in that wreck at Talladega.
“My dad always said, ‘If you’re going to be dumb, you better be tough.’ So, cheers.”
Logano is a three-time winner at Talladega. He has been involved in airborne crashes before at the 2.66-mile oval that is infamous for its big crashes.
After a similar incident in the April 2021 race at Talladega, Logano expressed frustration that his car had gotten up in the air and had its roof crushed. “I got a roll bar in my head,” Logano said. “That is not OK. I am one hit away from the same situation Ryan Newman just went through (in the 2020 Daytona 500). I just don’t feel like that is acceptable.”
NASCAR made safety enhancements to address airborne wrecks in recent years, and the Team Penske driver praised his car’s integrity after the wreck Sunday at Talladega.
“The car did a great job,” Logano said. ”The last time I flipped it was crushed on my head. This time, I don’t think any of the roll cage crushed at all, so I appreciate what NASCAR’s done. Thank you and the safety team for getting me out of there. There was some vicious hits in this one. Just happy to be alive.”

title: Walter Koenig, Ensign Chekov on original 'Star Trek' series, dies at 90
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Actor Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov, the youthful Russian navigator on the “ Star Trek ” television series and several movies, has died. He was 90.
Koenig died Monday at his home in the North Hollywood neighborhood of Los Angeles, talent agent Zachery McGinnis said in a statement.
In “Star Trek,” Ensign Chekov was the sole Communist-bloc member of the spaceship Enterprise bridge staff. His friendly, supportive presence showed how the rival nations (in the far-off future in which the show was set) were capable of working together.
Speaking heavily Russian-accented English, Chekov embodied stereotypical Russian personality traits, including fierce pride, love of poetry and blind loyalty.
“Star Trek” ran on NBC from 1966 to 1969 and has had an almost unprecedented afterlife as fans, or Trekkies, kept interest in the show alive.
“My heart is heavy,” Koenig’s castmate, George Takei, said in a post on the social platform X. “Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend.”
“Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it,” McGinnis said. “Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before.”
McGinnis said Koenig died surrounded by his daughter and niece.
Koenig played Chekov in seven “Star Trek” movies starting in 1979, as well as innumerable other spinoffs, including writing a “Star Trek” book, “Chekov’s Enterprise,” in 1980. The TV show has also inspired two spinoff TV series with new casts, and conventions that draw thousands of fans.
He returned to the science fiction genre with occasional appearances in the syndicated 1990s TV series “Babylon 5.”
