title: With tighter checks for flesh-eating screwworm, a border crossing reopens
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
With the all-clear from U.S. agriculture inspectors, Mexican cattle began moving on Monday through a border crossing in New Mexico that had been closed for nearly two years as both nations work to stop the flesh-eating New World screwworm from spreading.
The screwworm — actually a fly larva that burrows into the flesh of livestock, pets and even humans — has threatened the $113 billion U.S. cattle industry. Containment efforts have cost jobs and trade in border communities, and it cut off a source of cattle as the U.S. struggles to rebuild drought-depleted herds. Reopening crossings could help ease that squeeze, although experts caution that shoppers shouldn’t expect quick relief on beef prices.
The port at Columbus, New Mexico, is the third to resume Mexican cattle imports under new safeguards, which include tests, shots and inspections that happen before an animal even gets close to the border.
Officials and ranchers in the two countries say layers of treatment and inspection give them confidence that imported livestock won’t carry screwworm through the ports. But flies can buzz across the border on their own, meaning ranchers, hunters and pet owners should remain vigilant.
The parasite was an annual livestock scourge before being largely eradicated in the U.S. in the 1960s. It reappeared in Mexico in 2024, and the first confirmed U.S. case was in Texas in June.
More than 60 cases have been confirmed in Texas and New Mexico, with infestations of cattle, sheep, goats, horses and dogs. Last week, the first case in U.S. wildlife was confirmed after a hunter found screwworm in an elk.
Before the current outbreak, the U.S. was importing about 1 million head of cattle per year. It will take time to get back to that number while keeping a sharp eye on the risks to animal health, said Dudley Hoskins, undersecretary for the Department of Agriculture.
“As long as we can manage and mitigate that risk at an acceptable level, we will continue to process the safe and legal movement of cattle through these ports,” he said, watching as cattle lined up in the chutes at Columbus.
New Mexico is key for cattle imports
About a third of all Mexican cattle imported to the U.S. each year pass through Columbus and the Santa Teresa port near El Paso, Texas. Gerardo Fierro, executive director of the New Mexico Border Authority, pegged the value of the cattle trade for the area at $1 billion.
Fierro said the community watched as jobs, cattle sales and even tax revenue from the diesel fuel used to transport the animals evaporated due to the closures. Ranchers were no longer crossing into New Mexico and spending money on supplies, lodging and food, and farmers had no customers for their alfalfa and grain.
“This means a lot,” he said of the reopening.
Another border crossing for cattle in Arizona is due to open in late November.
Layers of safeguards ensure cows are clean
New Mexico state veterinarian Samantha Holeck said the rigorous process for getting cattle ready starts at their home ranches, where private veterinarians check for tuberculosis and other diseases and deliver medications that prevent screwworm.
At the next stop, veterinarians accredited by the Mexican government look for open wounds, signs of illness or other injuries. Then a head-to-tail inspection is done by the USDA while still in Mexico.
The last hurdle? Dipping — as it’s commonly known — involves the cows being immersed in vats of insecticide to get rid of any missed parasites.
Flies have lots of ways to move around
Holeck said the protocols developed over recent years helped to buy more time, and the USDA is using fly traps and drones to survey areas.
The government has a longstanding program to breed sterile male flies and drop swarms of them from planes to mate with wild females, causing the flies to die out. The government is building a $610 million factory in Texas that can produce 300 million sterile flies per week. That will augment production at facilities in Mexico and Panama.
“That’s our sharpest tool,” Hoskins said.
Beef prices are a bigger problem
Mexican ranchers once again have a market for their feeder cattle, but experts say it will take time for U.S. ranchers to rebuild herds that have dwindled to record lows due to years of persistent drought. Constrained supplies have pushed prices higher.
Tom Paterson, president of the New Mexico Cattle Grower’s Association, was among those who met with U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins last week in Columbus.
“I agree with the secretary,” he said, “when she says that food security is national security.”

title: When is it too late to get a flu shot?
text:
As the colder seasons approach, many people start preparing for fall and winter routines. For most people, this should include getting a yearly flu shot. The flu vaccine is effective and safe and provides protection against flu illness — both for you and for those around you.
Getting a flu vaccine can keep you from missing work or school due to illness. The flu vaccine also protects you against severe symptoms, which could require hospitalization. And the flu vaccine can be lifesaving for people at greater risk. This includes pregnant women, older adults, and children, as well as people with chronic medical conditions.
But what if it’s already flu season, or you’ve already had the flu? Is it ever too late to get the flu shot? Below, GoodRx, a platform for medication savings, has the answers.
Key takeaways:
- The best time to get a flu shot is right before flu season starts. Flu season usually starts by the end of October.
- The flu shot is safe, effective, and recommended for most people.
- The flu shot protects you even if you’ve already had the flu. So it’s almost never too late to get a flu shot.
Is it too late to get a flu shot?
It’s almost never too late to get a flu shot. A flu shot will provide protection as long as the flu is circulating in the community. Since the flu circulates until late May in most parts of the U.S., even getting your shot in late winter or early spring will help keep you healthy.
When is the best time to get a flu shot?
The best time to get a flu shot is right before flu season begins, which usually means in September or October. In most areas of the U.S., flu season is from October through May. Peak activity is usually from December through February.
It’s best to get your flu shot by the end of October. It takes two weeks for your immune system to fully respond to a vaccine. So, it’s important to plan accordingly and get the vaccine before flu activity increases in your community.
Early vaccination — that is, getting a flu shot in July or August — is sometimes an option. This can make sense for young children who need two doses of the flu vaccine in the same year. You may also benefit from early vaccination if you’re pregnant or close to delivery.
But, in general, most people shouldn’t get vaccinated early. The flu shot gets less effective over time, so it works best if you wait until closer to flu season.
How long does the flu shot last?
It’s not clear exactly how long a flu shot lasts. Studies show that vaccine protection likely lasts at least six months for most people — but fades over time. That’s why it’s important to get a yearly flu shot for the best protection against the flu virus during flu season.
Should you get a flu shot if you’ve already had the flu?
Yes, you should get a flu shot if you’ve already had the flu. Every year, several strains of flu spread through communities. Immunity to one strain of flu doesn’t protect you against other strains.
That means you can get the flu more than once in a single year. The flu shot is designed to protect you against several of the most troublesome strains each season. So it makes sense to get vaccinated even if you’ve already recovered from the flu.
Where to get a flu shot
Flu vaccines are widely available during the flu season. There are many places you can go to get a flu shot, including:
- Your doctor’s office
- Most large chain retail pharmacies
- Drive-thru flu-shot clinics
- Pop-up flu-shot clinics at community centers and hospitals
- Your local health department
There’s no “right” place to get the flu shot. You can go to any licensed healthcare professional offering a licensed flu vaccine.
When not to get a flu shot
Just about everyone should get a flu shot. However, the flu shot isn’t recommended for:
- Anyone with a severe allergy or anaphylaxis to the flu vaccine or its ingredients
- Infants younger than 6 months old
Anyone with a history of Guillain-Barré syndrome should talk with their healthcare team before getting a flu shot.
In rare situations, the risks of the flu shot can outweigh the benefits. In these cases, people need to talk with their healthcare team before getting a flu shot.
The flu shot is safe for people with egg allergies. Before 2023, people with egg allergies needed to take special precautions when getting a flu shot, but according to the CDC, that’s no longer the case.
If you or your child is sick on the day of your flu shot appointment, make sure you let the healthcare professional know. Some people can still get vaccinated if they only have a minor illness. In some cases, rescheduling the flu shot may be recommended.
Frequently asked questions
Is it too late to get a flu shot in January?
No, it’s not too late to get a flu shot in January. In the U.S., the flu tends to stick around through May. You can even get the flu in the summer. Getting a flu shot in January still provides important protection.
Can you get a flu shot anytime during the year?
Yes, you can get the flu shot pretty much any time of the year. But keep in mind that you’re more likely to have better protection if you get a flu vaccine right before the start of flu season, around September or October. Protection goes down over time, so the idea is to make sure you’re protected during the peak of flu season.
How effective is the flu shot this year?
The flu shot’s effectiveness varies from season to season, depending on how well the vaccine matches the strains actually circulating. In seasons with a good match, flu vaccination cuts the risk of a flu-related healthcare visit by 40% to 60%. But one thing holds up every year: Even when the match is imperfect, the vaccine still lowers your odds of severe illness and hospitalization.
Does the flu shot make you sick?
No, the flu shot doesn’t make you sick with the flu. Flu shots contain inactivated (killed) virus or single viral proteins. Neither of these can cause a flu infection. Some people can feel ill after a flu shot with:
- Low-grade fever
- Headache
- Muscle aches
- Fatigue
But that’s your immune system responding to the shot, not the flu.
What to avoid after a flu shot?
There’s not much you need to avoid after a flu shot. That being said, you may want to skip heavy arm workouts if your arm is sore and avoid alcohol for a day or so. Alcohol can cause dehydration, which could make any side effects feel worse.
The bottom line
The best time to get a flu shot is two weeks before the flu season begins — usually by the end of October. But it’s really never too late to get a flu shot, as the virus is normally circulating in communities through May of each year. The flu vaccine can keep people safe from flu illness, and it’s lifesaving for people at risk for severe flu disease. The flu shot is recommended for nearly everyone older than 6 months.

title: Bangor City Council bans remote public comments again
text:
“Can you hear me?” is usually George Lance’s first line when he unmutes and addresses the Bangor City Council via Zoom at its Monday night meetings.
Lance is one of the most consistent participants in the council’s public comment periods and usually continues his speech by advocating for a white heritage month or spewing racist, antisemitic slurs.
That’s what he did at Monday’s meeting — likely for the last time, because the City Council is again banning the use of Zoom by members of the public to speak remotely during public comment at its meetings.
Remote participation was reinstated less than a year ago after a temporary ban due to an influx of disruptive speakers who joined council meetings online, often using fake names, to deliver slurs and other hate speech that violated the city’s public comment policy.
Zoom comments resumed in January with a new registration system, but some people have continued to join meetings online and share offensive remarks that, in the council’s view, have little to do with city business.
City Councilor Susan Faloon proposed the rule change during a committee meeting last week. “In my opinion, it has really bogged down our meetings and been very distracting,” she said Monday.
Even with the registration requirement that city staff implemented this year, there’s no way to know whether someone is registering with their real name and place of residence, Assistant City Manager Courtney O’Donnell said at a Government Operations Committee meeting last week.
“They always put that they live in Bangor and that’s also, you know, questionable at times, but unfortunately there’s no way around that,” O’Donnell said.
She noted that community members will still be able to email councilors, call the city manager’s office, or send someone to speak for them at a City Council meeting if they can’t make it themselves, and that the city is still required by federal law to provide reasonable accommodations in the case of a disability.
Lance was the only person who offered remote comments at Monday’s meeting, requesting a proclamation recognizing white men.
“This is free speech, woman!” he said after Council Chair Susan Hawes interjected to tell him his comments were unrelated to city business.
Lance’s name appears in meeting minutes from several towns across the country, where he seemingly also joins remotely and offers similar comments to the ones he’s repeated regularly in Bangor, including one meeting where he claimed to live at an address in North Oaks, Minnesota.
The council voted 6-2 in favor of removing remote participation, with councilors Joe Leonard and Wayne Mallar voting against. Councilor Daniel Carson was absent.
“I definitely understand why councilor Faloon brought this forward,” Leonard said, but he added, “I don’t feel comfortable taking that privilege away from the average citizen” because of bad actors.
Residents were mixed on the measure.
Katie Coe said she thought it was a great idea, but noted that it’s hard for some people to get to the nighttime meetings after buses stop running and suggested that the city’s public transit operate later on Mondays to accommodate them.
Suzette Furrow spoke in opposition to the ban. “Just as you councilors have the privilege of participating remotely, I think the public should as well,” she said, adding that she’s participated remotely in the past due to sickness or travel.
Faloon also previously suggested moving the public comment period to the end of meetings, but the Government Operations Committee decided not to move forward with that proposal.
Correction: A previous version of this story misspelled Katie Coe’s name. It has been updated.

title: Woman’s 911 call was key in response to New Gloucester store fire
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sarenna Collins was driving through New Gloucester in the early hours of Oct. 11 when she saw a place near and dear to her heart on fire. Collins, who was driving with her mother on the way back from visiting a friend in Auburn, saw what looked like fog coming from Link’s Variety.
When Collins pulled up, she found smoke pouring out of the building and obscuring the area, and could see red in the back window of the kitchen. Worried that the fire would reach the gas pumps or propane tanks near the building, she immediately called 911.
Collins said she stayed at the scene while the fire was being extinguished, and watched as 12 fire trucks, from departments including Gray, Auburn, Raymond, Durham, Yarmouth and North Yarmouth, arrived to put out the blaze. Collins stayed until she asked the firefighters if she was allowed to take her mother, who has cancer, home.
Ashley Roberts, a manager at Link’s Variety, said the fire department told her that had they gotten the call just five or 10 minutes after they did, the store would have been completely engulfed in flames. Roberts said that while the store is not completely unsalvageable, the interior was significantly damaged, and she estimated it would take at least six months to get the store to a state where it can reopen.
Collins said Link’s Variety was a major part of her life. She said that whenever she was feeling down she would go to Link’s to get pizza and talk with the staff, all of whom knew her name.
Since the fire, Collins has stayed in contact with the owners. The morning after the fire, she drove back and spoke to them, and they were “very thankful” for her actions the previous night, she said, and even offered her a job once the store reopens.
“It’s (like) home,” said Collins, “and it really broke my heart it the way (that) it was. I don’t really care about recognition or anything like that, I just care that it can be saved.”
The Office of the Fire Marshal said on Oct. 19 that the cause of the blaze was still undetermined, though a press release in the immediate aftermath of the fire speculated it originated “in or around the furnace area.”

title: Walter Koenig, known for role in original 'Star Trek' series, dies at 90
text:
Walter Koenig, known for role in original 'Star Trek' series, dies at 90
Walter Koenig, best known for his role in the original "Star Trek" series, has died, according to reports. He was 90 years old.
Koenig played Pavel Chekov in the original Star Trek series. He appeared in 36 episodes of the show's 1960s TV run and in seven "Star Trek" movies, according to IMDb.
The Hollywood Reporter confirmed the death through his representative, saying he died of natural causes.
Fellow "Star Trek" star George Takei posted a remembrance about Koenig on Monday, saying his "heart is heavy" about the loss.
"Walter and I met on the bridge of the Enterprise in the 1960s, and we stayed friends for nearly six decades," Takei wrote in a Facebook post. "When Brad and I married in 2008, Walter stood beside us as our best man. Just last month, on Sept. 14, he turned 90, on the same day Brad and I celebrated our 18th wedding anniversary. I will always treasure that he and I shared that date.
"Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course," Takei added.
Koenig was married to his wife, Judy, from 1965 until she died in 2022. They had two children.

title: Microsoft offers 60,000 employees voluntary buyouts as AI spending accelerates
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - Microsoft has offered 60,000 employees, or about 27% of its global workforce, voluntary buyouts as the software giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence.
The company’s voluntary exit offer was available to eligible employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States, the company’s Chief People Officer Amy Coleman wrote in a blog post Monday.
“The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us,” Coleman wrote. “We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft.”
The company, which releases its quarterly financial results Wednesday, had approximately 223,000 full-time employees at the end of June.
Shares of Microsoft Corp., based in Redmond, Washington, hit an all-time high this month. The stock rose about 1% on Monday.
In May, Microsoft planned to offer buyouts to about 8,750 people, or 7% of its U.S. workforce, according to two people familiar with the plan who were not authorized to speak about it publicly. In July, the company said it was cutting 4,800 jobs, about 2.1% of its global workforce, including a large number of workers at its Xbox video game business.
The gusher of investment in data centers — likely topping $700 billion this year — to power artificial intelligence has made memory chips, computer processors and other equipment, as well as electricity, more expensive. Economists expect it will continue to push up inflation at least through the end of this year.
Microsoft has been ramping up its AI capabilities for several years. In 2024 the company revealed a new class of AI-imbued personal computers that centered on fusing its AI assistant, called Copilot, into the Windows operating system for PCs, where Microsoft already has the eyes of millions of consumers.
And in October 2025 Microsoft introduced a new artificial intelligence character called Mico, a floating cartoon face shaped like a blob or flame that embodies the software giant’s Copilot virtual assistant.

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Peter W. Nelson, 77, of Jefferson, passed away on the evening of Oct. 4, 2026 after a courageous battle with pulmonary fibrosis. Born in Schenectady, N.Y. on June 15, 1949, he was the son of Sven and Winnifred Nelson.
After his schooling, Pete served honorably in the U.S. Air Force. For several years after his service, he was a member of the fire department in Fonda, N.Y. and also served on the hazmat fire investigative team. In 2016 he moved from upstate New York to Maine.
Pete was an avid hunter and enjoyed fishing. He loved the water and was always excited to put his boat in lakes, oceans, and streams. He enjoyed camping, visiting state parks, and in the winter he loved to plow snow.
Pete also enjoyed photography, and liked taking pictures of family members and lighthouses. He also loved his many pets, cats, and dogs.
He is survived by his loving wife of 31 years, Debra Ann Nelson; a sister; brother-in-law; sisters-in-law; as well as several nieces, nephews, and cousins.
Pete was laid to rest privately with military honors in the Maine Veterans’ Memorial Cemetery in Augusta. In lieu of flowers, donations in his memory may be made to the American Lung Association or the ASPCA.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home, 612 Main St., Damariscotta, ME 04543. Condolences and messages for his family may be expressed by visiting stronghancock.com.

title: UMaine students and faculty weigh in on potential election outcomes
text:
Ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the Maine Campus asked members of the University of Maine community to share their outcome predictions, particularly for Maine’s closely watched U.S. Senate race.
The election between incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson has drawn national attention, including discussion surrounding Graham Platner’s suspended campaign and its potential impact on voters. Students and faculty offered their perspectives on the candidates and factors that could influence the outcome.
Robert Glover, an associate professor of political science and honors and co-leader of UMaine UVote, weighed in via email. He offered commentary on the effects various factors might have on the race and Mainers’ mindsets going into it, ranging from the distribution of media coverage between the candidates to the prevalence of attack ads.
“Maine is a state that tends to favor less alarmist, less extreme [and] more pragmatic political discourse. A lot of these ads are driven by large independent expenditures from entities unconnected with the campaigns. And Maine is a cheap media market. What might seem like a relatively small ad expenditure to someone from out of state saturates our airwaves for weeks. I think most Mainers are just trying to endure this and tune it out,” wrote Glover. “I hope that in the end, we’ll see voters driven to the polls by the positions of the candidates themselves, not what some out of state group is pouring into the state in advertising.”
Glover added that most Mainers had likely already decided which candidate they intended to vote for.
“This is, in part, because of the early rise of Platner. I don’t think there are too many Mainers at this point who are just totally unaware of this race. So really both campaigns are competing for a vanishingly small undecided electorate. I think this race will really come down to turnout.”
Autumn Carmona, a fourth-year botany student, said that college students may be more incentivized to vote because of the direct impact of politics on education.
“I think in college, people are a little more deeply involved because of how these issues impact them, and how it impacts their major,” said Carmona.
Carmona spoke at length about the way she felt people’s approach to the race was being shaped by social media, the campus environment and the character of each candidate’s campaign.
“I was pretty confident a month ago it was going to be Troy Jackson, and I’m still confident, but seeing the numbers recently, I’m a little surprised that he isn’t more popular,” she said. “I have a lot of hope for the movement, broadly. The transition from Platner to Jackson just shows that it’s about the movement, not the person. I think it really shows that people want real change, and they want it now.”
Amy Bradford, a fourth-year anthropology student, spoke to the Maine Campus about the transition from Platner to Jackson and her thoughts on the election.
“Maybe it’s wishful thinking, but I’m leaning towards Jackson winning just ’cause I’m hoping that people are tired of Susan Collins. I think that the fact that everyone was so gung-ho about Graham Platner before that imploded makes me think that a lot of people are ready for a change and are hopefully willing to go for the newer candidate.”
Bradford also spoke about the way she felt the scandals that plagued the Platner campaign followed Jackson’s in certain ways.
“There’s still the bad taste in people’s mouths when they remember Platner… now you see all these political ads bashing Troy Jackson by showing him with Graham Platner.”
When asked about the limited media coverage of other races, Bradford discussed how she believed it could influence voters.
“What it usually comes down to when you don’t know the candidate’s individual positions, that’s when you just go off of name recognition, ” Bradford said. “Like, Chellie Pingree, I recognize that name, so I feel like unless I do more research I might be tempted to be like, ‘oh, I’ll go with Pingree, because I recognize that name!’”
When asked about students who did not feel very well informed about the races and their candidates, Glover encouraged them to utilize resources such as VOTE411, the League of Women Voters Candidate guides, or local journalistic candidate guides.
“These are consequential races that have real implications for what our next two of four years look like,” he wrote. “And I have total faith in students to ‘do their homework’ and make an informed choice at the polls.”

title: Massachusetts woman allegedly attacked Maine man with ax
text:
A Massachusetts woman allegedly attacked a Rumford man with an ax Sunday morning during a dispute over payment for a motorcycle delivery.
Luciane Dezan, 46, of Medford, Massachusetts, has been charged with attempted elevated aggravated assault and aggravated criminal mischief, according to the Rumford Police Department.
The 44-year-old victim hired Dezan to deliver his red 1984 Honda GL1200 from his old home in Northborough, Massachusetts, to him at Madison’s Condos on Route 2 in Rumford.
But when Dezan arrived with the motorcycle, the victim discovered damage that he believed happened during the trip from Massachusetts to Maine. An argument broke out when he confronted Dezan and refused to pay the full sum, Rumford police said.
Dezan allegedly got an ax from her van and began hacking at the motorcycle, causing extensive damage, estimated at $2,000.
She allegedly swung the ax at the victim’s head when he intervened. The man dodged, and Dezan missed him.
The attack was caught on video, Rumford police said.
Dezan was taken to the Oxford County Jail in South Paris, where her bail was set at $10,000. Her bail conditions include not contacting the victim and staying away from his home.

title: Reject jail question so Penobscot County can pursue better community services
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Abigail Miller is a researcher, organizer, and advocate in Maine. She has a bachelor’s degree in sociology with a focus in criminal justice.
Question 1 on Penobscot County ballots asks if Penobscot County Jail (PCJ) should be able to move outside of Bangor. Though this is not a vote on expanding the jail, it’s one step in getting voters to fund a new and larger $80 million jail in Penobscot County.
Though crime rates have decreased in Maine over the last 50 years, the county spends millions each year boarding out incarcerated people to other facilities due to overcrowding at PCJ. However, I believe a new and larger jail is not the solution; affordable and humane alternatives exist.
I studied this in 2023-2024 for my undergraduate thesis with guidance from No PCJ Expansion. It became clear to me that high incarceration rates can be attributed to several unmet needs within the community, including a lack of accessible healthcare, mental health support, substance use disorder treatment, affordable housing, transportation, work, and access to community. When we respond to these issues with incarceration, jails become overcrowded and people do not receive meaningful support that changes outcomes.
One large increase in the jail population at PCJ was after an in-treatment mental health facility downsized in Bangor in the 1980s. Without alternative government-funded resources for these individuals, reliance on incarceration for those who need mental health support increased.
Beneficial mental health support is not fully offered in jail facilities. Incarceration can actually worsen these issues. I interviewed families of formerly incarcerated people at PCJ. Participants reported that some individuals at PCJ intentionally did not disclose their mental illnesses to correctional officers due to threats of solitary confinement. They also reported that many incarcerated people didn’t receive appropriate health services — even acquiring over-the-counter medication was challenging.
Many local nonprofits are already trying to bridge the gap between those in need and accessible services. Several organizations offer food security programs, housing, and free transportation. Food AND Medicine hosted a Peer Workforce Navigators program which helped connect people with jobs. Many organizations including Together Place and Breaking the Cycle offer support for substance use disorder, and access to community through peer-support and recovery. Needlepoint Sanctuary hosts a syringe service program. Several nonprofits offer other basic health and mental health support for no cost.
Inadequate funding and resources are typically the largest barriers for nonprofits to connect people with services. If collectively granted a sum of $10 million, nine of the local organizations interviewed reported they could run effective programming that could meet critical needs and address the root causes of incarceration. Through funding these programs, the county could potentially avoid the proposed $80 million jail expansion and save on the current excessive spending of maintaining the jail.
Research demonstrates that funding social programming instead of incarceration can lead to a lower likelihood of returning to jail and better public safety outcomes. Programs that aim to meet community needs like housing, work, healthcare, and education can improve long-term community well-being without involvement of the criminal justice system at all.
Additionally, research shows that when jails increase capacity, arrest rates increase and jails become full again, regardless of crime rates. If jail beds exist, they will be filled.
Penobscot County has an opportunity to make better choices for Mainers. There is humanizing and transformative work that nonprofits are already doing to accomplish this. We have to continue to support local nonprofits who serve our towns. Donate, volunteer, and vote in support of these organizations.
I believe we must reject Question 1. The county commissioners are already spending $100,000 to reserve land in Hampden. If this question passes, they have every intention of moving forward in the process of purchasing this land and building a larger jail.
Meeting community needs through programming is more humane, effective, and affordable than jail expansion. With just an eighth of the cost proposed for the jail expansion, Penobscot County could better protect our neighbors, families, and communities. Vote no on Question 1.

title: Cyclist fights off muggers with her Winnie the Pooh Stanley cup: ‘I was always a fighter’
text:
NEW YORK (WABC) - A New York woman fought off three men who tried to rob her while she was cycling in Central Park. She says her helmet, bag and Winnie the Pooh-themed Stanley cup helped her survive the attack.
Katherine Marroquin, 32, was riding her bike just before 10 p.m. last Sunday on her after-work commute through Central Park. She stopped after dropping her AirPods, and three men suddenly appeared from behind some bushes.
“They were hiding somewhere. It was really dark, and they waited for me to lean down and wait, and then, they appeared,” Marroquin said. “I think they were trying to steal phones, maybe, and they just saw me, saw the bike. They were like, ‘Oh, money.’”
Marroquin says the men struck her in the head, surrounded her and started going through her belongings. One of the men threw her stainless steel Stanley cup, which has a Winnie the Pooh design, on the ground in front of her.
Marroquin says she grabbed the tumbler from the ground and used it to defend herself.
“It’s three people by myself. I got to defend myself. I didn’t think about money or anything. I thought about my life and seeing my mom again. So, I grabbed the cup, and I hit one of the guys in the head,” she said.
The men soon ran off, taking her book bag with them.
Marroquin’s only injury was a cut next to her eye that was already there but reopened during the fight. She says her bag and helmet absorbed much of the attack.
Reflecting on the confrontation, Marroquin says she was determined not to surrender what she had worked for.
“I was always a fighter since I was little, you know? So, I feel like it’s unfair for people to come in and think that they could take whatever you work for. You know, I feel like it’s not fair,” she said.
The irony of all this is that Marroquin just started biking to work last year because she thought that would be safer than taking the subway.
“This is the reason why I started riding the bike because the subway was very dangerous,” she said.
The New York Police Department has released surveillance images of the people who are wanted in connection to the robbery. So far, there have been no arrests.

title: More than 60 former ambassadors, national security experts endorse Troy Jackson
text:
More than 60 former ambassadors, national security experts endorse US Senate candidate Troy Jackson
Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate Troy Jackson was endorsed by more than 60 former U.S. ambassadors and national security experts.
The group features those involved in administrations of both parties dating back to President Reagan. It includes President Barack Obama's National Security Advisor Susan Rice and former Deputy Secretary of State Wendy Sherman.
Maine's Total Coverage spoke with two members of the group who individually have decades of experience in foreign relations, and they say they've never been as concerned with the state of the nation as they are right now.
"We are at the most dangerous moment in U.S. history during my tenure, anyway, of working on all of these issues," stated former U.S. Ambassador to Algeria Craig Johnstone. "It is absolutely amazing how far we have fallen as a country. We have fallen way far. We were once the shining light on the hill. We are not the shining light on anybody's hill anymore."
The group critiqued President Donald Trump's policies on a variety of issues, but mainly the war in Iran, relations with Russia and the treatment of the nation's allies, pointing towards the tariffs put on Canadian goods.
"I am genuinely concerned about the direction of the country," said former U.S. Ambassador to Syria Robert Ford. "I have never been this concerned before. I have never been so concerned about respect for the rule of law inside our own country. I have never been as concerned about the deterioration of alliances, whether it be with Canada or with countries in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization."
While much of the criticism was on the Trump administration, both Ford and Johnstone voiced concerns with Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
They said the current majority in the Senate isn't asking the tough questions to properly check Trump's power. The pair added that they are confident Jackson would, if elected.

title: Singer Chris Brown to be sentenced over bottle attack at a London nightclub
text:
Chris Brown avoids prison time for brawling at a London nightclub
Grammy-winning singer Chris Brown avoided prison time Monday for beating a music producer with a tequila bottle at a London nightclub three years ago.
The 37-year-old was given an eight-month sentence, suspended for a year.
He had faced up to three years in prison after pleading guilty to a count of affray in July for the attack on the dance floor of Tape, a private club in the swanky Mayfair neighborhood in February 2023.
Video footage played in court showed Brown having to be pulled away from the victim, his former friend Abraham Diaw, after striking him twice in the head with a bottle.
“The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous, it carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained,” Judge Tony Baumgartner said in Southwark Crown Court.
Despite the seriousness of the attack, Baumgartner said Brown did not qualify for a custodial sentence because he pleaded guilty and there were several mitigating circumstances, including stable employment and charity work. The judge acknowledged Brown’s previous convictions but said he had maintained a clean record in recent years.
Previous brushes with the law
Brown has faced repeated legal trouble since his felony conviction in the 2009 assault of his then-girlfriend, Rihanna, hours before the pair were due to perform at the Grammys.
He has been arrested in several U.S. states over altercations but was either not charged or prosecutors later dropped the charges. In 2019 he was arrested in Paris and questioned on suspicion of rape, but was released without charge.
In return for his guilty plea, prosecutors dropped charges of assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm and having an offensive weapon, a bottle.
Brown’s friend and vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu also pleaded guilty to affray and was given a four-month suspended sentence.
Affray is the use or threat of unlawful violence that leads someone to fear for their safety.
Brown has apologized for the attack
Prosecutor Heidi Stonecliffe said Brown played a leading role in the attack.
“By any circumstances, when one watches that footage, it is Mr. Brown that moves first,” Stonecliffe said.
Defense lawyer Sallie Bennett-Jenkins said Brown apologized to all those at the club that night, though she emphasized the attack lasted no more than 20 seconds.
“This is an ugly and unattractive incident,” Bennett-Jenkins said. “It is something which undoubtedly would have caused distress to those who are present and for which Mr. Brown … offers a profound apology to all those present.”
Diaw was discharged from the hospital with head and knee injuries, Stonecliffe said.
Crowds greet Brown outside court
Brown was cheered outside the courthouse by fans who came from as far as Italy and the Netherlands.
His face was covered behind in a black mask and dark glasses and his bleached hair was mostly hidden from view under a black ball cap. He wore a black leather jacket and light-colored turtleneck.
He blew a kiss to one fan and appeared to sign an autograph for another as he moved through a pack of photographers and onlookers.
Not everyone was cheering for him. When he arrived at court in the morning, a lone voice could be heard shouting at him to ask when he was going to learn that violence is not OK.
Brown left the United Kingdom after the brawl but was arrested in May 2025 at a Manchester hotel after flying to the city for a concert. He had been free on bail of 5 million pounds ($6.7 million), which allowed him to tour Europe and North America the past two summers.
Brown rose to stardom as a teen in 2005 and won his first Grammy for best R&B album in 2011 for “F.A.M.E.” He earned his second in the same category for “11:11 (Deluxe)” in 2025.

title: Rumford Police Respond To Double Stabbing And Axe Attack In Separate Incidents
text:
It was a violent Sunday in Rumford, where knives and an axe were used in separate cases.
Rumford, Maine Police Encounter 2 Violent Calls in One Day
Police officers never know what types of situations they will encounter.
On Sunday, October 25, 2026, Rumford saw an especially busy day, with two violent calls back-to-back.
Three people now face charges for alleged attacks on three people.
Rumford, Maine Police Say 2 People Were Stabbed on Sunday and 2 Others Arrested
Rumford Police were called to 209 Waldo Street at approximately 8:48 am on Sunday, after 911 callers reported assaults involving two victims and two suspects who had fled on foot.
Police officers and Oxford County Sheriff's deputies arrived within minutes of the calls and found two victims suffering from stab wounds.
A 44-year-old man had a knife wound to his back, with significant bleeding, and a 37-year-old woman sustained a knife wound to the side of her abdomen. Both victims are from Rumford.
They were transported to Rumford Hospital for emergency treatment and are expected to survive their injuries.
While officers tended to the victims, other officers and deputies located the suspects, who took off on foot in different directions.
Tips from residents helped the police quickly apprehend the two suspects and take them into custody.
Jazya D. Swan, 19, of Lewiston, is charged with criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon and refusing to submit to arrest or detention.
A 15-year-old female from Lisbon, Maine, is charged with elevated aggravated assault, criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon, and refusing to submit to arrest or detention.
Rumford, Maine Police Report an Axe Attack Over a Motorcycle
In an unrelated call, Rumford Police Officers responded to a 911 call reporting a woman was attacking a resident of Madison's condos with an axe during an argument at approximately 11:57 am.
An investigation determined the 44-year-old male victim had arranged through social media for a Massachusetts woman to transport his red 1984 Honda GL 1200 motorcycle from his former home in Northborough, Massachusetts, to Rumford.
When Luciane Dezan, 46, of Medford, Massachusetts, arrived with the bike, the victim discovered damage he believed occurred in transit and told the woman he wouldn't pay the full agreed-upon fee.
The two argued, and Dezan allegedly retrieved an axe from her van and began repeatedly striking the motorcycle, causing extensive damage.
When the man attempted to stop her, she allegedly swung the axe at his head, narrowly missing him.
Police estimate the bike sustained approximately $2,000 in damage during the attack.
Dezan was charged with attempted elevated aggravated assault and aggravated criminal mischief and transported to the Oxford County Jail.

title: Halloween at Bates: How Do I Pick a Good Costume?
text:
Sprint to Spirit Halloween or quickly ship your costume to Post and Print, because Halloween is just around the corner.
While I’ve grown out of trick or treating, costumes are luckily still in style in college. Picking out my Halloween costume is always one of my favorite parts of the year. When else can you dress however you want and be whoever you wish to be?
When it comes to Halloween costumes, I would say that I have a solid resume. At Bates, I’m happy with the lineup of costumes that I’ve had so far. Freshman year, my roommate and I were the iconic twins from “The Shining.” Sophomore year, I was Lucy with two friends who were Charlie Brown and Snoopy. Junior year, I was Cody from “Surfs Up” and my friend was Chicken Joe. This year, I plan on being Paddington Bear.
I like to break Halloween costumes down into categories. My categories include: trendy this year, timeless, unique but known, funny, and creative.
It’s often hard to know what is trendy for the year. Some years it’s more obvious. For example, Barbie was a great pick for 2023. And Labubus, Belly Conklin’s, and Elphabas stole the show in 2025. However, 2026 is more up in the air.
Popular movies, shows, and trends generally inspire the main costumes of a year. Some popular movies this year, like “Obsession,” “Sheep Detectives,” “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “Backrooms,” “Project Hail Mary” and “The Odyssey,” will likely inspire costumes.
And yet, there are a lot of caveats that come with movie costumes. Given Bear and Nikki’s toxic relationship, dressing up as one of them isn’t the best idea. It’s hard to be someone from “Sheep Detectives” as a lot of the outfits aren’t recognizable and being a sheep doesn’t clearly point to this movie.
I predict there will be some astronaut costumes, inspired by “Project Hail Mary.” I also think that some people will still dress as Nikki from “Obsession.” I expect many Spider-Man’s. Also, given the new Hunger Games movie is coming out in November, I am predicting there will be a lot of Haymitch’s or other Hunger Games characters from some of the previous movies.
Then there are the popular television show inspired costumes. One big show that I’m guessing will inspire a lot of costumes is “Off Campus.” I can see a lot of hockey players, probably with Briar jerseys. It is also likely that people will dress as Hannah Wells or her best friend Allie Hayes. Additionally, given the new season of “Ted Lasso”, I’m guessing a lot of people will dress as Ted or other characters from the show. I also predict some Love Islanders like Bryce or Trinity.
In terms of timeless costumes, I’m definitely predicting vampires, angels, devils, witches, “Harry Potter” characters, “Wizard of Oz” characters, princesses, and fairies. Timeless costumes are fun to put together because there are many different parts of a costume to pick out: you can buy the pink corset or the pink dress, pick the green heels or the blue ones. This makes almost no costume truly identical.
One of my favorite categories of costumes is ‘unique but known.’ These are costumes that aren’t as popular, but can still be recognized. Costumes that fall into this category, and that I would recommend, are Coraline, Carrie, Jim and Pam, “Star Wars” characters, Care Bears, popular children’s book characters and Nick Wild and Judy Hops (or other known animated movie/television show characters).
In addition to this, it’s always entertaining to see a funny Halloween costume. Halloween doesn’t always need to be scary! I enjoy when people dress up as memes or TikToks trends like six-seven (for last year, please not this year) or the hyperpigmentation drawing. Inflatable costumes are hilarious and so are comedic characters from movies like Olaf or Michael Scott.
Finally, there is the creative costume. These are the costumes that I get most excited for. Generally, creative costumes are less popular characters from movies, like Ennui from “Inside Out” or Sandy from “SpongeBob SquarePants.” Out of the box ideas like dressing as a stoplight or dressing as a gumball machine with a matching gumball trick-or-treat bag, would definitely be part of this category. Most importantly, however, what classifies a creative costume is a homemade element. Maybe it is sewn by the person wearing it, maybe it has a stunning makeup look done by a friend, or maybe it’s a combination of finds from a thrift store.
Overall, you generally can’t go wrong with a Halloween costume. The most important thing is to wear something that you are excited about and feel comfortable wearing. Choose something that you have fun putting together. Decide what category of costume you want. Do you want to do a more timeless costume or a trendy costume for this year? Maybe you will have two costumes or three. The options are endless.
That’s the best advice I have for picking a costume! I already know that there will be a lot of crafty, whimsical, and scary costumes at the Bates Halloween Dance and I am so excited to see them.

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Linda L. Davis, of Westport Island, died on Oct. 19, 2026. She was 80 years old.
Linda was the third of four daughters born to Ella Britt and Warren Davis in Varina, Va.
Starting with the days of her English studies at Longwood College, nothing made Linda happier than a towering stack of books to devour.
After moving to Maine in the late 1960s, Linda taught public school in Jefferson, Hallowell, and Wiscasset.
Linda was well known as a gracious host. Her gravity-defying cheesecake, sumptuous lobster stew, and slow-roasted pulled pork won hearts (and probably clogged arteries).
She was exceedingly generous with her time and energy. Linda served on school boards, raised funds for libraries, and organized holiday meals and gift drives. Some of her most ambitious philanthropy was creating a fuel-assistance fund and thriving food pantry that served Westport Island until 2025.
Linda supported the care and dignity of her neighbors with dedication, ingenuity, and compassion.
Linda’s passing leaves her husband of 31 years, Richard DeVries; her daughter, Britt Morris and son-in-law, Keith Edwards; her daughter, Sarah Morris and son-in-law, James Mattson; her youngest sister, Ellen Glazman and brother-in-law, Alan Glazman; her daughter-in-law, Diana Kardia, her son-in-law Lee DeVries; and daughter-in-law, Laurie DeVries, and her three grandchildren, Joseph Kardia, Jake DeVries, and Dakota DeVries, grieving her loss.
Linda was a faithful reader of obituaries – we hope she would have liked this one.
Remembrance of Linda’s life and reception are planned for Saturday, Nov. 7 at The Montsweag in Woolwich from 11:30 a.m. to 2 p.m.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home, 612 Main St., Damariscotta, ME 04543. Condolences and messages for her family may be expressed by visiting stronghancock.com.

title: UMaine Extension hosts online talk about flower farming

text:
ONLINE — University of Maine Cooperative Extension will host an online panel discussion for current and aspiring flower farmers on Tuesday, Nov. 10, from 6 to 7:15 p.m. The discussion will focus on how to build a flower farming business that is resilient, rewarding and sustainable.
“Building a Resilient Flower Farming Business” will feature experienced flower farmers Lee Cline of Fox Hollow Flowers, Linda D’Arco of Ampersand Bulb and Mary Turner of Salt Farm Flowers, along with Ping Yu, assistant professor and ornamental specialist at the University of Georgia.

title: Maine Colleges Shine in New Ranking of America's 500 Best Schools
text:
Maine Colleges Shine in New Ranking of America’s 500 Best Schools
Whether it’s on the field, on the court, or in the classroom, college is all about competition. And nothing beats having bragging rights over a rival school.
That’s what makes this time of year so much fun. It’s college ranking season, when publications release their annual lists, giving schools plenty of reasons to celebrate...or complain.
The latest list to drop comes from the financial experts over at WalletHub. The popular publication releases an annual ranking of colleges and universities across the country, featuring the top 500 schools.
WalletHub evaluates numerous metrics, including cost, student selectivity, campus experience and safety, education and career outcomes, and faculty resources. Believe me when I say this is a very detailed ranking.
What Maine Colleges Have the Best National Rankings
Maine performed relatively well in this year’s rankings, with three schools earning top spots, particularly in the liberal arts college category. Here’s a closer look:
28. Colby College – Waterville
This Central Maine “Little Ivy” earned the highest ranking among Maine schools. It received high marks for its academic opportunities, campus facilities, and strong post-graduation salary outcomes. Its best ranking was 11th in campus experience.
29. Bowdoin College – Brunswick
The Brunswick college finished right behind its rival in the standings. Bowdoin is recognized for its high graduation rate, strong job placement, and outstanding faculty recommendations. Its highest ranking was 12th in education outcomes.
89. Bates College – Lewiston
Bates rounds out Maine’s trio of elite liberal arts colleges. It's particularly noted for student development, innovative learning environments, and its unique “Short Term” spring semester, which focuses on immersive, experiential learning. Its top ranking came in campus experience, finishing 39th.

What are Considered the Best Schools in America?
As for the number one spot? That honor went to Princeton University. The Ivy League school edged out MIT, Yale, Caltech, and Harvard to claim the top ranking.
It’s also worth noting that many other colleges across Maine offer an excellent education, including those in the community college system. There are plenty of great opportunities out there, so make sure to take advantage of them.

title: Bodycam video: Officers rescue man from burning Jeep in dramatic early morning crash
text:
Bodycam shows police pull alleged OUI driver from burning Jeep after Boston suburb crash
Three police officers rescued a man trapped in a burning vehicle after a crash early Sunday morning in a suburb of Boston, Massachusetts.
Sgt. Martin Faherty and officers Jonathan O'Brien and Matthew Richards responded to the collision around 3:20 a.m., according to the Holbrook Police Department.
O'Brien arrived first at the scene and saw a utility pole snapped in half and flames spreading across the front of a Jeep.
Bystanders told him the driver was still inside.
The driver tried to escape the vehicle, but his right foot was pinned beneath the damaged dashboard, according to police. The driver's foot and sneaker also caught fire.
Body camera video provided by Holbrook police shows the tense moments when O'Brien, Faherty and Richards pulled the driver to safety.
The driver was transported to South Shore Hospital in Weymouth, Massachusetts, with injuries that were not believed to be life-threatening.
O'Brien sustained minor burns to his fingers during the rescue.
Investigators said the Jeep left the roadway, hit a pole and a tree before crashing into a retaining wall.
The Jeep's driver, a 37-year-old Holbrook, Massachusetts, man, will be charged with operating under the influence (second offense), negligent operation of a motor vehicle, a marked lanes violation and speeding.
"These officers did an incredible job under dangerous conditions," Chief David Del Papa said. "The outcome would have been much different had they not arrived so quickly and acted immediately. Their quick response likely saved his life."
Boston sister station WCVB reports that this is the second time in the past year O'Brien has rescued a driver from a burning vehicle.

title: Drone Technology Helps Maine Emergency Crews Find Missing Bangor Woman
text:
Local Law Enforcement Employ Drone To Locate Lost Woman In Bangor City Forest Last Week
First Responders, at both the state and federal level across Maine, have started to make add drones into their toolkits.
Whether it be to locate fire hotspots, survey criminal activity from a safe distance, or in some cases, help finding missing people, drones are becoming more the norm in many departments.
This past April, Bangor PD started using a drone, and even put out a job posting to add a special drone technician to their team. That's a move that would pay off this when a woman went missing in the Bangor City Forest.
Read More: The Role Of Drones In Enhancing Public Safety In Maine
The woman was reported missing by her family, just before 3 PM on Thursday October 22nd, with her last known location being the woods.
The Bangor Police Department says that time was of the essence, as temperatures were expected to fall into the 30s Thursday night.
"Bangor Police coordinated a search effort that included K9 teams from the Maine Warden Service and the Bangor Police Department’s Unmanned Aircraft System (UAS) Team, and the Bangor Fire Department. The Warden was able to hear the missing woman but were unable to locate her. UAS Operator Det. Joe Orcutt was able to use the drone to pinpoint her location and assist in her recovery. "
Read More: The Role Of Drones In Finding Missing Pets In Maine
After locating the lost individual, first responders took the woman to a local hospital to be checked out.

title: Fire destroys home in rural Penobscot County township
text:
A fire destroyed a mobile home in Greenfield Township on Saturday night.
The residents awoke to the smell of smoke and smoke detectors and found fire spreading through the Cross Road home, according to Milford Fire and Rescue.
By the time firefighters arrived, the home was fully engulfed in flames and significantly damaged.
The home was a total loss.
Everyone inside the home, along with all pets, safely escaped the flames.
Greenfield Township is northeast of Old Town and on the Penobscot-Hancock county line.

title: Japan's former PM Yasuo Fukuda, proponent of ties with China, dies at 90
text:
Japan's former PM Yasuo Fukuda, proponent of ties with China, dies at 90
Former Japanese Prime Minister Yasuo Fukuda, who led the country for just one year and spent years afterward trying to build better ties with China, has died, officials said Monday. He was 90.
He died on Thursday, the governing Liberal Democratic Party said, without disclosing further details, including cause of his death.
Born in 1936, Fukuda grew up in a political family in Gunma, northwest of Tokyo. His father Takeo Fukuda also served as prime minister and worked to build Tokyo's ties with Beijing.
Related video: President Trump, Xi conclude state visit with extended trade truce, no major breakthroughs
After graduating from Waseda University in Tokyo, Yasuo Fukuda worked for a Japanese oil company for more than 17 years before entering politics, first serving as his father's private secretary just before the elder Fukuda became Japan's leader in 1976.
The younger Fukuda was first elected to parliament in 1990, taking his father's former seat. He landed his first ministerial post as Chief Cabinet Secretary, or top spokesperson, for gaffe-prone then-Prime Minister Yoshiro Mori in 2000. During that time Fukuda jokingly called himself the “secretary of explanations.”
As a lawmaker, Fukuda served in a number of foreign affairs-related roles and developed a reputation as a diplomacy expert. Like his father, he placed great importance on developing friendships with Asian countries.
During his 2007-2008 prime ministership, Fukuda developed stable ties with China's Hu Jintao. Fukuda's rule lasted only one year as he struggled to manage a divided parliament in which his Liberal Democratic Party held a majority in only one of the two houses.
After his retirement in 2012, Fukuda devoted his time to improving Japan’s relations with China during a period when their ties were disrupted by territorial disputes over a group of uninhabited islands in the East China Sea.
In 2014, Fukuda visited China to hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping, seeking a thaw in their chilly ties, paving the way for then-Prime Minister Shinzo Abe’s China visit to meet with Xi.
Fukuda also regularly headed political delegations to China and other Asian countries and attended international conferences.
“Lack of dialogue increases risks of misunderstanding ... and things that do not happen under normal circumstances could happen,” Fukuda said in an interview with The Associated Press in 2022, marking the 50th anniversary of the 1972 normalization of Japan-China ties.
Fukuda was often straight faced and known for his wry humor.
When Fukuda announced his resignation at an emergency news conference in September 2008 and a reporter said he sounded as though he was talking about someone else. Then Fukuda replied: "I can look at myself objectively. I'm not like you."
“I'm not like you” was chosen as one of the buzzwords of the year later in 2008 in an annual event hosted by a publisher, but Fukuda declined to accept the award.

Alexis Ingraham, of Burnham, has been twice convicted of animal cruelty
Maine woman back in court on new animal cruelty charges out of Montana
Alexis Ingraham, of Burnham, has been twice convicted of animal cruelty
A Maine woman with multiple animal cruelty convictions was back in court Monday on new, out-of-state allegations.
Alexis Ingraham, 41, was convicted of animal cruelty in August and had a prior conviction in 2011, according to WMTW media partner WABI. She was sentenced to two years in prison and two years of probation, plus a lifetime ban on owning animals, but that sentence is on hold pending appeal.
Ingraham appeared virtually in a Belfast courtroom Monday afternoon after being taken into custody on four new misdemeanor counts of animal cruelty out of Montana.
According to court documents, investigators allege Ingraham boarded two mares and two foals for months on a Montana property, where they were found emaciated in May with no feed and no water.
Despite being sent photos of their decline as early as March, Ingraham reportedly failed to intervene. All four horses were seized and taken to an equine medical center.
Ingraham waived extradition to Montana, saying she is not running from the charges. She is currently being held at the Waldo County Jail awaiting transfer to Montana.

title: Chris Brown avoids prison time for brawling at a London nightclub
text:
LONDON (AP) — Grammy-winning singer Chris Brown avoided prison time Monday for beating a music producer with a tequila bottle at a London nightclub three years ago.
The 37-year-old was given an eight-month sentence, suspended for a year.
He had faced up to three years in prison after pleading guilty to a count of affray in July for the attack on the dance floor of Tape, a private club in the swanky Mayfair neighborhood in February 2023.
Video footage played in court showed Brown having to be pulled away from the victim, his former friend Abraham Diaw, after striking him twice in the head with a bottle.
“The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous. It carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained,” Judge Tony Baumgartner said in Southwark Crown Court.
Despite the seriousness of the attack, Baumgartner said Brown did not qualify for a custodial sentence because he pleaded guilty and there were several mitigating circumstances, including stable employment and charity work. The judge acknowledged Brown’s previous convictions but said he had maintained a clean record in recent years.
Previous brushes with the law
Brown has faced repeated legal trouble since his felony conviction in the 2009 assault of his then-girlfriend, Rihanna, hours before the pair were due to perform at the Grammys.
He has been arrested in several U.S. states over altercations but was either not charged or prosecutors later dropped the charges. In 2019 he was arrested in Paris and questioned on suspicion of rape, but was released without charge.
In return for his guilty plea, prosecutors dropped charges of assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm and having an offensive weapon, a bottle.
Brown’s friend and vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu also pleaded guilty to affray and was given a four-month suspended sentence.
Affray is the use or threat of unlawful violence that leads someone to fear for their safety.
Brown has apologized for the attack
Prosecutor Heidi Stonecliffe said Brown played a leading role in the attack.
“By any circumstances, when one watches that footage, it is Mr. Brown that moves first,” Stonecliffe said.
Defense lawyer Sallie Bennett-Jenkins said Brown apologized to all those at the club that night, though she emphasized the attack lasted no more than 20 seconds.
“This is an ugly and unattractive incident,” Bennett-Jenkins said. “It is something which undoubtedly would have caused distress to those who are present and for which Mr. Brown … offers a profound apology to all those present.”
Diaw was discharged from the hospital with head and knee injuries, Stonecliffe said.
Crowds greet Brown outside court
Brown was cheered outside the courthouse by fans who came from as far as Italy and the Netherlands.
His face was covered by a black mask and dark glasses and his bleached hair was mostly hidden from view under a black ball cap. He wore a black leather jacket and light-colored turtleneck.
He blew a kiss to one fan and appeared to sign an autograph for another as he moved through a pack of photographers and onlookers.
Not everyone was cheering for him. When he arrived at court in the morning, a lone voice could be heard shouting at him to ask when he was going to learn that violence is not OK.
Brown left the United Kingdom after the brawl but was arrested in May 2025 at a Manchester hotel after flying to the city for a concert. He had been free on bail of 5 million pounds ($6.7 million), which allowed him to tour Europe and North America the past two summers.
Brown rose to stardom as a teen in 2005 and won his first Grammy for best R&B album in 2011 for “F.A.M.E.” He earned his second in the same category for “11:11 (Deluxe)” in 2025.

title: Central Maine Growth Council hires tech project manager
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Nathan Bernard, a former Waterville city official and technology entrepreneur, joined the Central Maine Growth Council as project manager for technology, innovation and infrastructure.
In the newly created role, he will work with municipalities on technology and infrastructure projects while supporting innovation programs involving businesses, academic institutions and community partners.
At Dirigo Labs, the growth council’s business incubator and accelerator, Bernard will help entrepreneurs develop and commercialize new products and services. He will also focus on expanding AI and data analytics capabilities.
“CMGC provides a unique opportunity to expand my public service work across the region and help central Maine navigate critical issues, including AI, economic resiliency, infrastructure, and affordability,” said Bernard.
Bernard brings experience in both the public and private sectors. He most recently served as a community development specialist in the Waterville city manager’s office.
Previously, he served as a grants and program manager at the Alfond Youth and Community Center and as a project manager for Code of America, a national nonprofit focused on improving government services through technology. He also founded a software company in New York City.
Bernard received his bachelor’s degree in operations, engineering and technology management from Boston University. He is pursuing a master’s degree in public policy, planning and management at the University of Southern Maine’s Muskie School of Public Service. He serves as a policy research fellow at Colby College’s Bram Public Policy Lab.
“Nathan brings a rare combination: he has built a technology company, delivered civic tech at the national level, and worked inside City Hall right here in Waterville,” said Garvan Donegan, president and CEO of the Central Maine Growth Council. “That blend of startup speed and public-sector know-how is exactly what our member municipalities and Dirigo Labs entrepreneurs need.”
“This role is a direct investment in our region’s capacity to innovate,” Donegan added. “With Nathan supporting this work, CMGC can help our communities adopt smarter tools, use data to plan for growth, support the next generation of startups, and turn good ideas into real projects that strengthen the Kennebec Valley and the State of Maine.”

title: A 10-year-old boy and his teacher drowned on a school trip. Here’s what officials say happened
text:
JOHNSON COUNTY, Iowa (KCRG/Gray News) - Officials in Iowa have revealed what happened just before a 10-year-old boy and his teacher drowned on a school field trip.
Hannah Jorgensen, a 24-year-old teacher at Borlaug Elementary, led a group of 14 students on a School of the Wild trip Sept. 22 at Lake Macbride State Park, according to the Johnson County Sheriff’s Office.
The woodland hike ended near the shore of the Coralville Reservoir, where the fifth grade students – including 10-year-old Ahmed Osman – stopped to eat lunch around noon.
During the lunch break, investigators say Ahmed stepped into the water flowing down the spillway. He slipped on the rocks and fell into the water.
Jorgensen jumped in the water to rescue Ahmed. She left her phone on the shore but told her students to call 911.
One student was able to make the call, and the others alerted a bystander. The bystander jumped into the water to rescue Ahmed and his teacher but was unable to do so.
First responders later recovered both Ahmed and Jorgensen’s bodies from the lake. The 10-year-old’s family has called Jorgensen a hero for trying to save him.
The bystander, who safely made it out of the water, stayed on the scene with the students and spoke with the investigators. The students were also interviewed as part of the investigation.
The investigation into the incident is ongoing.

title: Your vote matters | Letters To Editor
text:
To the Editor:
As a 99-year-old voter from Bangor, I’ve learned that one of the most important rights we have is the right to vote. Throughout my lifetime, I’ve seen how elections shape our communities, our state and our future.
That’s why I encourage every Mainer to make their voice heard this November. Whether you’re concerned about Social Security, rising costs, health care or the future you want for your family, voting is how we make those priorities known.
The good news is that older voters are engaged. A recent AARP Maine poll found that 87% of Mainers age 50 and older are motivated to vote this year.
No matter your age or political views, your vote matters. I’ve been voting for almost 80 years. Democracy works best when all of us participate.
Margie Higgins
Bangor

title: Three longtime conservation partners unite to protect rare older forests
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
New England Forestry Foundation and Seven Islands Land Company have signed an agreement to defer planned timber harvests on nearly 500 acres of rare, older, natural forest — also known as late-successional and old-growth forest — in Piscataquis County. These forests provide unique habitat to a range of sensitive species and store exceptional amounts of carbon.
This initiative builds on two conservation success stories in the forests managed by Seven Islands Land Company on behalf of the Pingree Family, one of the state’s longest tenured landowners. First, it expands the partnership between SILC, the Pingree Family and NEFF to prohibit development across more than 762,000 acres of working forests through the Pingree Forest Partnership: in March 2001, NEFF and the Pingree Family completed the largest working forestland conservation easement in the history of the United States. Furthermore, the LSOG forests covered by the timber harvest deferral are in the vicinity of the Big Reed Forest Reserve, Maine’s largest protected old growth forest, which SILC and the Pingree Family identified and proactively sold to the Nature Conservancy in 1987 to preserve the forest’s unique characteristics.
This new agreement is part of a broader NEFF effort to conserve some of Maine’s most ecologically unique forestland.
Under the agreement, NEFF will provide funding to Seven Islands Land Company in exchange for deferring planned timber harvests while partners investigate a longer-term conservation solution for the area. As part of the agreement, NEFF is also providing funds to support practices that will increase future timber production in younger forests by thinning dense young stands of commercial species like red spruce, sugar maple and yellow birch.
The area of the deferral covers 488.5 acres of mixed LSOG forests between Baxter State Park and the Allagash Wilderness Waterway. These forests are dominated by trees that are at least 150 years old and show only light evidence of past logging, or in some places none at all. The dominant species include sugar maple, yellow birch, American beech and red spruce. The older forest is ecologically rich and especially valuable for its ability to capture and store carbon, creating ecosystems that are critical in the fight against climate change.
“The Pingree Family and Seven Islands Land Company have long been conservation pioneers in Maine, and we are excited to explore this model for LSOG conservation with NEFF,” Dan LaMontagne, president and CEO of Seven Islands, said. “We continually look for creative ways to conserve the special and unique places on our lands while also maintaining economic viability, local employment and robust markets for a variety of forest products.”
The agreement demonstrates a new model for protecting natural forests through partnerships between conservation organizations and private landowners, while supporting sustainable timber production on the landscape.
“The Pingree timberlands managed by Seven Islands have always been a showcase for sustainable forestry,” Brian Milakovsky, NEFF senior forester, said. “Scattered through them are these LSOG gems that complement all the values of managed forests with their unique habitat features. We look forward to helping SILC conserve the best of them in a way that works for northern Maine’s economy.”
This work is supported by a $4.3 million grant from the U.S. Forest Service. The funding is part of a larger effort to protect the most exceptional old natural forests identified in northern Maine in 2024. The program also helps landowners improve forest health and productivity in other areas, supporting both carbon storage and wood production.
Through the application of its core expertise in conserving forestlands and advancing Exemplary Forestry, the New England Forestry Foundation helps the people of New England to sustain their way of life, protect forest wildlife habitat and ecosystem services and mitigate and adapt to climate change. In partnership with landowners, New England Forestry Foundation has conserved more than 1.2 million acres of forest since its founding in 1944, and owns and manages more than 150 Community Forests across the region. For more information, visit www.newenglandforestry.org.
Founded in 1964, Seven Islands Land Company manages the Pingree Family timberlands in northern and western Maine. Committed to a sustainable forest management mindset, Seven Islands is dedicated to bettering the environment, strengthening the forest industry and supporting the people in the communities in which we live and work. To learn more, visit www.sevenislands.com.
